zajjaj:17-17.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿مَثَلُهم كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي اسْتَوْقَدَ نارًا فَلَمّا أضاءَتْ ما حَوْلَهُ ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ﴾. This is a parable that Allah, Majestic and Mighty is He, struck for the hypocrites in their adorning themselves with the outward form of Islam and safeguarding their blood by what they displayed. The likeness of the Islam with which they adorned themselves is like the fire by which the one who kindles it seeks light. His saying: ”ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ“ means – and Allah knows best – Allah's acquainting the believers with their disbelief; so the light of Islam has gone from them through what Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, has made manifest of their disbelief. It is also possible that ”ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ“ refers to the Hereafter, that is: He punished them, so they have no light, because Allah, Majestic and Mighty is He, has made a light for the believers in the Hereafter and stripped the disbelievers of that light. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿انْظُرُونا نَقْتَبِسْ مِن نُورِكم قِيلَ ارْجِعُوا وراءَكم فالتَمِسُوا نُورًا﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 13].

zajjaj:18-18.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ فَهم لا يَرْجِعُونَ﴾ is put in the nominative (rufiʿa) as the khabar (predicate) of an ibtidāʾ (inchoative/subject), as though it were said: ”هَؤُلاءِ الَّذِينَ قِصَّتُهم هَذِهِ القِصَّةُ، صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ، فَهم لا يَرْجِعُونَ“ ("These, whose story is this story, are deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not return"). In speech it is permissible to say ”صُمًّا، بُكْمًا، عُمْيًا“ (accusative), on the reading ”وَتَرَكَهم صُمًّا، بُكْمًا، عُمْيًا“ ("and He left them deaf, dumb, blind"); but the Muṣḥaf is not to be contradicted by a reading that is not transmitted. The nominative is moreover stronger in meaning and weightier in expression.
The meaning of ”بُكْمٌ“ is that he is like one born mute; and it is said: al-abkam is the one bereft of understanding (literally "of heart"). ”صُمٌّ“ and ”بُكْمٌ“: their singulars are aṣamm and abkam. It is permissible for the plural of ”أصَمُّ“ to be ”صُمّانٌ“; and likewise every ”أفْعَلُ“ admits ”فُعْلانٌ“, as in ”أسْوَدُ“ (black), ”سُودٌ“ and ”سُودانٌ“; the meaning of ”سُودٌ“ and ”سُودانٌ“ is one. So too ”صُمٌّ“ and ”صُمّانٌ“, ”عُرْجٌ“ and ”عُرْجانٌ“ (lame), ”بُكْمٌ“ and ”بُكْمانٌ“.

zajjaj:19-19.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أوْ كَصَيِّبٍ مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾. ”اَلصَّيِّبُ“ in the language is rain; and everything that descends from above to below has ṣāba, yaṣūbu ("come down"). The poet said:
؎كَأنَّهم صابَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ سَحابَةٌ ∗∗∗ صَواعِقُها لِطَيْرِهِنَّ دَبِيبُ
(It is as if a cloud had poured down upon them, whose thunderbolts make their birds creep along [in fear].)
This too is a parable which Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, strikes for the hypocrites. The meaning was: "or like the people of a ṣayyib (rainstorm)". He made the religion of Islam a likeness for them with respect to the hardships and fear that befall them, and He made the lightning by which they seek light a likeness for the Islam by which they seek light, and the fear that befalls them in the lightning is in the position of the killing that they fear. The proof of this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يَحْسَبُونَ كُلَّ صَيْحَةٍ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn: 4].

zajjaj:20-20.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يَخْطَفُ أبْصارَهُمْ﴾. In ”يَخْطَفُ أبْصارَهم“ there are two dialects: one says ”خَطِفَ يَخْطَفُ“ and ”خَطَفَ يَخْطِفُ“, and the higher dialect, on which the reading is based, is ”خَطِفَ يَخْطَفُ“. This word is transmitted from the Arabs and from the Readers, and there are dialectal forms of it transmitted: from al-Ḥasan, ”يَخَطِّفُ أبْصارَهم“, with fatḥa on the yāʾ and the khāʾ and kasra on the ṭāʾ; it is also transmitted as ”يِخِطِّفُ“, with kasra on the yāʾ, the khāʾ and the ṭāʾ. Another form is also transmitted which is not acceptable in pronunciation because of its difficulty, namely making both the khāʾ and the ṭāʾ quiescent (sākin). Sībawayh transmitted something like this, and his associates rejected it from him, claiming that it is not acceptable in pronunciation and that poetry does not combine two quiescent letters within the body of the verse. [The poet] said:
؎وَمَسْحِهِ مَرُّ عُقابٍ كاسِرٍ ∗∗∗ .....................
(And his stroking [it] was like the passing of a swooping eagle …)
He replaces the hāʾ with a ḥāʾ and assimilates (yudghim) the first ḥāʾ into the second, while the sīn is quiescent, so he combines two quiescent letters.
As for what comes after ”يَخْطَفُ“, the good forms are ”يَخَطِّفُ“ and ”يِخِطِّفُ“. For whoever says ”يَخَطِّفُ“, the origin is ”يَخْتَطِفُ“: the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṭāʾ and the fatḥa of the tāʾ was cast onto the khāʾ. Whoever says ”يِخِطِّفُ“ gave the khāʾ a kasra because of its quiescence and the quiescence of the ṭāʾ. Some grammarians claimed that the kasra for the meeting of two quiescent letters here is a mistake, and that whoever says this is bound to say ”يَعِضُّ“ for ”يَعَضُّ“ and ”يَمِدُّ“ for ”يَمُدُّ“. This is a confusion that is not binding, because had he given it a kasra there, what is originally ”يَفْعَلُ“ and ”يَفْعُلُ“ would be confused with what is originally ”يَفْعِلُ“; whereas ”يَخْطِفُ“ has no origin other than this, and it is not at one time on the pattern ”يَفْتَعِلُ“ and at another on ”يَفْتَعَلُ“. So the kasra for the meeting of two quiescent letters was used in a place where it causes no confusion, and was refused where it would cause confusion, and [the word] was made to keep the vowel of the letter that was assimilated, so that the vowel indicates it. The meaning of ”خَطَفْتُ الشَّيْءَ“ and ”اِخْتَطَفْتُهُ“ in the language is: I took it swiftly.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿كُلَّما أضاءَ لَهم مَشَوْا فِيهِ﴾. One says ”ضاءَ الشَّيْءُ، يَضُوءُ“ and ”أضاءَ، يُضِيءُ“, and this second dialect is the preferred one. One also says ”أظْلَمَ“ and ”ظَلِمَ“, and ”أظْلَمَ“ is the preferred one.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَذَهَبَ بِسَمْعِهِمْ﴾. We have already explained the singular form of al-samʿ ("hearing"). One says ”أذْهَبْتُهُ“ and ”ذَهَبْتُ بِهِ“ ("I took it away"), and ”أذْهَبْتُ بِهِ“ is also transmitted, a rare dialect.
As for the mention of ”أوْ“ in His saying ”مَثَلُهم كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي...“ up to ”أوْ كَصَيِّبٍ“: ”أوْ“ has entered here not for doubt. This is what those skilled in the language call ”واوَ الإباحَةِ“ ("the wāw of permission") «[Translator's note: so in the text; the particle under discussion is أو, and the usual term is «أو الإباحة», "the aw of permission".]». You say: ”جالِسِ القُرّاءَ، أوِ الفُقَهاءَ، أوْ أصْحابَ الحَدِيثِ، أوْ أصْحابَ النَّحْوِ“ ("Sit with the Readers, or the jurists, or the people of ḥadīth, or the grammarians"). The meaning is that making the comparison is permitted to you concerning the hypocrites: if you liken them to the one who kindled a fire, that is their likeness; if you liken them to the people of the rainstorm, this is their likeness; or if you liken them to both together, both are their likenesses. Just as when you say ”جالِسِ الحَسَنَ، أوِ ابْنَ سِيرِينَ“ ("Sit with al-Ḥasan or Ibn Sīrīn"): each of them is worthy of being sat with; if you sit with al-Ḥasan you are obedient, and if you combine both you are obedient.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يَجْعَلُونَ أصابِعَهم في آذانِهِمْ مِنَ الصَّواعِقِ حَذَرَ المَوْتِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 19]. It is also transmitted as ”حِذارَ المَوْتِ“, but what our Readers follow is ”حَذَرَ المَوْتِ“. ”حَذَرَ المَوْتِ“ is in the accusative only because it is a mafʿūl lahu (object of purpose); the meaning is: they do that out of fear of death. Its accusative is not due to the dropping of the lām; rather, what puts it in the accusative is that it has the sense of a maṣdar (verbal noun), as though He said ”يَحْذَرُونَ حَذَرًا“ ("they fear with a fearing"), because their putting their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts indicates their fear of death. The poet said:
؎وَأغْفِرُ عَوْراءَ الكَرِيمِ ادِّخارَهُ ∗∗∗ وأُعْرِضُ عَنْ شَتْمِ اللَّئِيمِ تَكَرُّما
(I pardon the noble man's lapse, to keep him in store, and I turn away from the base man's abuse out of magnanimity.)
The meaning is: "for keeping him in store". And his saying ”وَأغْفِرُ عَوْراءَ الكَرِيمِ“ means: and I keep the noble man in store.

zajjaj:21-21.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يا أيُّها النّاسُ اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكم والَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكم لَعَلَّكم تَتَّقُونَ﴾. Its meaning is that Allah argued against the Arabs by the fact that He is their Creator and the Creator of those before them, because they acknowledged that. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿وَلَئِنْ سَألْتَهم مَن خَلَقَهم لَيَقُولُنَّ اللَّهُ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87]. It was said to them: if you acknowledge that He is your Creator, then worship Him and do not worship the idols. His saying ”لَعَلَّكم تَتَّقُونَ“ means: you guard the sanctities among you and refrain from what you commit of that which Allah has forbidden.
As for ”لَعَلَّ“, there are two views on it here from some of the people of the language. One of them: its meaning is "so that you may be God-fearing". What Sībawayh holds in the like of this is that it is a hope [expressed] on their behalf, as He said in the story of Pharaoh: ﴿لَعَلَّهُ يَتَذَكَّرُ أوْ يَخْشى﴾ [Ṭā Hā: 44], as though He said: "Go, both of you, upon your hope and your expectation", while Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, is behind that and knows what Pharaoh's affair will come to.
As for the iʿrāb of ”يا أيُّها“: ”أيُّ“ is a vague (mubham) noun, indeclinable (mabnī) on ḍamma because it is a single (mufrad) munādā (one addressed); ”اَلنّاسُ“ is a naʿt (adjective) of ”أيُّ“, obligatory. You say ”يا أيُّها الرَّجُلُ أقْبِلْ“ ("O man, come forward"), and ”يا الرَّجُلُ“ is not permissible, because ”يا“ is an alerting [particle] equivalent to the definiteness in ”اَلرَّجُلُ“, so ”يا“ and the alif-lām are not combined; hence you reach the alif-lām by means of ”أيُّ“. ”ها“ is obligatory with ”أيُّ“ for alerting (tanbīh), and it is a compensation for the iḍāfa (annexation) in ”أيُّ“, because the original state of ”أيُّ“ is to be annexed, in interrogation and in statement.
Sībawayh claimed, from al-Khalīl, that the single munādā is indeclinable, while its adjective is in a genuine nominative, because the vocative is regular with every single noun; and since the indeclinability is regular in the single noun specifically, it was likened to the nominative, and so its adjective was put in the nominative.
Al-Māzinī permits, in ”يا أيُّها الرَّجُلُ“, the accusative in ”اَلرَّجُلُ“, and no one among the Basrans held this view other than he. It is analogically valid, because the position of the single munādā is accusative, so its adjective was made to follow its position. This, in a case other than ”يا أيُّها الرَّجُلُ“, is permissible according to all the grammarians, as in your saying ”يا زَيْدُ الظَّرِيفُ“ and ”اَلظَّرِيفَ“ ("O Zayd the witty"). But the grammarians say only ”يا أيُّها الرَّجُلُ“, ”يا أيُّها النّاسُ“ [in the nominative]; the usage of the Arabs here is the nominative, and nothing else has come from them. The one truly addressed is ”اَلرَّجُلُ“, but ”أيُّ“ is a link (ṣila) to it. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash said that taking ”اَلرَّجُلُ“ to be a ṣila (relative clause) of ”أيُّ“ is more analogical, and none of the Basrans follows him in this view.

zajjaj:57-57.t:
His saying: ﴿وَظَلَّلْنا عَلَيْكُمُ الغَمامَ﴾: Allah made the clouds subservient to them, shading them when they went out to the Holy Land, and He sent down upon them «المَنّ» and «السَّلْوى». In sum, «المَنّ» is whatever Allah bestows as a favour (yamunnu bihi) in which there is no toil and no fatigue. The people of tafsīr (Quranic exegesis) say that «المَنّ» is something sweet that falls on trees and is drunk, and it is said that it is «التَّرَنْجِين» (manna of the camel-thorn). It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: «The truffle is of the manna (al-mann), and its water is a cure for the eye». The meaning of «المَنّ», as we have described it, in the language is: what Allah bestows without toil or fatigue. «السَّلْوى» is a bird like the quail (al-summānī), and it is mentioned that there used to come to them of these two whatever sufficed them.

His saying: ﴿كُلُوا مِن طَيِّباتِ ما رَزَقْناكُمْ﴾: they said its meaning is: of these good things; and they also said: of what is lawful for you.

zajjaj:58-58.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ قُلْنا ادْخُلُوا هَذِهِ القَرْيَةَ فَكُلُوا مِنها حَيْثُ شِئْتُمْ رَغَدًا﴾: «الرَّغَد» is what is ample and does not cause hardship.

His saying: ﴿وادْخُلُوا البابَ سُجَّدًا﴾: they were commanded to enter prostrating. ﴿وَقُولُوا حِطَّةٌ﴾: its meaning is "and say: our request is ḥiṭṭa", that is, the removal of our sins from us; and that is how it is read. Had it been read «حِطَّةً» (accusative), its justification in Arabic would be as though it had been said to them: "Say: remove from us our sins, a removing (ḥiṭṭatan)". But they distorted this saying and said a word other than the word they were commanded to say; and the gist of what they said is that it was a grave matter, for which Allah named them «فاسِقِين» (transgressors).

His saying: ﴿نَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ﴾ is jussive (majzūm) as the answer to the command (jawāb al-amr). The meaning is: "If you say what you were commanded to say, We will forgive you your sins (khaṭāyākum)". Some read: «نَغْفِرْ لَكم خَطِيئاتِكم», but the first reading is more widespread. Whoever says «خَطِيئاتِكم» takes it as the plural of «خَطِيئَة» with alif and tāʾ, like «سَفِينَة» / «سَفِينات» and «صَحِيفَة» / «صَحِيفات». The reading, as we have described, is «نَغْفِرْ لَكم خَطاياكم». The original form of «خَطايا» is «خَطائِئُ»: two hamzas come together, so the second is changed into a yāʾ, and it becomes «خَطائِيُ»; it is then made weak (uʿilla) like «حَظاعِيُ». Then the yāʾ and the kasra must be changed into a fatḥa and an alif, so it becomes «خَطاءا», like «حَظاعا». Then the hamza must be replaced by a yāʾ because it falls between two alifs, since the hamza is homogeneous with the alifs, and so three letters of one kind would have come together. What we have mentioned is the doctrine of Sībawayh. Sībawayh has another doctrine, whose origin is from al-Khalīl: he held that «خَطايا» was originally of the pattern «فَعائِل» and was inverted (qulibat) to «فَعالى», so the original according to him was «خَطائى», like «خَطائِعُ» — note this — then the hamza was moved forward and it became «خَطائِيُ», like «خَطاعِيُ», and after that it was changed according to the first doctrine. This doctrine has one stage fewer in the iʿlāl (weakening process), and the form in both cases ends up as «خَطايا».

zajjaj:59-59.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَأنْـزَلْنا عَلى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا رِجْزًا مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾: «الرِّجْز» is punishment, and so is «الرِّجْس». The poet said:
كَمْ رامَنا مِن ذِي عَدِيدٍ مُبْزى ∗∗∗ حَتّى وقَمْنا كَيْدَهُ بِالرِّجْزِ
(How many a one of great numbers and overbearing has sought us, until we crushed his scheme with punishment.)

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بِما كانُوا يَفْسُقُونَ﴾, that is: their substituting what they were commanded to say, namely «حِطَّةٌ». One says «فَسَقَ، يَفْسُقُ» and «يَفْسِقُ» and «يَفْسُقُ» according to the two dialects, and the readers follow them [Translator's note: the source lists «يَفْسُقُ» twice; presumably «يَفْسِقُ» and «يَفْسُقُ» are meant as the two forms]. The meaning of fisq is departing from the right course and from the truth; everything that departs from a thing has «فَسَقَ». However, the term was made specific to one who departs from the command of Allah, by saying «فاسِقٌ», with no need to say "he departed («فَسَقَ») from such-and-such", just as one says of everyone who believes in something «هو مُؤْمِنٌ بِكَذا» ("he is a believer in such-and-such"), while of one who believes in the command of Allah one says «مُؤْمِنٌ», and that suffices. The Arabs say «فَسَقَتِ الرُّطَبَةُ» when the fresh date comes out of its skin.

zajjaj:60-60.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذِ اسْتَسْقى مُوسى لِقَوْمِهِ﴾: the position of «إذْ» is accusative, following what preceded it, as though it were said: "And remember when Moses asked for water for his people". However, inflection does not appear on «إذْ», because it is not complete unless it is joined to a ṣila (complement clause), and everything among these vague words (mubhamāt) that is not complete without a ṣila is not inflected, because it is only part of a noun, and only a complete noun is inflected. «إذْ» was given a kasra here only because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. The meaning of «اسْتَسْقى» is: he sought that his people be given water; likewise «اسْتَنْصَرْتُ»: I sought help.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَقُلْنا اضْرِبْ بِعَصاكَ الحَجَرَ فانْفَجَرَتْ مِنهُ اثْنَتا عَشْرَةَ عَيْنًا﴾: most readers read «اثْنَتا عَشْرَةَ» with the shīn quiescent; another dialect has «اثْنَتا عَشِرَةَ عَيْنًا» with the shīn vowelled with kasra, and some readers have read «عَشِرَةَ» according to this dialect; both are good and eloquent. «عَيْنًا» is accusative as a tamyīz (specification). Everything made accusative as a tamyīz in numerals is so on the notion of the presence of tanwīn (nunation), even though it is not pronounced in «عَشْرَةَ», because the tanwīn has been dropped here together with the inflection. The meaning of people's saying "I have twenty dirhams (dirhaman)" is: I have twenty of the dirhams; the plural form was dropped — and this «مِن» is the one by which one genus is singled out from another — and the singular expressed the meaning of the plural. This is the sum of what is made accusative among numerals as a tamyīz. In tafsīr it is said that Allah made twelve springs gush out for them from a rock, for twelve groups, each group having a spring from which they drank; it gushed when they encamped, and when they departed the spring sank away, and they carried the rock with no water gushing from it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قَدْ عَلِمَ كُلُّ أُناسٍ مَشْرَبَهُمْ﴾: the water used to gush for them from twelve places, not varying at any stopping place, so each group of people knew its drinking place.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تَعْثَوْا في الأرْضِ مُفْسِدِينَ﴾: one says «عَثا، يَعْثى، عَثْوًا» and «عُثُوًّا»; «العَثْو» is the most severe corruption.

zajjaj:61-61.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فادْعُ لَنا رَبَّكَ يُخْرِجْ لَنا مِمّا تُنْبِتُ الأرْضُ﴾: «يُخْرِجْ» is jussive (majzūm), and there is more than one view about it. One of the grammarians said: the meaning is "Ask Him, and say to Him: bring forth for us, and He will bring forth for us". And he said about His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَقُلْ لِعِبادِي يَقُولُوا الَّتِي هي أحْسَنُ﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 53] — they said: the meaning is "Say to them: say what is best, that they may say". Others said: the meaning of «يُخْرِجْ لَنا» is the meaning of supplication, as though he said: bring forth for us; and likewise ﴿قُلْ لِعِبادِيَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا يُقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 31], the meaning being "Say to My servants: establish (the prayer)"; but since «ادْعُ» and «قُلْ» came before it, it was treated like the answer to a command (jawāb al-amr). Both views are a valid position, but taking it as the answer is better, because whatever in the Quran has the sense of a command without a jussive particle with it is nominative. Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿تُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ ورَسُولِهِ وتُجاهِدُونَ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Ṣaff: 11], and then, after the verse is complete, came «يَغْفِرْ لَكم»; the meaning is: believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive, and He will forgive you.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿مِن بَقْلِها وقِثّائِها وفُومِها﴾: «القِثّاء» has two dialectal forms: one says «القُثّاء» and «القِثّاء, O you». Some have read «قُثّائِها» with ḍamma, but the better and more widespread is «وَقِثّائِها» with kasra. «وَفُومِها»: «الفُوم» is wheat, and it is said: grains. One of the grammarians said that he holds it permissible that «الفُوم» here is «الثُّوم» (garlic); but this is something not known, that fūm is garlic, and there is here what decisively rules it out: it is absurd that the people would ask for food in which there is no wheat, when wheat is the basis of all nourishment. One says «فَوِّمُوا لَنا», that is, "bake bread for us". There is no disagreement among the lexicographers that fūm is wheat, and all the grains from which bread is baked fall under the name fūm.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أتَسْتَبْدِلُونَ الَّذِي هو أدْنى بِالَّذِي هو خَيْرٌ﴾ means that the manna and the quails are higher than what you have asked for. «أدْنى» is read without hamza, though some have read «أدْنَأُ بِالَّذِي هو خَيْرٌ»; both have a justification in the language, but leaving out the hamza is more deserving to be followed. As for «أدْنى» without hamza, its meaning is: that which is nearer and of less value, as you say "this is a middling (muqārib) garment". As for "base, vile", the usage for it is with hamza: one says «دُنُوء», «دَناءَة» and «هو دَنِيء» with hamza, and one says «هَذا أدْنَأُ مِنهُ» with hamza.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿اهْبِطُوا مِصْرًا﴾: most read it with the alif, though some have read «اهْبِطُوا مِصْرَ فَإنَّ لَكم» without alif. Whoever reads «مِصْرًا» with alif has two possibilities: it may mean a city among the cities, since they were in a wilderness; or he may mean «مِصْر» (Egypt) itself, making «مِصْرًا» a name of the country, and it is declined (fully) because it is a masculine word used as the name of a masculine thing. And it is possible that «مِصْرَ» without alif is read meaning «مِصْرًا», as He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿ادْخُلُوا مِصْرَ إنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ آمِنِينَ﴾ [Yūsuf: 99]; it is a diptote (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf) only because it refers to the city, so it is a masculine word used as the name of a feminine thing.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الذِّلَّةُ والمَسْكَنَةُ﴾: «الذِّلَّة» is abasement and «المَسْكَنَة» is submissiveness; its derivation is from «السُّكُون» (stillness): one says «مِسْكِين» only of one whom poverty has made still (askanahu), that is, has lessened his movement.

His saying, Majestic and Mighty is He: ﴿وَضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الذِّلَّةُ والمَسْكَنَةُ وباءُوا بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾: one says «بُؤْتُ بِكَذا وكَذا», that is, I bore it.

His saying, Majestic and Mighty is He: ﴿ذَلِكَ بِأنَّهم كانُوا يَكْفُرُونَ بِآياتِ اللَّهِ﴾: its meaning — and Allah knows best — is: the wrath befell them because of their disbelief.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَيَقْتُلُونَ النَّبِيِّينَ بِغَيْرِ الحَقِّ﴾: the reading agreed upon in «النَّبِيِّين», «الأنْبِياء» and «البَرِيَّة» is dropping the hamza. A group of the people of Medina pronounce with hamza everything of this kind in the Quran, reading «النَّبِيئِينَ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ» and «الأنْبِئاء». Its derivation is from «نَبَّأ» and «أنْبَأ», that is, "to inform". Leaving out the hamza is better, because usage requires that a «فَعِيل» with hamza has its plural as «فُعَلاء», like «ظَرِيف» / «ظُرَفاء» and «نَبِيء» / «نُبَآء», while if it is of those with yāʾ, its plural is «أفْعِلاء», as in «غَنِيّ» / «أغْنِياء» and «نَبِيّ» / «أنْبِياء». «أفْعِلاء» has occurred among sound words, but rarely; they said «خَمِيس» / «أخْمِساء» and «أخْمُس», and «نَصِيب» / «أنْصِباء». So «نَبِيّ» may be from «أنْبَأْتُ», one whose hamza was dropped because of frequent use; and it may be from «نَبَأ، يَنْبُؤُ» when it rose high, so that it is a «فَعِيل» from elevation.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا والَّذِينَ هادُوا والنَّصارى والصّابِئِينَ مَن آمَنَ بِاللَّهِ واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ وعَمِلَ صالِحًا فَلَهم أجْرُهُمْ﴾ [al-Baqara: 62]: it is not possible for any of them to have faith except together with his faith in the Prophet ﷺ. The proof of that is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وصَدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أضَلَّ أعْمالَهُمْ﴾ [Muḥammad: 1] ﴿والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ وآمَنُوا بِما نُـزِّلَ عَلى مُحَمَّدٍ وهو الحَقُّ مِن رَبِّهِمْ كَفَّرَ عَنْهم سَيِّئاتِهِمْ﴾ [Muḥammad: 2]. So its interpretation is: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, and believes in the Prophet ﷺ, they shall have their reward. It is permissible to say «فَلَهم» (plural) because «مَن» has the form of a singular but applies to one, two and many, feminine and masculine; so the discourse may follow its form, being made singular and masculine, or follow its meaning, being made dual, plural and feminine. The poet said:
تَعالَ فَإنْ عاهَدْتَنِي لا تَخُونُنِي ∗∗∗ نَكُنْ مِثْلَ مَن يا ذِئْبُ يَصْطَحِبانِ
(Come, and if you pledge to me that you will not betray me, we shall be, O wolf, like two (man … yaṣṭaḥibāni) who keep company together.)
«هادُوا»: its original meaning in the language is "they repented"; likewise His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنّا هُدْنا إلَيْكَ﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 156], that is, we have repented to You. As for the singular of «النَّصارى», two views are given about it. They said: its singular may be «نَصْران», as you see, so that «نَصْران» / «نَصارى» is on the pattern of «نَدْمان» / «نَدامى». The poet said:
فَكِلْتاهُما خَرَّتْ وأسْجَدَ رَأْسَها ∗∗∗ كَما أسْجَدَتْ نَصْرانَةٌ لَمْ تَحَنَّفِ
(Both of them fell down and bowed its head, as a Christian woman (naṣrāna) who has not become a ḥanīf bows.)
So «نَصْرانَة» is the feminine of «نَصْران». And the singular of «النَّصارى» may be «نَصْرِيّ», like «بَعِير مَهْرِيّ» (a Mahrī camel) and «إبِل مَهارى». The meaning of «الصّابِئِين» is: those who go out from one religion to another. One says «صَبَأ فُلانٌ — if he leaves his religion — يَصْبَأُ, O you», and one says «صَبَأتِ النُّجُومُ» when the stars appear, and «صَبَأ نابُهُ» when his canine tooth comes out.

zajjaj:22-22.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الأرْضَ فِراشًا﴾ means: a smooth bed; He did not make it rugged and rough ground on which it is impossible to settle.
His saying: ﴿والسَّماءَ بِناءً﴾: everything that rises above the earth is called ”بِناءٌ“ (a structure), and its meaning is that He made it a roof, as He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿وَجَعَلْنا السَّماءَ سَقْفًا مَحْفُوظًا﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 32]. In His saying ”جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الأرْضَ“ two ways are permissible: idghām (assimilation) and iẓhār (clear articulation). You say ”جَعَلَ لَكم“ and ”جَعَلْ لَكُمُ الأرْضَ“. Whoever assimilates does so because two letters of one kind come together and because of the many vowels; whoever articulates clearly – and that is the proper way, followed by most of the Readers – does so because the two are separate, belonging to two words.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَلا تَجْعَلُوا لِلَّهِ أنْدادًا وأنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾: this is an argument against them, based on their acknowledgement that He is Allah their Creator. So it was said to them: do not make equals to Allah while you know that they do not create and that Allah is the Creator. In the language: ”فُلانٌ نِدُّ فُلانٍ“ and ”نَدِيدُ فُلانٍ“ ("so-and-so is the equal of so-and-so"). Jarīr said:
؎أتَيْمًا تَجْعَلُونَ إلَيَّ نِدًّا ∗∗∗ وما تَيْمٌ لِذِي حَسَبٍ نَدِيدُ
(Is it Taym that you make an equal to me? Taym is no equal to a man of noble lineage.)
So this verse and the one before it are an argument against them in establishing the oneness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

zajjaj:23-23.t:
Then, in what follows this verse, He argued against them by establishing the matter of the Prophet ﷺ, saying: ﴿وَإنْ كُنْتُمْ في رَيْبٍ مِمّا نَـزَّلْنا عَلى عَبْدِنا فَأْتُوا بِسُورَةٍ مِن مِثْلِهِ﴾. ”في رَيْبٍ“ means: in doubt. And His saying ”فَأْتُوا بِسُورَةٍ مِن مِثْلِهِ“: the scholars have two views on it. One of them – some said – is that ”مِن مِثْلِهِ“ means: of the like of the Qurʾān, as He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿فَأْتُوا بِعَشْرِ سُوَرٍ مِثْلِهِ مُفْتَرَياتٍ﴾ [Hūd: 13]. Others said: ”مِن مِثْلِهِ“ means: from a human being like him.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وادْعُوا شُهَداءَكم مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾, that is: call upon those whose obedience you have sought and whose help you have hoped for in producing a sūra of the like of it.

zajjaj:24-24.t:
His saying: ﴿فَإنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا ولَنْ تَفْعَلُوا فاتَّقُوا النّارَ﴾. This was said to them after the matter of tawḥīd and the matter of the Prophet ﷺ had been established against them; so they were threatened with punishment if they did not believe after the proof had been established against them.
”لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا“ is in the jussive (majzūm) because ”لَمْ“ introduced into the future [i.e. imperfect] verb the meaning of the past, and so it put it in the jussive. Every particle that cleaves to the verb and introduces a meaning into it has an effect on its iʿrāb in proportion to its meaning. If that particle is ”أنْ“ and its sisters, as in ”لَنْ تَفْعَلُوا“ and ”يُرِيدُونَ أنْ يُطْفِئُوا“, it is accusative, because ”أنْ“ and what follows it are equivalent to a noun; the light ”أنْ“ resembles the doubled ”أنَّ“ with what follows it. For when you say ”ظَنَنْتُ أنَّكَ قائِمٌ“ ("I thought that you were standing"), its meaning is: I thought your standing; and when you say ”أرْجُو أنْ تَقُومَ“ ("I hope that you will stand"), its meaning is: I hope for your standing. So the meaning of ”أنْ“ and what it governs is like the meaning of the doubled ”أنَّ“ and what it governs. For that reason ”أنْ“ puts [the verb] in the accusative, while ”لَمْ“ puts it in the jussive, because what follows it has departed from the sense of a noun; likewise it and what follows it together depart from the sense of a noun.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الَّتِي وقُودُها النّاسُ والحِجارَةُ﴾. They were made to know the punishment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, through the severest of the things they know, because there is nothing in this world more extreme in causing pain than fire. So it was said to them that Allah's punishment is of the severest kinds they know, except that it is of this severe thing that they know. It is said that the stones here are interpreted as stones of sulphur.
His saying ”وَقُودُها“: al-waqūd is firewood, and everything with which a fire is kindled is waqūd. One says ”هَذا وُقُودُكَ“ ("this is your fuel"), and one says ”قَدْ وقَدْتُ النّارَ وُقُودًا“ ("I have kindled the fire, a kindling"); so the maṣdar (verbal noun) has ḍamma, and fatḥa is permissible in it. It has been transmitted: ”وَقَدْتُ النّارَ وقُودًا“ and ”قَبِلْتُ الشَّيْءَ قَبُولًا“ ("I accepted the thing, an acceptance"); so the pattern ”فَعُولٌ“ has occurred in the maṣdar, but the rule [for this word] is the ḍamma.

zajjaj:25-25.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَبَشِّرِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ أنَّ لَهم جَنّاتٍ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِها الأنْهارُ﴾. He mentioned this for the believers, and what He has prepared for them as a reward for their belief, after mentioning to them the recompense of the disbelievers. The position of ”أنَّ“ is accusative; its meaning is: give them the glad tidings that (bi-anna) theirs are gardens. When the bāʾ was dropped, the verb reached ”أنَّ“ directly, and so it was put in the accusative.
Some grammarians have said that it is possible for the position of the like of this to be genitive, even though the bāʾ has been dropped from ”أنَّ“. ”جَنّاتٍ“ is in the position of the accusative through ”أنَّ“, except that the tāʾ is the tāʾ of the feminine plural, which has one and the same form in the genitive and the accusative, just as the yāʾ of the [sound masculine] plural has one form in the accusative and the genitive. You say ”رَأيْتُ الزَّيْدِينَ“ ("I saw the Zayds") and ”مَرَرْتُ بِالزَّيْدِينَ“ ("I passed by the Zayds"), and ”رَأيْتُ الهِنْداتِ“ ("I saw the Hinds") and ”رَغِبْتُ في الهِنْداتِ“ ("I desired the Hinds"). ”اَلْجَنَّةُ“ in the language of the Arabs is an orchard, and ”اَلْجَنّاتُ“ are orchards; they are what Allah has promised the God-fearing, and in them is whatever souls desire and eyes delight in.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿كُلَّما رُزِقُوا مِنها مِن ثَمَرَةٍ رِزْقًا قالُوا هَذا الَّذِي رُزِقْنا مِن قَبْلُ وأُتُوا بِهِ مُتَشابِهًا﴾. The people of the language said: the meaning of ”مُتَشابِهًا“ is: its parts resemble one another in excellence and beauty. The people of tafsīr and some of the people of the language said: ”مُتَشابِهًا“ means its parts resemble one another in form and differ in taste. The proof of the exegetes is His saying ”هَذا الَّذِي رُزِقْنا مِن قَبْلُ“, because its form is the first form; but a difference of tastes with an agreement of form is more striking and better known among people: if you saw an apple containing the taste of every fruit, it would be the utmost marvel and an indication of [divine] wisdom.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَهم فِيها أزْواجٌ مُطَهَّرَةٌ﴾, that is, they do not need what the women of the people of this world need of eating and drinking; they do not menstruate, nor do they need anything from which one purifies oneself. Moreover they are pure with the purity of character and chastity. So ”مُطَهَّرَةٌ“ gathers all purity, because ”مُطَهَّرَةٌ“ (purified) is more emphatic in speech than ”طاهِرَةٌ“ (pure), and because ”مُطَهَّرَةٌ“ is used only for what is abundant.
The iʿrāb of ”أزْواجٌ“: nominative through ”وَلَهم“, or, if you wish, through the ibtidāʾ (being a subject). In ”أزْواجٌ“ it is possible that the singular of them is ”زَوْجًا“ or ”زَوْجَةً“. Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, said: ﴿اسْكُنْ أنْتَ وزَوْجُكَ الجَنَّةَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 35], and the poet said:
؎فَبَكى بَناتِي شَجْوَهُنَّ وزَوْجَتِي ∗∗∗ والطّامِعُونَ إلَيَّ ثُمَّ تَصَدَّعُوا
(My daughters wept their grief, and my wife, and those who had hopes of me; then they dispersed.)

zajjaj:26-26.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَسْتَحْيِي أنْ يَضْرِبَ مَثَلا ما بَعُوضَةً فَما فَوْقَها﴾. If someone asks: what is the meaning of mentioning this parable right after what He promised the people of Paradise and what He prepared for the disbelievers? It is answered: this is connected to His saying ﴿فَلا تَجْعَلُوا لِلَّهِ أنْدادًا﴾ [al-Baqara: 22], because Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ لَنْ يَخْلُقُوا ذُبابًا﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 73], and He said: ﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ أوْلِياءَ كَمَثَلِ العَنْكَبُوتِ اتَّخَذَتْ بَيْتًا﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 41]. The disbelievers said: "The god of Muḥammad strikes parables with the fly and the spider." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَسْتَحْيِي أنْ يَضْرِبَ مَثَلا ما بَعُوضَةً فَما فَوْقَها﴾, that is, for these rivals whom you have taken besides Allah, because this is in reality the likeness of these rivals.
As for the iʿrāb of ”بَعُوضَةً“: the accusative is from two directions in our view, and some grammarians mentioned a third. The best of these is that ”ما“ is redundant (zāʾida) and emphasising, as though He said: ”إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَسْتَحْيِي أنْ يَضْرِبَ بَعُوضَةً مَثَلًا، ومَثَلًا بَعُوضَةً“ ("Allah is not ashamed to strike a gnat as a parable / a parable, a gnat"), with ”ما“ redundant and emphasising, as in His saying: ﴿فَبِما رَحْمَةٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ لِنْتَ لَهُمْ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 159], the meaning being: "by a mercy from Allah, truly". So ”ما“ in emphasis is equivalent to "truly", except that it has no iʿrāb, and the governor of the genitive or the accusative steps over it to what comes after it; its meaning is emphasis. Like it in emphasis is ”لا“ in His saying: ﴿لِئَلا يَعْلَمَ أهْلُ الكِتابِ﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 29], meaning: "so that the People of the Book may know".
It is [also] possible that ”ما“ is an indefinite noun, so that the meaning is: ”إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَسْتَحْيِي أنْ يَضْرِبَ شَيْئًا مَثَلًا“ ("Allah is not ashamed to strike something as a parable"), with ”بَعُوضَةً“ as it were in the position of a description of "something", as though He said: ”إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَسْتَحْيِي أنْ يَضْرِبَ مَثَلًا شَيْئًا مِنَ الأشْياءِ، بَعُوضَةً فَما فَوْقَها“ ("… to strike as a parable some thing among things, a gnat or what is above it"). Some grammarians said its meaning may be: "what is between a gnat and what is above it". The first two views are the view of the early grammarians, and the preferred view among the body of the Basrans is that ”ما“ is superfluous (laghw).
The nominative in ”بَعُوضَةً“ is permissible in iʿrāb, but I do not recall anyone who read it so, and I do not know whether anyone read it so or not. The nominative would be on the suppression of ”هو“, as though He said: ”مَثَلًا الَّذِي هو بَعُوضَةٌ“ ("a parable which is a gnat"). This, according to Sībawayh, is weak, and there is room to avoid it; but whoever reads ”تَمامًا عَلى الَّذِي أحْسَنُ“ – and it has been read so – may read ”مَثَلًا ما بَعُوضَةٌ“, though it is stronger in ”اَلَّذِي أحْسَنُ“, because ”اَلَّذِي“ is longer and ”اَلَّذِي“ has no function other than that of nouns.
On the meaning of His saying ”فَما فَوْقَها“ they gave two views: they said ”فَما فَوْقَها“ means what is larger than it; and they said ”فَما فَوْقَها“ means [what is above it] in smallness. Some grammarians prefer the first, because the gnat is, as it were, the limit of smallness among the things with which a parable is struck. The second view is also preferred, because what is sought here, and the purpose, is smallness and the belittling of the parable of the rivals.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَأمّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾, meaning those who believed, ﴿فَيَعْلَمُونَ﴾ that this parable is true; ﴿وَأمّا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا فَيَقُولُونَ ماذا أرادَ اللَّهُ بِهَذا مَثَلا﴾, that is: what did He intend by the fly and the spider as a parable? So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿يُضِلُّ بِهِ كَثِيرًا﴾, that is: He calls all creatures to believe in it, and the disbelievers deny it and so are led astray by it.
﴿وَما يُضِلُّ بِهِ إلا الفاسِقِينَ﴾ indicates that they are the ones led astray by it. ”وَيَهْدِي بِهِ كَثِيرًا“: the believers are increased in guidance by it, because whenever they increase in belief they have increased in guidance.
The fāʾ entered the jawāb (answer) of ”أمّا“ in His saying ”فَيَعْلَمُونَ“ because ”أمّا“ comes with the meaning of condition and requital (sharṭ and jazāʾ). When one says ”أمّا زَيْدٌ فَقَدْ آمَنَ، وأمّا عَمْرٌو فَقَدْ كَفَرَ“ ("As for Zayd, he has believed; as for ʿAmr, he has disbelieved"), the meaning is: whatever may be the case, Zayd has believed; and whatever may be the case, ʿAmr has disbelieved.
His saying ”ماذا“: it is possible that ”ما“ and ”ذا“ are a single noun, whose position is accusative, the meaning being: what thing did Allah intend by this as a parable? It is also possible that ”ذا“ with ”ما“ is equivalent to ”اَلَّذِي“ (which), so that the meaning is: what is it that Allah intended by this as a parable? Or: what thing is it that Allah intended by this as a parable? In that case ”ما“ here is nominative by ibtidāʾ (as mubtadaʾ, subject), and ”ذا“ has the meaning of ”اَلَّذِي“ and is the khabar (predicate) of the mubtadaʾ.
The iʿrāb of ”اَلْفاسِقِينَ“ is accusative, as though the meaning were: ”وما يَضِلُّ بِهِ أحَدٌ إلّا الفاسِقِينَ“ ("and no one goes astray by it except the transgressors"). «[Translator's note: so in the text; the verb is vocalised as intransitive يَضِلُّ with أحدٌ as its agent, which would ordinarily leave الفاسقين as an excepted noun in the accusative after a negated clause with the agent expressed.]»

zajjaj:62-62.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ﴾: the good reading is the nominative (rafʿ). Likewise when «لا» is repeated in speech you say: «لا رَجُلٌ عِنْدِي، ولا زَيْدٌ» ("no man is with me, nor Zayd"), and ﴿لا فِيها غَوْلٌ ولا هم عَنْها يُنْـزَفُونَ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 47]. If it is read «وَلا خَوْفَ عَلَيْهِمْ» (with the lā of generic negation), that is good, extremely good, and it has been read so.

zajjaj:63-63.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ أخَذْنا مِيثاقَكم ورَفَعْنا فَوْقَكُمُ الطُّورَ﴾: the meaning is: remember when We took your covenant. «الطُّور» here is the mountain. As for the meaning of «أخَذْنا مِيثاقَكم», it may be what Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, took when He brought forth mankind like tiny particles (al-dharr). The proof of this is His saying: ﴿وَإذْ نَتَقْنا الجَبَلَ فَوْقَهم كَأنَّهُ ظُلَّةٌ﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 171], and then He said, after the end of the verse: ﴿وَإذْ أخَذَ رَبُّكَ مِن بَنِي آدَمَ مِن ظُهُورِهِمْ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 172]; so this verse is like the verse in al-Baqara, and this is the best of the views about it. It has also been said that the taking of the covenant is the covenant Allah took from the messengers and those who followed them; its proof is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ أخَذَ اللَّهُ مِيثاقَ النَّبِيِّينَ لَما آتَيْتُكم مِن كِتابٍ وحِكْمَةٍ ثُمَّ جاءَكم رَسُولٌ مُصَدِّقٌ لِما مَعَكم لَتُؤْمِنُنَّ بِهِ ولَتَنْصُرُنَّهُ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 81]; so the taking of the covenant from the prophets — Allah's blessings and peace be upon them — includes those who followed them. «رَفَعْنا فَوْقَكُمُ الطُّورَ», that is: We brought you a mighty sign, namely that «الطُّور», which is the mountain, was raised above them until it overshadowed them and they thought it was going to fall upon them. So Allah told of the greatness of the sign they were shown after the taking of the covenant, and told of the thing after which, had He punished them, He would have been just in doing so; but He granted them repentance after that.

zajjaj:64-64.t:
And He said: ﴿ثُمَّ تَوَلَّيْتُمْ مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾, that is, after the mighty signs. ﴿فَلَوْلا فَضْلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكم ورَحْمَتُهُ﴾, that is: were it not that Allah favoured you with repentance after you had disbelieved, despite the greatness of these signs, ﴿لَكُنْتُمْ مِنَ الخاسِرِينَ﴾. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿خُذُوا ما آتَيْناكم بِقُوَّةٍ﴾ [al-Baqara: 63]: the position of «ما» is accusative, and «ما آتَيْناكم» is the Book, which is the Torah. The meaning of "take it with strength" is: take it with earnestness, and abandon doubt and uncertainty, because of the mighty signs that have become clear to you.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واذْكُرُوا ما فِيهِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 63]: its meaning is: study what is in it. It is permissible in the language to say «خُذْ» and «وخْذًا» [Translator's note: so in the source; the intended form is unclear, perhaps «أُوخُذْ» is meant], whose original form is «اُوْخُذْ»; likewise «كُلْ», whose original form is «اُوْكُلْ». But in «خُذْ» and «كُلْ» there came together frequent usage, the meeting of two hamzas, and a ḍamma, so the fāʾ of the verb (its first radical) was dropped — namely the hamza that was in «أخَذَ» and «أكَلَ». It was dropped for what we have described: frequent usage and the combination of things they find heavy.

zajjaj:65-65.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَقَدْ عَلِمْتُمُ الَّذِينَ اعْتَدَوْا مِنكم في السَّبْتِ﴾: the meaning of «عَلِمْتُمْ» here is "you knew (ʿaraftum)"; similar to it is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لا تَعْلَمُونَهُمُ اللَّهُ يَعْلَمُهُمْ﴾ [al-Anfāl: 60], whose meaning is: you do not know them; Allah knows them. The meaning of «اعْتَدَوْا» is: they did wrong and transgressed the limit set for them. They had been commanded not to fish on the Sabbath, and the fish used to gather on the Sabbath because they were safe on it; so they penned them in on the Sabbath and took them on Sunday. Thus they transgressed on the Sabbath, because their catching them prevented them from moving freely. So Allah made their recompense in this world — after the mighty signs He had shown them — that He made them «قِرَدَةً خاسِئِينَ», apes despised. The meaning of «خاسِئِين» is: driven far away. One says «خَسَأْتُ الكَلْبَ، أخْسَؤُهُ خَسْئًا», that is, I drove the dog away and chased it off.

zajjaj:66-66.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَجَعَلْناها نَكالا لِما بَيْنَ يَدَيْها وما خَلْفَها﴾: this «ها» refers back to the community that was transformed, and it may refer to the deed. The meaning of «لِما بَيْنَ يَدَيْها» admits two interpretations: «لِما بَيْنَ يَدَيْها» may mean: for the sins it had committed before; and «لِما بَيْنَ يَدَيْها» may mean: for the nations that see it, while «وما خَلْفَها» is what comes after it. The meaning of your saying "nakkaltu bihi" (I made an example of him) is: I caused others to shrink back (yankulu) from doing the like of what he did, lest the like of what befell him befall them.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَمَوْعِظَةً لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾, that is: the people of piety take admonition from it and hold fast to what they are upon.

zajjaj:67-67.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْمُرُكم أنْ تَذْبَحُوا بَقَرَةً﴾: the meaning is: and remember when Moses said to his people. They were commanded to slaughter a cow, part of which a slain man would be struck with; they had disputed about who killed him, and his killer was not known. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, commanded that the slain man be struck with one of the parts of the cow. They claim in the tafsīr that they were commanded to strike him with the right thigh, or the tail. Allah the Exalted wished to show them how the dead are brought to life. In this verse there is an argument against the polytheists of the Arabs, because they did not believe in the resurrection; so the Prophet ﷺ informed them of this report, which none could know except one who had read the scriptures or to whom it had been revealed. The polytheists knew that the Prophet ﷺ was unlettered (ummī), and that the People of the Book — while opposing him — knew that what he related of these narratives was true. ﴿قالُوا أتَتَّخِذُنا هُزُوًا﴾: so Moses disavowed mockery, because the mocker is ignorant and frivolous, and said: ﴿أعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ أنْ أكُونَ مِنَ الجاهِلِينَ﴾.

zajjaj:68-68.t:
When it became clear to them that it was from Allah, they said: ﴿ادْعُ لَنا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّنْ لَنا ما هِيَ﴾. They asked "What is it?" only because they did not know that a cow, with part of which a dead man is struck, would bring him to life. ﴿قالَ إنَّهُ يَقُولُ إنَّها بَقَرَةٌ لا فارِضٌ ولا بِكْرٌ﴾: «فارِضٌ» is nominative by an implied (muḍmar) «هي». The meaning of «لا فارِضٌ» is "not old", and «وَلا بِكْرٌ» is "not young", that is, she is neither old nor young. ﴿عَوانٌ﴾: «العَوان» is below the aged and above the young. Of fāriḍ one says «فَرَضَتْ، تَفْرِضُ، فُرُوضًا», and of ʿawān «قَدْ عَوَّنَتْ، تُعَوِّنُ». One says «حَرْبٌ عَوانٌ» when it is not the first war but a second one. Zuhayr said:
إذا لَقِحَتْ حَرْبٌ عَوانٌ مُضِرَّةٌ ∗∗∗ ضَرُوسٌ تَهُزُّ النّاسَ أنْيابُها صُعْلُ
(When a repeated (ʿawān), harmful war conceives, a biting one whose fangs shake people, small-headed [i.e. fierce].)
The meaning of «بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ» is: between the young and the old, between the small and the aged. «بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ» is permissible, although «بَيْنَ» is used only with two or more, because «ذَلِكَ» stands in for whole sentences: you say "I thought Zayd standing", and someone says "I thought that (dhālika)".

zajjaj:69-69.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ادْعُ لَنا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّنْ لَنا ما لَوْنُها﴾: the position of «ما» is nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject), because its interpretation is interrogative, as in your saying "Pray to your Lord for us to make clear to us what thing (ayyu shayʾin) her colour is"; similar to it is ﴿فَلْيَنْظُرْ أيُّها أزْكى طَعامًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. It is not permissible in recitation to read «ادْعُ لَنا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّنْ لَنا ما لَوْنُها» taking «ما» as superfluous (laghw) [Translator's note: the source prints the same vowelling as the Quranic text; the intended disallowed reading is presumably «ما لَوْنَها», with «لَوْنَها» accusative as the object of «يُبَيِّنْ»], for the Quran is recited only as the readers did on whom there is consensus in taking from them.

﴿قالَ إنَّهُ يَقُولُ إنَّها﴾: what comes after "saying" (qawl), of the category of «إنَّ», is always with kasra, as though you were mentioning the saying at the head of your speech. «قُلْتُ» occurs in the speech of the Arabs only to report with it what was speech standing by itself before it entered, so that with its mention it conveys that same wording. You say «قُلْتُ: زَيْدٌ مُنْطَلِقٌ» ("I said: Zayd is leaving"), as though you said «زَيْدٌ مُنْطَلِقٌ»; and likewise «إنَّ زَيْدًا مُنْطَلِقٌ». There is no disagreement among the grammarians about that, except that a people among the Arabs, namely the Banū Sulaym, treat the whole category of «قُلْتُ» like that of «ظَنَنْتُ», saying «قُلْتُ زَيْدًا مُنْطَلِقًا». This is a dialect of which nothing may be found in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He; and «قالَ أنَّهُ يَقُولُ إنَّها» is not permissible: only the kasra is permissible.

As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿صَفْراءُ فاقِعٌ لَوْنُها﴾: «فاقِعٌ» is a naʿt (adjective) for a yellow of intense yellowness. One says «أصْفَرُ فاقِعٌ» (bright yellow), «أبْيَضُ ناصِعٌ» (pure white) and «أحْمَرُ قانٍ» (deep red). The poet said:
يَسْقِي بِها ذُو تُومَتَيْنِ كَأنَّما ∗∗∗ قَنَأتْ أنامِلُهُ مِنَ الفُرْصادِ
(With it pours one wearing two pearl earrings, as though his fingertips had turned deep red from mulberry.)
That is, they became intensely red. One also says «أحْمَرُ قاتِمٌ» (dark red), «أبْيَضُ يَقَقٌ», «لَهِقٌ» and «لِهاقٌ» (brilliant white), and «أسْوَدُ حالِكٌ», «حَلُوكٌ», «حَلْوَكِيٌّ» and «دَجُوجِيٌّ» (jet black). All of these are intensive descriptions of colours. They have also said that «صَفْراء» here means black. The meaning of ﴿تَسُرُّ النّاظِرِينَ﴾ is: it pleases the onlookers.

zajjaj:1-1.t:
And from Sūrat "al-Baqara"
﷽
His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿الم﴾: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā held that they are letters of the alphabet (ḥurūf al-hijāʾ), an opening of speech; and likewise "المر" and "المص". Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash held that it is an opening of speech, the proof of this being that the speech mentioned before the sura has been completed. Quṭrub held that "الم", "المص", "المر", "كهيعص", "ق", "يس" and "نون" are letters of the alphabet (ḥurūf al-muʿjam), mentioned to indicate that this Qur'an is composed of these separated letters, which are the letters "أ ب ت ث"; so some of them came separated, and the whole of them came composed, to show the people upon whom the Qur'an was sent down that it is in their own letters, which they understand — there is no doubt in it.

It is transmitted from al-Shaʿbī that he said: Allah has a secret in every Book, and His secret in the Qur'an is the letters of the alphabet mentioned at the beginnings of the suras. Three views are transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās on "الم" and what resembles it. One of them is that he said: Allah swore by these letters that this Book which was sent down upon Muḥammad ﷺ is the Book that is with Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, in which there is no doubt. The second view from him is that "الر", "حم" and "نون" are a name of al-Raḥmān, Mighty and Majestic is He, separated in pronunciation and joined in meaning. The third from him is that he said: "الم" means "أنا اللَّهُ أعْلَمُ" (I am Allah; I know best); "الر" means "أنا اللَّهُ أرى" (I am Allah; I see); "المص" means "أنا اللَّهُ أعْلَمُ وأفْصِلُ" (I am Allah; I know best and I distinguish); and "المر" means "أنا اللَّهُ أعْلَمُ وأرى" (I am Allah; I know best and I see). This is all that has reached us from the views of the philologists and the grammarians on the meaning of "الم", and all that has reached us from the scholars of exegesis.

We say concerning the i'rab of "الم", "الر", "كهيعص" and letters like these: this is the chapter on spelling-out (al-tahajjī).

This is the chapter on the letters of spelling-out (ḥurūf al-tahajjī)
They are: alif, bāʾ, tāʾ, thāʾ and the rest of them that occur in the Qur'an. The consensus of the grammarians is that these letters are indeclinable (mabnī) on the pause (waqf); they are not inflected. The meaning of our saying "indeclinable on the pause" is that you assume you can stop on each one of them, so the pronunciation is: "ألِفْ لامْ مِيمْ ذَلِكَ...". The proof that you assume a stop on them is your combining two vowelless letters in your saying "لامْ" and in your saying "مِيمْ". The proof that the letters of the alphabet are built on the stop, just as numbers (in counting) are built on the stop, is that you pronounce them with the pause, combining two vowelless letters, just as you say when you count: "واحِدْ، اِثْنانْ، ثَلاثَهْ، أرْبَعَهْ..." (one, two, three, four…). Were it not that you assume a stop, you would say "ثَلاثَةٌ" with tāʾ, as you say "ثَلاثًا يا هَذا" (three, O you), where the hāʾ becomes tāʾ with nunation and connected speech. Their proper inflection is that their endings be vowelless. Sībawayh held that what you mean is that the alphabet consists of letters by which one reproduces what is in nouns composed of letters, so they are treated like what is used to reproduce a sound, such as "غاقْ" and "غاقْ يا فَتى" — one merely reproduces the cry of the crow. Further proof that they are in pause form is the saying of the poet:
أقْبَلْتُ مِن عِنْدِ زِيادٍ كالخَرِفْ ∗∗∗ تَخُطُّ رِجْلايَ بِخَطٍّ مُخْتَلِفْ
تُكَتِّبانِ في الطَّرِيقِ لامَ الِفْ
(I came away from Ziyād like a dotard, my two feet tracing an uneven line, writing on the road lām-alif.)
As though he said "لامْ ألِفْ" with the lām vowelless, but he cast the vowel of the hamza of "ألِفْ" onto the mīm and gave it fatḥa.

Abū Isḥāq said: The explanation and interpretation of these letters is that they are not treated like fully declinable nouns (al-asmāʾ al-mutamakkina) and imperfect verbs, which must be inflected; rather, they are the separation (taqṭīʿ) of a composed noun, in which inflection is required only once it is complete. In your saying "جَعْفَرٌ", it is not required that the jīm, the ʿayn, the fāʾ or the rāʾ be inflected separately without completing the noun. They are only reproductions placed upon these letters. If you treat them like nouns and speak about them, you say: "هَذِهِ كافٌ حَسَنَةٌ" and "هَذا كافٌ حَسَنٌ" (this is a fine kāf), and likewise the rest of the letters of the alphabet. Whoever says "هَذِهِ كافٌ" makes it feminine in the sense of "word" (kalima), and whoever makes it masculine does so in the sense of "letter" (ḥarf). Inflection occurs in them because you take them out of the category of reproduction (ḥikāya). The poet said:
كافًا ومِيمَيْنِ وسِينًا طاسِما
(A kāf, two mīms and an effaced sīn.)
He also said:
كَما بَيَّنَتْ كافٌ تَلُوحُ ومِيمُها
(As a gleaming kāf and its mīm have made plain.)
He made "طاسِما" masculine because he made it a qualification of the sīn and took the sīn in the sense of "letter"; and he said "تَلُوحُ", making the kāf feminine, taking it in the sense of "word". The poet said — satirising the grammarians, and he is Yazīd ibn al-Ḥakam:
إذا اجْتَمَعُوا عَلى ألِفٍ وواوٍ ∗∗∗ وياءٍ لاحَ بَيْنَهُمُ جِدالُ
(When they gather over an alif, a wāw and a yāʾ, a quarrel flares up among them.)

As for the i'rab of "أبِي جادٍ", "هَوَزٍ" and "حُطِّي", Sībawayh held that these have known derivations in the speech of the Arabs and are triptotes (fully declinable): you say "عَلِمْتُ أبا جادٍ" (I learned Abū Jād) and "اِنْتَفَعْتُ بِأبِي جادٍ" (I benefited from Abū Jād); likewise "هَوَزٌ": you say "نَفَعَنِي هَوَزٌ" and "اِنْتَفَعْتُ بِهَوَزٍ"; and likewise "حُطِّي". They are declinable and take nunation. As for "كَلَمْوَنُ", "سَعْفَصُ" and "قُرَيْشِياتٌ", they are foreign: you say "هَذِهِ كَلَمْوَنُ يا هَذا", "تَعَلَّمْتُ كَلَمْوَنَ" and "اِنْتَفَعْتُ بِكَلَمْوَنَ", and likewise "سَعْفَصُ". As for "قُرَيْشِياتٌ", it is a name for a plural, declinable because of the alif and tāʾ: you say "هَذِهِ قُرَيْشِياتٌ يا هَذا" and "عَجِبْتُ مِن قُرَيْشِياتٍ يا هَذا".

Quṭrub has another view on "الم". He held it possible that, when the people talked nonsense about the Qur'an and would not try to understand it — when they said: "لا تَسْمَعُوا لِهَذا القُرْآنِ والغَوْا فِيهِ" (Do not listen to this Qur'an and make noise during it) — mention of these letters was sent down; so they fell silent when they heard the letters, hoping to gain what they wanted, so that — after the letters — they would come to understand the Qur'an and what is in it, and the proof against them would be firmer if they denied after understanding and learning.

Abū Isḥāq said: What I choose among these views that have been stated on His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, "الم", is part of what is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah's mercy be upon him: namely that the meaning of "الم" is "أنا اللَّهُ أعْلَمُ" (I am Allah; I know best), and that each letter of them has its own interpretation. The proof of this is that the Arabs pronounce a single letter, indicating by it the word of which it is part. The poet said:
قُلْنا لَها قِفِي قالَتْ قافْ ∗∗∗ لا تَحْسَبِي أنّا نَسِينا الإيجافْ
(We said to her: "Stop!" She said: "Qāf" [I stop]. Do not think that we have forgotten the hard riding.)
So he pronounced only qāf, meaning that she said: "أقِفُ" (I stop). The poet also said:
نادَوْهُمُ أنْ ألْجِمُوا ألاتا ∗∗∗ قالُوا جَمِيعًا كُلُّهم ألا فا
(They called to them: "Bridle! Will you not…?" They all said together: "Then…!")
Its interpretation: "They called to them: Bridle! Will you not ride (ألا تَرْكَبُونَ)? They all said together: Then ride (ألا فارْكَبُوا)!" He pronounced only a tāʾ and a fāʾ, just as the first poet pronounced a qāf. Some of the philologists recited, by al-Qayyim ibn Saʿd ibn Mālik:
إنْ شِئْتَ أشْرَفْنا كِلانا فَدَعا ∗∗∗ اللَّهَ رَبًّا جُهْدَهُ فَأسْمَعا
بِالخَيْرِ خَيْراتٍ وإنْ شَرًّا فَآ ∗∗∗ ولا أُرِيدُ الشَّرَّ إلّا أنْ تَآ
(If you wish, we both shall go up high and each call upon Allah as Lord with all his strength and make himself heard: for good, good things; and if evil, then [evil]; and I do not want evil unless you [will it].)
And the grammarians recited:
بِالخَيْرِ خَيْراتٍ وإنْ شَرًّا فا ∗∗∗ ولا أُرِيدُ الشَّرَّ إلّا أنْ تا
(For good, good things; and if evil, then [evil]; and I do not want evil unless you [will it].)
They mean: "إنْ شَرًّا فَشَرٌّ، ولا أُرِيدُ الشَّرَّ إلّا أنْ تَشاءَ" (if evil, then evil; and I do not want evil unless you will it). All the Basrans recited this. This is what I choose concerning these letters, and Allah knows best their true nature.

As for "ص", al-Ḥasan read: "صادِ والقُرْآنِ", giving the dāl kasra. The philologists said: its meaning is "صادِ القُرْآنَ بِعَمَلِكَ" (confront the Qur'an with your deeds), i.e. aim at it; the yāʾ dropped because of the imperative. It is also possible that the dāl was given kasra because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, if you intend connected speech. Likewise ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Isḥāq read: "صادِ والقُرْآنِ", and he also read: "قافِ والقُرْآنِ المَجِيدِ"; the kasra in the view of Ibn Abī Isḥāq is because of the meeting of two vowelless letters. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read: "صادَ والقُرْآنِ", with fatḥa on the dāl, and likewise he read "نُونَ والقَلَمِ" and "قافَ والقُرْآنِ", also with fatḥa, because of the meeting of two vowelless letters. Sībawayh said: if you call "أسْحارَّ" in the vocative — "اَلْأسْحارُّ" being the name of a plant, with doubled rāʾ — you say in its curtailed form (tarkhīm): "يا أسْحارَ أقْبِلْ" (O Asḥār, come), giving fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, just as you choose fatḥa in your saying "عَضَّ يا فَتى" (bite, young man); making fatḥa follow fatḥa is like making alif follow fatḥa. "يا أسْحارِ أقْبِلْ" is also permissible, giving kasra because of the meeting of two vowelless letters. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash said: it is possible that "صادَ", "قافَ" and "نُونَ" are names of suras, in the accusative, except that they are diptotes, just as feminine names in general are diptotes. The first view — I mean the meeting of two vowelless letters, and the fatḥa and kasra on account of their meeting — is more in accordance with analogy (aqyas), because he (al-Akhfash) holds that he puts these things in the accusative as though he said: "أذْكُرُ صادَ" (I mention Ṣād); likewise he allows the accusative in "حم" and "طس", and also "ياسِينْ", as names of suras. Had it been read so, its explanation would be fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters. As for "كهيعص", the nūn is not pronounced distinctly before the ṣād in recitation; likewise "حم عسق": the nūn is not pronounced distinctly before the sīn. Al-Akhfash and other grammarians said: the nūn was not pronounced distinctly because its point of articulation is close to that of the sīn and the ṣād. As for "نُونْ والقَلَمِ", the reading in it is with the nūn pronounced distinctly before the wāw of "والقَلَمِ", and also without distinct pronunciation: if you wish you pronounce it distinctly and if you wish you do not, saying "نُونْ والقَلَمِ", because the nūn is somewhat distant from the wāw.

As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, "الم اَللَّهُ", there are two views on the fatḥa of the mīm. One of them belongs to a group of grammarians: these letters are built on the pause, so after them the connecting alif must be made disjunctive (a hamza of qaṭʿ), so that the original is "أ ل م اَللَّهُ لا إلَهَ إلّا هو"; then the fatḥa of the hamza was cast onto the mīm and the hamza dropped, just as you say "واحِدْ، اِثْنانِ", and if you wish you say "واحِدِ اثْنانِ", casting the kasra of "اِثْنَيْنِ" onto the dāl. Some other grammarians said: it is not possible in pronunciation to utter three vowelless letters, so the mīm in "المَ اللَّهُ" must have fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters — meaning the mīm, the lām and the one after it. This view is correct; nothing else is possible in pronunciation.

As for whoever holds that it was only the vowel of the hamza that was cast, he ought to read: "المِ اللَّهُ" «[Translator's note: so the text as printed; the argument seems to require the reverse attribution — the kasra "المِ" would follow from the view that the vowel is due to the meeting of two vowelless letters, while casting the hamza's fatḥa yields "المَ". The text is translated as written.]». I know of no one who read so, except what is reported from al-Ruʾāsī; and as for whoever transmits it from ʿĀṣim, it is not a sound transmission. Some grammarians said: if it were vowelled because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, it would have kasra. This is a mistake: if we did that in the meeting of two vowelless letters where the first of them is (preceded by) a yāʾ, you would have to say "كَيْفِ زَيْدٍ؟" and "أيْنِ زَيْدٍ؟", and this is not permissible. The fatḥa occurred only because kasra is heavy after yāʾ.

zajjaj:27-27.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الَّذِينَ يَنْقُضُونَ عَهْدَ اللَّهِ مِن بَعْدِ مِيثاقِهِ﴾. The covenant of Allah here – and Allah knows best – is what Allah took from the prophets and those who followed them: that they would not disbelieve in the matter of the Prophet ﷺ. The proof of this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ أخَذَ اللَّهُ مِيثاقَ النَّبِيِّينَ لَما آتَيْتُكم مِن كِتابٍ وحِكْمَةٍ ثُمَّ جاءَكم رَسُولٌ مُصَدِّقٌ لِما مَعَكم لَتُؤْمِنُنَّ بِهِ ولَتَنْصُرُنَّهُ قالَ أأقْرَرْتُمْ وأخَذْتُمْ عَلى ذَلِكم إصْرِي قالُوا أقْرَرْنا قالَ فاشْهَدُوا﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 81]. This is the covenant taken from everyone who followed the prophets, peace be upon them: that they believe in the Messenger who confirms what is with them. ”إصْرِي“ is like "my covenant".
It is also possible that the covenant of Allah is the one He took from the children of Adam from their backs, when He said: ﴿وَأشْهَدَهم عَلى أنْفُسِهِمْ ألَسْتُ بِرَبِّكم قالُوا بَلى شَهِدْنا﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 172]. Some people said that the covenant of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, is the drawing of inferences to His oneness, and that every being endowed with discernment knows that Allah is a Creator, and so belief in Him is incumbent upon him. For the first two views there is in the Qurʾān what confirms their interpretation.
As for the iʿrāb of ”الَّذِينَ“: it is accusative as a ṣifa (adjective) of ”اَلْفاسِقِينَ“. The position of His saying ﴿أنْ يُوصَلَ﴾ is genitive as a badal (substitute) for the hāʾ, the meaning being: what Allah commanded to be joined (bi-an yūṣala). The position of ”أُولَئِكَ“ is nominative by ibtidāʾ (as mubtadaʾ, subject), ”اَلْخاسِرُونَ“ is the khabar (predicate) of the mubtadaʾ, and ”هم“ has the sense of faṣl (separation), which is what the Kufans call ”اَلْعِمادَ“ (the support). It is also possible that ”أُولَئِكَ“ is nominative by ibtidāʾ, ”هم“ a second mubtadaʾ, ”اَلْخاسِرُونَ“ its khabar, and ”هُمُ الخاسِرُونَ“ the khabar of ”أُولَئِكَ“.

zajjaj:28-28.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿كَيْفَ تَكْفُرُونَ بِاللَّهِ وكُنْتُمْ أمْواتًا فَأحْياكم ثُمَّ يُمِيتُكم ثُمَّ يُحْيِيكم ثُمَّ إلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾. Their being dead at first is that they were sperm-drops; then they were made living beings, then they were caused to die, then they were brought to life, and then they will be returned to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, after the resurrection, as He said: ﴿مُهْطِعِينَ إلى الدّاعِ﴾ [al-Qamar: 8], that is, hastening, and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يَوْمَ يَخْرُجُونَ مِنَ الأجْداثِ سِراعًا﴾ [al-Maʿārij: 43]; al-ajdāth are the graves.
The interpretation of ”كَيْفَ“ is that it is a question with the meaning of wonder (taʿajjub), and this wonder is only for creatures and for the believers, that is: wonder at these people, how they disbelieve when Allah's proof has been established against them. The meaning of ”وَكُنْتُمْ“ is: "when you had been" (wa-qad kuntum); this wāw is the wāw of the ḥāl (circumstantial), and suppressing ”قَدْ“ is permissible when there is an indication of it in the speech. Likewise His saying: ﴿أوْ جاءُوكم حَصِرَتْ صُدُورُهُمْ﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 90], ﴿وَإنْ كانَ قَمِيصُهُ قُدَّ مِن دُبُرٍ﴾ [Yūsuf: 27].

zajjaj:29-29.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ لَكم ما في الأرْضِ جَمِيعًا﴾. The position of ”ما“ is mafʿūl bihi (direct object). Its interpretation is that everything on the earth is a favour bestowed upon you, so it is for you. There is another view on it: that this is a proof of the oneness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ثُمَّ اسْتَوى إلى السَّماءِ﴾: there are two views on it. Some said: ”اِسْتَوى إلى السَّماءِ“ means He turned and directed Himself to the heaven, as you say: ”قَدْ فَرَغَ الأمِيرُ مِن بَلَدِ كَذا وكَذا، ثُمَّ اسْتَوى إلى بَلَدِ كَذا“ ("the emir finished with such-and-such a town, then istawā to such-and-such a town"), meaning: he directed himself to it. It has also been said: ”اِسْتَوى“ means His command ascended to the heaven; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.
”اَلسَّماءِ“: its form is the form of a singular and its meaning is the meaning of a plural; the proof of this is His saying: ﴿فَسَوّاهُنَّ سَبْعَ سَماواتٍ﴾. It is also possible that ”اَلسَّماءِ“ is a plural, just as al-samawāt is a plural, as though its singular were ”سَماةٌ“ or ”سَماوَةٌ“, with ”سَماءٌ“ for the whole. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash claimed that ”اَلسَّماءُ“ may be a singular by which the plural is meant, as you say: ”كَثُرَ الدِّرْهَمُ والدِّينارُ في أيْدِي النّاسِ“ ("the dirham and the dinar have become plentiful in people's hands"). ”اَلسَّماءُ“ in the language is the roof (ceiling); and of everything that rises high and is elevated it is said: ”قَدْ سَما يَسْمُو“ ("it has risen high"). Every roof is a samāʾ, young man; and from this the clouds are so called, because they are high.

zajjaj:30-30.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ قالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلائِكَةِ إنِّي جاعِلٌ في الأرْضِ خَلِيفَةً﴾. Abū ʿUbayda said: ”إذْ“ here is redundant (zāʾida). This is rashness on the part of Abū ʿUbayda, because nothing should be said about the Qurʾān except with an aim that runs towards the truth. ”إذْ“ means time, and it is a noun, so how can it be superfluous (laghw)? Its meaning is time. The argument concerning ”إذْ“ is that Allah the Exalted mentioned the creation of people and others, so it is as though He said: ”اِبْتَدَأ خَلْقَكم إذْ قالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلائِكَةِ إنِّي جاعِلٌ في الأرْضِ خَلِيفَةً“ ("He began your creation when your Lord said to the angels: I am placing a vicegerent on the earth").
In the mention of this verse there is an argument against the People of the Book establishing the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ: the account of Adam, and the angels' prostration to him that Allah commanded, was known to them, and this was not part of the knowledge of the Arabs which they used to know. So in the Prophet's ﷺ reporting it there is a proof establishing his messengership, since he brought them what was not part of the knowledge of the Arabs; rather it is an account known only to one who has read the Book or to whom it has been revealed.
«[Translator's note: the following paragraph is marked in the source with the verse sign ؎, although it is prose.]» The interpretation of His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أتَجْعَلُ فِيها مَن يُفْسِدُ فِيها ويَسْفِكُ الدِّماءَ﴾: it is related that a creation called ”اَلْجانُّ“ (the jinn) were on the earth, and they caused corruption and shed blood, so Allah sent His angels, who expelled them from the earth. It is said that these angels became the inhabitants of the earth after the jinn, and they said: "O Lord, will You place on it one who will cause corruption on it and shed blood, while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You?" The interpretation of this inquiry of theirs is that it was by way of seeking knowledge and seeking the wisdom, not by way of objection; as though they said: "O Allah, if this is our supposition, then make known to us the true aspect of it."
Some people said the meaning in it is other than this: namely that Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, informed the angels that He was placing a vicegerent on the earth and that among the creation would be a group that sheds blood, a group of the children of Adam, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, gave the angels leave to ask Him about that. His informing them of this was an increase in establishing in their souls that He knows the unseen. So it is as though they said: "Will You create on it a people who shed blood and disobey You? Rather, when they know that You created them, they ought to glorify You with Your praise as we glorify, and sanctify as we sanctify." They did not say this except after He had given them leave; it is not permissible to attribute to the angels that they say something they merely conjecture, because Allah the Exalted has described them as doing what they are commanded.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنِّي أعْلَمُ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, that is: I test the one whom you suppose will obey, and the test guides him. The alif [of interrogation] here is only for affirming the "placing" in this saying, as Jarīr said:
ألَسْتُمْ خَيْرَ مَن رَكِبَ المَطايا ∗∗∗ وأنْدى العالَمِينَ بُطُونَ راحِ
(Are you not the best of those who ride mounts, and the most generous of all people in the palms of the hands?)
The meaning of ”يَسْفِكُ“ is: pours out. One says ”سَفَكَ الشَّيْءَ“ when he poured it out. The meaning of ”نُسَبِّحُ بِحَمْدِكَ“ is: we declare You free of evil. Everyone who does a deed by which he intends Allah has made tasbīḥ; one says ”فَرَغْتُ مِن تَسْبِيحِي“, that is: from my prayer. Sībawayh and other grammarians said that the meaning of ”سُبْحانَ اللَّهِ“ is: Allah's being free of evil and His being declared transcendent above evil. Al-Aʿshā said:
؎أقُولُ لَمّا جاءَنِي فَخْرُهُ ∗∗∗ سُبْحانَ مِن عَلْقَمَةَ الفاخِرِ
(I say, when his boasting reached me: how far removed [I am] from ʿAlqama the boaster!)
The meaning is: dissociation from him and from his boasting.
The meaning of ”نُقَدِّسُ لَكَ“ is: we purify ourselves for You; and likewise whoever obeys You, we sanctify him, that is, we purify him. From this is ”بَيْتُ المَقْدِسِ“, that is: the purified house, or the place in which one is purified of sins.

zajjaj:31-31.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَعَلَّمَ آدَمَ الأسْماءَ كُلَّها ثُمَّ عَرَضَهم عَلى المَلائِكَةِ﴾. The people of the language said: He taught Adam the names of the genera, and He presented the bearers of the names – people and others – to the angels. For this reason He said ”ثُمَّ عَرَضَهم“ (with the masculine plural pronoun), because among them were those endowed with reason, and for every group of rational beings one says ”هم“. ”هم“ is said of people, it is said of angels, it is said of the jinn, it is said of al-jānn, and it is said of the devils; so every discerning being in pronominal reference is ”هم“. This is the doctrine of the people of the language.
Some of the people of speculative reasoning have said that the benefit in bringing the names – more far-reaching than that – is the benefit of the names of the meanings (qualities) of each kind of these. «[Translator's note: the Arabic sentence here is awkwardly constructed; it is rendered as closely as possible.]» For the argument in this is that when horses were presented and it was asked "What is the name of these?", it would be said "Horses"; so whatever name were placed on these would tell about them. The benefit is rather that you tell the name of every meaning in every genus, so it is said: "This is suited to such-and-such." This is the clear benefit; for it is agreed that you may call the riding-beast and the camel by whatever name you wish, while the meaning in it, which is its special property, is a single meaning, even if the names for it differ. And Allah knows best.

zajjaj:2-2.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ذَلِكَ الكِتابُ لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ هُدًى لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾: al-Akhfash and Abū ʿUbayda held that its meaning is "هَذا الكِتابُ" (this Book). The poet said:
أقُولُ لَهُ والرُّمْحُ يَأْطُرُ مَتْنُهُ ∗∗∗ تَأمَّلْ خُفافًا إنَّنِي أنا ذَلِكا
(I say to him, while the spear bends its shaft: "Look closely at Khufāf — I am that one.")
He said: the meaning is "إنَّنِي أنا هَذا" (I am this one). Other grammarians said: its meaning is "The Qur'an is that Book which they were promised on the tongue of Moses and Jesus, may Allah bless them both and grant them peace." The proof of this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَكانُوا مِن قَبْلُ يَسْتَفْتِحُونَ عَلى الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا فَلَمّا جاءَهم ما عَرَفُوا كَفَرُوا بِهِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 89], and likewise His saying: ﴿الَّذِينَ آتَيْناهُمُ الكِتابَ يَعْرِفُونَهُ كَما يَعْرِفُونَ أبْناءَهم وإنَّ فَرِيقًا مِنهم لَيَكْتُمُونَ الحَقَّ وهم يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 146]. So the meaning is: "هَذا ذَلِكَ الكِتابُ" (this is that Book). It is also possible that His saying is "الم ذَلِكَ الكِتابُ", and "ذَلِكَ" is said of a thing that has already been mentioned: if you wish you say "هَذا" of it, and if you wish you say "ذَلِكَ" of it, as in your saying: "أنْفَقْتُ ثَلاثَةً وثَلاثَةً، فَذَلِكَ سِتَّةٌ" (I spent three and three, so that is six), and if you wish you say "هَذا سِتَّةٌ" (this is six); or as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, in the story of Pharaoh: ﴿فَحَشَرَ فَنادى﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 23] ﴿فَقالَ أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 24] ﴿فَأخَذَهُ اللَّهُ نَكالَ الآخِرَةِ والأُولى﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 25], after which He said: ﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَعِبْرَةً لِمَن يَخْشى﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 26]; and He said in another place: ﴿وَلَقَدْ كَتَبْنا في الزَّبُورِ مِن بَعْدِ الذِّكْرِ أنَّ الأرْضَ يَرِثُها عِبادِيَ الصّالِحُونَ﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 105], then He said: ﴿إنَّ في هَذا لَبَلاغًا لِقَوْمٍ عابِدِينَ﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 106]. And He said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿المر تِلْكَ آياتُ الكِتابِ والَّذِي أُنْـزِلَ إلَيْكَ مِن رَبِّكَ الحَقُّ﴾ [al-Raʿd: 1]. So He said ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ «[Translator's note: so in the text; the verse just cited has تِلْكَ.]», and it is possible that the meaning is: "تِلْكَ عَلاماتُ الكِتابِ" (those are the signs of the Book) — i.e. the Qur'an — spoken in the letters of the Arabs which we understand, as we described in the explanation of the letters of the alphabet.

The position of "ذَلِكَ" is nominative, because it is the khabar (predicate) of a mubtadaʾ (subject), according to the view of whoever said: "هَذا القُرْآنُ ذَلِكَ الكِتابُ" (this Qur'an is that Book). "اَلْكِتابُ" is nominative; the grammarians call it ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition), as in your saying: "هَذا الرَّجُلُ أخُوكَ" (this man is your brother), where الرَّجُلُ is the ʿaṭf bayān, i.e. it makes clear who it is you pointed at. The noun in "ذَلِكَ" is "ذا"; the kāf was added for address and has no share in inflection. Sībawayh said: if it had a share in inflection, you would say "ذاكَ نَفْسِهِ زَيْدٌ", and this is wrong; only "هَذاكَ نَفْسُهُ زَيْدٌ" is permissible. And thus "ذانِكَ" testifies that the kāf has no grammatical position: if it had a position, it would be genitive by annexation, and the nūn does not enter together with annexation. The lām is added to "ذَلِكَ" for emphasis — I mean emphasis of the noun — because when it is added, "ها" is dropped along with it. You say "ذَلِكَ الحَقُّ", "ذاكَ الحَقُّ" and "ها ذاكَ الحَقُّ", but "هَذَلِكَ الحَقُّ" is ugly, because the lām has already emphasised the meaning of pointing. The lām was given kasra because of the meeting of two vowelless letters — I mean the alif of "ذا" and the lām after it. It ought to have been vowelless, but it was given kasra for the reason we stated. Likewise the position of "ذَلِكَ" must be nominative for whoever makes "ذَلِكَ" the khabar of "الم".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾: its meaning is: there is no doubt in it. You say "رابَنِي فُلانٌ" when you know there is cause for suspicion (rība) in someone, and "أرابَنِي" when he makes me imagine there is cause for suspicion. The poet said:
أخُوكَ الَّذِي إنْ رِبْتَهُ قالَ إنَّما ∗∗∗ أُرِبْتُ وإنْ عاتَبْتَهُ لانَ جانِبُهْ
(Your brother is the one who, if you suspect him, says: "I was only made to seem suspect", and if you reproach him, he becomes gentle.)
The position of "لا رَيْبَ" is accusative. Sībawayh said: "لا" governs what follows it and puts it in the accusative; its putting what follows it in the accusative is like "إنَّ" putting what follows it in the accusative, except that it puts it in the accusative without nunation. He held that it, together with what follows it, is like a single thing, as though it were the answer to someone's saying: "هَلْ مِن رَجُلٍ في الدّارِ؟" (Is there any man in the house?), where "مِن" is not separable from "رَجُلٍ".

If someone says: "Why do you reject its being the answer to 'هَلْ رَجُلَ في الدّارِ؟'?", it is replied: the meaning of "لا رَجُلَ في الدّارِ" is universal negation: when you say "لا رَجُلَ في الدّارِ" (there is no man at all in the house), it is not possible that there be in the house a man or more than one man. Likewise "هَلْ مِن رَجُلٍ في الدّارِ؟" is a question about one or more than one. But when you say "هَلْ رَجُلٌ في الدّارِ؟" or "لا رَجُلٌ في الدّارِ", it is possible that there are two men in the house, because you have only stated that there is not one in it, so it is possible that there are more. When you say "لا رَجُلَ في الدّارِ", it is a general negation; and likewise "لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ".

In His saying ﴿فِيهِ﴾ there are four possibilities, of which the reading follows only one, and one should not go beyond it to another: namely "فِيهِ هُدًى", with kasra on the hāʾ. In ordinary speech — and in recitation, had it been read so — "فِيهُو هُدًى", with the wāw retained, and "فِيهِي هُدًى", with the yāʾ retained, are permissible. We have explained these possibilities in the i'rab of "al-Ḥamd".

As for the reading "فِيهْ هُدًى", with the hāʾ assimilated (idghām) into the hāʾ, it is heavy in pronunciation.
