It is permissible by analogy, because the two letters are of one kind, except that it is heavy in pronunciation, because the guttural letters are not basic to assimilation, and the two letters belong to two words. Al-Akhfash reported that it is a reading.

The position of "هُدًى" is accusative, and its meaning is clarification (bayān). Its accusative has two explanations. One of them is that it is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from your saying: "اَلْقُرْآنُ ذَلِكَ الكِتابُ هُدًى" (the Qur'an is that Book, as guidance). It is also possible that it is accusative through your saying "لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ" — in the state of its guiding — so that it is a ḥāl, from your saying: "لا شَكَّ فِيهِ هادِيًا" (there is no doubt in it, as a guide). It is possible that its position is nominative, from several aspects. One of them is that it is a khabar after a khabar, as though He said: "هَذا ذَلِكَ الكِتابُ هُدًى", i.e. it combines being the Book they were promised and being guidance; as you say: "هَذا حُلْوٌ حامِضٌ" (this is sweet and sour), meaning that it combines the two tastes. It is possible that its nominative is through an implied "هو", as though, when the speech was complete and it was said "الم ذَلِكَ الكِتابُ لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ", it was then said: "هو هُدًى" (it is guidance). It is also possible that its nominative is on your saying "ذَلِكَ الكِتابُ لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ", as though you said "ذَلِكَ الكِتابُ حَقًّا" (that is the Book, truly), because "لا شَكَّ فِيهِ" means "it is true"; and then He said after that: "فِيهِ هُدًى لِلْمُتَّقِينَ" (in it is guidance for the God-fearing).

zajjaj:70-70.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ البَقَرَ تَشابَهَ عَلَيْنا﴾: the reading of this goes several ways. The best and most widespread is «تَشابَهَ عَلَيْنا» with fatḥa on the hāʾ and without doubling. Also permissible are «تَشّابَهُ عَلَيْنا» and «يَشّابَهُ عَلَيْنا», with tāʾ and with yāʾ. It has also been read «إنَّ الباقِرَ يَشّابَهُ عَلَيْنا». The Arabs say, for the collective of «البَقَر» (cattle) and «الجِمال» (camels): «الباقِر» and «الجامِل», making it a generic noun (ism li-l-jins). Ṭarafa ibn al-ʿAbd said:
وَجامِلٍ خَوَّعَ مِن نِيبِهِ ∗∗∗ زَجْرُ المُعَلّى أُصُلًا والسَّفِيحْ
(And many a herd of camels whose old she-camels were thinned by the shouts over the winning arrow (al-muʿallā) and the blank arrow (al-safīḥ) at eventide.)
It is also transmitted as «مِنِّي بِهِ», which is the more common transmission, but it is nothing. Another poet said:
ما لِي رَأيْتُكَ بَعْدَ عَهْدِكَ مُوحِشًا ∗∗∗ خَلَقًا كَحَوْضِ الباقِرِ المُتَهَدِّمِ
(Why do I see you, after the time I knew you, desolate and worn, like the crumbling trough of the cattle?)
Whatever is like «بَقَرَة» / «بَقَر», «نَخْلَة» / «نَخْل» and «سَحابَة» / «سَحاب», the Arabs treat as masculine and as feminine, saying «هَذا بَقَرٌ» and «هَذِهِ بَقَرٌ», «هَذا نَخْلٌ» and «هَذِهِ نَخْلٌ». Whoever makes it masculine does so because the collective word can express its genus, so you say "this is a collection (jamʿ)"; and the word can express a party and a portion, so you say "this is a group (jamāʿa)" and "this is a party (firqa)". Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿ألَمْ تَرَ أنَّ اللَّهَ يُزْجِي سَحابًا ثُمَّ يُؤَلِّفُ بَيْنَهُ﴾ [al-Nūr: 43], making it masculine, while its singular is «سَحابَة»; and He said: ﴿والنَّخْلَ باسِقاتٍ﴾ [Qāf: 10], using the plural according to the meaning of "a group", while its form is singular. So whoever reads «إنَّ البَقَرَ تَشّابَهَ عَلَيْنا» [Translator's note: the source prints «البَقْرَ» with sukūn on the qāf, presumably a misprint], its meaning is: the group of cattle resemble one another to us; the tāʾ was assimilated into the shīn because the point of articulation of the tāʾ is near that of the shīn. Whoever reads «تَشّابَهُ عَلَيْنا» means «تَتَشابَهُ», and dropped the second tāʾ because two tāʾs came together, as «لَعَلَّكم تَذَكَّرُونَ» has been read [Translator's note: the stated explanation (dropping a tāʾ) fits «تَشابَهُ» without doubling; the doubled form «تَشّابَهُ» would rather reflect assimilation. Translated as written]. And whoever reads «يَشّابَهُ عَلَيْنا» with yāʾ also means the genus of cattle; the original is «يَتَشابَهُ عَلَيْنا», and the tāʾ was assimilated into the shīn.

zajjaj:71-71.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لا ذَلُولٌ تُثِيرُ الأرْضَ ولا تَسْقِي الحَرْثَ﴾: its meaning is: she is not broken in (dhalūl), nor ploughing the earth. His saying «وَلا تَسْقِي الحَرْثَ»: one says «سَقَيْتُهُ» when you hand someone a drink and he drinks, and «أسْقَيْتُهُ» means you provided him with irrigation (water supply); so «وَلا تُسْقِي» with ḍamma would be sound here.

His saying: ﴿لا شِيَةَ فِيها﴾, that is: there is no colour in her differing from her colour. «الوَشْي» in the language is the mixing of one colour with another, and likewise in speech. One says «وَشَّيْتُ الثَّوْبَ، أشِيهِ، شِيَةً، ووَشْيًا» [Translator's note: so in the source with doubled shīn; the paradigm given («أشِيهِ») is that of «وَشَيْتُ»], like your saying «وَدَيْتُ فُلانًا، أدِيهِ، دِيَةً» (I paid the blood-money for so-and-so). «لا شِيَةَ فِيها» is accusative by negation (the lā of generic negation). Were it read «لا شِيَةٌ فِيها» it would be permissible, but the reading is with the accusative.

His saying: ﴿الآنَ جِئْتَ بِالحَقِّ﴾: there are four ways (of pronouncing it), some of which al-Akhfash reported. The best is «قالُوا الآنَ», with the lām quiescent and the wāw dropped from pronunciation. Al-Akhfash claimed that it is permissible to cut off the connecting alif (alif al-waṣl) here, saying «قالُوا ألْآنَ جِئْتَ بِالحَقِّ». This is a transmitted report, but it has no justification in analogy (qiyās), nor is it permissible in my view. But there are two ways besides these two, and both are good in Arabic: it is permissible to say «قالُوا لانَ», casting off the hamza, giving the lām of «الآن» a fatḥa, and leaving the wāw dropped because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, the fatḥa of the lām not being taken into account; and it is permissible to say «قالُوا لانَ جِيتَ بِالحَقِّ», but I know of no one who read it so, so let no one recite with a reading that has not been recited, even if it is established in Arabic. Those who pronounced the wāw did so because of the vowelling of the lām: they had dropped it because of its quiescence, so when it was vowelled they restored it. The better in Arabic is dropping it, because it has been read so. You say «الأحْمَرُ», and they cast off the hamza and say «الَحْمَرُ», giving the lām a fatḥa while keeping the connecting alif, because the lām is regarded as quiescent; and some say «لَحْمَرُ», not keeping the connecting alif, meaning «الأحْمَرُ». As for the accusative-looking ending of «الآنَ», it is a vowel for the meeting of two quiescent letters. Do you not see that you say «أنا الآنَ أُكْرِمُكَ» ("I now honour you") and «مِنَ الآنَ فَعَلْتُ كَذا وكَذا» ("from now I did such-and-such")? It was originally indeclinable (mabnī) and was vowelled for the meeting of two quiescent letters. «الآنَ» is indeclinable even though it has the alif and lām, because the alif and lām entered it with a reference not previously established: you say "the boy (al-ghulām) did such-and-such" only when you and your addressee are both familiar with him. These alif and lām stand in for the meaning of pointing; the meaning is: you do this up to this time. So «الآنَ» is not inflected, just as «هَذا» is not inflected.

zajjaj:72-72.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ قَتَلْتُمْ نَفْسًا فادّارَأْتُمْ فِيها﴾: its meaning is «فَتَدارَأْتُمْ فِيها», that is, you pushed it off onto one another, i.e. some of you cast it upon others. One says «دَرَأْتُ فُلانًا» when you push him off, «دارَيْتُهُ» when you treat him gently, and «دَرَّيْتُهُ» when you deceive him. But the tāʾ was assimilated into the dāl because they are of one point of articulation; when it was assimilated it became quiescent, so a connecting alif was brought for it, and you say «ادّارَأ القَوْمُ», that is, the people pushed against one another.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿مُخْرِجٌ ما كُنْتُمْ تَكْتُمُونَ﴾: the better in «مُخْرِجٌ» is the tanwīn (nunation), because it refers only to what is future, or to the present. It is permissible to drop the tanwīn for lightness, so that one would read «مُخْرِجُ ما كُنْتُمْ تَكْتُمُونَ» — if it has been read so; otherwise the Quran is not to be departed from, as we have explained.

zajjaj:74-74.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ثُمَّ قَسَتْ قُلُوبُكم مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾: the interpretation of «قَسَتْ» in the language is: became coarse, dry and hard. So the interpretation of hardness (qasw) in the heart is the departure of softness, mercy, humility and submissiveness from it.

The meaning of «مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ» is: after the bringing to life of the dead man for you by one of the parts of the cow. This is a mighty sign; whoever witnessed it — and thereby witnessed of His power, Mighty and Majestic is He, what removes every doubt — ought to have had his heart soften and submit. And «مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ» may mean: after the bringing to life of the dead man and the signs that preceded it, such as the transformation into apes and swine, the raising of the mountain above them, and the gushing of water from a rock they carried with them. This is permissible — «ذَلِكَ» while this group is being addressed, without saying «ذَلِكم», though had He said «ذَلِكم» it would have been good — it is permissible to say to a group both «بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ» and «بَعْدَ ذَلِكم» because a group can be rendered by a word such as «الجَمِيع» (the whole) or «الفَرِيق» (the party), so the address is in a singular word with the meaning of "a group".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَهِيَ كالحِجارَةِ أوْ أشَدُّ قَسْوَةً﴾ — and «أوْ أشَدَّ قَسْوَةً» has also been transmitted. We have explained the meaning of likening hardness to stones. «أوْ» enters here not for the meaning of doubt; rather it is the «أوْ» that comes for permission (ibāḥa). You say: "Those from whom knowledge should be taken: al-Ḥasan or Ibn Sīrīn", and you are not in doubt; the meaning here is rather: these two are worthy of having knowledge taken from them; if you take it from al-Ḥasan you are right, if you take it from Ibn Sīrīn you are right, and if you take it from both together you are right. So the interpretation is: "Know that the hearts of these people — if you liken their hardness to stones you are right, or to what is harder, you are right". «أوْ» here cannot properly be in the sense of «و» (and). Likewise His saying: «مَثَلُهم كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي اسْتَوْقَدَ نارًا ... أوْ كَصَيِّبٍ», that is: "If you compare them to the one who kindled a fire, that is their likeness; and if you compare them to the rainstorm, it is a likeness for them". We have explained it in its place sufficiently and satisfactorily, if Allah wills. Whoever reads «أشَدُّ قَسْوَةً» makes «أشَدُّ» nominative by an implied «هي», as though He said: "or it is harder". Whoever makes it accusative, «أوْ أشَدَّ قَسْوَةً», takes it as originally genitive, in the sense of the kāf (of comparison); but «أشَدّ», being of the pattern «أفْعَل», is a diptote, because it has the form of a verb and is an adjective, so it took a fatḥa while being in the position of the genitive. It is permissible in His saying, Exalted is He, «فَهي كالحِجارَةِ» to say «فَهْيَ كالحِجارَةِ» with the hāʾ quiescent, because the fāʾ together with «هي» has made the word like «فَخِذ», so the kasra is dropped as heavy. One of the grammarians related that it is permissible in «هي» to make the yāʾ of «هي» quiescent, but I know of no one who read it so; in my view it is not permissible to make it quiescent, nor to make the wāw in «هو» quiescent: «هُوْ رَبُّكم» is not permissible. Some grammarians have related the quiescence, but it is poor, because every pronoun, when standing alone, has fatḥa as its vowel, as in «أنا رَبُّكم»; and just as the nūn of «أنا» is not made quiescent, this wāw is not made quiescent.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإنَّ مِنَ الحِجارَةِ لَما يَتَفَجَّرُ مِنهُ الأنْهارُ﴾: He, Mighty and Majestic is He, made clear how their hearts were: that they were harder and firmer than stones. He made known that from stones rivers gush forth, and of them is that which splits so that water comes out of it — meaning the springs that come out of stones but are not rivers — and of them is that which falls down for fear of Allah. They said: what falls down for fear of Allah is like the mountain to which Allah manifested Himself when He spoke to Moses, peace be upon him. Some said: it is the trace of craftsmanship which shows that they are created. This is an error, because there is none of them in which the trace of craftsmanship is not evident — it is in all of them. Rather, discernment (tamyīz) has been placed in the one of them that falls down, as He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿لَوْ أنْـزَلْنا هَذا القُرْآنَ عَلى جَبَلٍ لَرَأيْتَهُ خاشِعًا مُتَصَدِّعًا مِن خَشْيَةِ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 21], and as He said: ﴿ألَمْ تَرَ أنَّ اللَّهَ يَسْجُدُ لَهُ مَن في السَّماواتِ﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 18], then said: ﴿والنُّجُومُ والجِبالُ﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 18]. So He made known that this is a discernment that Allah willed from them; and had craftsmanship been meant by that, He would not have said: ﴿وَكَثِيرٌ مِنَ النّاسِ وكَثِيرٌ حَقَّ عَلَيْهِ العَذابُ﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 18], because the trace of craftsmanship includes the believer and others.

zajjaj:75-75.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أفَتَطْمَعُونَ أنْ يُؤْمِنُوا لَكُمْ﴾: this alif is an alif of enquiry (istikhbār), and in many places it functions as disapproval and prohibition when there is no negation with it; it is as though He made them despair of hoping for the faith of this party of the Jews. When there is a negation at the beginning of the speech, the disapproval of the negation is affirmation, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ألَمْ يَأْتِكم نَذِيرٌ﴾ [al-Mulk: 8] ﴿قالُوا بَلى﴾ [al-Mulk: 9]. So the answer to «أفَتَطْمَعُونَ» is "No", as we have described.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقَدْ كانَ فَرِيقٌ مِنهم يَسْمَعُونَ كَلامَ اللَّهِ ثُمَّ يُحَرِّفُونَهُ مِن بَعْدِ ما عَقَلُوهُ﴾: it is related in the tafsīr that they heard the speech of Allah to Moses, peace be upon him, and distorted it. So it was said of these whom the Prophet ﷺ witnessed: they disbelieved and distorted, so they have a precedent in their disbelief.

zajjaj:76-76.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذا لَقُوا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قالُوا آمَنّا وإذا خَلا بَعْضُهم إلى بَعْضٍ قالُوا أتُحَدِّثُونَهم بِما فَتَحَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾: the meaning is: do you inform them that the mention of the Prophet ﷺ and his description are found in your Book, so that they may argue against you with it before your Lord? That is, so that they have the argument against you in their believing in the Prophet ﷺ, since you acknowledge him, telling of the truth of his matter from your Book; this makes clear His argument against you before Allah.

﴿أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾, that is: do you not understand Allah's argument against you in this?

zajjaj:34-34.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ قُلْنا لِلْمَلائِكَةِ اسْجُدُوا لآدَمَ﴾. The Readers read ”لِلْمَلائِكَةِ اسْجُدُوا“ with kasra, while Abū Jaʿfar al-Madanī alone read ”لِلْمَلائِكَةُ اسْجُدُوا“ with ḍamma. Abū Jaʿfar is among the eminent people of Medina and the reliable authorities in reading, except that he erred in this word, because al-malāʾika is in the position of the genitive, and it is not permissible for the genitive to be put in the nominative. Rather, he likened the [vowel of the] tāʾ of the feminine to the kasra [sic] of the alif of connection (alif al-waṣl), because when you begin [with the verb] you say ”اُسْجُدُوا“. «[Translator's note: so in the text; the vowel of the initial hamza in ”اُسْجُدُوا“ is a ḍamma, as the author himself explains below, and it is this ḍamma that Abū Jaʿfar is said to have carried over.]» The Qurʾān ought not to be read on the basis of a fancied notion that is not correct.
”إذْ“ is in the position of the accusative, conjoined to the ”إذْ“ before it. ”اَلْمَلائِكَةُ“: their singular is ”مَلَكٌ“, whose origin is ”مَلْأكٌ“. Sībawayh recited:
؎فَلَسْتَ لِإنْسِيٍّ ولَكِنْ لِمَلْأكٍ ∗∗∗ تَنَزَّلَ مِن جَوِّ السَّماءِ يَصُوبُ
(You are not [born] of a human, but of an angel who came down from the vault of the sky, descending.)
Its meaning is: a bearer of a message. One says ”مَأْلُكَةٌ“ and ”مَأْلَكَةٌ“ (a message), and ”مَأْلُكٌ“ is the plural of ”مَأْلُكَةٌ“. The poet said:
؎أبْلِغِ النُّعْمانَ عَنِّي مَأْلُكًا ∗∗∗ أنَّهُ قَدْ طالَ حَبْسِي وانْتِظارْ
(Convey to al-Nuʿmān a message from me: that my detention and my waiting have grown long.)
His saying ”لِآدَمَ“: ”آدَمَ“ is in the position of the genitive, except that it is a diptote (lā yanṣarif), because it is on the pattern ”أفْعَلَ“. The people of the language say that its derivation is from ”أدِيمُ الأرْضِ“ (the surface of the earth), because he was created from dust; likewise ”اَلْأُدْمَةُ“ (brownness) is only likened to the colour of dust.
If you say ”مَرَرْتُ بِآدَمَ، وآدَمَ آخَرَ“ ("I passed by Adam and another Adam"): the grammarians differ concerning an ”أفْعَلَ“ that is used as a name while its origin is an adjective. Sībawayh, al-Khalīl and those who hold their view say that it is declinable (yanṣarif) when indefinite, because when you make it indefinite you return it to a state in which it was declinable. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash said: when you name a man with it you have taken it out of the category of the adjective, so when you make it indefinite you must make it declinable, and say: ”مَرَرْتُ بِآدَمٍ، وآدَمٍ آخَرَ“. «[Translator's note: as written, the positions attributed to the two sides appear to be reversed: Sībawayh and al-Khalīl are normally reported to keep such a name diptote when made indefinite, and al-Akhfash to make it declinable; the text is translated as it stands.]»
The meaning of the prostration to Adam is the worship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, not the worship of Adam, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, created rational beings only for His worship.
When you begin [with the verb] you say ”اُسْجُدُوا“ and give the alif a ḍamma. The alif has no share in vowelling – I mean this hamza with which one begins; it was only brought in for the quiescent letter after it, because one does not begin with a quiescent letter. Its due was the kasra, because a quiescent letter follows it and it is itself notionally quiescent, so it should take kasra for the meeting of two quiescent letters; but it was given ḍamma because a ḍamma after a kasra is felt to be heavy. The same applies to every verb whose third letter has ḍamma in the imperfect, as in His saying: ﴿انْظُرْ كَيْفَ يَفْتَرُونَ عَلى اللَّهِ الكَذِبَ﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 50], and like ﴿اقْتُلُوا يُوسُفَ﴾ [Yūsuf: 9], because they are from ”نَظَرَ، يَنْظُرُ“ and ”قَتَلَ، يَقْتُلُ“. The ḍamma after the kasra was disliked only because it does not occur in the speech of the Arabs after it, owing to its heaviness; so there is nothing in the language like ”فِعُلَ“, nor like ”إفْعُلْ“.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَسَجَدُوا إلا إبْلِيسَ أبى﴾. Some people said that Iblīs was one of the angels and so he was excepted from them in the prostration. Some of the people of the language said that Iblīs was not one of the angels, and the proof of that is His saying: ﴿إلا إبْلِيسَ كانَ مِنَ الجِنِّ﴾ [al-Kahf: 50]. It was said to these: then how was it permissible for him to be excepted from them? They said: the angels and he were [all] commanded to prostrate. They said: our proof that he was commanded along with them is His saying ﴿إلا إبْلِيسَ أبى﴾, for he would not have refused unless he had been commanded. This view is the one we prefer, because Iblīs was of the jinn, as He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said. The other view is not impossible: [then] "he was of the jinn" would mean he was astray, just as the jinn were astray, and so he was counted among them, as He said in his story: ﴿وَكانَ مِنَ الكافِرِينَ﴾; its interpretation is that he did their deeds and so became part of them, as He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿المُنافِقُونَ والمُنافِقاتُ بَعْضُهم مِن بَعْضٍ﴾ [al-Tawba: 67].
In this verse there is an indication establishing the messengership of the Prophet ﷺ, as in the verse before it and the one following it, because it is a report of what was not part of the knowledge of the Arabs and is known only to the People of the Book or a prophet to whom it was revealed.
”إبْلِيسُ“ is not declined (as a triptote) because it is a foreign noun: foreignness and definiteness are combined in it, and so it is barred from full declension (a diptote).

zajjaj:35-35.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَكُلا مِنها رَغَدًا حَيْثُ شِئْتُما﴾. ”اَلرَّغَدُ“ is the abundant that does not trouble you.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تَقْرَبا هَذِهِ الشَّجَرَةَ فَتَكُونا مِنَ الظّالِمِينَ﴾, that is: if you do the deeds of the wrongdoers you become of them. The meaning of ”لا تَقْرَبا“ here is: do not eat; the proof of this is His saying ﴿وَكُلا مِنها رَغَدًا حَيْثُ شِئْتُما ولا تَقْرَبا هَذِهِ الشَّجَرَةَ﴾, that is: do not approach it in eating. ”وَلا تَقْرَبا“ is in the jussive through the prohibition.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَتَكُونا مِنَ الظّالِمِينَ﴾ is accusative, because the answer to a prohibition with the fāʾ is accusative; its accusative, according to Sībawayh and al-Khalīl, is by a suppressed ”أنْ“. The meaning is: let there be no approaching of this tree on your part, and [thus] a being among the wrongdoers. It is also possible that ”فَتَكُونا“ is jussive by conjunction with His saying: ”وَلا تَقْرَبا، فَتَكُونا“.

zajjaj:36-36.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَأزَلَّهُما الشَّيْطانُ عَنْها﴾. Its meaning is that the two of them were made to slip through Satan's leading them astray, so it became as though he made them slip; as you say to someone who does something that becomes a means to making you slip from a fine state to another: ”أنْتَ أزْلَلْتَنِي عَنْ هَذا“ ("you made me slip from this"), that is: my accepting from you made me slip, so you became the one who removed me.
The meaning of ”اَلشَّيْطانُ“ in the language is: the one, of jinn and humans, who is extreme in disbelief and has gone far in it. ”اَلشَّطَنُ“ in the language of the Arabs is the rope, and ”اَلْأرْضُ الشَّطُونُ“ is the distant land; al-shayṭān is ”فَيْعالٌ“ from this.
It has been read: ”فَأزالَهُما الشَّيْطانُ“ ("Satan removed them"), from ”زُلْتُ“ and ”أزالَنِي غَيْرِي“; and ”أزَلَّهُما“ is from ”زَلَلْتُ“ and ”أزَلَّنِي غَيْرِي“. For ”زَلَلْتُ“ here there are two aspects: ”فَأزَلَّهُما الشَّيْطانُ“ may mean he caused them to incur the slip and the sin, and ”فَأزَلَّهُما“ may mean he moved them aside. Both readings are correct and good.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقُلْنا اهْبِطُوا بَعْضُكم لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ﴾. Allah combined for the Prophet ﷺ the story of their descent, although Iblīs had been sent down first; the proof of that is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فاخْرُجْ مِنها فَإنَّكَ رَجِيمٌ﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 34]; Adam and Eve were sent down afterwards. So He combined the report for the Prophet ﷺ because they were together in the descent, even if their times in it were separate.
His saying ﴿بَعْضُكم لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ﴾: Iblīs is an enemy of the believers among Adam's offspring, and his enmity towards them is disbelief; and the believers are enemies of Iblīs, and their enmity towards him is faith.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَكم في الأرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ﴾, that is: a dwelling and a settling.
His saying ﴿إلى حِينٍ﴾: some people said the meaning of al-ḥīn here is "until the Day of Resurrection"; others said "until the ending of the terms", that is, each one settles until the end of his term. ”اَلْحِينُ“ and ”اَلزَّمانُ“ are, in the language, of one standing. Some people make al-ḥīn, in a place other than this, six months; their proof is His saying: ﴿تُؤْتِي أُكُلَها كُلَّ حِينٍ بِإذْنِ رَبِّها﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 25]. But "every ḥīn" there was only made to stand for a known period. ”اَلْحِينُ“ is suitable for all times, except that in usage it is more common for long ones; one says ”ما رَأيْتُكَ مُنْذُ حِينٍ“ ("I have not seen you for a ḥīn"), meaning: for a long time. The basic sense is as we have told.

zajjaj:37-37.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَتَلَقّى آدَمُ مِن رَبِّهِ كَلِماتٍ فَتابَ عَلَيْهِ﴾. The words – and Allah knows best – are the confession of Adam, peace be upon him, and Eve of the sin, because they said: ”رَبَّنا ظَلَمْنا أنْفُسَنا وإنْ لَمْ تَغْفِرْ لَنا وتَرْحَمْنا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الخاسِرِينَ“ ("Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we shall surely be among the losers"). They confessed their sin and repented. In this verse there is an admonition for their offspring and a teaching of how the way to free oneself from sins is, and that nothing avails except confession and repentance, because failing to acknowledge what Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, has forbidden is forbidden and is disbelief in Allah; so confession together with repentance is indispensable. This meaning ought to be understood, for it is among the greatest benefits that are needed.
Ibn Kathīr read: ”فَتَلَقّى آدَمَ مِن رَبِّهِ كَلِماتٌ“ (with Adam in the accusative and "words" as the agent). The preferred reading is that on which there is consensus, and it is stronger in Arabic, because Adam learnt these words, so it was said: "he received these words". The Arabs say ”تَلَقَّيْتُ هَذا مِن فُلانٍ“ ("I received this from so-and-so"), the meaning being: my understanding of his saying from his utterance.

zajjaj:3-3.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾: its meaning is: they believe as true (yuṣaddiqūn). Everyone who believes (muʾmin) in something affirms it as true. When you mention a muʾmin without saying "he is a believer in such-and-such", it is (a usage) that is proper only with respect to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He «[Translator's note: i.e. the unqualified term "believer" is understood as belief in Allah.]». The position of "اَلَّذِينَ" is genitive, following "اَلْمُتَّقِينَ". It is also possible that their position «[Translator's note: the text has the dual "مَوْضِعُهُما", "their (two) position".]» is nominative, as praise (madḥ), as though, when it was said "هُدًى لِلْمُتَّقِينَ" (guidance for the God-fearing), it was asked "مَن هُمْ؟" (Who are they?), and it was said: "اَلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالغَيْبِ" (those who believe in the unseen). It is also possible that the position of "اَلَّذِينَ" is accusative, likewise as praise, as though it were said: "أذْكُرُ الَّذِينَ" (I mention those who…). In "اَلَّذِينَ" inflection does not appear: you say — in the accusative, nominative and genitive — "أتانِي الَّذِينَ في الدّارِ" (those in the house came to me), "رَأيْتُ الَّذِينَ في الدّارِ" (I saw those in the house) and "مَرَرْتُ بِالَّذِينَ في الدّارِ" (I passed by those in the house); and likewise "اَلَّذِي في الدّارِ". It was denied inflection only because inflection occurs at the end of nouns, and "اَلَّذِي" and "اَلَّذِينَ" are vague (mubham) and are only complete with their ṣila (relative clause); therefore they were denied inflection. The origin of "اَلَّذِي" is "لَذٍ", on the pattern of "عَمٍ" — know this. So said al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, al-Akhfash and all whose knowledge is trusted.

If someone says: "Why then do you say 'أتانِي اللَّذانِ في الدّارِ' (the two who are in the house came to me) and 'رَأيْتُ اللَّذَيْنِ في الدّارِ' (I saw the two who are in the house), inflecting in the dual everything that is not inflected (in the singular), such as 'هَذانِ' and 'هَذَيْنِ', while you do not inflect 'هَذا' or 'هَؤُلاءِ'?", the answer to that is: everything that is not inflected in the singular resembles the particle that comes for a meaning (ḥarf maʿnā); when you put it in the dual, its resemblance to the particle that comes for a meaning is cancelled, because particles of meaning are not put in the dual.

If someone says: "Why then did you deny it inflection in the plural?", I say: because a plural that is not formed on the pattern of the dual is like the singular. Do you not see that you said, for the plural of this, "هَؤُلاءِ يا فَتى", making it a single noun for the plural? Likewise your saying "اَلَّذِينَ" is only a noun for the plural, just as your saying "سِنِينُ يا فَتى" is a noun for the plural; so you made it indeclinable as you made the singular indeclinable. Whoever forms the plural of "اَلَّذِينَ" on the pattern of the dual says: "جاءَنِي الَّذُونَ في الدّارِ" and "رَأيْتُ الَّذِينَ فِي الدّارِ". This ought not to occur, because in the plural one can dispense with the pattern of the dual, whereas the dual has only one form.

The meaning of His saying ﴿بِالغَيْبِ﴾ is: what was hidden from them of what the Prophet ﷺ told them concerning the matter of the unseen, the resurrection and the Day of Rising. Everything hidden from them of what he informed them about is unseen (ghayb).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَيُقِيمُونَ الصَّلاةَ﴾: its meaning is: they perform the prayer completely, as He said: ﴿وَأتِمُّوا الحَجَّ والعُمْرَةَ لِلَّهِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 196]. The yāʾ of "يُؤْمِنُونَ" and "يُقِيمُونَ" was given ḍamma because every verb of four letters — such as "أكْرَمَ", "أحْسَنَ", "أقامَ" and "آمَنَ" — has as its imperfect "يُكْرِمُ", "يُحْسِنَ", "يُؤْمِنُ" and "يُقِيمُ". The beginnings of the imperfect were given ḍamma only to distinguish between three-letter verbs — such as "ضَرَبَ" — and four-letter verbs — such as "دَحْرَجَ". What is of three letters is "ضَرَبَ يَضْرِبُ", or "تَضْرِبُ", or "نَضْرِبُ"; so the ḍamma separated the two.

If someone says: "Why were they not separated by kasra?", it is replied: kasra may enter in forms like "تِعْلَمُ" and "تِبْيَضُّ"; and because ḍamma is used with yāʾ, whereas kasra is not used with yāʾ: whoever says "أنْتَ تِعْلَمُ" «[Translator's note: the text prints "تَعْلَمُ" with fatḥa here; the argument requires the dialectal "تِعْلَمُ".]» does not say "هو يِعْلَمُ". So the distinguishing mark between them had to be the ḍamma and nothing else. The origin of "يُقِيمُ" is "يُؤَقْيِمُ", and the origin of "يُكْرِمُ" is "يُؤَكْرِمُ" «[Translator's note: the text gives the origin of يُقِيمُ here as يُؤَقْيِمُ (with yāʾ) but below as أُؤَقْوِمُ (with wāw); the root is q-w-m.]». But the hamza was deleted because the ḍamma is an indication of four-letter verbs. Had it been retained, you would have to say — when speaking of yourself — "أنا أُؤَقْوِمُ" and "أنا أُؤَكْرِمُ", and two hamzas would come together, which was felt to be heavy; so the hamza which is the fāʾ of the verb «[Translator's note: so in the text; the hamza of أفْعَلَ is an augment, not the first radical (fāʾ).]» was deleted, and the rest of the verb followed the pattern of the hamza (form), so you said "أنْتَ تُكْرِمُ" (you honour), "نَحْنُ نُكْرِمُ" (we honour) and "هي تُكْرِمُ" (she honours); just as from the pattern of "يَعِدُ" the wāw was deleted because it falls between a yāʾ and a kasra — its origin being "يَوْعِدُ" — and then it was deleted in "تَعِدُ", "نَعِدُ" and "أعِدُ".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَمِمّا رَزَقْناهم يُنْفِقُونَ﴾: its meaning is: they give in charity. He said, Mighty and Majestic is He: "وأنْفِقُوا مِمّا رَزَقْناكم" (and spend out of what We have provided you), up to His saying: "قَرِيبٍ فَأصَّدَّقَ" (a short term, so that I might give in charity).

zajjaj:4-4.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بِما أُنْـزِلَ إلَيْكَ﴾: if you wish, you lighten (takhfīf) the hamza in "أُنْزِلَ", and likewise in His saying "أُولَئِكَ"; this is the dialect of those other than the people of the Hijaz. As for the people of the Hijaz, they lighten the hamza between the wāw and the hamza «[Translator's note: so in the text; the phrase probably refers to pronouncing the hamza "between" (bayna bayna), i.e. midway between hamza and the letter of its vowel.]». Sībawayh said: this was done to the hamza alone among the letters only because its point of articulation is distant, and because it is a stress (nabra) in the chest, being the most distant of the letters in articulation. As for "إلَيْكَ", "إلَيْهِمْ", "عَلَيْكَ" and "عَلَيْهِمْ", the origin of these is "إلاكَ", "عَلاكَ", "إلاهم" and "عَلاهم", just as you say "إلى زَيْدٍ" (to Zayd) and "عَلى إخْوَتِكَ" (upon your brothers); except that the alif was changed with the pronoun and replaced by yāʾ, in order to distinguish between the alif at the end of fully declinable (mutamakkin) words and the alif at the end of non-declinable words to which annexation is necessary. Do you not see that "إلى", "عَلى" and "لَدى" never stand apart from annexation? That is why the Arabs said — of "كِلا" in the accusative and genitive —: "رَأيْتُ كِلَيْهِما" (I saw both of them), "كِلَيْكُما" (both of you), "مَرَرْتُ بِكِلَيْهِما" (I passed by both of them) and "كِلَيْكُما". They distinguished between annexation to an overt noun and to a pronoun, since "كِلا" does not stand alone and does not form speech except with annexation.

zajjaj:78-78.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَمِنهم أُمِّيُّونَ﴾: the meaning of «الأُمِّيّ» in the language is: one attributed to the natural state of his community (umma), that is, he does not write; so in not writing he remains as he was born. «أُمِّيُّونَ» is nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject), and «مِنهم» is the khabar (predicate). According to the view of al-Akhfash, «أُمِّيُّونَ» is nominative by its verb, the meaning being: "and there are established among them unlettered ones".

The meaning of «إلّا أمانِيَّ»: people have given two views on its meaning. They said: its meaning is that they do not know the Book except as recitation, as He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿وَما أرْسَلْنا مِن قَبْلِكَ مِن رَسُولٍ ولا نَبِيٍّ إلا إذا تَمَنّى ألْقى الشَّيْطانُ في أُمْنِيَّتِهِ﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 52], that is, when he recited, Satan cast into his recitation. It has also been said: «الأمانِيّ» are falsehoods; the Arabs say "you are only making up (tatamannā) this saying", that is, inventing it. And «أمانِيَّ» may be attributed to a speaker when he says what he does not know, as though he were merely wishing for it; this is used in people's speech: you say to one who says what has no reality while he loves it: "this is a wish (munan)" and "this is a desire (umniyya)". In the form of «أمانِيَّ» there are two ways: the Arabs say «هَذِهِ أمانٍ» and «أمانِيُّ, O you», with doubling and without. Whoever says «أمانِيَّ» with doubling, it is like «أُحْدُوثَة» / «أحادِيث» and «قُرْقُورَة» / «قَراقِير». Whoever says «أمانٍ» without doubling, it is [Translator's note: the source has «أكْثَرُ» here, apparently misplaced; translated as written] among words in which two yāʾs come together, more commonly so, because of the heaviness of the yāʾ.

The Arabs say for «أثْفِيَة» both «أثافِيّ» and «أثافٍ», and the lightened form is more common because of their frequent use of «أثافٍ»; «الأثافِيّ» are the stones placed under the cooking pot.

zajjaj:79-79.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَوَيْلٌ لِلَّذِينَ يَكْتُبُونَ الكِتابَ بِأيْدِيهِمْ﴾: «الوَيْل» in the language is a word used by everyone who falls into destruction; its origin is in punishment and perdition. «وَيْلٌ» is nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject), and its khabar (predicate) is «لِلَّذِينَ». Were it outside the Quran, «فَوَيْلًا لِلَّذِينَ» would be permissible, in the sense of "Allah has assigned woe to those who…"; the nominative is in the sense of the established fact of woe for those who write the Book with their hands and then say "This is from Allah", in order to sell it for a small price. It is said that this concerns the description of the Prophet ﷺ: they wrote his description otherwise than as it was in the Torah. It is said in the tafsīr that they wrote his description as being tawny and tall, whereas his description in it was tawny and of medium height; so they altered it, and Allah fastened woe upon them for what their hands wrote and for what they earned from it, because they took money for it and accepted gifts.

zajjaj:80-80.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقالُوا لَنْ تَمَسَّنا النّارُ إلا أيّامًا مَعْدُودَةً﴾: «تَمَسَّنا» is accusative (manṣūb) by «لَنْ». The grammarians have disagreed about the cause of the accusative by «لَنْ». Two views are related from al-Khalīl. One of them is that it governs the accusative as «أنْ» does, but what follows it is not its ṣila (complement), because «لَنْ يَفْعَلَ» is the negation of «سَيَفْعَلُ»; so what comes after it may be placed before it, as in your saying «زَيْدًا لَنْ أضْرِبَ» ("Zayd I will not strike"), just as you say «زَيْدًا لَمْ أضْرِبْ». Sībawayh related from one of the companions of al-Khalīl, from al-Khalīl, that he said: the origin of «لَنْ» is «لا أنْ», but the omission occurred for lightness. Sībawayh held that this is not good: were it so, «زَيْدًا لَنْ أضْرِبَ» would not be permissible. All the grammarians follow the doctrine of Sībawayh. Hishām related from al-Kisāʾī about «لَنْ» a view like this anomalous view from al-Khalīl, but neither Sībawayh nor his companions adopted it. The meaning of «أيّامًا مَعْدُودَةً»: they said, "We will be punished only because we worshipped the calf for some days". Two views are given about their number: it was said seven days, and it was said forty days. This is a report about the Jews; it is they who said: ﴿لَنْ تَمَسَّنا النّارُ إلا أيّامًا مَعْدُودَةً﴾.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قُلْ أتَّخَذْتُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ عَهْدًا﴾, with a disjunctive alif (alif al-qaṭʿ): it is read in two ways, «أتَّخَذْتُمْ» with the dhāl pronounced distinctly, and «أتَّخَتُّمْ» with the dhāl assimilated into the tāʾ. The alif is disjunctive because it is the alif of interrogation and of making one acknowledge (taqrīr).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿عِنْدَ اللَّهِ عَهْدًا﴾: the meaning is: has Allah pledged to you that He will not punish you beyond this measure?

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَلَنْ يُخْلِفَ اللَّهُ عَهْدَهُ﴾, that is: if you have a pledge, Allah will not break it; or do you say about Allah what you do not know?

zajjaj:81-81.t:
Then He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿بَلى مَن كَسَبَ سَيِّئَةً﴾, as a rebuttal of their saying «لَنْ تَمَسَّنا النّارُ إلّا أيّامًا مَعْدُودَةً».

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَأحاطَتْ بِهِ خَطِيئَتُهُ فَأُولَئِكَ أصْحابُ النّارِ هم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾: the truth about this verse, and the consensus, is that this is specifically for the Jews, because He, Mighty and Majestic is He, is speaking about them. It has also been said: «مَن كَسَبَ سَيِّئَةً» is associating partners with Allah (shirk), and «أحاطَتْ بِهِ خَطِيئَتُهُ» is the major sins. What runs through these narratives is only information about the Jews.

zajjaj:83-83.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ أخَذْنا مِيثاقَ بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ لا تَعْبُدُونَ إلا اللَّهَ﴾: the reading is of two kinds: «تَعْبُدُونَ» and «يَعْبُدُونَ», with yāʾ and with tāʾ. A third way has been transmitted which is not adopted because it contradicts the Muṣḥaf: Ibn Masʿūd read «لا تَعْبُدُوا».

«لا تَعْبُدُونَ» with tāʾ is nominative in two ways. First, that «لا» is the answer to an oath (jawāb al-qasam), because the taking of the covenant is equivalent to an oath; the proof of that is His saying: ﴿وَإذْ أخَذَ اللَّهُ مِيثاقَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ لَتُبَيِّنُنَّهُ لِلنّاسِ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 187], where the answer to the oath came with the lām; likewise it comes with negation by «لا». Second, it may be nominative through the dropping of «أنْ», in the sense of «ألّا تَعْبُدُوا»: when «أنْ» was dropped, it became nominative. This is the doctrine of al-Akhfash and other grammarians. As for the reading with tāʾ, it is in the sense of address and reported speech, as though it were said: "We said to them: you shall not worship except Allah". As for «لا يَعْبُدُونَ» with yāʾ, it is because they are absent, and the sign of the absent (third person) is the yāʾ.

The meaning of taking the covenant and pledge we have explained before this place.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَبِالوالِدَيْنِ إحْسانًا﴾ is accusative in the sense of "and do good to parents, a doing good (iḥsānan)", standing in place of the word «أحْسِنُوا». «ذِي القُرْبى واليَتامى»: it (al-yatāmā) is a plural on the pattern «فَعالى», as «أسِير» is pluralised as «أُسارى». One says «يَتِمَ، يَيْتَمُ، يُتْمًا، ويَتْمًا» when he loses his father; this is for human beings, while for others orphanhood is from the side of the mother. Muḥammad ibn Yazīd [al-Mubarrad] informed me of that, from al-Riyāshī, from al-Aṣmaʿī: the orphan among people is from the side of the father, and among other than people from the side of the mother. «المَساكِين» is taken from «السُّكُون» (stillness); its singular is «مِسْكِين», as though poverty has made him still.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقُولُوا لِلنّاسِ حُسْنًا﴾: there are three views about it: «حُسْنًا» with tanwīn and the sīn quiescent; «حَسَنًا» with tanwīn and fatḥa on the sīn; and al-Akhfash related «حُسْنى» without tanwīn. As for the first two ways, people have read them, and both are good and eloquent in the language. As for «حُسْنى», it ought not to be read, because it belongs to the category of «الأفْعَل» / «الفُعْلى», such as «الأحْسَن» / «الحُسْنى» and «الأفْضَل» / «الفُضْلى», which is used only with the alif and lām, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ سَبَقَتْ لَهم مِنّا الحُسْنى﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 101], and said: ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أحْسَنُوا الحُسْنى وزِيادَةٌ﴾ [Yūnus: 26]. About His saying «حُسْنًا» with tanwīn there are two views: the meaning is "speak to people speech possessing goodness"; and al-Akhfash held that «حُسْنًا» may be in the sense of «حَسَنًا». As for «حَسَنًا», it is an adjective, the meaning being "good speech (qawlan ḥasanan)". The interpretation of ﴿وَقُولُوا لِلنّاسِ حُسْنًا﴾ is that it is an address to the scholars of the Jews: they were told, be truthful about the description of the Prophet ﷺ.

﴿وَأقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ وآتُوا الزَّكاةَ﴾: know that He took the covenant from them and pledged them in it to truthfulness about the description of the Prophet ﷺ.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ثُمَّ تَوَلَّيْتُمْ إلا قَلِيلا مِنكُمْ﴾ means their forebears from whom He took the covenant.

His saying: ﴿وَأنْتُمْ مُعْرِضُونَ﴾, that is: and you too are like your forebears in turning away from what you were pledged to. «إلّا قَلِيلًا» is accusative as an exception (istithnāʾ), the meaning being: "I except a few of you".

zajjaj:84-84.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ أخَذْنا مِيثاقَكم لا تَسْفِكُونَ دِماءَكُمْ﴾: one says «سَفَكْتُ الدَّمَ، أسْفِكُهُ، سَفْكًا» when you pour it out. «لا تَسْفِكُونَ» is nominative on the basis of the oath, and on the basis of the omission of «أنْ», as we described regarding His saying «لا تَعْبُدُونَ». Similar to the omission of «أنْ» is the saying of Ṭarafa:
ألا أيُّهَذا الزّاجِرِي أحْضُرَ الوَغى ∗∗∗ وأنْ أشْهَدَ اللَّذّاتِ هَلْ أنْتَ مُخْلِدِي
(O you who forbid me to attend the battle and to witness the pleasures — can you make me live forever?)
The singular of «الدِّماء» is «دَمٌ, O you», light (without doubling), and its origin is «دَمَيٌ» according to most grammarians. The proof of those who say its origin is «دَمَيٌ» is the saying of the poet:
فَلَوْ أنّا عَلى حَجَرٍ ذُبِحْنا ∗∗∗ جَرى الدَّمَيانِ بِالخَبَرِ اليَقِينِ
(Were we slaughtered on one stone, the two bloods (al-damayān) would flow with the certain news.)
Others said: its origin is «دَمْيٌ», but when it was shortened and then had restored to it what had been dropped from it, the mīm was vowelled, so that the vowel indicates that it had been used in shortened form.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تُخْرِجُونَ أنْفُسَكم مِن دِيارِكُمْ﴾ is conjoined to «لا تَسْفِكُونَ دِماءَكم».

His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ أقْرَرْتُمْ﴾, that is: you acknowledged that this was imposed on you in the covenant and imposed on your fathers, and you, O remaining ones being addressed, bear witness that this is true.

zajjaj:38-38.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَإمّا يَأْتِيَنَّكم مِنِّي هُدًى فَمَن تَبِعَ هُدايَ فَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾. The benefit in mentioning the verse is that He, Mighty and Majestic is He, informed them that He would test them with obedience, that He would recompense them with Paradise for it and with the Fire for abandoning it, and that this testing took place at the descent to earth.
The iʿrāb of ”إمّا“ in this place is the iʿrāb of the particles of condition and requital (sharṭ and jazāʾ), except that when the requital comes with the heavy or light nūn on the verb, ”ما“ cleaves to it [i.e. to in]; and the meaning of its cleaving to it is emphasis, just as the meaning of the entry of the nūn into the condition is emphasis. The most effective thing in what servants are commanded is to emphasise it to them. The letter before the nūn in His saying ﴿يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ﴾ was given fatḥa because of the quiescence of the yāʾ and the quiescence of the first nūn.
The apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is in the fāʾ together with the second condition and its apodosis, namely ”فَمَن تَبِعَ هُدايَ“; and the apodosis of ”فَمَن تَبِعَ هُدايَ“ is His saying: ﴿فَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ﴾.
”هُدايَ“: the prevalent form in the reading and in transmission from the Arabs is ”هُدايَ فَلا خَوْفٌ“. The yāʾ in ”هُدايَ“ was given fatḥa because it came after a quiescent letter, and its original vowel is the fatḥa. The original is to say ”هَذا غُلامِيَ قَدْ جاءَ“ ("this is my servant, he has come") with fatḥa on the yāʾ, because it is a letter in the position of a pronoun, denied iʿrāb and therefore made to keep a vowel, as ”هو“ was made to keep one. Dropping the vowel is permissible, because the yāʾ is one of the letters of prolongation and softness; but when the letter before it is quiescent there is no avoiding giving it a vowel, so it was given the share of vowel it had originally, which is the fatḥa.
Some of the Arabs say ”هُدَيَّ“ and ”عَصَيَّ“. Whoever reads with this reading has only turned the alif into a yāʾ because of the yāʾ after it; for the rule of the yāʾ of annexation (possession) is that the letter before it takes kasra, so, in place of the kasra of the preceding letter – since the alif cannot have the letter before it given kasra nor can it itself take kasra – its conversion into yāʾ was made. Ṭayyiʾ say, for ”هُدًى“, ”عَصًا“, ”أفْعًى“ and the like, in pause: ”هُدَيْ“, ”عَصَيْ“, ”أفْعَيْ“, without annexation. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash and other grammarians recited:
؎تَبَشَّرِي بِالرَّفْهِ والماءِ الرَّوِيْ ∗∗∗ وفَرَجٍ مِنكِ قَرِيبٍ قَدْ أتَيْ
(Rejoice at the good tidings of ease and thirst-quenching water, and of relief for you, near, that has come.)
Some of the Arabs treat what they treat [this way] in pause – in the basic [connected] form – as they treat it in pause, and this is not the good way. Sībawayh claimed that those who replaced the alif with yāʾ did so in pause in order to make it clearer. He also reported that some people say in pause ”حُبْلَوْ“ and ”أفْعَوْ“. The people of the language and those learned in it report everything in it only so that the good, sound and regular may be distinguished from the rest, and what is not good avoided. The rule in these things is that they are pronounced in connected speech and in pause with an alif; it is not for you to change something for a cause and then pronounce it according to its origin while the cause has not gone away.
So the reading that ought to be adhered to is ﴿هُدايَ فَلا خَوْفٌ﴾, unless ”هُدَيَّ“ is established by a sound transmission, in which case it is read so; and its analogical justification is as we have described.
As for His saying ”هَذا صِراطٌ عَلَيَّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ“ and His saying ”إلَيَّ مَرْجِعُكم“, it is not permissible to read ”هَذا صِراطٌ عَلايَّ“ nor ”ثُمَّ إلايَّ مَرْجِعُكم“, because the connected form in these was ”إلايَ“ and ”عَلايَ“, but the alif was replaced with yāʾ with pronouns in order to distinguish between that whose ending is of what must be declined and be fully a noun (mutamakkin) and that whose ending is of what need not be declined; so this alif was turned into yāʾ for this reason.

zajjaj:40-40.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يا بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَتِيَ الَّتِي أنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾. ”بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ“ is accusative because it is an annexed (muḍāf) vocative, and the basic case of the vocative is the accusative, because its meaning is the meaning of "I called" and "I summoned". ”إسْرائِيلُ“ is in the position of the genitive, except that its ending has fatḥa because it is a diptote. There are two things in it that require barring full declension: it is foreign and it is definite; and when a noun is so it is a diptote, if it exceeds three letters, according to the grammarians.
In His saying ”نِعْمَتِيَ الَّتِي أنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكم“ there are two ways. The better of them is fatḥa on the yāʾ, because what follows it is quiescent, namely the lām of definiteness; its use is frequent in speech, so fatḥa on the yāʾ was chosen with it, for the meeting of two quiescent letters; and also because, even if no quiescent letter followed the yāʾ, its fatḥa would be stronger in the language. It is permissible for the yāʾ to be dropped in pronunciation because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, so that one reads ”نِعْمَتِ الَّتِي أنْعَمْتُ“ with the yāʾ dropped. The preferred way is to keep the yāʾ and give it fatḥa, because it is stronger in Arabic, weightier in expression and more complete in reward, since the reader is rewarded for everything he reads of the Book of Allah, a good deed for every letter; and since keeping it is more proper in the language, it ought to be kept for the reasons we described.
As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿هارُونَ أخِي﴾ [Ṭā Hā: 30] ﴿اشْدُدْ بِهِ أزْرِي﴾ [Ṭā Hā: 31], the Readers did not often give this yāʾ fatḥa, while most of them read it with fatḥa before the alif-lām. By my life, the defining lām is more frequent in use, but I say: the preferred reading is ”أخِيَ اشْدُدْ“ with fatḥa on the yāʾ, for the meeting of two quiescent letters, just as they gave it fatḥa before the lām, because the meeting of two quiescent letters with the lām and with others is one and the same matter. If it is dropped, the dropping is permissible and good, but better is what we have described.
As for the meaning of the verse in its reminder of the favour: they were reminded of what had been bestowed upon their forefathers before them and what had been bestowed upon themselves. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿إذْ جَعَلَ فِيكم أنْبِياءَ وجَعَلَكم مُلُوكًا﴾ [al-Māʾida: 20]; those whom the Prophet ﷺ encountered were not prophets; rather they were reminded of what had been bestowed upon their forefathers, and upon them in themselves and in their forefathers. This meaning exists in the speech of the Arabs and is known to them: a man boasts against another man, saying ”هَزَمْناكم يَوْمَ ذِي قارٍ“ ("we routed you on the day of Dhū Qār") and saying ”قَتَلْناكم يَوْمَ كَذا“ ("we killed you on such-and-such a day"), meaning: our forefathers killed your forefathers.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَأوْفُوا بِعَهْدِي أُوفِ بِعَهْدِكُمْ﴾. Its meaning – and Allah knows best – is His saying: ﴿وَإذْ أخَذَ اللَّهُ مِيثاقَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ لَتُبَيِّنُنَّهُ لِلنّاسِ ولا تَكْتُمُونَهُ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 187]. The completion of making it clear is that they report what is in it of the mention of the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ. We have already explained, before this, what indicates the mention of the covenant, and that is sufficient.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإيّايَ فارْهَبُونِ﴾ is accusative through the command, as though its meaning were ”اِرْهَبُونِي“ ("fear me"), the second [verb] being the explanation of this suppressed verb. Were it outside the Qurʾān, ”وَأنا فارْهَبُونِ“ would be permissible; but the preferred form in speech, in the Qurʾān and in poetry is ”وَإيّايَ فارْهَبُونِ“. The yāʾ was dropped – its origin being ”فارْهَبُونِي“ – because it is a fāṣila; the meaning of "fāṣila" is the end of a verse, so that the composition runs on a consistent sound. The people of the language call the ends of verses (of the Qurʾān) ”اَلْفَواصِلَ“ (al-fawāṣil) and the ends of poetic lines ”اَلْقَوافِيَ“ (rhymes).
One says ”وَفَيْتُ لَهُ بِالعَهْدِ، فَأنا وافٍ بِهِ“ and ”أوْفَيْتُ لَهُ بِالعَهْدِ، فَأنا مُوفٍ بِهِ“ ("I fulfilled the covenant to him, so I am fulfilling it"), and the preferred form is ”أوْفَيْتُ“; on it the whole Qurʾān was revealed. Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿وَأوْفُوا بِعَهْدِي أُوفِ بِعَهْدِكُمْ﴾, and He said: ﴿وَأوْفُوا بِعَهْدِ اللَّهِ إذا عاهَدْتُمْ﴾ [al-Naḥl: 91], and He said: ﴿فَأوْفُوا الكَيْلَ والمِيزانَ﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 85]; everything in the Qurʾān is with the alif. The poet said, concerning ”أوْفَيْتُ“ and ”وَفَيْتُ“, combining the two dialects in a single line:
؎أمّا ابْنُ عَوْفٍ فَقَدْ أوْفى بِذِمَّتِهِ ∗∗∗ كَما وفى بِقِلاصِ النَّجْمِ حادِيها
(As for Ibn ʿAwf, he has fulfilled his pledge, just as the driver of the young she-camels of the star fulfilled [his duty] by them.)

zajjaj:41-41.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَآمِنُوا بِما أنْـزَلْتُ مُصَدِّقًا لِما مَعَكم ولا تَكُونُوا أوَّلَ كافِرٍ بِهِ﴾, meaning the Qurʾān. It can also be: "and do not be the first to disbelieve in your Book and in the Qurʾān", if you wish, with the hāʾ referring back to His saying ”لِما مَعَكم“. It was said to them ”وَلا تَكُونُوا أوَّلَ كافِرٍ“ only because the address was directed at their learned men: if they disbelieved, the followers would disbelieve with them; that is why it was said to them ”وَلا تَكُونُوا أوَّلَ كافِرٍ“.
If someone asks: how can the hāʾ be for their Book? It is said to him: when they concealed the mention of the Prophet ﷺ in their Book they disbelieved in it, just as whoever conceals a verse of the Qurʾān has disbelieved in it. The meaning of ”وَلا تَكُونُوا أوَّلَ كافِرٍ بِهِ“, when it refers to the Qurʾān, involves no difficulty, because they openly professed that they disbelieved in the Qurʾān.
The meaning of ”أوَّلَ كافِرٍ“ is "the first of the disbelievers". Some Basrans gave two views on this: al-Akhfash said its meaning is "the first one who disbelieved in it"; and the Basrans also said its meaning is "and do not be the first party that disbelieves in it", that is, in the Prophet ﷺ. Both views are correct and good.
Some grammarians said that this is permissible only with ”فاعِلٌ“ (active participle) and ”مَفْعُولٌ“ (passive participle): you say ”اَلْجَيْشُ مُنْهَزِمٌ“ ("the army is routed") and ”اَلْجَيْشُ مَهْزُومٌ“ ("the army is defeated"), but it is not permissible, in what has been mentioned, to say ”اَلْجَيْشُ رَجُلٌ“ ("the army is a man") and ”اَلْجَيْشُ فَرَسٌ“ ("the army is a horse"). This is clearer with ”فاعِلٌ“ and ”مَفْعُولٌ“, because when you say ”اَلْجَيْشُ مُنْهَزِمٌ“ it is known that you mean "this army", and you uttered it with a fāʿil form «[Translator's note: the text has «فنقطت», evidently for «فنطقت», "you uttered".]», because the meaning for which ”اَلْجَيْشُ“ was coined is a meaning indicating a group; so it [the participle], ”فاعِلٌ“ or ”مَفْعُولٌ“, indicates what ”اَلْجَيْشُ“ indicates. When you say ”اَلْجَيْشُ رَجُلٌ“, what is disliked in this is only that it may be fancied that you are belittling it; but when its meaning is known, it is acceptable and good. You say ”جَيْشُهم إنَّما هو فَرَسٌ ورَجُلٌ“ ("their army is but horse and man"), that is, it does not have many followers, and the meaning indicates that you mean "the army is horses and men". This is clearer with ”فاعِلٌ“ and ”مَفْعُولٌ“, as we have described.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أوَّلَ كافِرٍ بِهِ﴾: the highest and oldest dialect is fatḥa on the kāf, the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz. Imāla (inclining the ā towards ē) on the kāf is also good and eloquent in the language, because when a fāʿil form is free of the covering letters (ḥurūf al-iṭbāq) and the elevated letters (al-ḥurūf al-mustaʿliya), imāla in it is acceptable – except in the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz. Imāla is the dialect of Banū Tamīm and others among the Arabs, and the tongue of the people in Iraq runs according to the pronunciation with imāla. So the Arabs say ”هَذا عابِدٌ“ and ”هو عابِدٌ“ ("he is a worshipper") with imāla, giving kasra to what follows it, unless the covering letters enter, which are ṭāʾ, ẓāʾ, ṣād and ḍād. It is not permissible in your saying ”فُلانٌ ظالِمٌ“ ("so-and-so is a wrongdoer") to say ”ظالِمٌ“ with imāla, nor in ”طالِبٌ“ to say ”طالِبٌ“ with imāla, nor in ”صابِرٌ“ to say ”صابِرٌ“ with imāla, nor in ”ضابِطٌ“ to say ”ضابِطٌ“ with imāla. Likewise the elevated letters, which are khāʾ, ghayn and qāf: it is not permissible in ”غافِلٌ“ to say ”غافِلٌ“ with imāla, nor in ”خادِمٌ“ to say ”خادِمٌ“ with imāla, nor in ”قاهِرٌ“ to say ”قاهِرٌ“ with imāla. The chapter of imāla is long to explain, but this is what is intended in this place, and as much as is needed.

zajjaj:5-5.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلى هُدًى مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾: the position of "أُولَئِكَ" is nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject; ibtidāʾ), and the khabar (predicate) is "عَلى هُدًى مِن رَبِّهِمْ", except that أُولَئِكَ is not inflected, because it is a demonstrative noun; the hamza in it was given kasra because of the meeting of two vowelless letters. Likewise His saying: ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ المُفْلِحُونَ﴾, except that "هم" has entered as a separating pronoun (faṣl); or, if you wish, it is a repetition of the noun, as you say: "زَيْدٌ هو العالِمُ" (Zayd — he is the learned one), putting "زَيْدًا" in the nominative as mubtadaʾ, putting "هو" in the nominative as a second mubtadaʾ, and putting "اَلْعالِمُ" in the nominative as khabar of "هو", and "اَلْعالِمُ" as khabar of "زَيْدٌ" «[Translator's note: so in the text; on this analysis it is the clause "هو العالِمُ" that is the khabar of زَيْدٌ.]». So it is with His saying: "وَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ المُفْلِحُونَ". If you wish, you make "هو" a faṣl and put "زَيْدًا" and "اَلْعالِمُ" in the nominative as mubtadaʾ and its khabar. The faṣl is what the Kufans call "ʿimād" (support).

Sībawayh says that the faṣl is proper only with verbs that are not complete (i.e. that need a predicate), as in "كانَ زَيْدٌ هو العالِمَ" (Zayd was the learned one) and "ظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا هو العالِمَ" (I thought Zayd to be the learned one). Sībawayh said: the faṣl has entered in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿تَجِدُوهُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ هو خَيْرًا﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], in His saying: ﴿وَلا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَبْخَلُونَ بِما آتاهُمُ اللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ هو خَيْرًا لَهُمْ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 180], in His saying: ﴿وَيَرى الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا العِلْمَ الَّذِي أُنْـزِلَ إلَيْكَ مِن رَبِّكَ هو الحَقَّ﴾ [Sabaʾ: 6], and in His saying: ﴿وَإذْ قالُوا اللَّهُمَّ إنْ كانَ هَذا هو الحَقَّ مِن عِنْدِكَ﴾ [al-Anfāl: 32], and in what resembles this of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, has mentioned.

Likewise you have this in speech in the mubtadaʾ and khabar, and in your saying "كانَ زَيْدٌ هو العالِمَ": the mention of "هو", "أنْتَ", "أنا" and "نَحْنُ" — they enter to signal that the khabar is guaranteed (to follow) and that the speech is not yet complete. The place where they enter is when the khabar is definite or what resembles a definite noun. And "هو" is equivalent to the superfluous (laghw) "ما" in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَبِما رَحْمَةٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ لِنْتَ لَهُمْ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 159]; it enters only as an emphasiser.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿المُفْلِحُونَ﴾: everyone who attains good is called "مُفْلِحٌ". He said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قَدْ أفْلَحَ المُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 1], and He said: ﴿قَدْ أفْلَحَ مَن زَكّاها﴾ [al-Shams: 9]. Al-falāḥ is continuance (baqāʾ). Labīd ibn Rabīʿa said:
نَحُلُّ بِلادًا كُلُّها حُلَّ قَبْلَنا ∗∗∗ ونَرْجُو الفَلاحَ بَعْدَ عادٍ وتُبَّعا
(We settle in lands every one of which was settled before us, and we hope for continuance after ʿĀd and Tubbaʿ.)
That is: we hope for continuance. And ʿAbīd said:
أفْلِحْ بِما شِئْتَ فَقَدْ يُدْ ∗∗∗ رَكُ بِالضَّعْفِ وقَدْ يُخْدَعُ الأرِيبُ
(Prosper by whatever you wish, for success is sometimes reached through weakness, and the clever man is sometimes deceived.)
That is: attain good by whatever you wish. "اَلْفَلّاحُ" is the ploughman, and al-filāḥa is his craft. He was called "اَلْفَلاحُ" «[Translator's note: so vowelled in the text, without doubling of the lām.]» only because he splits the earth. It is said "فَلَحْتُ الحَدِيدَ" when you have cut iron. The poet said:
قَدْ عَلِمَتْ خَيْلُكَ أنِّي الصَّحْصَحُ ∗∗∗ إنَّ الحَدِيدَ بِالحَدِيدِ يُفْلَحُ
(Your horsemen know that I am the hardy one: iron is split by iron.)
The one who hires out animals (al-mukārī) is also called "اَلْفَلّاحُ"; he was called "فَلّاحٌ" only by comparison with the ploughman. The poet said:
لَها رِطْلٌ تَكِيلُ الزَّيْتَ فِيهِ ∗∗∗ وفَلّاحٌ يَسُوقُ لَها حِمارا
(She has a raṭl measure in which she measures oil, and a hireling who drives a donkey for her.)

zajjaj:6-6.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا سَواءٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أأنْذَرْتَهم أمْ لَمْ تُنْذِرْهُمْ﴾: "إنَّ" puts "اَلَّذِينَ" in the accusative. It puts nouns in the accusative and predicates in the nominative; its meaning in speech is emphasis (tawkīd), and it is one of the instruments of the oath. It puts in the accusative and the nominative only because it is likened to the verb. Its resemblance to it is that it is not followed by verbs and does not govern them; only the noun and the predicate are mentioned after it, just as the agent and the object are mentioned after the verb — except that the object is put first with it, to distinguish between what is likened to the verb while its form is the form of a verb, and what is likened to it while its form is not the form of a verb. Its khabar here is a whole clause, I mean His saying: ﴿سَواءٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أأنْذَرْتَهم أمْ لَمْ تُنْذِرْهُمْ﴾. ﴿سَواءٌ﴾ is put in the nominative as mubtadaʾ, and ﴿أأنْذَرْتَهم أمْ لَمْ تُنْذِرْهُمْ﴾ stands in the place of the khabar, as though it were equivalent to your saying: "سَواءٌ عَلَيْهِمُ الإنْذارُ وتَرْكُهُ" (warning and leaving it are alike to them). "سَواءٌ" is placed in the position of "مُسْتَوٍ" (equal), because you do not put maṣdars (verbal nouns) in the place of active participles unless their interpretation is the interpretation of those participles.

As for the entry of the alif of interrogation and the entry of the interrogative "أمْ" while the speech is a statement, that occurred only for the meaning of equalisation (taswiya); the instrument of equalisation is the alif of interrogation and "أمْ". You say: "أزَيْدٌ في الدّارِ، أمْ عَمْرٌو" (Is Zayd in the house, or ʿAmr?); the alif and "أمْ" entered only because your knowledge is equal regarding Zayd and ʿAmr: you know that one of them is in the house without doubt, but you want what you know to be made clear to you, and your knowledge of it to be singled out from the other. Therefore you say: "قَدْ عَلِمْتُ أزْيَدٌ في الدّارِ أمْ عَمْرٌو" (I know whether Zayd or ʿAmr is in the house), and you only want to make equal, for the one you inform, the knowledge that has become clear to you. Likewise "سَواءٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أأنْذَرْتَهم أمْ لَمْ تُنْذِرْهم": the alif and "أمْ" entered for equalisation.

As for "أأنْذَرْتَهم", Sībawayh held that among the Arabs are those who pronounce the hamza fully (taḥqīq) but do not combine two hamzas, even if they belong to two words. As for the people of the Hijaz, they do not pronounce either of them fully. As for some of the readers — Ibn Abī Isḥāq and others — they combine the two in recitation and read "أأنْذَرْتَهم". Many of the readers lighten one of them. Sībawayh held that al-Khalīl favoured lightening the second, saying "آنْذَرْتَهم", making the second (hamza) between hamza and alif, without making it a pure alif. Whoever makes it a pure alif errs in two respects: first, he combines two vowelless letters; second, he replaces with an alif a vowelled hamza that is preceded by a vowel, the vowel being fatḥa. The proper treatment of a hamza that is vowelled and preceded by fatḥa is to make it "between-between" (bayna bayna), I mean between the hamza and the letter from which its vowel comes. So you say for "سَألَ": "سالَ"; for "رَؤُوفٌ": "رَوُوفٌ"; and for "بِئْسَ": "بِيسَ" — between-between. This is one rule; only oral transmission (mushāfaha) settles it. Others than al-Khalīl allowed, in the like of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿فَقَدْ جاءَ أشْراطُها﴾ [Muḥammad: 18], the lightening of the first. Sībawayh held that a group of the Arabs read: "فَقَدَ جا أشْراطُها", pronouncing the second fully and lightening the first; this is the doctrine of Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ. As for al-Khalīl, he holds the full pronunciation of the first, saying: "فَقَدْ جاءَ اشْراطُها". Al-Khalīl said: I chose lightening the second only because people agree on replacing the second in your saying "آدَمُ" and "آخَرُ", since the origin of "آدَمُ" is "أادَمُ" and of "آخَرُ" is "أاخَرُ". Al-Khalīl's view is more in accordance with analogy, and Abū ʿAmr's view is also good.

Abū Isḥāq said: the hamza of interrogation is an initial alif, and an initial hamza cannot be lightened. But if the hamza of the alif of interrogation is cast onto the vowelless mīm of "عَلَيْهِمْ", so that you say "عَلَيْهِمَ أنْذَرْتَهم", it is permissible; but no one has read it so. The two hamzas in His saying "فَقَدْ جاءَ أشْراطُها" are two hamzas in the middle of the word (i.e. of the utterance), and lightening the first is possible. As for whoever lightens the first hamza in His saying "أأنْذَرْتَهم", he drops it entirely and casts its vowel onto the mīm; I know of no one who read so. What is required — according to the dialect of the people of the Hijaz — is "عَلَيْهِمَ اَنْذَرْتَهم", giving the mīm fatḥa and making the second hamza between-between; this is the doctrine of all the people of the Hijaz.

It is also possible that "لا يُؤْمِنُونَ" is the khabar of "إنَّ", as though it were said: "إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لا يُؤْمِنُونَ، سَواءٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أأنْذَرْتَهم أمْ لَمْ تُنْذِرْهم" (Those who disbelieve will not believe — it is alike to them whether you warn them or do not warn them). These are people about whom Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, informed the Prophet ﷺ that they would not believe, as He said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا أنا عابِدٌ ما عَبَدْتُمْ﴾ [al-Kāfirūn: 4] ﴿وَلا أنْتُمْ عابِدُونَ ما أعْبُدُ﴾ [al-Kāfirūn: 5].

As for two hamzas when both have kasra — as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿عَلى البِغاءِ إنْ أرَدْنَ تَحَصُّنًا﴾ [al-Nūr: 33] — and when both have ḍamma — as in His saying: ﴿أوْلِياءُ أُولَئِكَ﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 32] — Abū ʿAmr lightens the first hamza in both, saying: "عَلى البِغا إنْ أرَدْنَ" and "أوْلِيا أُولَئِكَ". He makes the first hamza, that of "اَلْبِغاءِ", between hamza and yāʾ, and gives it kasra; and he makes the first hamza in your saying "أوْلِيا أُولَئِكَ" between wāw and hamza, and gives it ḍamma.

Abū ʿUbayda reported that Abū ʿAmr used to put in place of the first hamza a kasra in "اَلْبِغاءِ إنْ" and a ḍamma in "أوْلِياءُ أُولَئِكَ". Abū ʿUbayda reports only what he heard, for he is reliable and trustworthy in the eyes of the scholars; but he does not record a place like this precisely, because what he said is impossible: if the hamza dropped and a kasra or ḍamma replaced it — as he described — the two vowels would remain on no letter, and this is impossible, because a vowel cannot exist except on a vowelled letter.

Abū Isḥāq said: what we reported just now is Sībawayh's transmission from Abū ʿAmr, and he is more precise in this. As for His saying: ﴿السُّفَهاءُ ألا﴾ [al-Baqara: 13],

and His saying: ﴿وَإلَيْهِ النُّشُورُ﴾ [al-Mulk: 15] ﴿أأمِنتُمْ مَن في السَّماءِ أنْ﴾ [al-Mulk: 16] — where the two hamzas differ — Abū ʿUbayda reported that Abū ʿAmr used to replace the second with a fatḥa. This contradicts what Sībawayh reported, and the statement is likewise impossible, because a fatḥa does not stand by itself; it only stands on a letter.

The sum of what the grammarians say on the first question — in the like of His saying "عَلى البِغاءِ إنْ" or "أوْلِياءُ أُولَئِكَ" — is three views, according to the dialect of those other than the people of the Hijaz. The first of these three — the doctrine of Sībawayh and al-Khalīl — is to put in place of the second hamza a between-between hamza: when it has ḍamma, he makes the hamza between wāw and hamza, saying "أوْلِياءُ اُولَئِكَ"; and when it has kasra, he makes the hamza between yāʾ and hamza, saying "عَلى البِغاءِيِنْ". As for Abū ʿAmr, he read as we mentioned. As for Ibn Abī Isḥāq — whose doctrine is the doctrine of a group of the readers — he combines the two hamzas, reading "أوْلِياءُ أُولَئِكَ" and "عَلى البِغاءِ إنْ أرَدْنَ" with both hamzas fully pronounced. As for the case where the two hamzas differ, as in "اَلسُّفَهاءُ ألا", most readers follow the doctrine of Ibn Abī Isḥāq. As for Abū ʿAmr, in Sībawayh's transmission he pronounces the second hamza fully and lightens the first, making it between wāw and hamza, saying "اَلسُّفَهااُ ألا", between-between; and he says "مَن في السَّمايِ أنْ", pronouncing the second fully. As for Sībawayh and al-Khalīl, they say "اَلسُّفَهاءُ ولا", making the second hamza a pure wāw, and in His saying "مَن في السَّماءِ يَنْ" a pure yāʾ with fatḥa. This is all there is in this chapter.

Abū ʿUbayda mentioned that someone transmitted from Abū ʿAmr that, when two hamzas came together, he would drop one of them. This is not established, because analogy does not require it; and Abū ʿUbayd «[Translator's note: so in the text ("أبُو عُبَيْدٍ"), although the passage has been speaking of Abū ʿUbayda.]» did not verify his transmission, because he said: "someone transmitted it"; and in the matter of transmitting a reading from a teacher of recitation, disagreement ought to be slight. If this is sound from him, then he allows it in cases like "سَواءٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أأنْذَرْتَهم أمْ لَمْ تُنْذِرْهم", and in the like of His saying: ﴿آلذَّكَرَيْنِ حَرَّمَ أمِ الأُنْثَيَيْنِ﴾ [al-Anʿām: 143], dropping the hamza of interrogation, because "أمْ" indicates it. The poet said:
لَعَمْرُكَ ما أدْرِي وإنْ كُنْتُ دارِيًا ∗∗∗ شُعَيْثُ بْنُ سَهْمٍ أمْ شُعَيْثُ بْنُ مِنقَرِ
(By your life, I do not know — though I am one who knows — whether it is Shuʿayth ibn Sahm or Shuʿayth ibn Minqar.)
And ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa said:
لَعَمْرُكَ ما أدْرِي وإنْ كُنْتُ دارِيًا ∗∗∗ بِسَبْعٍ رَمَيْنَ الجَمْرَ أمْ بِثَمانِ
(By your life, I do not know — though I am one who knows — whether they threw the pebbles with seven or with eight.)
The first verse was recited by al-Khalīl and Sībawayh, and the second verse is also sound.

zajjaj:85-85.t:
﴿ثُمَّ أنْتُمْ هَؤُلاءِ﴾: the address is to the Jews of Banū Qurayẓa and Banū al-Naḍīr, because they broke faith: some of them killed others, and some of them expelled others from their homes, and this was the breaking of their covenant.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿تَظاهَرُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِالإثْمِ والعُدْوانِ﴾ has been read light and doubled: «تَظاهَرُونَ» and «تَظّاهَرُونَ». Whoever reads it doubled, its original form is «تَتَظاهَرُونَ», and the tāʾ was assimilated into the ẓāʾ because the two points of articulation are close. Whoever reads it light, its original form is also «تَتَظاهَرُونَ», and the second tāʾ was dropped because two tāʾs came together. The interpretation of «تَظاهَرُونَ» is: you aid one another. One says «قَدْ ظاهَرَ فُلانٌ فُلانًا» when he aids him; from it is His saying: ﴿وَكانَ الكافِرُ عَلى رَبِّهِ ظَهِيرًا﴾ [al-Furqān: 55], that is, a helper.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بِالإثْمِ والعُدْوانِ﴾: «العُدْوان» is excess in wrongdoing. One says «عَدا فُلانٌ في ظُلْمِهِ، عَدْوًا، وعُدُوًّا، وعُدْوانًا، وعَداءً»; all of this means overstepping in wrongdoing.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لا تَعْدُوا في السَّبْتِ﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 154] is only from this, that is: do not do wrong on it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإنْ يَأْتُوكم أُسارى تُفادُوهُمْ﴾: the reading of this goes several ways: «أسْرى تَفْدُوهم», «أسْرى تُفادُوهم» and «أُسارى تُفادُوهم»; «أسارى» (with fatḥa) is also permissible, but I know of no one who read it so. The original of the plural is «فُعالى».

Allah made known their self-contradiction regarding their Book: that He had forbidden them to kill them and to expel them from their homes, yet they ransom them when they are taken captive, while they kill them and expel them from their homes. So He rebuked them, saying: ﴿فَما جَزاءُ مَن يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ مِنكم إلا خِزْيٌ في الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾, meaning what befell Banū Qurayẓa and Banū al-Naḍīr: Banū al-Naḍīr were exiled to Syria, and Banū Qurayẓa were annihilated — judgement was passed on them that the fighting men be killed and the offspring taken captive. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿ذَلِكَ لَهم خِزْيٌ في الدُّنْيا﴾ [al-Māʾida: 33]; and for others among the rest of the disbelievers the disgrace in this world is killing, and the taking of the jizya together with abasement and humiliation. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, made known that this does not expiate their sins, and that they will go after that to a mighty punishment, saying: ﴿ذَلِكَ لَهم خِزْيٌ في الدُّنْيا﴾ [al-Māʾida: 33] ﴿وَيَوْمَ القِيامَةِ يُرَدُّونَ إلى أشَدِّ العَذابِ وما اللَّهُ بِغافِلٍ عَمّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾. The meaning of «ثُمَّ أنْتُمْ هَؤُلاءِ تَقْتُلُونَ أنْفُسَكم»: «هَؤُلاءِ» is in the sense of «الَّذِينَ» (relative noun), and «تَقْتُلُونَ» is the ṣila (relative clause) of «هَؤُلاءِ», as in your saying "then you are those who kill yourselves". Similar to it is His saying: ﴿وَما تِلْكَ بِيَمِينِكَ يا مُوسى﴾ [Ṭāhā: 17]. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَهُوَ مُحَرَّمٌ عَلَيْكم إخْراجُهُمْ﴾: «هو» is of two kinds. It may be the pronoun of the expulsion previously mentioned — He said: «وَتُخْرِجُونَ فَرِيقًا مِنكم مِن دِيارِهِمْ ... وهو مُحَرَّمٌ عَلَيْكم إخْراجُهم» — and then, because of the length of the discourse, He made clear that what He forbade is the expulsion. And it may be (the pronoun) of the story, the account, the report (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), as though He said: "and the matter is: their expulsion is forbidden to you", as He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿قُلْ هو اللَّهُ أحَدٌ﴾ [al-Ikhlāṣ: 1], that is: the matter which is the truth is the oneness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

﴿خِزْيٌ﴾: regarding evil and harm one says «خَزِيَ الرَّجُلُ خِزْيًا», and regarding shame one says «خَزِيَ، يَخْزى، خِزايَةً». The meaning of ﴿يُرَدُّونَ إلى أشَدِّ العَذابِ﴾, «عَذابٌ عَظِيمٌ» and «عَذابٌ ألِيمٌ» is that punishment is of two kinds, according to the measure of the sins. The proof of that is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَأنْذَرْتُكم نارًا تَلَظّى﴾ [al-Layl: 14] ﴿لا يَصْلاها إلا الأشْقى﴾ [al-Layl: 15] ﴿الَّذِي كَذَّبَ وتَوَلّى﴾ [al-Layl: 16]; this fire described here is entered only by the disbelievers.

zajjaj:87-87.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنا مُوسى الكِتابَ﴾ means the Torah.

His saying: ﴿وَقَفَّيْنا مِن بَعْدِهِ بِالرُّسُلِ﴾, that is: We sent messenger following messenger in calling to the oneness of Allah and upholding the laws of His religion. One says of that: «فُلانٌ يَقْفُو فُلانًا» when he follows him.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَآتَيْنا عِيسى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ البَيِّناتِ﴾: the meaning of «آتَيْنا» is "We gave", and the meaning of «البَيِّنات» is the signs which creatures [Translator's note: the source reads «المُخَلِّقُون», presumably for «المَخْلُوقُون»] are incapable of, among what ʿĪsā ﷺ was given: his bringing the dead to life and his healing of the one born blind and the leper.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَأيَّدْناهُ بِرُوحِ القُدُسِ﴾: the meaning of «أيَّدْنا» in the language is "We strengthened and fortified". The poet said:
مِن أنْ تَبَدَّلْتَ بِآدٍ آدا
(… because you exchanged strength for strength.)
He means «مِن أنْ تَبَدَّلْتَ بِأيْدٍ آدًا», meaning one strength for another; «الآد» and «الأيْد» are strength.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بِرُوحِ القُدُسِ﴾: «رُوحُ القُدُس» is Jibrīl, peace be upon him, and «القُدُس» is purity; we have explained it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أفَكُلَّما جاءَكم رَسُولٌ بِما لا تَهْوى أنْفُسُكُمُ اسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ﴾: «كُلَّما» is accusative like the accusative of other adverbs (ẓurūf). The meaning of «اسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ» is: you disdained and held yourselves too great to be followers, because they had leadership and were followed, so they preferred this world to the Hereafter.

zajjaj:88-88.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقالُوا قُلُوبُنا غُلْفٌ﴾ is read in two ways: «غُلْفٌ» and «غُلُفٌ». The better of the two readings is «غُلْفٌ» with the lām quiescent, because it has a supporting witness from the Quran. The meaning of «غُلْفٌ» is: having coverings; its singular is «أغْلَف», and «غُلْف» is like «أحْمَر» / «حُمْر». It is as though they said: "our hearts are in containers". The proof of that is His saying: ﴿وَقالُوا قُلُوبُنا في أكِنَّةٍ مِمّا تَدْعُونا إلَيْهِ وفي آذانِنا وقْرٌ ومِن بَيْنِنا وبَيْنِكَ حِجابٌ﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 5]. Whoever reads «غُلُفٌ», it is the plural of «غِلاف»: «غِلاف» / «غُلُف» like «مِثال» / «مُثُل» and «حِمار» / «حُمُر»; the meaning of this would be: "our hearts are containers of knowledge". The first is more likely. «غُلُفٌ» may also be made quiescent, so that one says «غُلْفٌ», as one says «مُثْل» for the plural of «مِثال». So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, made known that the matter is contrary to what they said, and said: ﴿بَلْ لَعَنَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾. The meaning of «لَعَنَهم» in the language is: He put them far away. So the interpretation — and Allah knows best — is: rather, Allah has set a seal upon their hearts, as He said: ﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ﴾ [al-Baqara: 7]. Then He, Mighty and Majestic is He, told that this is a recompense from Him to them for their disbelief, saying: «بَلْ لَعَنَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِكُفْرِهِمْ». «اللَّعْن», as we have described, is putting far away. Al-Shammākh said:
وَماءٍ قَدْ ورَدْتُ لِوَصْلِ أرْوى ∗∗∗ عَلَيْهِ الطَّيْرُ كالوَرَقِ اللَّجِينِ
(Many a water I have come to for the sake of union with Arwā, birds upon it like crushed leaves,)
ذَعَرْتُ بِهِ القَطا ونَفَيْتُ عَنْهُ ∗∗∗ مَقامَ الذِّئْبِ كالرَّجُلِ اللَّعِينِ
(I startled the sand-grouse at it and drove away from it the wolf's haunt, like the banished (laʿīn) man.)

zajjaj:89-89.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلَمّا جاءَهم كِتابٌ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ مُصَدِّقٌ لِما مَعَهُمْ﴾: «جاءَهم» is read with fatḥa on the jīm and full (non-inclined) articulation (tafkhīm), which is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, the highest and oldest dialect; and inclination (imāla) towards kasra is the dialect of Banū Tamīm and many of the Arabs. Its justification is that it is originally of the verbs with yāʾ, so it was inclined to indicate that. The meaning of the Book of Allah here is the Quran. Its derivation is from «الكَتْب», which is the plural of «كَتْبَة», a leather stitch [Translator's note: the source has «الخَرَزَة»]; anything some of which you join to some other by way of bringing together and assembling, you have "written" (katabtahu). «الكَتِيبَة» is the fighting troop; its derivation is from this, because its parts are joined to one another. The speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, which was sent down upon His Prophet was named «كِتاب» (Book), «قُرْآن» (Quran) and «فُرْقان» (Criterion). We have explained the meaning of «كِتاب».
