The meaning of «قُرْآن» is the meaning of gathering: one says «ما قَرَأتْ هَذِهِ النّاقَةُ سَلًى قَطُّ», that is, her womb never closed upon an offspring. The poet said:
هِجانِ اللَّوْنِ لَمْ تَقْرَأْ جَنِينا
(Of pure white colour, she has never borne (lam taqraʾ) a foetus.)
Most people said: she has not gathered a foetus, that is, she has not closed her womb upon a foetus. Quṭrub gave two views on «قُرْآن»: one of them is this, which is the well-known one that most people hold; the other view is not beyond soundness, and it is good. He said: «لَمْ تَقْرَأْ جَنِينًا» means she has not cast it forth gathered; and he said: the meaning of «قَرَأتْ» may be "she uttered it gathered", just as «لَفَظْتُ» (I uttered), from «اللَّفْظ», is derived from «لَفَظْتُ كَذا وكَذا» when you cast it out; so it is as though «قَرَأْتُ القُرْآنَ» means "I uttered it gathered".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿مُصَدِّقٌ لِما مَعَهُمْ﴾, that is: it confirms the Torah and the Gospel and informs them of what is in their books which can only be known through revelation or the reading of books; and they knew that the Prophet ﷺ was unlettered and did not write.

His saying: ﴿وَكانُوا مِن قَبْلُ يَسْتَفْتِحُونَ عَلى الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾: «قَبْلُ» has ḍamma because it is a ghāya (a word cut off from its genitive complement). By right of inflection it would take kasra and fatḥa; but when it was diverted from its normal category it was made indeclinable (mabnī) on ḍamma, so it was built on what would not enter it by right of inflection. It was diverted from its category only because its origin is to be in construct (iḍāfa), and it was made single, indicating the construct; the meaning is "and they were, before this". As for the meaning of «يَسْتَفْتِحُونَ عَلى الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا», there are two views about it. Some said: they used to tell of the truth of the matter of the Prophet ﷺ. And it was said: «وَكانُوا [مِن قَبْلُ] يَسْتَفْتِحُونَ عَلى الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا»: they used to seek victory by mentioning the Prophet ﷺ. «فَلَمّا جاءَهم ما عَرَفُوا», that is, what they used to seek victory through and whose truth they used to tell of, they disbelieved, while they were certain — they deliberately chose schism out of enmity to Allah.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَلَعْنَةُ اللَّهِ عَلى الكافِرِينَ﴾: we have explained «اللَّعْنَة». The apodosis (jawāb) of «وَلَمّا جاءَهم كِتابٌ» is omitted, because its meaning is known; «فَلَمّا جاءَهم ما عَرَفُوا كَفَرُوا بِهِ» indicates it.

zajjaj:42-42.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تَلْبِسُوا الحَقَّ بِالباطِلِ وتَكْتُمُوا الحَقَّ﴾. One says ”لَبَسْتُ عَلَيْهِمُ الأمْرَ، ألْبِسُهُ“ when you have obscured the matter for them, and ”لَبِسْتُ الثَّوْبَ، ألْبَسُهُ“ ("I put on the garment"). The meaning of the verse: do not confound the truth; the truth here is the matter of the Prophet ﷺ and what he brought of the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. His saying ”بِالباطِلِ“ means: with what they distort.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَأنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, that is: you commit your confounding of the truth and your concealing of it with knowledge and insight on your part.
The iʿrāb of ”وَلا تَلْبِسُوا“: jussive through the prohibition, and the sign of the jussive is the dropping of the nūn; its origin is ”تَلْبِسُونَ“.
”تَكْتُمُونَ“ may be jussive, in the sense of ”وَلا تَكْتُمُوا الحَقَّ“ ("and do not conceal the truth"), and it may be accusative, the sign of the accusative also being the dropping of the nūn. If you make it accusative, it is in the sense of the answer with the wāw. The doctrine of al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, al-Akhfash and a group of the Basrans is that everything that is accusative in this chapter is so by a suppressed ”أنْ“, as though you said: ”لا يَكُنْ مِنكم إلْباسُ الحَقِّ وكِتْمانُهُ“ ("let there be from you no confounding of the truth and concealing of it"), as though He said ”وَأنْ تَكْتُمُوهُ“; and ”تَلْبِسُوا“ indicates a "confounding", just as you say ”مَن كَذَبَ كانَ شَرًّا“ ("whoever lies, it is an evil"), where what is at the head of your speech indicates the lying, so you omitted it.

zajjaj:44-44.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أتَأْمُرُونَ النّاسَ بِالبِرِّ وتَنْسَوْنَ أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾. The alif is the alif of interrogation, and its meaning here is affirmation (taqrīr) and rebuke, as though it were said to them: "You are upon this way." The meaning of this speech – and Allah knows best – is that they used to command their followers to hold fast to their Book while they themselves abandoned holding fast to it, because their denial of the Prophet ﷺ is their abandoning of holding fast to it. It is also possible – and Allah knows best – that they used to command the giving of charity while being miserly with it, because they were described as having hardened hearts and as consuming usury and illicit gain, and they had been forbidden usury; so withholding charity falls within this category.

zajjaj:45-45.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّبْرِ والصَّلاةِ﴾. If someone asks: why was it said to them ”اِسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّبْرِ“ ("seek help through patience")? And what is the benefit in it? [The answer is that] this address was originally an address to the People of the Book, who had leadership among their followers; so it was said to them: seek help, against what [stands in your way], through prayer, which will remove from you the craving for leadership, because in prayer is recited what makes one desire what is with Allah and makes one renounce all the affairs of this world. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿إنَّ الصَّلاةَ تَنْهى عَنِ الفَحْشاءِ والمُنْكَرِ﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 45].
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإنَّها لَكَبِيرَةٌ إلا عَلى الخاشِعِينَ﴾: the meaning is that the prayer accompanied by belief in the Prophet ﷺ is great: it weighs heavily on the disbelievers and is grievous to them along with belief in the Prophet ﷺ. The humble one (al-khāshiʿ) – the lowly, obedient, submissive one – does not care about a leadership he had along with disbelief, when he moves over to faith.

zajjaj:46-46.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الَّذِينَ يَظُنُّونَ أنَّهم مُلاقُو رَبِّهِمْ﴾. ”اَلظَّنُّ“ here has the meaning of certainty, and the meaning is: "those who are certain of that"; had they been doubting, they would have been astray disbelievers. ”اَلظَّنُّ“ in the meaning of certainty exists in the language. Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma said:
؎فَقُلْتُ لَهم ظُنُّوا بِألْفَيْ مُقاتِلٍ ∗∗∗ سَراتُهم في الفارِسِيِّ المُسَرَّدِ
(So I said to them: be sure of two thousand warriors, their chiefs clad in close-knit Persian mail.)
Its meaning is: be certain. One of the earlier scholars said that ẓann is used in the sense of a knowledge you have not witnessed, even if its reality has become established in your soul. This is a view, except that the people of the language did not mention it. Abū Isḥāq [al-Zajjāj] said: I heard this from Ismāʿīl ibn Isḥāq al-Qāḍī, may Allah have mercy on him, who transmitted it from Zayd ibn Aslam.
His saying ”أنَّهم“ here: ”إنَّهم“ with kasra is not suitable in its place, because the ẓann is operative (wāqiʿ), so it must be followed by ”أنَّ“, unless there is a lām in the khabar (predicate). In ”أنَّهم إلَيْهِ راجِعُونَ“ both fatḥa and kasra are suitable, but the fatḥa is the proper way, on which the reading is based. If you say in ordinary speech ”وَإنَّهم إلَيْهِ راجِعُونَ“, you construe the speech according to the meaning, as though it were ”وَهم إلَيْهِ راجِعُونَ“ ("and they are returning to Him"), with ”أنَّ“ «[Translator's note: so vocalised in the text; the context indicates the kasra form إنَّ.]» entering for emphasis. Were it not for that, it would not be permissible for you to cancel the operation of ẓann with the lām when you say ”ظَنَنْتُ إنَّكَ لَعالِمٌ“ ("I thought: you are indeed learned").
The meaning of ”مُلاقُو رَبِّهِمْ“ is ”مُلاقُونَ رَبَّهُمْ“, because the active participle here is indefinite; but the nūn is dropped for lightness. It is not permissible in the Qurʾān to retain it, because that is contrary to the Muṣḥaf, and it is not permissible for anything in the Muṣḥaf that is agreed upon to be contradicted, because following the Muṣḥaf is the root of following the Sunna.

zajjaj:47-47.t: His saying: ﴿يا بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَتِيَ الَّتِي أنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكم وأنِّي فَضَّلْتُكم عَلى العالَمِينَ﴾. Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, reminded them of His favour upon them in their forebears. The proof of this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ نَجَّيْناكم مِن آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 49], whereas those addressed by the Qurʾān had not seen Pharaoh nor his people; but He, Mighty and Majestic is He, reminded them that He had never ceased bestowing favour upon them, because His bestowing favour on their forebears is a bestowing of favour upon them. The proof of this is that the Arabs and all people say ”أكْرَمْتُكَ بِإكْرامِي أخاكَ“ ("I honoured you by my honouring your brother"), although the preference reached only his brother. The Arabs in particular regard what belonged to their forefathers as a glory for themselves, and whatever contained blame they count as a disgrace upon themselves, even if it was in the past of their forefathers and forebears.

zajjaj:7-7.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ وعَلى سَمْعِهِمْ وعَلى أبْصارِهِمْ غِشاوَةٌ﴾: the meaning of "خَتَمَ" (seal) — in the language — and "طَبَعَ" (stamp) is one meaning, namely covering a thing and making sure that nothing enters it, as He said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أمْ عَلى قُلُوبٍ أقْفالُها﴾ [Muḥammad: 24], and He said, exalted be His mention: ﴿كَلا بَلْ رانَ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 14], meaning: what they used to earn has overpowered their hearts. Likewise He stamped them because of their disbelief. They did hear, see and understand, but they did not use these senses in a way that would avail them, so they became like one who does not hear and does not see. The poet said:
أصَمُّ عَمّا ساءَهُ سَمِيعُ
(Deaf to what displeases him, hearing [otherwise].)
Likewise His saying, Majestic and Mighty is He: "وَعَلى أبْصارِهِمْ غِشاوَةٌ": it is the covering. As for His saying "وَعَلى سَمْعِهِمْ" while He means "وَعَلى أسْماعِهِمْ" (their hearings), there are three explanations of it. One of them is that السَّمْع has the meaning of a maṣdar (verbal noun), so it was put in the singular, as you say: "يُعْجِبُنِي حَدِيثُكم" (your talk pleases me) and "يُعْجِبُنِي ضَرْبُكم" (your striking pleases me); it is singular because it is a maṣdar. It is also possible that, since He annexed السَّمْع to them, it indicated the meaning of "أسْماعِهِمْ". The poet said:
بِها جِيَفُ الحَسْرى فَأمّا عِظامُها ∗∗∗ فَبِيضٌ وأمّا جِلْدُها فَصَلِيبُ
(In it are the carcasses of exhausted camels: as for their bones, they are white; and as for their skin [lit. its skin], it is dry and hard.)
The poet also said:
لا تُنْكِرِي القَتْلَ وقَدْ سُبِينا ∗∗∗ في حَلْقِكم عَظْمٌ وقَدْ شَجِينا
(Do not deny the killing when we have been taken captive: in your throat [i.e. throats] is a bone, and we have choked.)
Its meaning is: in your throats (حُلُوقِكُمْ). And he said:
كَأنَّهُ وجْهُ تُرْكِيَّيْنِ قَدْ غَضِبا ∗∗∗ مُسْتَهْدَفٍ لِطِعانٍ غَيْرِ تَذْيِيبِ
(As though it were the face [i.e. faces] of two Turks who have grown angry, set up as a target for thrusting that does not falter.)
«[Translator's note: the text announces three explanations but states two explicitly.]»

As for "غِشاوَةٌ": everything that envelops a thing is built, in the speech of the Arabs, on the pattern "فِعالَةٌ", such as "اَلْغِشاوَةُ" (covering), "اَلْعِمامَةُ" (turban), "اَلْقِلادَةُ" (necklace) and "اَلْعِصابَةُ" (headband). Likewise the names of crafts, because the meaning of a craft is the comprehending of everything in it, such as "اَلْخِياطَةُ" (tailoring) and "اَلْقِصارَةُ" (fulling). Likewise for everyone who takes control of something, the pattern al-fiʿāla applies to it, as in "اَلْحِلاقَةُ" «[Translator's note: so in the text; probably a misprint for اَلْخِلافَةُ (the caliphate).]» and "اَلْإمارَةُ" (governorship). The nominative in "غِشاوَةٌ" is the standard, and it is the way of the readers. The accusative is permissible grammatically, on the basis that the meaning is "وَجَعَلَ عَلى أبْصارِهِمْ غِشاوَةً" (and He placed a covering over their eyes), as Allah said, Mighty and Majestic is He, in another place: ﴿وَخَتَمَ عَلى سَمْعِهِ وقَلْبِهِ وجَعَلَ عَلى بَصَرِهِ غِشاوَةً﴾ [al-Jāthiya: 23]. Its like in poetry, of what is construed according to its meaning, is his saying:
يا لَيْتَ بَعْلَكِ قَدْ غَدا ∗∗∗ مُتَقَلِّدًا سَيْفًا ورُمْحا
(Would that your husband had gone out in the morning girded with a sword and a spear.)
Its meaning is: girded with a sword and carrying a spear. It is also transmitted as "غَشْوَةٌ", but the right form is what we have mentioned; "غَشْوَةٌ" is only a reversion to the origin, because all maṣdars revert to "فَعْلَةٌ". The nominative and accusative in "غَشْوَةٌ" are as in "غِشاوَةٌ".

zajjaj:8-8.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَمِنَ النّاسِ مَن يَقُولُ آمَنّا بِاللَّهِ وبِاليَوْمِ الآخِرِ وما هم بِمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾: by this He meant the hypocrites. The inflection of "مِن" is the pause (i.e. it is indeclinable with sukūn), except that it was given fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters: the vowelless nūn of your saying "مِن" and the vowelless first nūn of "اَلنّاسِ" «[Translator's note: so in the text; the vowelless letter at the start of اَلنّاسِ is the lām of the article.]». Basically it should have been given kasra because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, but it was given fatḥa because of the heaviness of two kasras coming together: if it were "مِنِ النّاسِ", that would be heavy. As for "عَنِ النّاسِ", only kasra is permissible in it, because the first letter of "عَنْ" has fatḥa. As for "مَن", its inflection is the pause, because in a statement it is not a complete noun except with a ṣila (relative clause), and inflection does not occur in part of a noun. As for the assimilation (idghām) into the yāʾ in "مَن يَقُولُ", nothing else is possible: you say "مَن يُقَوَّمُ", assimilating with nasalisation (ghunna) and without nasalisation.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَما هم بِمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾: the bāʾ entered to emphasise the meaning of negation, because if you say "ما زَيْدٌ أخُوكَ" (Zayd is not your brother) and the listener does not hear "ما", he will think you are affirming; but if you say "ما زَيْدٌ بِأخِيكَ" and "ما هم بِمُؤْمِنِينَ", the listener knows that you are negating. And so it is with everything in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

zajjaj:9-9.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: by it He also means the hypocrites. The meaning of "يُخادِعُونَ" is: they display something other than what is in their souls. Dissimulation (al-taqiyya) is also called "خِداعًا" (deception); so, as it were, when they displayed Islam and concealed disbelief, their dissimulation became deception. The pattern fāʿala is used here for other than two parties, because this pattern often occurs in the language for a single agent, as in "عاقَبْتُ اللِّصَّ" (I punished the thief) and "طارَقْتُ النَّعْلَ" (I sewed one sole upon another).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَما يَخْدَعُونَ إلا أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾: its interpretation is that the deception returns upon them as torment and punishment. ﴿وَما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾: that is, they do not know that it returns upon them as torment. It is said "ما شَعُرْتُ بِهِ", i.e. I did not know of it; and "لَيْتَ شِعْرِي ما صَنَعْتَ" means: would that I knew what you did.

zajjaj:10-10.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ﴾: its meaning is hypocrisy. Sickness and illness (marad) are said both of the body and of religion, just as health is said both of the body and of religion. As for the meaning of His saying "مَرَضٌ", Abū ʿUbayda said: its meaning is doubt and hypocrisy. Illness in the heart applies to everything by which a person departs from soundness in religion.

His saying: ﴿فَزادَهُمُ اللَّهُ مَرَضًا﴾: there are two answers on it. Some said: Allah increased them (in sickness) through their disbelief, as He said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بَلْ طَبَعَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْها بِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 155]. Some of the philologists said: Allah increased them (in sickness) through what He sent down to them of the Qur'an, for they doubted it as they doubted what came before it. He said: the proof of this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذا ما أُنْـزِلَتْ سُورَةٌ﴾ [al-Tawba: 124], up to His saying: ﴿فَأمّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا فَزادَتْهم إيمانًا وهم يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ﴾ [al-Tawba: 124] ﴿وَأمّا الَّذِينَ في قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ فَزادَتْهم رِجْسًا إلى رِجْسِهِمْ﴾ [al-Tawba: 125]. This is a clear and evident view, and Allah knows best.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَهم عَذابٌ ألِيمٌ﴾: its meaning is painful, its pain reaching their hearts. The interpretation of "ألِيمٌ" in the language is "مُؤْلِمٌ" (causing pain). The poet — ʿAmr ibn Maʿdī Karib al-Zubaydī — said:
أمِن رَيْحانَةِ الدّاعِي السَّمِيعِ ∗∗∗ يُؤَرِّقُنِي وأصْحابِي هُجُوعُ
(Is it from Rayḥāna that the caller who makes himself heard keeps me awake, while my companions are asleep?)
The meaning of "اَلسَّمِيعُ" (here) is "اَلْمُسْمِعُ" (the one who makes heard).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بِما كانُوا يَكْذِبُونَ﴾; it is also read "يُكَذِّبُونَ". Whoever reads "يَكْذِبُونَ" without doubling: their lie is their saying that they are believers; Allah said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَما هم بِمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 8]. As for "يُكَذِّبُونَ" with doubling, its meaning is: because of their denying the Prophet ﷺ.

zajjaj:90-90.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بِئْسَما اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾: when «بِئْسَ» falls upon «ما», «ما» is treated with it as an indefinite noun. That is so only with «نِعْمَ» and «بِئْسَ», because they do not govern a proper name; they govern only an indefinite noun indicating a genus, or a noun with alif and lām indicating a genus. They are like that only because «نِعْمَ» comprehends all praise and «بِئْسَ» comprehends all blame: when you say «نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ» ("an excellent man is Zayd"), Zayd has merited the praise found in the whole of his genus. Abū Isḥāq [al-Zajjāj] said: in «نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ» there are four dialectal forms: «نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ», «نَعِمَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ», «نِعِمَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ» and «نَعْمَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ». Likewise when you say «بِئْسَ الرَّجُلُ», you indicate that he has comprehended the blame found in the whole of his genus.

So, since it comprehends the praise of genera, it was not permissible for it to govern anything but a word for a genus. When there is with it a generic noun without alif and lām, it is always accusative, and when it has alif and lām it is always nominative, as in your saying «نِعْمَ رَجُلًا زَيْدٌ» and «نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ». When «رَجُل» is accusative, it is as a tamyīz (specification), and in «نِعْمَ» there is an implied (muḍmar) noun on condition of being explained (ʿalā sharīṭat al-tafsīr), and «زَيْدٌ» makes clear who this praised one is, because when you say «نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ» it is not known whom you mean; so by your saying «زَيْدٌ» you mean "this praised one is Zayd". Sībawayh and al-Khalīl said all that we have said about «نِعْمَ» and «بِئْسَ», and they said: if you wish, you may make «زَيْد» nominative because it is a postponed mubtadaʾ (subject), as though, when you said «نِعْمَ رَجُلًا زَيْدٌ», you said «نِعْمَ زَيْدٌ نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ» [Translator's note: so in the source; the intended paraphrase is presumably «زَيْدٌ نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ», "Zayd — an excellent man"]. Likewise «ما» with «نِعْمَ» is without a ṣila (relative clause), because a ṣila clarifies and specifies, while the purpose with «نِعْمَ» is that an indefinite noun or a genus should follow it. So His saying ﴿بِئْسَما اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ means "evil is a thing (shayʾan) for which they have sold themselves".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أنْ يَكْفُرُوا بِما أنْـزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾: its position is nominative; the meaning is: that blamed thing is that they disbelieve in what Allah has sent down.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَنِعِمّا هِيَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 271] is as though He said: "excellent is it as a thing". Some said: «نِعْمَ» with «ما» is equivalent to «حَبَّ» with «ذا»: you say «حَبَّذا زَيْدٌ», «حَبَّذا هي» and «نِعِمّا هي». The first view is the doctrine of the grammarians. All the grammarians related: «بِئْسَما تَزْوِيجٌ ولا مَهْرٌ» ("an evil thing is marriage without a dowry"), the meaning in it being: "evil as a thing is marriage without a dowry".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أنْ يَكْفُرُوا بِما أنْـزَلَ اللَّهُ بَغْيًا أنْ يُنَـزِّلَ اللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ عَلى مَن يَشاءُ مِن عِبادِهِ﴾: its meaning is that they disbelieved out of envious transgression (baghy) and enmity towards the Prophet ﷺ, because they did not doubt his prophethood ﷺ; they only envied him for the favour Allah gave him. The meaning is: they disbelieved out of envy, because Allah sent down the favour upon the Prophet ﷺ. «بَغْيًا» is accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun) that is a mafʿūl lahu (object of purpose), as you say «فَعَلْتُ ذَلِكَ حَذَرَ الشَّرِّ» ("I did that for fear of evil"), that is, «لِحَذَرِ الشَّرِّ», as though you said "I feared a fearing". Similar to it in poetry is the saying of the poet — Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī:
وَأغْفِرُ عَوْراءَ الكَرِيمِ ادِّخارَهُ ∗∗∗ وأُعْرِضُ عَنْ شَتْمِ اللَّئِيمِ تَكَرُّما
(I forgive the noble man's lapse, to keep him in store, and I turn away from the base man's insult out of magnanimity.)
The meaning is: I forgive the noble man's lapse for keeping him in store, and I turn away from the base man's insult for magnanimity; and it is as though he said: "I keep the noble man in store, a keeping (iddikhāran), and I act magnanimously towards the noble man, a magnanimity" [Translator's note: so in the source; «الكَرِيم» in the second clause is presumably for «اللَّئِيم», as the following sentence shows], because his saying «أغْفِرُ عَوْراءَ الكَرِيمِ» means "I keep the noble man in store", and his saying «وَأُعْرِضُ عَنْ شَتْمِ اللَّئِيمِ تَكَرُّمًا» means "I act magnanimously towards the base man". The position of the second «أنْ» is accusative; the meaning is: "that they disbelieve in what Allah sent down because Allah sends down", that is, they disbelieved for this reason; its explanation is like what we have explained.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَباءُوا بِغَضَبٍ عَلى غَضَبٍ﴾: the meaning of «باؤُوا» in the language is "they bore"; one says «قَدْ بُؤْتُ بِهَذا الذَّنْبِ», that is, I have borne it. As for the meaning of «بِغَضَبٍ عَلى غَضَبٍ», there are two views about it. Some said: with wrath because of disbelief in the Prophet ﷺ, upon wrath for disbelief in ʿĪsā ﷺ — meaning by them the Jews. And it was said: «فَباؤُوا بِغَضَبٍ عَلى غَضَبٍ», that is, with a sin by which they deserved the Fire, upon a previous sin by which they also deserved the Fire.

zajjaj:91-91.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذا قِيلَ لَهم آمِنُوا بِما أنْـزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾, that is, in the Quran which Allah sent down upon the Prophet ﷺ, ﴿قالُوا نُؤْمِنُ بِما أُنْـزِلَ عَلَيْنا﴾. Allah has made clear that they do not believe in what was sent down upon them, and we have explained that previously. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَيَكْفُرُونَ بِما وراءَهُ وهو الحَقُّ﴾ means: and they disbelieve in what is after it, that is, in what came after that which was sent down upon them, ﴿وَهُوَ الحَقُّ مُصَدِّقًا لِما مَعَهُمْ﴾. This shows that they have disbelieved in what is with them, since they disbelieved in what confirms what is with them.

«مُصَدِّقًا» is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), and this is a corroborative ḥāl (ḥāl muʾakkida). Sībawayh, al-Khalīl and all the grammarians whose knowledge is relied upon held that your saying «هو زَيْدٌ قائِمًا» is an error, because your saying «هو زَيْدٌ» is a pronoun standing for a previously mentioned noun, so there is no benefit in the ḥāl: the ḥāl here would entail that when he is standing he is Zayd, and when he leaves off standing he is not Zayd, and this is an error. As for your saying «هو زَيْدٌ مَعْرُوفًا» and ﴿هُوَ الحَقُّ مُصَدِّقًا﴾ [Fāṭir: 31], there is benefit in the ḥāl, as though you said "take note of him as known", and it is as though it were equivalent to your saying «هو زَيْدٌ حَقًّا» ("he is Zayd truly"). So «مَعْرُوفًا» is a ḥāl, because he is Zayd only in that he is known as Zayd; and likewise «الحَقّ»: the Quran is the truth, since it confirms the books of the messengers.

Allah gave them the lie in their saying «نُؤْمِنُ بِما أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْنا», and said: ﴿قُلْ فَلِمَ تَقْتُلُونَ أنْبِياءَ اللَّهِ مِن قَبْلُ إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾, that is: in what book was the killing of a prophet permitted?! And what religion and faith permitted that?! If someone says: "Why was it said to them ﴿فَلِمَ تَقْتُلُونَ أنْبِياءَ اللَّهِ مِن قَبْلُ﴾ when these people never killed a prophet?", it is said to him: the lexicographers have given two views on this. One of them: the address to those of the people of Mecca [Translator's note: so in the source; the context concerns the Jews of Medina] who were present and to those absent is one address; so if their forebears killed the prophets and they persist in that way, they have shared with them in killing them. It was also said: why were you content with that deed? This second view comes back to the meaning of the first. It is permissible to use here the form of the imperfect while the meaning is past because of His saying «مِن قَبْلُ» (before). The proof of that is His saying: ﴿قُلْ قَدْ جاءَكم رُسُلٌ مِن قَبْلِي بِالبَيِّناتِ وبِالَّذِي قُلْتُمْ فَلِمَ قَتَلْتُمُوهُمْ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 183]; so His saying «فَلِمَ تَقْتُلُونَ» is equivalent to «فَلِمَ قَتَلْتُمْ» ("why did you kill"). Two views have been given about His saying «إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ»: one of them is "you were not believers", and it was said: "your faith is no faith". Faith (īmān) here applies to the basis of creed and religion; so it was said to them: "a faith is no faith if it calls to the killing of the prophets".

zajjaj:93-93.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ أخَذْنا مِيثاقَكم ورَفَعْنا فَوْقَكُمُ الطُّورَ﴾: we have explained it previously.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَأُشْرِبُوا في قُلُوبِهِمُ العِجْلَ بِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾: its meaning is "they were made to drink the love of the calf"; «حُبَّ» (love) was dropped and «العِجْل» was put in its place, as the poet said:
وَكَيْفَ تُواصِلُ مَن أصْبَحَتْ ∗∗∗ خِلالَتُهُ كَأبِي مَرْحَبِ
(And how can you keep up ties with one whose friendship has become like Abū Marḥab?)
That is, "like the friendship of Abū Marḥab". And as he said:
وَشَرُّ المَنايا مَيِّتٌ بَيْنَ أهْلِهِ ∗∗∗ كَهَلْكِ الفَتى قَدْ أسْلَمَ الحَيَّ حاضِرُهْ
(The worst of deaths is one dying among his family, like the perishing of a young man whose people present have abandoned the tribe.)
The meaning is: "the worst of deaths is the death of one dying …".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾, that is: Allah did that to them as a recompense for disbelief, as He said: ﴿بَلْ طَبَعَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْها بِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 155].

His saying: ﴿بِئْسَما يَأْمُرُكم بِهِ إيمانُكم إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾: we have explained it, that is: you were not believers, for evil is the faith that commands you to disbelief.

zajjaj:48-48.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واتَّقُوا يَوْمًا لا تَجْزِي نَفْسٌ عَنْ نَفْسٍ شَيْئًا﴾, by which He means the Day of Resurrection. The Jews used to claim that their forefathers the prophets would intercede for them with Allah, so Allah made them despair of that.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا يُؤْخَذُ مِنها عَدْلٌ﴾: ”اَلْعَدْلُ“ here is the ransom. The meaning of ”لا تَجْزِي نَفْسٌ عَنْ نَفْسٍ شَيْئًا“ is: no soul will avail in it (fīhi); and it was [also] said: will not avail it (tajzīhi). Omitting ”فِيهِ“ here is acceptable, because ”في“ with an adverb of time (ẓarf) may be omitted: you say ”أتَيْتُكَ اليَوْمَ“ ("I came to you today") and ”أتَيْتُكَ في اليَوْمِ“ ("I came to you in the day"); when you use a pronoun you say ”أتَيْتُكَ فِيهِ“ ("I came to you in it"), and you may also say ”أتَيْتُكَهُ“. The poet said:
؎وَيَوْمًا شَهِدْناهُ سُلَيْمًا وعامِرًا ∗∗∗ قَلِيلًا سِوى الطَّعْنِ النِّهالِ نَوافِلُهْ
(And many a day on which we witnessed Sulaym and ʿĀmir, whose spoils were few apart from thirsty spear-thrusts.)
He meant: we witnessed on it. Some grammarians said that what is omitted here is the hāʾ, because adverbs of time, in his view, may not be omitted; this is the view of al-Kisāʾī.
The Basrans and a group of the Kufans say that what is omitted is ”فِيهِ“. The grammarians distinguished between adverbs and nouns other than adverbs, saying: omission with adverbs is permissible; just as it was with its overt form, so also is the omission with its pronoun. If you said ”اَلَّذِي سِرْتُ اليَوْمُ“ ("the day [that] I travelled is …"), meaning ”اَلَّذِي سِرْتُ فِيهِ“, it is permissible, because you say ”سِرْتُ اليَوْمَ“ and ”سِرْتُ فِيهِ“. But if you said ”اَلَّذِي تَكَلَّمْتُ فِيهِ زَيْدٌ“ ("the one I spoke about is Zayd"), ”اَلَّذِي تَكَلَّمْتُ زَيْدٌ“ would not be permissible: for you say ”تَكَلَّمْتُ اليَوْمَ“ and ”تَكَلَّمْتُ فِيهِ“ [of a day], but in your saying ”تَكَلَّمْتُ في زَيْدٍ“ ("I spoke about Zayd") you may not say ”تَكَلَّمْتُ زَيْدًا“.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ”تُقْبَلُ مِنها شَفاعَةٌ“ – [shafāʿa] is nominative because it is the noun of a verb whose agent is not named (i.e. nāʾib fāʿil, deputy agent). When the one who did the act to a noun is not named, it is put in the nominative, because the verb becomes a statement about it just as it becomes a statement about the fāʿil (agent). You say ”لا يُقْبَلُ مِنها شَفاعَةٌ“ and ”لا تُقْبَلُ“, because the femininity of what does not procreate is not real (ghayr ḥaqīqī), so in the verb you have the choice of masculine or feminine form: you say ”قُبِلَ مِنكَ الشَّفاعَةُ“ and ”قَدْ قُبِلَتْ مِنكَ الشَّفاعَةُ“ ("the intercession was accepted from you"). Likewise ﴿فَمَن جاءَهُ مَوْعِظَةٌ﴾ [al-Baqara: 275], because the meaning of ”مَوْعِظَةٌ“ and ”وَعْظٌ“, and of ”شَفاعَةٌ“ and ”شَفْعٌ“, is one; that is why the masculine and the feminine came, according to the form and the meaning.
As for what is rational, or from which there is offspring and birth, such as ”اِمْرَأةٌ“ (woman), ”رَجُلٌ“ (man), ”ناقَةٌ“ (she-camel) and ”جَمَلٌ“ (he-camel), the masculine form is valid for its feminine «[Translator's note: so in the text; the following sentences treat this usage as ugly though tolerable, and «لا يصح», "is not valid", may have been intended.]»: if you said ”قامَ جارَتُكَ“ ("your [female] neighbour stood", with masculine verb) or ”نُحِرَ ناقَتُكَ“ ("your she-camel was slaughtered", with masculine verb), it would be ugly, though it is permissible despite its ugliness, because "she-camel" and "neighbour (f.)" indicate the meaning of femininity, so their form is deemed sufficient in place of putting the verb in the feminine. But for names that apply to males and to female bearers, the mark of the feminine is indispensable, because speech is for conveying information and its purpose is clarity. If a woman were named ”قاسِمٌ“ (Qāsim), it would not be permissible to say ”جاءَنِي قاسِمٌ“ ("Qāsim came to me", masculine verb), for it would not be known whether you meant a male or a female. There is no way to omit this tāʾ when it distinguishes between two meanings; just as, when two men have been mentioned, you may not say ”قَدْ قامَ“ ("he has stood") but only ”قاما“ ("they two stood"). So the mark of the feminine, where there is ambiguity, is like the mark of the dual here.

zajjaj:49-49.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ نَجَّيْناكم مِن آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾. The position of ”إذْ“ is accusative, as though He said: ”واذْكُرُوا إذْ نَجَّيْناكم مِن آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ“ ("and remember when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh"). ”آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ“ means his followers and those who were on his religion. Likewise "the family (āl) of the prophets", Allah's blessings be upon them, means those who were on their religion; and likewise our saying ”صَلّى اللَّهُ عَلى مُحَمَّدٍ وآلِهِ“: the meaning of ”آلِهِ“ is those of his household and others who followed him. The meaning of addressing them here is to remind them of the favour upon them in their forebears, as we have described.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يَسُومُونَكم سُوءَ العَذابِ﴾. The meaning of ”يَسُومُونَكم“ in the language is: they inflict upon you. The meaning of ”سُوءَ العَذابِ“ is: severe punishment. Although all punishment is evil, it was made indefinite (nukkira) in this place only because it is the most extreme treatment that a subject can be dealt «[Translator's note: so in the text («فإنما نُكِّر … مرعيّ»); the wording appears corrupt and is rendered as closely as possible.]»; that is why it was said ”سُوءَ العَذابِ“, that is, what reaches in harm a point beyond which there is no limit. He explained it by His saying: ﴿يُذَبِّحُونَ أبْناءَكُمْ﴾.
The reading agreed upon is ”يُذَبِّحُونَ“ with doubling (tashdīd), and an irregular (shādhdh) transmission has ”يَذْبَحُونَ أبْناءَكم“. The agreed reading is more emphatic, because ”يُذَبِّحُونَ“ is for multiplicity, while ”يَذْبَحُونَ“ may be for little or much; so the meaning of multiplicity is more emphatic here.
”أبْناءَكم“ is the plural of ”اِبْنٌ“ (son). The origin is as if it were the plural of ”بَنَيٌ“ or ”بَنَوٌ“. One says ”اِبْنٌ بَيِّنُ البُنُوَّةِ“ ("a son of evident sonship"), so it could be ”فَعَلٌ“ or ”فِعْلٌ“, as though its origin were ”بَنايَةٌ“. Those who said ”بَنُونَ“ seem to have made the plural of ”بَنَيًا“ ”بَنُونَ“; so ”أبْناءُ“ is the plural of ”فَعَلٌ“ or ”فِعْلٌ“.
”بِنْتٌ“ (daughter) shows that it may properly be ”فِعْلًا“; and it may be ”فَعَلٌ“ transferred to ”فِعْلٌ“, just as ”أُخْتٌ“ (sister) was transferred from ”فَعَلٌ“ to ”فُعْلٌ“. As for ”بَناتٌ“, it is not the plural of ”بِنْتٌ“ according to its form; rather it was returned to its origin and pluralised as ”بَناتٌ“, on the basis that the origin of ”بِنْتٌ“ is ”فِعْلَةٌ“, as though it were one of the words whose final radical (lām) has been dropped.
Al-Akhfash prefers that what has been dropped from ”اِبْنٌ“ is the wāw; he said: because it is more often the wāw that is dropped, owing to its heaviness. But the yāʾ is also dropped for heaviness. Abū Isḥāq [al-Zajjāj] said: the proof of that is that for ”يَدًا“ (hand) they agreed that what was dropped from it is the yāʾ, and they have a decisive proof of this consensus: one says ”يَدَيْتُ إلَيْهِ يَدًا“ ("I did him a favour"). And ”دَمٌ“ (blood) has had the yāʾ dropped from it; one says ”دَمٌ“ and ”دَمَيانِ“ (two bloods). The poet said:
؎فَلَوْ أنّا عَلى حَجَرٍ ذُبِحْنا ∗∗∗ جَرى الدَّمَيانِ بِالخَبَرِ اليَقِينِ
(Were we slaughtered upon a stone, the two bloods would flow [apart], bringing the certain news.)
”اَلْبُنُوَّةُ“ is not decisive evidence for the wāw, because they say ”اَلْفُتُوَّةُ“ (youth) yet ”اَلْفَتَيانِ“ in the dual; He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿وَدَخَلَ مَعَهُ السِّجْنَ فَتَيانِ﴾ [Yūsuf: 36]. So for ”اِبْنٌ“ it is possible that what was dropped is the wāw or the yāʾ, and in my view the two are equal.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَفِي ذَلِكم بَلاءٌ مِن رَبِّكم عَظِيمٌ﴾, meaning: in the deliverance from the people of Pharaoh. ”اَلْبَلاءُ“ here is the favour. It is related that al-Aḥnaf said: ”اَلْبَلاءُ، ثُمَّ الثَّناءُ“, that is: the bestowing of favour, then the thanks. Zuhayr said:
؎جَزى اللَّهُ بِالإحْسانِ ما فَعَلا بِنا ∗∗∗ وأبْلاهُما خَيْرَ البَلاءِ الَّذِي يَبْلُو
(May Allah repay with kindness what the two did for us, and grant them the best of the favours that He bestows.)
And Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿وَلِيُبْلِيَ المُؤْمِنِينَ مِنهُ بَلاءً حَسَنًا﴾ [al-Anfāl: 17].

zajjaj:50-50.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ فَرَقْنا بِكُمُ البَحْرَ فَأنْجَيْناكم وأغْرَقْنا آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ وأنْتُمْ تَنْظُرُونَ﴾. The position of ”إذْ“ is accusative, like the one before it. The meaning of ”فَرَقْنا بِكُمُ البَحْرَ“ has come explained in another verse, namely His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَأوْحَيْنا إلى مُوسى أنِ اضْرِبْ بِعَصاكَ البَحْرَ فانْفَلَقَ فَكانَ كُلُّ فِرْقٍ كالطَّوْدِ العَظِيمِ﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 63], that is: the sea parted and became like great mountains, and they were on its bed. Likewise His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فاضْرِبْ لَهم طَرِيقًا في البَحْرِ يَبَسًا لا تَخافُ دَرَكًا ولا تَخْشى﴾ [Ṭā Hā: 77], meaning: a road possessing dryness.
His saying ﴿وَأغْرَقْنا آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ وأنْتُمْ تَنْظُرُونَ﴾: there are two views on it. They said: "while you see them drowning". It is also possible that ”وَأنْتُمْ تَنْظُرُونَ“ means: while you are witnesses, knowing that, even if something occupied them from seeing it at that time. From this one says: ”دُورُ آلِ فُلانٍ تَنْظُرُ إلى دُورِ بَنِي فُلانٍ“ ("the houses of so-and-so's family look at the houses of the sons of so-and-so"), that is, they face them, and it is known that houses see nothing.

zajjaj:51-51.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ واعَدْنا مُوسى أرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً﴾. It is [also] read ”وَإذْ واعِدْنا مُوسى“ «[Translator's note: so in the text; from the discussion that follows, the two readings meant are «واعَدْنا» and «وَعَدْنا».]», and both are permissible and good. A group of the people of the language preferred ”وَإذْ وعَدْنا“ without alif, and said: we preferred this only because mutual appointment (muwāʿada) occurs only for other than human beings «[Translator's note: so in the text; the argument requires the sense "occurs only between human beings".]»; so they preferred ”وَعَدْنا“, and said: our proof is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ وعَدَكم وعْدَ الحَقِّ﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 22] and the like. What they mentioned is not like this case. ”واعَدْنا“ here is good and eloquent, because obedience in accepting is equivalent to mutual appointment: it is a promise from Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and acceptance and following from Moses, so it is treated as mutual appointment.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ثُمَّ اتَّخَذْتُمُ العِجْلَ مِن بَعْدِهِ وأنْتُمْ ظالِمُونَ﴾. He reminded them of the disbelief of their forefathers despite these great signs, and informed them that their disbelief in the Prophet ﷺ, despite the clarity of his matter and what they had come upon of his description in their books, is like the disbelief of their forefathers. In the mention of these stories there was an indication establishing the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ, because these stories are not part of the knowledge of the Arabs but of the knowledge of the People of the Book. The Prophet ﷺ informed them of what is in their books, and they knew that he was of the Arabs who had not read their books, so they knew that he could only have known these stories by way of revelation. So in these verses there is a reminder to them of the favour upon them in their forebears, and an establishing of the matter of the messengership, as we have described.

zajjaj:11-11.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذا قِيلَ لَهم لا تُفْسِدُوا في الأرْضِ قالُوا إنَّما نَحْنُ مُصْلِحُونَ﴾: its meaning is: do not turn people away from the religion of Allah. "إنَّما نَحْنُ مُصْلِحُونَ" (we are only reformers) admits two kinds of answer. One of them is that they think they are reformers. The second is that they mean: "This which they call corruption is, in our view, reform." As for the inflection of "قِيلَ", its end is indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa, as is every past verb indeclinable on fatḥa. The origin of "قِيلَ" is "قُوِلَ", but the kasra was transferred to the qāf, because the ʿayn (second radical) of the verb in your saying "قالَ" was transferred from a vowel to vowellessness, so it must keep this vowellessness throughout the rest of the verb's inflections. Some pronounce "قِيلَ" with a slight ḍamma (rawm). Outside the Qur'an "قَدْ قُولَ ذاكَ" (that has been said) is also permissible. The most eloquent of the dialects is "قِيلَ", "غِيضَ" and ﴿وَسِيقَ الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا رَبَّهُمْ﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]; and if you wish you may say "قُِيلَ", "غُِيضَ" and "سُِيقَ", giving a slight ḍamma (rawm) to the beginnings of all passive verbs (verbs whose agent is not named) in this category.

zajjaj:13-13.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قالُوا أنُؤْمِنُ كَما آمَنَ السُّفَهاءُ﴾: the root meaning of al-safah (foolishness) in the language is lightness of forbearance. Likewise it is said "ثَوْبٌ سَفِيهٌ" when a garment is thin and worn out.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ألا إنَّهم هُمُ السُّفَهاءُ﴾: the meaning of "ألا" is opening and alerting (istiftāḥ wa-tanbīh). His saying "هُمُ السُّفَهاءُ": it is possible that (السُّفَهاءُ) is the khabar (predicate) of "إنَّ", with "هم" a faṣl (separating pronoun) — which is what the Kufans call "اَلْعِمادَ" (the support). It is also possible that "هم" is a mubtadaʾ (subject), "اَلسُّفَهاءُ" the khabar of the mubtadaʾ, and "هُمُ السُّفَهاءُ" the khabar of "إنَّ".

zajjaj:14-14.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذا لَقُوا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قالُوا آمَنّا وإذا خَلَوْا إلى شَياطِينِهِمْ قالُوا إنّا مَعَكُمْ﴾: Allah informed the believers of the disbelief that the hypocrites conceal. The meaning of "شَياطِينِهِمْ" in the language is: "their rebels and their insolent ones in disbelief". It is said "خَلَوْتُ إلَيْهِ" and "(خَلَوْتُ) مَعَهُ" (I was alone with him), and it is said "خَلَوْتُ بِهِ". This is of two kinds. One of them is "جَعَلْتُ خَلْوَتِي مَعَهُ" (I made my privacy with him), as he said "خَلَوْتُ إلَيْهِ", i.e. I made my privacy with him — and likewise it is said "خَلَوْتُ إلَيْهِ". And "خَلَوْتُ بِهِ" can also mean "سَخِرْتُ مِنهُ" (I mocked him).

The accusative of "مَعَكم" is like the accusative of adverbs (ẓurūf): you say "إنّا مَعَكم" (we are with you) and "إنّا خَلْفَكم" (we are behind you), meaning: we are settled with you, and settled behind you. The reading agreed upon is with fatḥa on the ʿayn (of مَعَ). Making the ʿayn vowelless is permissible under poetic necessity (iḍṭirār), but it is not permissible to read it so. "إنّا مَعْكم" is permissible for the poet when he is constrained. The poet said:
قَرِيشِي مِنكُمُ وهَوايَ مَعْكم ∗∗∗ وإنْ كانَتْ زِيارَتُكم لِماما
(My kin is of you and my love is with you, even if your visits are only now and then.)

In His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿خَلَوْا إلى﴾, there are two ways. If you wish, you leave the wāw vowelless and lighten the hamza, giving it kasra, saying "خَلَوْا اِلى". If you wish, you drop the hamza and give the wāw kasra, saying "خَلَوِ لى"; this is how the people of the Hijaz read, and it is good and eloquent. "إنّا": its origin is "إنَّنا", as Allah said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّنِي مَعَكُما﴾ [Ṭā Hā: 46]; but the nūn was deleted because of the multitude of nūns. The deleted one is the second nūn of "إنَّ", for there are two nūns in "إنَّ", the first vowelless and the second vowelled.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾: "نَحْنُ" is indeclinable on ḍamma, because "نَحْنُ" indicates a group, and a group of pronouns is indicated — when you form from the singular's own form — by mīm and wāw, as in "فَعَلُوا" and "أنْتُمْ"; and the wāw is of the same kind as the ḍamma. "نَحْنُ" had to be vowelled, so it was vowelled with ḍamma, because ḍamma comes from wāw. Do you not see that the wāw of the plural, when vowelled because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, is given ḍamma, as in ﴿اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 16]? Some vowelled it with kasra, saying "اِشْتَرَوِا الضَّلالَةَ", because the meeting of two vowelless letters requires kasra on the first when they belong to two words. The reading agreed upon is ﴿اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 16], with ḍamma. It has also been transmitted as "اِشْترَوا الضَّلالَةَ" with fatḥa, and this is extremely anomalous (shādhdh). As for "مُسْتَهْزِئُونَ", the good reading in it is full pronunciation (taḥqīq) of the hamza. If you lighten the hamza, you make it between wāw and hamza, saying "مُسْتَهْزِوُونَ"; this is the preferred option after full pronunciation. It is also permissible to replace the hamza with a yāʾ, saying "مُسْتَهْزِيُونَ". As for "مُسْتَهْزُونَ", it is weak, with no justification except as an anomaly, in the dialect of those who replace the hamza with yāʾ, saying for "اِسْتَهْزَأْتُ" "اِسْتَهْزَيْتُ"; in the dialect of "اِسْتَهْزَيْتُ" one must say "مُسْتَهْزُونَ".

zajjaj:102-102.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واتَّبَعُوا ما تَتْلُو الشَّياطِينُ عَلى مُلْكِ سُلَيْمانَ﴾ — that is, what they used to recite. What the devils had recited during the reign of Solomon was a book of sorcery. Out of the slander and lying of the Jews, they claimed that they had taken this sorcery from Solomon and that it was the Greatest Name of Allah, and they made a living by it. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made known that they had rejected His Book and followed sorcery. The meaning of "﴿عَلى مُلْكِ سُلَيْمانَ﴾" is: in the time of Solomon's reign over them. Thus Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cleared Solomon of sorcery and gave Muhammad ﷺ the upper hand over their lies, and said: ﴿وَما كَفَرَ سُلَيْمانُ﴾, because Allah made the practising of sorcery by Solomon [would-be] disbelief, so He cleared him of it, and made known that the devils were the ones who disbelieved, saying: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ الشَّياطِينَ كَفَرُوا يُعَلِّمُونَ النّاسَ السِّحْرَ﴾. Whoever reads "لَكِنَّ" with shadda puts "اَلشَّياطِينَ" in the accusative (naṣb), and whoever reads it light (without shadda) puts it in the nominative (rafʿ), saying: "وَلَكِنِ الشَّياطِينُ كَفَرُوا". Both have been read.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يُعَلِّمُونَ النّاسَ السِّحْرَ وما أُنْـزِلَ عَلى المَلَكَيْنِ﴾. It has also been read "عَلى المَلِكَيْنِ" (upon the two kings), but "اَلْمَلَكَيْنِ" (the two angels) is better established both in transmission and in exegesis. The meaning is: they teach people sorcery, and they teach what was sent down upon the two angels. So the position of "ما" is accusative, conjoined (nasaq, i.e. maʿṭūf) to "اَلسِّحْرَ". It is also permissible that it means "they followed what the devils recited, and they followed what was sent down upon the two angels", so that the second "ما" is conjoined to the first.

His saying: ﴿وَما يُعَلِّمانِ مِن أحَدٍ حَتّى يَقُولا إنَّما نَحْنُ فِتْنَةٌ فَلا تَكْفُرْ﴾. There is more than one view on this. The first of them — and the best established — is that the two angels used to teach people about sorcery; "عَلَّمْتُ" and "أعْلَمْتُ" both have one and the same meaning in the language. They used to teach [people] the account of sorcery and order them to avoid it, and in that there is wisdom: if someone were to ask, "What is fornication? What is false accusation (qadhf)?", he would have to be informed and taught that it is forbidden. Likewise is the sense of the two angels informing people, and their ordering them to avoid it after informing them points to what we have described. This is sound and clear. On this interpretation, learning sorcery is not disbelief; only practising it is disbelief, just as whoever knows what fornication is does not sin by knowing it, but sins only by committing it.

There is another view on it: it is possible that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, tested people through the two angels at that time, and made the test one of disbelief and faith: that whoever accepted to learn sorcery became a disbeliever by learning it, and by refraining from learning it a believer — because sorcery had become widespread and was found in every nation. The proof of that is that Pharaoh, in the matter of Moses ﷺ, resorted to sorcery and said: "﴿ائْتُونِي بِكُلِّ ساحِرٍ عَلِيمٍ﴾ [Yūnus: 79]". It is possible that Allah tested by this, just as He tested by the river in His saying: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ مُبْتَلِيكم بِنَهَرٍ فَمَن شَرِبَ مِنهُ فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي ومَن لَمْ يَطْعَمْهُ فَإنَّهُ مِنِّي إلا مَنِ اغْتَرَفَ غُرْفَةً بِيَدِهِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 249]. It has also been said that sorcery was not sent down upon the two angels, nor did they command it, nor did Solomon, peace be upon him, bring it. So a group said: "﴿وَما كَفَرَ سُلَيْمانُ ولَكِنَّ الشَّياطِينَ كَفَرُوا يُعَلِّمُونَ النّاسَ السِّحْرَ وما أُنْـزِلَ عَلى المَلَكَيْنِ﴾" with "ما" as a negation (jaḥd), and "هارُوتُ" and "مارُوتُ" as a description of the devils according to these people's interpretation; the interpretation according to their doctrine is: "the devils were Hārūt and Mārūt". According to their doctrine, the meaning of the two saying "﴿إنَّما نَحْنُ فِتْنَةٌ فَلا تَكْفُرْ﴾" would be like the saying of a misguided, dissolute person: "I am in error, so do not seek what I am in." These are three approaches. The first two are closer to the [correct] interpretation and closer to the truth according to many of the people of language. The third view has some basis, except that the ḥadīth and what has come down in the story of the two angels is more fitting and more deserving to be adopted. We mention the meaning and exegesis alongside the i'rab only because the Book of Allah ought to be made clear; do you not see that Allah says: ﴿أفَلا يَتَدَبَّرُونَ القُرْآنَ﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 82]? We have been urged to reflect and consider; but no one should speak except according to the usage of the language, or what agrees with the transmitters among the people of knowledge. And Allah knows best the true exegesis of this verse, for many of the grammarians refrained from speaking about it because of its difficulty, while a group of them did speak about it, and we have spoken only according to their doctrines. Some of the people of language said: what was sent down upon the two angels was speech that was not sorcery, except that it separates a man and his wife, so it belongs to the category of sorcery as regards prohibition. This needs the same kind of explanation that sorcery needs.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَيَتَعَلَّمُونَ مِنهُما﴾. "يَتَعَلَّمُونَ" is not an answer (jawāb) to His saying "فَلا تَكْفُرْ". The grammarians have two views on this. Some of them said: His saying "يَتَعَلَّمُونَ" is conjoined to His saying "يُعَلِّمُونَ"; but this is a mistake, because His saying "مِنهُما" is here proof that the learning is from the two angels specifically. It has also been said: "فَيَتَعَلَّمُونَ" is conjoined to what the meaning of the speech entails; the meaning being: "﴿إنَّما نَحْنُ فِتْنَةٌ فَلا تَكْفُرْ﴾" = "so do not learn, and do not practise sorcery; but they refuse, and so they learn". This is a good view. The best in this is that "فَيَتَعَلَّمُونَ" is conjoined to "يُعْلِّمانِ" [understood], and mention of "يُعْلِّمانِ" was dispensed with because of what in the speech points to it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَما هم بِضارِّينَ بِهِ مِن أحَدٍ إلا بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾. "Permission" (idhn) here cannot be a command from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because Allah does not command indecency; rather the meaning is: "except with the knowledge of Allah".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَيَتَعَلَّمُونَ ما يَضُرُّهم ولا يَنْفَعُهُمْ﴾. The meaning is: it harms them in the Hereafter, even if they gain some quick benefit from it in this world.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَقَدْ عَلِمُوا لَمَنِ اشْتَراهُ ما لَهُ في الآخِرَةِ مِن خَلاقٍ﴾. Al-khalāq is an ample share of good. By this He means those who teach sorcery, because they were among the scholars of the Jews.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَبِئْسَ ما شَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهم لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾. There are two views on it. They said: "﴿لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾" refers to those who teach sorcery, while those who knew that whoever knows it has no share are the ones who were taught. Abū Isḥāq [al-Zajjāj] said: The best in my view is that "﴿لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾" refers back to these same people who knew that they have no share in the Hereafter, i.e. whoever is taught sorcery; but it was said "لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ", i.e. if their knowledge had benefited them, they would have been called knowers, but they cast their knowledge behind their backs, so it was said of them "﴿لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾", i.e. they do not give knowledge its due, because when a knower abandons acting on his knowledge, it is said to him: "You are no knower." The lām in "لَقَدْ" comes in by way of oath and tawkīd (emphasis). The grammarians have two views on "لَمَنِ اشْتَراهُ ما لَهُ في الآخِرَةِ مِن خَلاقٍ": some made "مَن" conditional and made "ما لَهُ في الآخِرَةِ مِن خَلاقٍ" its answer (jawāb). But this is not a place for condition and apodosis (jazāʾ); rather the meaning is: "they certainly knew that the one who purchased it has no share in the Hereafter", just as you say: "واللَّهِ لَقَدْ عَلِمْتَ لَلَّذِي جاءَكَ ما لَهُ مِن عَقْلٍ" (By Allah, you certainly knew that the one who came to you has no sense). As for the lām entering the apodosis elsewhere — and for whoever made this a place of condition and apodosis — it is like His saying: ﴿وَلَئِنْ جِئْتَهم بِآيَةٍ لَيَقُولَنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ [al-Rūm: 58], and like: ﴿وَلَئِنْ أتَيْتَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ بِكُلِّ آيَةٍ ما تَبِعُوا قِبْلَتَكَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 145]. The second lām is in reality the lām of the oath, because you swear only about your own action, not about someone else's action, in your saying: "واللَّهِ لَئِنْ جِئْتَنِي لَأُكْرِمَنَّكَ" (By Allah, if you come to me I shall surely honour you). Some grammarians claimed that when the lām entered at the start of the speech it resembled the oath, and so was answered with the oath's answer. This is a mistake, because the answer of an oath does not resemble the oath; rather the first lām entered to signal that the whole sentence is bound to the oath, because the apodosis, even though the oath is upon it, has come to have a share of the condition in it; that is why the lām entered.

zajjaj:15-15.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿اللَّهُ يَسْتَهْزِئُ بِهِمْ﴾: there are several answers on it. The meaning of Allah's mocking them is that He displayed to them, of His rulings in this world, the opposite of what awaits them in the Hereafter, just as they displayed of Islam the opposite of what they concealed. It is also possible that His mocking them is His seizing them from where they do not know, as He said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿سَنَسْتَدْرِجُهم مِن حَيْثُ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 182]. It is also possible — and Allah knows best — and this is the explanation preferred by the philologists, that the meaning of "يَسْتَهْزِئُ بِهِمْ" is: He recompenses them for their mockery with torment; so He called the recompense of the sin by the sin's name, as He said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَجَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ سَيِّئَةٌ مِثْلُها﴾ [al-Shūrā: 40]: the second is not in reality an evil deed, but it was called "سَيِّئَةً" (an evil deed) for the pairing of the expression (izdiwāj al-kalām). Likewise His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَمَنِ اعْتَدى عَلَيْكم فاعْتَدُوا عَلَيْهِ بِمِثْلِ ما اعْتَدى عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [al-Baqara: 194]: the first is wrongdoing and the second is not wrongdoing, but in the language the name of the sin was used so that it would be known that it is a punishment for it and a recompense for it. These are three explanations, and Allah knows best.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ وهو خادِعُهُمْ﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 142], and ﴿وَيَمْكُرُونَ ويَمْكُرُ اللَّهُ﴾ [al-Anfāl: 30], follow the same course.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَيَمُدُّهم في طُغْيانِهِمْ يَعْمَهُونَ﴾: the meaning of "وَيَمُدُّهم" is: He grants them respite; and this points to the first answer. "في طُغْيانِهِمْ" means: in their excess and their disbelief. The meaning of "يَعْمَهُونَ" in the language is: they wander in bewilderment. It is said "رَجُلٌ عَمِهٌ" and "عامِهٌ", i.e. bewildered. The rajaz poet said:
وَمَهْمَهٌ أطْرافُهُ في مَهْمَهِ ... أعْمى الهُدى بِالجاهِلِينَ العُمَّهِ
(Many a waterless desert whose edges lie in another desert, its guiding marks blind to the ignorant who wander bewildered.)

zajjaj:16-16.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ بِالهُدى﴾: "أُولَئِكَ" is in the nominative position as mubtadaʾ (subject), and its khabar (predicate) is "اَلَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ". We have already explained the wāw of "اِشْتَرَوْا" and its kasra. As for whoever replaces the ḍamma with a hamza, saying "اِشْتَرَؤُ الضَّلالَةَ", he is in error, because the wāw with ḍamma that is replaced by a hamza is treated so only when its quality (the ḍamma) is permanent, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذا الرُّسُلُ أُقِّتَتْ﴾ [al-Mursalāt: 11], whose origin is "وُقِّتَتْ"; and likewise "أدْؤُرٌ" (houses), whose origin is "أدْوُرٌ". The ḍamma of the wāw in His saying "اِشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ" is only because of the meeting of two vowelless letters. Its like is ﴿لَتُبْلَوُنَّ في أمْوالِكم وأنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 186]: the wāw in it ought not to be given a hamza.

The meaning of the statement is that whenever someone leaves something and holds fast to something else, the Arabs say of the one who holds fast to it: "قَدِ اشْتَراهُ" (he has bought it), though there is no buying or selling there; rather, his desire for it, shown by his holding fast to it, is like the desire of the buyer who gives his money for what he desires. The poet said:
أخَذْتُ بِالجُمَّةِ رَأْسًا أزْعَرا ∗∗∗ وبِالثَّنايا الواضِحاتِ الدَّرْدَرا
وَبِالطَّوِيلِ العُمْرِ عُمْرًا أقْصَرا ∗∗∗ كَما اشْتَرى الكافِرُ إذْ تَنَصَّرا
(I took, in exchange for the thick locks, a sparse-haired head; for the gleaming front teeth, toothless gums; and for the long life, a shorter life — as the unbeliever bought when he turned Christian.)

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَما رَبِحَتْ تِجارَتُهُمْ﴾: its meaning is: they did not profit in their trade, because trade itself does not profit; rather, profit and loss are made in it. The Arabs say "قَدْ خَسِرَ بَيْعُكَ" (your sale has lost) and "رَبِحَتْ تِجارَتُكَ" (your trade has profited), intending by that concision and breadth of expression. The poet said:
وَكَيْفَ تُواصِلُ مَن أصْبَحَتْ ∗∗∗ خِلالَتُهُ كَأبِي مَرْحَبِ
(How can you keep ties with one whose friendship has become like Abū Marḥab?)
He means: like the friendship of Abū Marḥab. And Allah said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بَلْ مَكْرُ اللَّيْلِ والنَّهارِ﴾ [Sabaʾ: 33]; the night and the day do not plot; its meaning is only: rather, their plotting by night and by day.

zajjaj:94-94.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قُلْ إنْ كانَتْ لَكُمُ الدّارُ الآخِرَةُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ خالِصَةً مِن دُونِ النّاسِ﴾: this was said to them because they said: ﴿لَنْ يَدْخُلَ الجَنَّةَ إلا مَن كانَ هُودًا أوْ نَصارى﴾ [al-Baqara: 111], and said: ﴿نَحْنُ أبْناءُ اللَّهِ وأحِبّاؤُهُ﴾ [al-Māʾida: 18]. So it was said to them: if you are, in your own estimation, truthful in what you claim, then wish for death; for whoever does not doubt that he is going to Paradise, Paradise is preferable to him over this world; so if you are truthful, wish for what is preferable and better.

For the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims there is in this verse the greatest argument, the clearest sign and proofs for Islam and for the soundness of establishing the messengership of the Prophet ﷺ. For he said to them, "Wish for death", and informed them that they would never wish for it; and not one of them wished for it, because had they wished for it they would have died at that very hour. The proof of their knowing that the matter of the Prophet ﷺ is true is that they refrained from wishing, and not one of them ventured on it — so that his venturing would have refuted His saying ﴿وَلَنْ يَتَمَنَّوْهُ أبَدًا﴾ [al-Baqara: 95], or he would have lived after wishing, and so would have rebutted what the Prophet ﷺ brought. So praise be to Allah, who made the truth plain and clear, and suppressed falsehood and made it vanish.

zajjaj:95-95.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَنْ يَتَمَنَّوْهُ أبَدًا بِما قَدَّمَتْ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾ means: what their hands sent forth of their disbelief in the Prophet ﷺ, because they disbelieved while knowing that he is true, and that if they wished for it they would die; the proof of that is their refraining from wishing for it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِالظّالِمِينَ﴾: Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers and of those who are not wrongdoers; the point here is only that He knows how to requite them. This occurs in the speech people use among themselves: when a man turns to another who has done him a wrong, he says "I know you" and "I see you well", its interpretation being: I know how I will deal with you and what I will apply to you. So the meaning is: He is All-Knowing of them and All-Seeing of what they do, that is, He will requite them for it by killing in this world, or by abasement and humiliation and the paying of the jizya. «لَنْ» governs the accusative as «أنْ» does; we have explained its accusative previously and mentioned what the grammarians said about it. «أبَدًا» is accusative because it is an adverb of time (ẓarf zamān); the meaning is: they will not wish for it throughout their lives until their death. Likewise your saying «لا أُكَلِّمُكَ أبَدًا» ("I will never speak to you") means "I will not speak to you as long as I live". The meaning of «بِما قَدَّمَتْ أيْدِيهِمْ» is "because of what their hands send forth", and it may properly be "because of that which their hands sent forth".

zajjaj:96-96.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَتَجِدَنَّهم أحْرَصَ النّاسِ عَلى حَياةٍ﴾ means by it these scholars of the Jews. The meaning is: you will find them, when they are called to wish for death, the most eager of people for life. The meaning of «لَتَجِدَنَّهم» is "you will surely know them (to be)". The meaning of ﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ أشْرَكُوا﴾ is: and you will find them more eager than those who associate partners, and this is the utmost in comparison. Those who associate partners are the Magians and whoever does not believe in the resurrection.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يَوَدُّ أحَدُهم لَوْ يُعَمَّرُ ألْفَ سَنَةٍ﴾: the "thousand" is mentioned because it was the utmost with which the Magians used to pray for their kings; the king used to be greeted with the words: "Live a thousand Nawrūz and a thousand Mihrajān". He is saying: these people who claim that Paradise is theirs, and that the bliss of Paradise is superior, do not wish for death, and they are more eager than those who do not believe in the resurrection. And that is how these people must be, because they disbelieve in the Prophet ﷺ while he is true in their own view, so they know that they are going to the Fire without doubt; so they are more eager for this reason, and because they know that if they wished for death they would die, since they knew that the Prophet ﷺ is true. Were it not for that, they would not have refrained from wishing, because the wishing of one of them would have established their claim. We have gone to lengths in explaining these verses only because they are the utmost in argument for establishing the matter of the Prophet ﷺ.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَما هو بِمُزَحْزِحِهِ مِنَ العَذابِ أنْ يُعَمَّرَ﴾: this (هو) is a pronoun referring to «أحَدُهم», who has been mentioned, as though He said: "and as for any one of them, his long life is not going to remove him from the punishment". And «هو» may properly be a pronoun for the long life that has been mentioned, so that it would be: "and his long life is not going to remove him from the punishment"; then He made «أنْ يُعَمَّرَ» an explanation of «هو» [Translator's note: the source has «مَبْنِيًّا», presumably for «مُبَيِّنًا»], as though He said: "that which is not going to remove him: that he be given long life". Some said that «هو» is for something unspecified (majhūl, i.e. the pronoun of the matter). In the view of some this is not proper with «ما» when the bāʾ comes in its predicate together with the sentence: the Basrans do not permit «ما هو قائِمًا زَيْدٌ» meaning "the matter is not: Zayd standing", nor «كانَ هو قائِمًا زَيْدٌ» [Translator's note: the source reads «لا كانَ هو قائِمًا زَيْدٌ»] meaning "the matter was: Zayd standing"; likewise they do not permit «ما هو بِقائِمٍ زَيْدٌ» meaning "the matter is not …".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واللَّهُ بَصِيرٌ بِما يَعْمَلُونَ﴾: its explanation has preceded in the verse before this one. You say regarding «يَوَدُّ»: «وَدِدْتُ الرَّجُلَ، أوَدُّهُ، وُدًّا», or «وِدادًا، ومَوَدَّةً، ووِدادَةً». Al-Kisāʾī related «وَدَدْتُ الرَّجُلَ» (with fatḥa), while what all people know is «وَدِدْتُهُ». He related only what he heard, but he heard it from someone whose dialect should not be adopted, because there is consensus on the correctness of «أوِدُّ» [Translator's note: so in the source] and «أوَدُّ», and «أوَدُّ» cannot have «وَدَدْتُ» as its past; so the consensus invalidates «وَدَدْتُ» — I mean the consensus on their saying «أوَدُّ».

zajjaj:97-97.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قُلْ مَن كانَ عَدُوًّا لِجِبْرِيلَ﴾: there are several dialectal forms of the name «جِبْرِيل»; some of them have been read and some have not. The best of the forms is «جَبْرَئِيل», with fatḥa on the jīm and with hamza, because what is related from the Prophet ﷺ concerning the one with the Trumpet is: "Jabraʾīl is on his right and Mīkāʾīl on his left"; this is how the people of ḥadīth recorded it precisely. One also says «جِبْرِيل», with fatḥa or kasra on the jīm; and one also says «جِبْرَألّ», dropping the yāʾ, keeping the hamza and doubling the lām; and one says «جِبْرِين» with nūn, but this is not permissible in the Quran — I mean keeping the nūn — because it contradicts the Muṣḥaf. The poet said:
شَهِدْنا فَما تَلْقى لَنا مِن كَتِيبَةٍ ∗∗∗ يَدَ الدَّهْرِ إلّا جَبْرَئِيلُ أمامَها
(We were present, and you will never meet a troop of ours, for all time, without Jabraʾīl before it.)
This verse follows the wording in the ḥadīth and what many of the readers follow. «جِبْرِيل» has also come in poetry; the poet said:
وَجِبْرِيلٌ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ فِينا ∗∗∗ ورُوحُ القُدْسِ لَيْسَ لَهُ كِفاءُ
(And Jibrīl, the messenger of Allah, is among us, and the Holy Spirit, who has no equal.)
This was mentioned only because the Jews said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Jibrīl is our enemy; had Mīkāʾīl come to you, we would have accepted from you". So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿قُلْ مَن كانَ عَدُوًّا لِجِبْرِيلَ فَإنَّهُ نَـزَّلَهُ عَلى قَلْبِكَ بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ مُصَدِّقًا لِما بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾, meaning the previous scriptures, ﴿وَهُدًى وبُشْرى لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾. «مُصَدِّقًا» is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial).

zajjaj:98-98.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَمِيكالَ فَإنَّ اللَّهَ عَدُوٌّ لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾: «مِيكائِيل» has several dialectal forms: «مِيكائِيل» and «مِيكال» — both of which have been read — and «مِيكَأْل», with a hamza and no yāʾ. These are foreign names that reached the Arabs, and they pronounced them in different forms — I mean «جِبْرِيل» and «مِيكائِيل».

«إسْرائِيل» also has several forms: «إسْرايِيل», «إسْرال» and «إسْرايِل».

And «إبْراهِيم», «إبْراهَم», «أبْرَهْم» and «إبْراهام»; but the Quran has come only with «إبْراهِيم», and the reading follows it. Most of what I relate of readings in this book of ours is from Abū ʿUbayd, from what Ismāʿīl ibn Isḥāq related from Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Abū ʿUbayd.

zajjaj:99-99.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَقَدْ أنْـزَلْنا إلَيْكَ آياتٍ بَيِّناتٍ﴾ means the signs that have been mentioned, which we have explained. «الآيَة» in the language is a sign (ʿalāma), and «بَيِّناتٍ» means clear. «قَدْ» enters speech only for people who are not expecting the news [Translator's note: so in the source («لا يَتَوَقَّعُونَ»); the usual definition of «قَدْ» is that it is for people who are expecting the news (li-qawm yatawaqqaʿūna al-khabar), so the negation may be a slip], and the lām in «لَقَدْ» is a lām of oath.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَما يَكْفُرُ بِها إلا الفاسِقُونَ﴾ means those who have departed from the right course. We have explained that the Arabs' saying «فَسَقَتِ الرُّطَبَةُ» means the fresh date came out of its skin.

zajjaj:100-100.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أوَكُلَّما عاهَدُوا عَهْدًا نَبَذَهُ فَرِيقٌ مِنهُمْ﴾: the meaning of «نَبَذَهُ» is: rejected it and threw it away. The poet said:
نَظَرْتُ إلى عُنْوانِهِ فَنَبَذْتُهُ ∗∗∗ كَنَبْذِكَ نَعْلًا أخْلَقَتْ مِن نِعالِكا
(I looked at its address and threw it away, as you throw away a sandal of yours that has worn out.)
﴿أوَكُلَّما عاهَدُوا﴾ is accusative as an adverb (ẓarf). This wāw in ﴿أوَكُلَّما﴾ has the alif of interrogation entering upon it, because the interrogation is a fresh start, and the alif is the mother of the interrogative particles. This wāw also enters upon «هَلْ», so you say «وهَلْ زَيْدٌ عاقِلٌ؟» ("and is Zayd intelligent?"), because the meaning of the interrogative alif is present in «هَلْ»; so it is as though the implied form were «أوَهَلْ», except that the interrogative alif and «هَلْ» do not come together, since «هَلْ» makes the alif unnecessary.

zajjaj:101-101.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَمّا جاءَهم رَسُولٌ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ مُصَدِّقٌ لِما مَعَهُمْ﴾ means by it the Prophet ﷺ, because what he brought confirms the Torah and the Gospel. «لَمّا» is that by which a thing occurs because of the occurrence of something else. «مُصَدِّقٌ» is nominative, an adjective (ṣifa) of «رَسُولٌ», because both are indefinite. Were it accusative, that would be permissible, because «رَسُولٌ» has already been qualified by His saying ﴿مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾; for that reason the accusative (as a ḥāl) becomes acceptable. The position of «ما» in «مُصَدِّقٌ لِما مَعَهم» is genitive by the lām of annexation (lām al-iḍāfa), and «مَعَ» is its ṣila (relative clause); what makes «مَعَ» accusative is (the implied notion of) being settled (al-istiqrār); the meaning is: "of what is settled with them".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿نَبَذَ فَرِيقٌ مِنَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ كِتابَ اللَّهِ وراءَ ظُهُورِهِمْ﴾: by ﴿الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ﴾ He means the Jews, and the Book here is the Torah. About ﴿كِتابَ اللَّهِ وراءَ ظُهُورِهِمْ﴾ there are two views: it may be the Quran, and it may be the Torah, because those who disbelieved in the Prophet have cast away the Torah.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿كَأنَّهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾: He made known that they are learned in their Book and that they rejected it knowingly and out of enmity to the Prophet ﷺ, and He made known that they cast away the Book of Allah.

zajjaj:53-53.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ آتَيْنا مُوسى الكِتابَ والفُرْقانَ لَعَلَّكم تَهْتَدُونَ﴾. ”آتَيْنا“ means "We gave"; ”اَلْكِتابَ“ is mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and ”اَلْفُرْقانَ“ is conjoined to it. It is possible that ”اَلْفُرْقانَ“ is the Book itself, except that it was mentioned again, and He meant by it that it distinguishes between truth and falsehood. One of the grammarians – Quṭrub – said the meaning is: "and We gave Muḥammad the Criterion (al-furqān)"; his proof is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿تَبارَكَ الَّذِي نَـزَّلَ الفُرْقانَ عَلى عَبْدِهِ﴾ [al-Furqān: 1], by which He means the Qurʾān.
The first view is the [correct] view, because al-furqān has been mentioned for Moses in a place other than this; Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنا مُوسى وهارُونَ الفُرْقانَ وضِياءً وذِكْرًا لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 48].
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لَعَلَّكم تَهْتَدُونَ﴾: ”لَعَلَّ“ is mentioned here – while Allah knows whether they will be guided or not – according to what servants do and how they address one another, that is, that this is something through which guidance is hoped for; so they were addressed according to their hope. Like it is His saying: ﴿لَعَلَّهُ يَتَذَكَّرُ أوْ يَخْشى﴾ [Ṭā Hā: 44]; the meaning is only: go, both of you, upon your hope, while Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, knows what will be, and He is behind it.

zajjaj:54-54.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ قالَ مُوسى لِقَوْمِهِ يا قَوْمِ إنَّكم ظَلَمْتُمْ أنْفُسَكم بِاتِّخاذِكُمُ العِجْلَ﴾. The reading is ”يا قَوْمِ“ with kasra on the mīm; it is an annexed (muḍāf) vocative, and the preferred form in it is dropping the yāʾ, because the yāʾ is a single letter, the vocative is a domain of omission, and it is at the end of the noun just as the tanwīn is at its end; so the yāʾ was dropped and the kasra remained to indicate it.
Four ways are permissible in ordinary speech; but in the Qurʾān [only] the kasra with dropping of the yāʾ, because it is the best of the ways and it is the consensus of the Readers. What is permissible in speech is that you say ”يا قَوْمِ إنَّكم“, as it is read in the Qurʾān; ”يا قَوْمِي“, with the yāʾ kept and quiescent; and ”يا قَوْمِيَ“, with the yāʾ vowelled. These are three ways with annexation. And ”يا قَوْمُ“, with ḍamma on the mīm, is permissible, in the sense of ”يا أيُّها القَوْمُ“ ("O people").
The meaning of His saying ”ظَلَمْتُمْ أنْفُسَكم بِاتِّخاذِكُمُ العِجْلَ“: of everyone who does a deed that returns upon him with harm it is said: ”إنَّما أسَأْتَ إلى نَفْسِكَ“ ("you have only harmed yourself") and ”ظَلَمْتَ نَفْسَكَ“ ("you have wronged yourself"). The root meaning of ”اَلظُّلْمُ“ in the language is putting a thing in other than its place. The Arabs say: ”وَمَن أشْبَهَ أباهُ فَما ظَلَمَ“ ("whoever resembles his father has done no ẓulm"), meaning: the resemblance did not fall for him in other than its place. One says ”ظُلِمَ الرَّجُلُ سِقاءَهُ مِنَ اللَّبَنِ“ when [the milk in his skin] is drunk and served before it has properly set; and ”أرْضٌ مَظْلُومَةٌ“ ("wronged ground") when it is dug where it had not been dug before, or when the rain came near it and passed it by. Al-Nābigha said:
؎إلّا الأوارِيَّ لَأْيًا ما أُبَيِّنُها ∗∗∗ والنُّؤْيَ كالحَوْضِ بِالمَظْلُومَةِ الجَلَدِ
(Except the tethering-posts, which I can make out only with difficulty, and the trench, like a cistern, in the hard, "wronged" ground.)
The meaning of His saying ”بِاتِّخاذِكُمُ العِجْلَ“ is: you took it as a god.
The meaning of His saying ﴿فَتُوبُوا إلى بارِئِكُمْ﴾ is: to your Creator. One says ”بَرَأ اللَّهُ الخَلْقَ“ ("Allah created the creatures"); so ”اَلْبارِئُ“ is the Creator, and ”اَلْبَرِيَّةُ“ and ”اَلْخَلْقُ“ are the created beings, except that ”اَلْبَرِيَّةُ“ occurs in most of their speech without hamza; its origin [is hamzated], as in ﴿أُولَئِكَ هم خَيْرُ البَرِيَّةِ﴾ [al-Bayyina: 7]. Most of the Readers and of speech have ”اَلْبَرِيَّةُ“ without hamza, though some people read ”اَلْبَرِيئَةِ“ with hamza; the preferred form is that of the majority.
It is related from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ that he read ”إلى بارِئْكم“ with the hamza made quiescent, while Sībawayh transmitted this with the kasra pronounced fleetingly (ikhtilās). I reckon that the correct transmission is what Sībawayh transmitted, for he is more exact concerning what is transmitted from Abū ʿAmr, and [this] iʿrāb is more in keeping with the transmission from Abū ʿAmr, because dropping the kasra in the like of this, and dropping the ḍamma, occur only under the constraint of poetry. Sībawayh recited – and he claimed that it is among what is permissible in poetry specifically:
؎إذا اعْوَجَجْنَ قُلْتُ صاحِبْ قَوِّمِ
(When they [the camels] veer off course, I say: "Companion, straighten [them]!")
with the bāʾ quiescent; and he also recited:
؎فاليَوْمَ أشْرَبْ غَيْرَ مُسْتَحْقِبٍ ∗∗∗ إثْمًا مِنَ اللَّهِ ولا واغِلِ
(So today I drink, not bearing a sin before Allah, nor as an uninvited intruder.)
Correct speech is to say ”يا صاحِبُ أقْبِلْ“ or ”يا صاحِبِ أقْبِلْ“ ("O companion, come forward"); there is no justification for the quiescence. Likewise ”فاليَوْمَ أشْرَبُ يا هَذا“. Others than Sībawayh transmitted these verses in the regular form, as it ought to be in speech and poetry; they transmitted this verse in two ways: they transmitted ”فاليَوْمَ فاشْرَبْ غَيْرَ مُسْتَحْقِبٍ“, and they also transmitted ”فاليَوْمَ أُسْقى غَيْرَ مُسْتَحْقِبٍ“; and they also transmitted ”إذا اعْوَجَجْنَ قُلْتُ صاحِ قَوِّمِ“. Sībawayh – Allah willing – would only transmit what he had heard; but what these others heard is what is established in the language, and Sībawayh himself mentioned that analogy is other than what he transmitted. So it ought to be read only as ”إلى بارِئِكم“ with kasra, and likewise ”عِنْدَ بارِئِكم“.
The meaning of ”فاقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكم“: Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, tested them by making their repentance consist in their killing one another. It is said that they were lined up in two rows, killing one another: whoever was killed was a martyr, and whoever was not killed was a penitent whose past sins were forgiven. It is also said that the seventy whom Moses ﷺ chose were not among those who worshipped the calf, and that they were the ones who did the killing. The first is more in keeping with the verse, because His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فاقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ indicates that it was the repentance of the calf-worshippers. Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, tested them with this great trial only because of their disbelief after the proofs and the great signs.

zajjaj:55-55.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ قُلْتُمْ يا مُوسى لَنْ نُؤْمِنَ لَكَ حَتّى نَرى اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً فَأخَذَتْكُمُ الصّاعِقَةُ وأنْتُمْ تَنْظُرُونَ﴾. The meaning of ”جَهْرَةً“ is: not screened from us by anything. One says ”فُلانٌ يُجاهِرُ بِالمَعاصِي“ ("so-and-so commits sins openly"), that is, he does not screen himself from people in any of them.
His saying ﴿فَأخَذَتْكُمُ الصّاعِقَةُ﴾: the meaning of ”اَلصّاعِقَةُ“ is what they are struck down by, that is, they die. So the thunderbolt seized them and they died; the proof that they died «[Translator's note: the source text breaks off here; the proof follows in the next entry with ﴿ثُمَّ بَعَثْناكم مِن بَعْدِ مَوْتِكم﴾.]»

zajjaj:56-56.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ثُمَّ بَعَثْناكم مِن بَعْدِ مَوْتِكم لَعَلَّكم تَشْكُرُونَ﴾. In this verse there is mention of resurrection after a death that occurred in this world, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿فَأماتَهُ اللَّهُ مِائَةَ عامٍ ثُمَّ بَعَثَهُ﴾ [al-Baqara: 259], and like His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَقالَ لَهُمُ اللَّهُ مُوتُوا ثُمَّ أحْياهُمْ﴾ [al-Baqara: 243]. That is an argument against the idolaters of the Arabs, who were not certain of the resurrection: the Prophet ﷺ brought reports of those who were raised after death in this world, in which the Jews, the Christians and the possessors of scriptures agree with him; so he ﷺ argued with Allah's proof, on which all those of the People of the Scriptures who opposed him agree with him.
His saying ﴿لَعَلَّكم تَشْكُرُونَ﴾, that is: for His raising you after death, and His informing you that His power over you is this power, and that the reprieve after death has nothing after it; it is as though it compels [one] to the worship of Allah.

zajjaj:103-103.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَوْ أنَّهم آمَنُوا واتَّقَوْا لَمَثُوبَةٌ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ خَيْرٌ﴾. "مَثُوبَةٌ" is in the position of the answer (jawāb) of "لَوْ", because it conveys the sense of your saying "لَأُثِيبُوا" (they would have been rewarded). The meaning of the speech is that Allah's reward is better for them than what they earn through disbelief and sorcery.
