His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾, i.e. if they acted upon their knowledge and knew the reality of that in which excellence lies.

zajjaj:104-104.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تَقُولُوا راعِنا وقُولُوا انْظُرْنا واسْمَعُوا﴾. Al-Ḥasan read: "لا تَقُولُوا راعِنًا" with tanwīn (nunation), while what the people [of reading] follow is "راعِنا" without tanwīn. Three views have been given on "راعِنا" without tanwīn. Some said: "راعِنا" means "أرْعِنا سَمْعَكَ" (lend us your hearing). It has also been said: the Muslims used to say to the Prophet ﷺ "راعِنا", and the Jews used to revile one another with this word; they used to revile the Prophet ﷺ inwardly, so when they heard this word they seized the chance to voice their reviling of him with an audible expression for which nothing could be held against them on the surface. So Allah informed the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims of that and forbade this word. And some said: "لا تَقُولُوا راعِنا" is from murāʿāh (mutual regard) and mukāfaʾa (requital); they were commanded to address the Prophet ﷺ with esteem and reverence, so it was said to them: "لا تَقُولُوا راعِنا", i.e. "match us in speech", as some of them say to others; "وَقُولُوا أنْظِرْنا", i.e. "grant us respite"; "واسْمَعُوا", as if it were said to them: "listen". And some said that "راعِنا" is a word used in mockery and ridicule, so the Muslims were forbidden to utter it in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ. As for al-Ḥasan's reading "راعِنًا", its meaning is: do not say folly — from al-ruʿūna (foolishness).

zajjaj:105-105.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ما يَوَدُّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِن أهْلِ الكِتابِ ولا المُشْرِكِينَ﴾. The meaning is: nor [do those] among the polytheists [wish it] — [alongside] those who disbelieved among the People of the Book.

The Jews [are meant by the first], and the polytheists in this place are the idol-worshippers. ﴿أنْ يُنَـزَّلَ عَلَيْكم مِن خَيْرٍ مِن رَبِّكُمْ﴾: it is read "أنْ يُنْزَلَ عَلَيْكم" both with the light form and the heavy form (with shadda). In Arabic "أنْ يَنْزِلَ عَلَيْكم" is also permissible, but it should not be read in this third way, since none of the well-known readers read it so. The position of "مِن خَيْرٍ" is nominative (rafʿ); the meaning is: those who disbelieved and the polytheists do not wish that good (خَيْرٌ) be sent down upon you from your Lord. If this occurred in [ordinary] speech, "ولا المُشْرِكُونَ" (in the nominative) would be permissible, but the muṣḥaf is not to be contradicted, and what is established in the muṣḥaf is also the better. The entry of "مِن" here is by way of tawkīd (emphasis) and redundancy (ziyāda), as in "ما جاءَنِي مِن أحَدٍ" and "ما جاءَنِي أحَدٌ" (no one came to me).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واللَّهُ يَخْتَصُّ بِرَحْمَتِهِ مَن يَشاءُ واللَّهُ ذُو الفَضْلِ العَظِيمِ﴾, i.e. He singles out for His prophethood whomever He wills — those whom He, Mighty and Majestic, has told us are chosen.

zajjaj:106-106.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ما نَنْسَخْ مِن آيَةٍ أوْ نُنْسِها﴾. In "نُنْسِها" more than one form has been read: "أوْ نُنْسِها", "نَنْسَها" and "نَنْسَأْها". As for al-naskh in the language, it is annulling a thing and setting another in its place. The Arabs say: "نَسَخَتِ الشَّمْسُ الظِّلَّ", meaning: the sun removed the shade and took its place. The people of language have two views on the meaning of "أوْ نُنْسِها". Some of them said: "أوْ نُنْسِها" is from al-nisyān (forgetting), and they said: our proof of that is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿سَنُقْرِئُكَ فَلا تَنْسى﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 6] ﴿إلا ما شاءَ اللَّهُ﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 7]; so Allah has made known that He wills that [something] be forgotten. This view is not permissible in my opinion, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed the Prophet ﷺ in His saying ﴿وَلَئِنْ شِئْنا لَنَذْهَبَنَّ بِالَّذِي أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 86] that He does not will to take away what He revealed to the Prophet ﷺ. And in His saying ﴿فَلا تَنْسى﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 6] ﴿إلا ما شاءَ اللَّهُ﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 7] there are two views that invalidate this view we have reported from some of the people of language. One of them: "فَلا تَنْسى", i.e. you will not abandon anything except what Allah wills that you abandon. [The other:] it is possible that "إلّا ما شاءَ اللَّهُ" refers to what befalls [a person] by human nature, after which you remember — not that it is by way of depriving the Prophet ﷺ of something of the wisdom he was given. Another view has been given on "﴿أوْ نُنْسِها﴾", and it too is a mistake: they said it means "or We leave it". Of this one says "نَسِيتُ" when I have left [something], but one does not say "أُنْسِيتُ" in the sense of "I left". Rather the meaning of "﴿أوْ نُنْسِها﴾" is "أوْ نَتْرُكْها", i.e. We command that it be left. [Translator's note: the text as it stands both rejects and then adopts the sense "leave it"; the distinction intended seems to be between "We leave it" and "We command that it be left".]

If someone asks: what is the meaning of leaving it, other than abrogation? And what is the difference between leaving (al-tark) and abrogation (al-naskh)? The answer is that abrogation in the Book comes in the form of one verse abrogating another, so that the second annuls acting upon the first. The meaning of leaving is that a verse comes with some practice, and then the Muslims are commanded to leave that without a verse coming that abrogates the one before it — for example: ﴿إذا جاءَكُمُ المُؤْمِناتُ مُهاجِراتٍ فامْتَحِنُوهُنَّ﴾ [al-Mumtaḥana: 10]; then afterwards the Muslims were commanded to leave off the examination. This is the meaning of leaving, and we have explained the meaning of abrogation; this is the truth. Whoever reads "أوْ نَنْسَأْها" means "نُؤَخِّرْها" (We postpone it). Al-nasʾ in the language is postponement; one says "نَسَأ اللَّهُ في أجَلِهِ" and "أنْسَأ اللَّهُ أجَلَهُ", i.e. He postponed his appointed term.

His saying: ﴿نَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ مِنها﴾ — the meaning is: with something better than it for you — ﴿أوْ مِثْلِها﴾. As for a case in which something better than the abrogated is brought, it is the completion of fasting, which abrogated the permission to break the fast for whoever was able to fast. The proof of that is His saying: ﴿وَلِتُكْمِلُوا العِدَّةَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 185]; this is better for us, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said. As for His saying ﴿أوْ مِثْلِها﴾, it means: We bring a verse whose reward is like the reward of the one before it. The benefit in that is that the abrogating [verse] is easier to take up than the abrogated, belief in it more readily acceptable, and people quicker to [accept] it — like the qibla, which was in one direction; then Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to make the House [the Kaʿba] the qibla of the Muslims, and turned it away from facing Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis). Even though prostrating towards any direction is equal in practice and reward, what Allah commanded at that time was the most beneficial and the most inviting for the Arabs and others to Islam.

zajjaj:196-196.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَأتِمُّوا الحَجَّ والعُمْرَةَ لِلَّهِ﴾. In ”اَلْعُمْرَةَ“ both the accusative (naṣb) and the nominative (rafʿ) are permissible. The meaning with the accusative is: complete both of them; the meaning with the nominative is: complete the Hajj, and the ʿumra is for Allah, i.e. it is among the things by which you draw near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and it is not obligatory. More than one view has also been given on His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَأتِمُّوا الحَجَّ والعُمْرَةَ﴾. It is narrated from ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah have mercy on them both, that they said: completing them is that you enter iḥrām from the home of your family. It is narrated from others that one said: completing them is that the expenditure be lawful and that one refrain from what Allah has forbidden. Some of them said: the Hajj and the ʿumra have stations and rites, such as the ṭawāf, the standing at ʿArafa and other things, so completing them is performing everything that is in them; and this is clear. As for the meaning of ”اِعْتَمَرَ“ in the language, two views have been given on it. Some of them said: ”اِعْتَمَرَ“ means "he aimed at, set out for". The poet said:
؎لَقَدْ سَما ابْنُ مُعَمَّرٍ حِينَ اعْتَمَرْ ∗∗∗ مَغْزًى بَعِيدًا مِن بَعِيدٍ وضَبَرْ
(Ibn Muʿammar rose high when he set out for a distant campaign-goal from afar, and gathered his strength.)
The meaning is: when he aimed at a distant campaign-goal. Some of them said: the meaning of ”اِعْتَمَرَ“ is "he visited", from ”اَلزِّيارَةُ“ (visiting). The meaning of ”اَلْعُمْرَةُ“ in practice is: the ṭawāf around the House and the running between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa, only. The ʿumra is available to a person throughout the whole year, whereas the time of the Hajj is a single time of the year. In my view, the meaning of ”اِعْتَمَرَ“ with respect to setting out for the House is that it was singled out for this — I mean, for the mention of ”اِعْتَمَرَ“ — because it is setting out to perform a deed in an inhabited (ʿāmir) place; for this reason it is said: muʿtamir.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَإنْ أُحْصِرْتُمْ فَما اسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ الهَدْيِ﴾. What is transmitted among the authorities on the language is that of a man whom fear or illness prevents from moving about freely it is said: ”قَدْ أُحْصِرَ“, so he is muḥṣar; and of a man who has been confined it is said: ”قَدْ حُصِرَ“, so he is maḥṣūr. Al-Farrāʾ said: if ”أُحْصِرَ“ were said of one who has been confined, it would be permissible, as though he treats the one confining him as equivalent to the illness and fear that prevented him from moving about. The truth in this is what the authorities on the language hold: that of the one whom fear or illness prevents one says ”أُحْصِرَ“, and of the confined one ”حُصِرَ“. That is the truth only because when a man refrains from moving about he has confined himself, so it is as though the illness "made him confined", i.e. made him confine himself; whereas one's saying ”حَصَرْتُ فُلانًا“ means only "I confined him", not that he confined himself, and ”أُحْصِرَ“ is not permissible in it.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَما اسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ الهَدْيِ﴾. The position of ”ما“ is nominative; the meaning is: then incumbent upon him is whatever is easily obtainable of the sacrificial animals. It has been said in place of ”اَلْهَدْيُ“: ”اَلْهَدِيُّ“; and ”اَلْهَدِيُّ“ is the plural of ”هَدِيَّةٌ“, as is ”هَدْيٌ“, like their saying regarding the ḥadhya of the saddle: ”حَذِيَّةٌ“ and ”حَذْيٌ“. Some of them said: ”ما اسْتَيْسَرَ“ means whatever is easy, of camels and cattle. Some of them said: a camel, or a cow, or a sheep; and this is the best view.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تَحْلِقُوا رُءُوسَكم حَتّى يَبْلُغَ الهَدْيُ مَحِلَّهُ﴾. They said regarding ”مَحِلَّهُ“: for whoever is performing the Hajj, its place/time of lawfulness is the Day of Sacrifice, and for whoever is performing the ʿumra, the day he enters Mecca.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَمَن كانَ مِنكم مَرِيضًا أوْ بِهِ أذًى مِن رَأْسِهِ فَفِدْيَةٌ﴾, i.e. then upon him is a ransom. If it were put in the accusative it would be permissible in the language, by implying "then let him give a ransom" or "then let him bring a ransom". The ransom is due from him only if he shaves his head and comes out of his iḥrām.
His saying: ﴿أوْ نُسُكٍ﴾, i.e. or a nasīka which he slaughters; and the nasīka is the slaughtered animal.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَإذا أمِنتُمْ فَمَن تَمَتَّعَ بِالعُمْرَةِ إلى الحَجِّ فَما اسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ الهَدْيِ﴾, i.e. then upon him is whatever is easily obtainable of the sacrificial animals. The position of ”ما“ is nominative, and it may be accusative by implying "then let him offer whatever is easily obtainable of the sacrificial animals".
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَصِيامُ ثَلاثَةِ أيّامٍ في الحَجِّ وسَبْعَةٍ إذا رَجَعْتُمْ﴾. Its meaning is: then upon him is the fasting of…; the accusative is permissible, on the sense "then let him fast this fasting", but reciting is not permissible with what has not been recited.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿تِلْكَ عَشَرَةٌ كامِلَةٌ﴾. More than one view has been given on it. Some of them said: ”كامِلَةٌ“ means it completes the reward. Some of them said: ”كامِلَةٌ“ in being a substitute for the sacrificial animal. What applies here — and Allah knows best — is that when it was said: ”فَصِيامُ ثَلاثَةِ أيّامٍ في الحَجِّ وسَبْعَةٍ إذا رَجَعْتُمْ“, someone might imagine that the obligation is three days during the Hajj or seven on returning; so Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, made known that all ten are obligatory. The meaning, then, is: what is obligatory upon you is the fasting of ten complete days, divided as mentioned between the Hajj and the return.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ذَلِكَ لِمَن لَمْ يَكُنْ أهْلُهُ حاضِرِي المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾, i.e. this obligation is upon whoever is not one whose family is in Mecca. As for ”حاضِرِي المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ“, its origin is ”حاضِرِينَ المَسْجِدَ الحَرامَ“; the nūn dropped because of the iḍāfa (genitive construct), and the yāʾ dropped in continuous speech because it is vowelless and the lām in ”اَلْمَسْجِدِ“ is vowelless. As for the pause, you say in it — whenever you are compelled to pause: ”حاضِرِي“.

zajjaj:107-107.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ألَمْ تَعْلَمْ أنَّ اللَّهَ لَهُ مُلْكُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾. The wording of "ألَمْ" here is the wording of a question (istifhām), but its meaning is tawqīf (bringing the addressee to acknowledge). The jussive (jazm) of "ألَمْ" here is like the jussive of "لَمْ", because the interrogative particle does not alter the governing word (ʿāmil) from its government. The meaning of al-mulk in the language is complete power and its firm establishment. Whatever is such that one says of [its holder] "مَلِكٌ" (king) is called "اَلْمُلْكَ" (sovereignty), and whatever power has attained, of which one says "مالِكٌ" (owner), is "مِلْكٌ" (possession). You say: "مَلَكْتُ الشَّيْءَ، أمْلِكُهُ، مِلْكًا" (I owned the thing). And it is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿عَلى مُلْكِ سُلَيْمانَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 102], i.e. in his dominion and power. The root of this is from their saying "مَلَكْتُ العَجِينَ، أمْلُكُهُ" when you have kneaded the dough thoroughly; and from this it is said of marriage: "شَهِدْنا إمْلاكَ فُلانٍ" (we witnessed so-and-so's imlāk), i.e. we witnessed the contracting of his marriage and its making firm. The meaning of the verse is: Allah owns the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them, so He knows best the way of benefit in what He prescribes for them in worship — abrogating, abrogated, left, and so on.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَما لَكم مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ مِن ولِيٍّ ولا نَصِيرٍ﴾. This is an address to the Muslims, in which they are told that whoever opposes them is against them, and that Allah, Majestic and Mighty, is their helper. The benefit in it is that through His helping them they will overcome everyone else.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أمْ تُرِيدُونَ أنْ تَسْألُوا رَسُولَكم كَما سُئِلَ مُوسى مِن قَبْلُ﴾ [al-Baqara: 108]. The best reading is with the hamza fully pronounced (taḥqīq). It is permissible to make it bayna bayna (in-between), between hamza and yāʾ, so that it is pronounced "سُيِلَ"; this is governed only by oral transmission, because writing does not distinguish between the fully pronounced [hamza], the softened one, and what is made a pure yāʾ. It is also permissible: "كَما سِيلَ مُوسى مِن قَبْلُ", from your saying "سِلْتُ، أسالُ" in the sense of "سُئِلْتُ، أسْألُ"; this is a dialect of the Arabs that all the grammarians have reported [Translator's note: the text has «حجاها», evidently for «حكاها», "reported it"], but reading follows only the two ways we explained before this one: taḥqīq of the hamza and its softening (talyīn). The meaning of "أمْ" here, and in every place where it does not occur conjoined to the interrogative alif — except that it is not used at the very start [of speech] — is that it signals the meaning of "بَلْ" (rather) together with the meaning of the interrogative alif. The meaning is: "Rather, do you want to ask your Messenger as Moses was asked before?" The meaning of the verse is that they were forbidden to ask the Prophet ﷺ about that in asking about which there is no good for them, and what would make them disbelieve. They were addressed thus only after the proofs had become clear to them and been established against their opposition; we have explained that in His saying ﴿فَتَمَنَّوُا المَوْتَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 94] and in similar passages explained earlier. So the Muslims were told that asking after the proofs have been established is disbelief, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تَسْألُوا عَنْ أشْياءَ إنْ تُبْدَ لَكم تَسُؤْكُمْ﴾ [al-Māʾida: 101]. And His saying: ﴿وَمَن يَتَبَدَّلِ الكُفْرَ بِالإيمانِ فَقَدْ ضَلَّ سَواءَ السَّبِيلِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 108], i.e. whoever asks the Prophet ﷺ about what does not concern him after the truth has become clear has strayed from سَواءَ السَّبِيلِ, i.e. the straight course of the way.

zajjaj:109-109.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَدَّ كَثِيرٌ مِن أهْلِ الكِتابِ لَوْ يَرُدُّونَكم مِن بَعْدِ إيمانِكم كُفّارًا﴾. By this He means the scholars of the Jews.

His saying: ﴿حَسَدًا مِن عِنْدِ أنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ is connected to the wishing (wadd) of those who disbelieved, not to His saying "حَسَدًا", because a person's envy does not come from [anywhere but] himself [Translator's note: i.e. saying it is "from themselves" would add nothing]; rather the meaning is: their wish for your disbelief comes from themselves — not that in their view disbelief is the truth, nor that their Book commanded them the disbelief in the Prophet ﷺ that they hold. The proof of that is His saying: ﴿مِن بَعْدِ ما تَبَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الحَقُّ﴾. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فاعْفُوا واصْفَحُوا حَتّى يَأْتِيَ اللَّهُ بِأمْرِهِ﴾ — this was at a time when the Muslims had not yet been commanded to fight the polytheists; they used only to call with clear proofs and the utmost gentleness, until Allah made clear that they were only being obstinate after the truth had become clear to them; after that the Muslims were commanded to fight.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾, i.e. able to call to His religion by whatever He likes of what is, in His view, wisest and most effective. One says: "أقْدَرَ عَلى الشَّيْءِ، قَدْرًا، وقَدَرًا، وقُدْرَةً، وقُدْرانًا، ومَقْدِرَةً، وَمَقْدُرَةً، ومَقْدَرَةً" — these are seven forms, all transmitted, and the weakest of them is "مَقْدِرَةٌ" with kasra.

zajjaj:111-111.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقالُوا لَنْ يَدْخُلَ الجَنَّةَ إلا مَن كانَ هُودًا أوْ نَصارى﴾. The report in this is about the People of the Book, and He bound the Christians together with them in His saying "وَقالُوا", because both groups read the Torah and differ over affirming the messengership of Moses and Jesus; that is why Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said "وَقالُوا", mentioning them together. The meaning is that the Jews said: "None will enter Paradise except whoever is a Jew (هُودًا)", and the Christians said: "None will enter Paradise except whoever is a Christian". It was permissible to use plural wording because the meaning of "مَن" is the meaning of "a group", so the predicate (khabar) was construed according to the meaning; the meaning is: "except those who were Jews and were Christians". [هُود] is the plural of "هائِدٌ", [like] "هَوْدٌ" [Translator's note: as printed], like "حائِلٌ" and "حَوْلٌ", and "بازِلٌ" and "بَزْلٌ". We have explained the singular of al-naṣārā and its plural earlier in the book.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿تِلْكَ أمانِيُّهُمْ﴾. This is as is said to someone who claims what he cannot prove: "You are merely wishing." "أمانِيُّهم" is with shadda; "تِلْكَ أمانِيهِمْ" is permissible in Arabic, but the reading is with shadda and nothing else, because of the consensus on it and because it is better in Arabic.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قُلْ هاتُوا بُرْهانَكم إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾, i.e. if you are truthful in your own estimation, then make clear what has shown you that Paradise is assured for you.

zajjaj:112-112.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بَلى مَن أسْلَمَ وجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ وهو مُحْسِنٌ فَلَهُ أجْرُهُ﴾, i.e. this one enters Paradise.

If someone asks: what then is the proof of the one who believes, according to your position? It is said: what we have explained of the argumentation for the Prophet ﷺ, and the demonstration of proofs by his informing them of what can be known only from a scripture or revelation, and by what was said to them about wishing for death, and the signs the Prophet ﷺ brought that establish the messengership. This is the proof of the one who submits his face to Allah.

zajjaj:113-113.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقالَتِ اليَهُودُ لَيْسَتِ النَّصارى عَلى شَيْءٍ وقالَتِ النَّصارى لَيْسَتِ اليَهُودُ عَلى شَيْءٍ وهم يَتْلُونَ الكِتابَ﴾. By this He means that both groups recite the Torah, yet this disagreement has occurred between them while their Book is one. By this He pointed to their misguidance, and by this He warned against disagreement occurring over the Qurʾān, because the disagreement of the two groups led them out into disbelief. So understand this place well, for in it there is a great argument and an admonition concerning the Qurʾān.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿كَذَلِكَ قالَ الَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ مِثْلَ قَوْلِهِمْ﴾. By this He means those who are not people of a scripture, such as the polytheists of the Arabs and the Magians. The meaning is that these too said: "None will enter Paradise except whoever follows our religion."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فاللَّهُ يَحْكُمُ بَيْنَهم يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾. The meaning is: He will show them openly who enters Paradise and who enters the Fire; this is the decisive judgement regarding the destination of each group. As for judging between them in creed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has already made it clear in the arguments of the Muslims that He has made manifest, and in the inability of creation to produce the like of the Qurʾān.

zajjaj:145-145.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلَئِنْ أتَيْتَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ بِكُلِّ آيَةٍ ما تَبِعُوا قِبْلَتَكَ﴾ — some grammarians claimed that "لَئِنْ" has been given the answer (jawāb) of "لَوْ", because the past verb follows it just as it follows "لَوْ" «[Translator's note: the source text here reads "الماضِيَ-٩", the "٩" apparently being a stray page or footnote marker]», so it was given the answer of "لَوْ", and each of the two enters upon the domain of its sister. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿وَلَئِنْ أرْسَلْنا رِيحًا فَرَأوْهُ مُصْفَرًّا لَظَلُّوا مِن بَعْدِهِ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾ [al-Rūm: 51], and it ran in the manner of "وَلَوْ أرْسَلْنا رِيحًا" ("and if We had sent a wind"). Al-Akhfash also held this view. Sībawayh and all his followers said that the meaning of "لَظَلُّوا مِن بَعْدِهِ يَكْفُرُونَ" is "لَيَظَلُّنَّ" ("they would surely remain"), and that the meaning of "لَئِنْ" is other than the meaning of "لَوْ", in the view of the majority. And even if those others said that the answer is the same, they do not deny that the meaning of "لَئِنْ" concerns what is in the future, while the meaning of "لَوْ" is past. The true meaning of "لَوْ" is that by it a thing is prevented because of the prevention of something else. You say: "لَوْ أتَيْتَنِي لَأكْرَمْتُكَ" ("had you come to me, I would have honoured you"), that is: "you did not come to me, so I did not honour you"; my honouring was prevented only because of your coming being prevented. The meaning of "إنْ" and "لَئِنْ" is that with them a thing occurs because of the occurrence of something else in the future. You say: "إنْ تَأْتِنِي أُكْرِمْكَ" ("if you come to me, I will honour you"); the honouring occurs with the occurrence of the coming. This is the true meaning of the two.

As for the interpretation (taʾwīl): the People of the Book knew that the Prophet ﷺ is true, and that his description and his prophethood are in their Book, and they were certain in their knowledge of that; so signs avail nothing with one who finds what he already knows.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَما بَعْضُهم بِتابِعٍ قِبْلَةَ بَعْضٍ﴾ — because the People of the Book backed one another against the Prophet ﷺ; the Jews do not follow the qibla of the Christians, nor do the Christians follow the qibla of the Jews, yet with that they are in agreement in backing one another against the Prophet.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿إنَّكَ إذًا لَمِنَ الظّالِمِينَ﴾, that is: you would surely be one of them if you followed their desires. This address is to the Prophet ﷺ and to the rest of his community, because whatever he was addressed with of this kind, the community has been addressed with it. The proof of that is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿يا أيُّها النَّبِيُّ إذا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّساءَ﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]: the beginning of the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the wording of the community is not with him, yet its end is proof that the address is general.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿الَّذِينَ آتَيْناهُمُ الكِتابَ يَعْرِفُونَهُ كَما يَعْرِفُونَ أبْناءَهُمْ﴾ [al-Baqara: 146] — by this He means the scholars of the Jews.

"اَلَّذِينَ" is nominative (marfūʿ) by being the mubtadaʾ (subject; lit. "by inception"), and the khabar (predicate) of "اَلَّذِينَ" is "يَعْرِفُونَهُ". Concerning "يَعْرِفُونَهُ" there are two views. Some said: they know that the matter of the qibla, and the Prophet's ﷺ turning from the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) to the Sacred House, is true, just as they know their sons. And it was said: the meaning of "يَعْرِفُونَهُ" is: they know the Prophet ﷺ and the soundness of his affair.

zajjaj:146-146.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَإنَّ فَرِيقًا مِنهم لَيَكْتُمُونَ الحَقَّ وهم يَعْلَمُونَ﴾, that is: they know that it is the truth; that is: they conceal his description, and [conceal it from] whoever does not know the matter of the Prophet ﷺ and what he brought, while they know that it is the truth.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿الحَقُّ مِن رَبِّكَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 147], that is: this is the truth from your Lord. ﴿فَلا تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ المُمْتَرِينَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 147], that is: of those who doubt. The address here too is general, that is: so do not be [plural] among those who doubt.

zajjaj:148-148.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلِكُلٍّ وِجْهَةٌ هو مُوَلِّيها﴾ — one says "هَذِهِ جِهَةٌ" ("this is a direction"), and "وَجْهَةٌ", and "وِجْهَةٌ"; likewise one says "ضَعَةٌ", "وَضْعَةٌ" and "ضِعَةٌ" (lowliness). Concerning His saying "هو مُوَلِّيها" two views have been given. Some of the people of language said — and it is the predominant view — that "هو" refers to "كُلٍّ" ("each"): the meaning is "he turns his face towards it", that is: the people of each direction are the ones who have turned their faces towards that direction. It has also been read: "هو مُوَلّاها" ("he is made to turn towards it"), and that is good. Others said: that is, Allah — according to what they claim — turns the people of every religion towards the qibla He wills. Both views are permissible, and Allah knows best.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فاسْتَبِقُوا الخَيْراتِ﴾, that is: hasten to acceptance from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and turn your faces wherever He has commanded you to turn them.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿أيْنَ ما تَكُونُوا يَأْتِ بِكُمُ اللَّهُ جَمِيعًا﴾, that is: He will return you to Himself. ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾, so you will be paid in full for what you did. "أيْنَما" puts what follows it in the jussive (majzūm), because when it is joined with "ما" it puts what follows it in the jussive, and the speech is a condition (sharṭ), and the answer (jawāb) is jussive like the condition. If it is interrogative — as in "أيْنَ زَيْدٌ" ("where is Zayd?") — then if you answer it, you answer in the jussive; you say: "أيْنَ بَيْتُكَ أزُرْكَ" ("where is your house, [so that] I may visit you?"), the meaning being: "if I know your house, I will visit you".

Some grammarians claimed that His saying: ﴿هَلْ أدُلُّكم عَلى تِجارَةٍ تُنْجِيكم مِن عَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾ [al-Ṣaff: 10] has as its answer "يَغْفِرْ لَكم" ("He will forgive you"). This is an error, because forgiveness does not become due by the guidance [to the transaction]; forgiveness becomes due only by their accepting what the Prophet ﷺ conveys to them. Rather, "يَغْفِرْ لَكم ذُنُوبَكم" is the answer to ﴿تُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ ورَسُولِهِ وتُجاهِدُونَ﴾ [al-Ṣaff: 11], for it is a command in the wording of a statement; the meaning is: believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive, [and] He will forgive you.

zajjaj:150-150.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿لِئَلا يَكُونَ لِلنّاسِ عَلَيْكم حُجَّةٌ﴾, that is: Allah has made known to you the matter of the argumentation concerning the qibla — of what we have already explained — so that people would have no argument against Allah regarding His saying: "ولِكُلٍّ وِجْهَةٌ هو مُوَلِّيها", that is: "He turns towards it so that there should not be…" («[Translator's note: the source writes "لِئَلّا يَكُونُ" with the imperfect in the nominative in this paraphrase; translated as written]»).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿إلا الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا مِنهم فَلا تَخْشَوْهُمْ﴾ — some said: [it means] "but those of them who did wrong, do not fear them". My view is that the meaning here is clear. The meaning is: so that people would have no argument against you, except one who does wrong by his argumentation concerning what has become clear to him; just as you say: "ما لَكَ عَلَيَّ مِن حُجَّةٍ إلّا الظُّلْمَ" ("you have no argument against me except wrongdoing"), that is: except that you wrong me. The meaning is: "you have no argument against me at all, but you are wronging me", and [likewise] "ما لَكَ عَلَيَّ حُجَّةٌ إلّا ظُلْمِي" ("you have no argument against me except wronging me"). His wrongdoing is called an "argument" here only because the one arguing by it called it an "argument", while his argument is void in the sight of Allah. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿حُجَّتُهم داحِضَةٌ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ [al-Shūrā: 16]; it was called an "argument", except that it is a nullified argument, so it is not an argument that establishes a right. This is a sufficient explanation, if Allah wills.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلأُتِمَّ نِعْمَتِي عَلَيْكُمْ﴾, that is: "I made [this] known to you so that there would be no argument against you, and so that I may complete My favour upon you, and that perhaps you may be guided".

zajjaj:151-151.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿كَما أرْسَلْنا فِيكم رَسُولا مِنكُمْ﴾ — "كَما" may be an answer to what precedes it, so that it would be: "that perhaps you may be guided, just as We sent among you a messenger from among you". The better [view] is that "كَما" is attached (muʿallaqa) to His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فاذْكُرُونِي أذْكُرْكُمْ﴾ [al-Baqara: 152], that is: remember Me with gratitude and sincerity, just as We sent among you….

If someone says: how can the answer of "كَما أرْسَلْنا" be "فاذْكُرُونِي أذْكُرْكم"? The answer here is that it is fit to be two answers, because His saying "فاذْكُرُونِي" is a command, and His saying "أذْكُرْكم" is the requital (jazāʾ) of "اُذْكُرُونِي"; the meaning is: if you remember Me, I will remember you.

The meaning of the verse is that it is an address to the Arab polytheists. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, addressed them with what guided them to the affirmation of the message of the Prophet ﷺ, and said: just as We sent among you Muḥammad ﷺ, a man from among you, unlettered, who you know did not recite any book before his message nor after it, except by what was revealed to him; and [you know] that you were people of the Jāhiliyya, not knowing wisdom, nor the reports of the prophets, nor of their forefathers, nor their stories; then He sent the Prophet ﷺ to you, and he informed you of the reports of the prophets and of what happened in their reports with their nations, and the People of the Book could not refute what he reported. So just as I bestowed favour upon you by sending him, remember Me by affirming My oneness and by believing him ﷺ, and be grateful to Me; I will remember you with My mercy, My forgiveness and praise of you.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا تَكْفُرُونِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 152] — what most of the readers (qurrāʾ) brought is the omission of the yāʾs along with the nūn.

zajjaj:231-231.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّساءَ فَبَلَغْنَ أجَلَهُنَّ﴾ means: the time at which their ʿidda (waiting period) comes to an end. ﴿فَأمْسِكُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ أوْ سَرِّحُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ﴾ means: leave them until the whole of their term is completed and they become more in possession of themselves.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تُمْسِكُوهُنَّ ضِرارًا﴾ means: do not retain them while you have no need of them. It has also been said that a man used to divorce a woman and leave her until the end of her term drew near, then take her back in order to harm her; so Allah forbade them this harming of women.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَمَن يَفْعَلْ ذَلِكَ فَقَدْ ظَلَمَ نَفْسَهُ﴾ means: he has exposed it to the punishment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, because doing what Allah has forbidden is exposing oneself to His punishment. The root meaning of ”اَلظُّلْمُ“ (wrongdoing) is putting a thing in other than its proper place, and we have already explained that.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تَتَّخِذُوا آياتِ اللَّهِ هُزُوًا﴾ means: what He has made clear to you of His indications and signs concerning divorce and other matters. Two views have been given on this. Some said: a man used to divorce or free a slave and then say: ”كُنْتُ لاعِبًا“ ("I was only joking"); so Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, made known that His obligations admit no joking. Others said: the meaning of ”وَلا تَتَّخِذُوا آياتِ اللَّهِ هُزُوًا“ is: do not abandon acting upon what Allah has defined for you, so that you become negligent and trifling — as you say to a man who does not carry out what he is charged with and is slack in it: ”إنَّما أنْتَ لاعِبٌ“ ("you are just playing").

zajjaj:232-232.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَلا تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ أنْ يَنْكِحْنَ أزْواجَهُنَّ﴾: this is addressed to the guardians (al-awliyāʾ), and in it is proof that the matter of guardians is clear, because the divorced woman who is being taken back is in possession of her own marital right (buḍʿ), yet a guardian is still indispensable. The meaning of ”تَعْضُلوهُنَّ“ is: prevent them and hold them back from marrying their husbands. The origin of this — according to what has been narrated — is «that the husband of Maʿqil ibn Yasār's sister divorced her, and Maʿqil ibn Yasār refused to marry her to him again and prevented her from that by right of guardianship. When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited it to him, and Maʿqil said: "My nose is humbled before the command of Allah."» The root of ”اَلْعَضْلُ“ is from their saying ”عَضَلَتِ الدَّجاجَةُ، فَهي مُعْضَلٌ“ ("the hen is egg-bound"), when her egg is held back and stuck and does not come out. One also says ”عَضَلَتِ النّاقَةُ، فَهي مُعْضَلٌ“ of a she-camel, when what is in her belly is held back.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ذَلِكَ يُوعَظُ بِهِ مَن كانَ مِنكم يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ﴾ means: by the command of Allah which He has recited to you, ”يُوعَظُ بِهِ مَن كانَ مِنكم يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ“, that is: whoever believes in the command of Allah, His threat and the Resurrection, and obeys Allah in these limits. He said ”ذَلِكَ يُوعَظُ بِهِ“ while addressing a plurality; we have already explained the view on this earlier. One of the philologists said that ”ذا“ together with the definite forms was imagined (tuwuhhima) to be a single word. I do not know who, other than the one who said this, holds this "imagining". Allah addressed the Arabs with what they understand, and addressed them in the most eloquent of dialects; there is no "imagining" in the Qurʾān — Allah is exalted far above that. Rather, the reality is that ”ذَلِكَ“ and ”ذَلِكم“ are both addresses to a plurality: the plurality's expression is a single expression, so the meaning is: ”ذَلِكَ أيُّها القَبِيلُ يُوعَظُ بِهِ مَن كانَ مِنكم يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ“ ("that, O company, is what whoever of you believes in Allah is admonished by").
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, after this: ﴿ذَلِكم أزْكى لَكم وأطْهَرُ﴾ shows that ”ذَلِكَ“ and ”ذَلِكم“ are an address to a group. The meaning of ﴿واللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ وأنْتُمْ لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ is: Allah knows what is in your best interest in this world and the next, and you do not know except what He has taught you.

zajjaj:233-233.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿والوالِداتُ يُرْضِعْنَ أوْلادَهُنَّ حَوْلَيْنِ كامِلَيْنِ﴾: the wording is that of a statement (khabar) and the meaning is a command, just as you say ”حَسْبُكَ دِرْهَمٌ“ ("a dirham is enough for you"), whose wording is a statement and whose meaning is ”اِكْتَفِ بِدِرْهَمِ“ ("be content with a dirham"). Likewise the meaning of the verse is ”لِتُرْضِعِ الوالِداتُ“ ("let the mothers suckle"). One says ”أرْضَعَتِ المَرْأةُ، فَهي مُرْضِعَةٌ“; their saying ”اِمْرَأةٌ مُرْضِعٌ“, without the hāʾ, means "a woman who is in the state of suckling". If you want the active participle (ism fāʿil) of ”أرْضَعَتْ“, you say ”مُرْضِعَةٌ“ and nothing else. One says ”رُضِعَ المَوْلُودُ، يُرْضَعُ“ and ”رَضَعَ، يَرْضَعُ“; the first is more common and clearer. One says ”اَلرَّضاعَةُ“ and ”اَلرِّضاعَةُ“, with fatḥa and with kasra; the fatḥa is the commonest and most correct usage, and the reading is according to it: ﴿لِمَن أرادَ أنْ يُتِمَّ الرَّضاعَةَ﴾. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash reported that some of Banū Tamīm say ”اَلرِّضاعَةُ“ with kasra on the rāʾ, and others besides him have also reported the kasra. One also says ”اَلرَّضاعُ“ and ”اَلرِّضاعُ“. One says ”ما حَمَلَهُ عَلى ذَلِكَ إلّا اللُّؤْمُ والرَّضاعَةُ“ ("nothing drove him to that but meanness and base nursing"), with fatḥa only here; and one says ”ما حَمَلَهُ عَلَيْهِ إلّا اللُّؤْمُ والرِّضْعُ“, like ”اَلْحِلْفُ“; and ”اَلرَّضْعُ“ — both are said. The meaning of ﴿حَوْلَيْنِ كامِلَيْنِ﴾ is twenty-four months, from the day he is born to the day he is weaned. It only says ”كامِلَيْنِ“ (complete) because a speaker may say "two years (ʿāmān, sanatān) have passed for that", allowing that the two years have passed while some part of them still remains, when there is an indication in the speech of what the speaker intends; but when He says ”كامِلَيْنِ“, it is not permissible that they fall short at all. It is read ”لِمَن أرادَ أنْ تَتِمَّ الرَّضاعَةُ“ and ”لِمَن أرادَ أنْ يُتِمَّ الرَّضاعَةَ“. This is the right of nursing, unless the two of them — I mean the parents — agree to weaning before the two years and consult each other about it.
The meaning of ﴿وَعَلى المَوْلُودِ لَهُ رِزْقُهُنَّ وكِسْوَتُهُنَّ﴾ is: the husband owes the divorced woman her provision if she suckles the child, and he owes the clothing. The meaning of ﴿بِالمَعْرُوفِ﴾ is: according to what they know to be just, in proportion to what is possible. The meaning of «لا تُكَلَّفُ نَفْسٌ إلّا وُسْعَها» is: it is charged only with the measure of what it is able to do.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لا تُضارَّ والِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِها﴾ has been read in two ways. ”لا تُضارُّ والِدَةٌ“, with ḍamma on the rāʾ, on the sense of ”لا تُكَلَّفُ نَفْسٌ“, as a statement (khabar) carrying the meaning of a command. Whoever read ”لا تُضارَّ والِدَةٌ“, with fatḥa on the rāʾ, the position is that of jazm (jussive) as a prohibition; the original is ”لا تُضارَرْ“, then the first rāʾ was assimilated into the second, and the second was given fatḥa because of the meeting of two sukūns. This is the preferred option with a doubled consonant when a fatḥa or an alif precedes it; the preferred form is ”عَضَّ يا رَجُلُ“ and ”ضارَّ زَيْدًا يا رَجُلُ“. ”لا تُضارِّ والِدَةٌ“ with kasra is also permissible, but I do not know anyone who read it so, so do not read it that way. Kasra is permissible only because of the meeting of two sukūns, since it is the original vowel for moving one of two sukūns. The meaning of ”لا تُضارَّ والِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِها“ is: she should not abandon suckling her child out of anger at his father and so harm him, because the mother is more tender towards her child than a stranger. ﴿وَلا مَوْلُودٌ لَهُ بِوَلَدِهِ﴾ means: he should not take him from his mother in order to harm her, and so harm his child. «وعَلى الوارِثِ مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ» means: he too is bound to refrain from harming.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَإنْ أرادا فِصالا عَنْ تَراضٍ مِنهُما وتَشاوُرٍ﴾ means: weaning, and they have agreed to that after consulting each other and knowing that it will not bring harm upon the child.
﴿فَلا جُناحَ عَلَيْهِما﴾ means: there is no sin on them in weaning, as we have described.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإنْ أرَدْتُمْ أنْ تَسْتَرْضِعُوا أوْلادَكُمْ﴾ means: that you seek a wet-nurse other than the mother for your children; then there is no sin on you. ﴿إذا سَلَّمْتُمْ ما آتَيْتُمْ بِالمَعْرُوفِ﴾: it has been said about it: when you hand the matter over to the wet-nurse; and it has been said: when you hand over what some of you have given to others, by mutual agreement in that.

zajjaj:272-272.t:
His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿لَيْسَ عَلَيْكَ هُداهُمْ﴾: its meaning is: your duty is only to convey [the message], just as He — Majestic and Mighty is He — said: ﴿وَلا تُسْألُ عَنْ أصْحابِ الجَحِيمِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 119]. And the meaning of ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ يَهْدِي مَن يَشاءُ﴾ is: He grants success (yuwaffiqu) to whomever He wills for guidance. Some people said: had Allah willed, He would have guided them, i.e. He would have compelled them to be guided, as He said: ﴿إنْ نَشَأْ نُنَـزِّلْ عَلَيْهِمْ مِنَ السَّماءِ آيَةً فَظَلَّتْ أعْناقُهم لَها خاضِعِينَ﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 4], and as He — Mighty and Majestic is He — said: ﴿وَلَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَمَعَهم عَلى الهُدى﴾ [al-Anʿām: 35]. But this [verse] is not like that; in this one there is: ”وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ يَهْدِي مَن يَشاءُ“, so no one is guided except through Allah's granting of success (tawfīq), as He said: ﴿وَما تَوْفِيقِي إلا بِاللَّهِ﴾ [Hūd: 88].

The meaning of ﴿وَما تُنْفِقُونَ إلا ابْتِغاءَ وجْهِ اللَّهِ﴾: this is specific to the believers. He informed them that He knew that by their spending they seek what is with Allah — Majestic and Mighty is He —, because when He informed them of that, they knew that they would be rewarded for it, as He said: ﴿وَما تُنْفِقُوا مِن خَيْرٍ يُوَفَّ إلَيْكم وأنْتُمْ لا تُظْلَمُونَ﴾.

His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكم ويُكَفِّرُ عَنْكم مِن سَيِّئاتِكُمْ﴾ [al-Baqara: 271]: the nominative (rafʿ) in ”يُكَفِّرُ“ and the jussive (jazm) are both permissible. It is also read ”وَنُكَفِّرُ عَنْكم“, with the nūn, and with the yāʾ. Sībawayh held that he prefers the nominative in ”وَيُكَفِّرُ“; he said: because what comes after the fāʾ has become equivalent to [what it would be] outside a conditional apodosis (jazāʾ). And he permitted the jussive on the basis of the position of ”فَهو خَيْرٌ لَكم“, because the meaning is: ”يَكُنْ خَيْرًا لَكم“ (it will be better for you). He mentioned that some read: ”مَن يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَلا هادِيَ لَهُ ويَذَرْهم“ with a jussive rāʾ, while the preferred choice in his view is the nominative in His saying ”وَيَذَرُهم“ and in ”وَنُكَفِّرُ“. He said: as for the accusative (naṣb), it is very weak; he does not allow ”وَنُكَفِّرَ عَنْكم“ except by way of poetic necessity (iḍṭirār), and he held that it is like the saying of the poet:
؎سَأتْرُكُ مَنزِلِي لِبَنِي تَمِيمٍ ∗∗∗ وألْحَقَ بِالحِجازِ فَأسْتَرِيحا
(I shall leave my dwelling to the Banū Tamīm and join the Ḥijāz, and so find rest.)
except that the accusative [in the verse] is slightly stronger, because [in it] one thing becomes necessary only through the necessity of another, so it resembles the interrogative and what is similar to it. This is the view of all the Basrans, and it is clear and evident.

zajjaj:273-273.t:
His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿لِلْفُقَراءِ الَّذِينَ أُحْصِرُوا في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾: ”فُقَراءُ“ is the plural of ”فَقِيرٌ“, like ”ظَرِيفٌ“ and ”ظُرَفاءُ“. They gave two views about ”أُحْصِرُوا“: they said the obligation of jihad confined them (aḥṣarahum) and so prevented them from moving about [for their livelihood]; and they said: their enemy confined them, because it kept them occupied with fighting it. The meaning of ”أُحْصِرُوا“ is: they reached the point of confining themselves to jihad, just as you say: ”رابَطَ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ“ (he stood guard in the path of Allah).

The meaning of ﴿لا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ ضَرْبًا في الأرْضِ﴾ is: they have bound themselves to the matter of jihad, and that prevented them from moving about — not because they are unable to move about. This is like your saying: ”أمَرَنِي المَوْلى أنْ أُقِيمَ، فَما أقْدِرُ عَلى أنْ أبْرَحَ“ (my master ordered me to stay, so I cannot leave): the meaning is that I have bound myself to obeying him, not that he is unable to move while being healthy and sound. One says: ”ضَرَبْتُ في الأرْضِ ضَرْبًا“ (I travelled in the land), and ”ضَرَبَ الفَحْلُ النّاقَةَ“ (the stallion covered the she-camel), when he mounts her — ضِراب. And ”اَلضَّرِيبُ“ is the frost that falls on the ground; one says: ”ضَرَبَتِ الأرْضُ“, and ”جُلِدَتِ الأرْضُ“ and ”جَلِدَتِ الأرْضُ“ (the ground was frosted). Al-Kisāʾī transmitted: ”ضَرِبَتِ الأرْضُ“ and ”جَلِدَتْ“, but the more common is ”ضَرَبَتْ“ and ”جُلِدَتْ“.

The meaning of ﴿يَحْسَبُهُمُ الجاهِلُ أغْنِياءَ مِنَ التَّعَفُّفِ﴾ is: the ignorant one reckons them and supposes them to be rich, because of their restraint from begging and their display of dignified appearance.

The meaning of ﴿لا يَسْألُونَ النّاسَ إلْحافًا﴾: it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: ”«مَن سَألَ ولَهُ أرْبَعُونَ دِرْهَمًا، فَقَدْ ألْحَفَ»“ (Whoever begs while he has forty dirhams has begged importunately). The meaning of ”ألْحَفَ“ is: he wrapped himself in begging while being in no need of it; and ”اَللِّحافُ“ (the coverlet) is derived from this, because it envelops a person in covering. The meaning is that there is no begging from them at all, such that there could be importunity from them, as Imruʾ al-Qays said:
؎عَلى لاحِبٍ لا يُهْتَدى بِمَنارِهِ ∗∗∗ إذا سافَهُ العَوْدُ الدَّيافِيَّ جَرْجَرا
(Upon a beaten track whose waymarks give no guidance; when the old Dayāfī camel sniffs it, it groans.)
The meaning is: it has no waymark by which one could be guided. Likewise, there is no begging from these people, such that importunity could occur in it.

zajjaj:274-274.t: His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم بِاللَّيْلِ والنَّهارِ سِرًّا وعَلانِيَةً فَلَهم أجْرُهُمْ﴾: ”اَلَّذِينَ“ is put in the nominative by inchoation (ibtidāʾ, i.e. as mubtadaʾ (subject)), and it is permissible for the khabar (predicate) to be what comes after the fāʾ. In [ordinary] speech one may not say ”زَيْدٌ فَمُنْطَلِقٌ“, because the fāʾ has no meaning there; it is only valid with ”اَلَّذِينَ“ because it comes with the sense of condition and apodosis (al-sharṭ wa-l-jazāʾ).

zajjaj:275-275.t:
His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿الَّذِينَ يَأْكُلُونَ الرِّبا لا يَقُومُونَ إلا كَما يَقُومُ الَّذِي يَتَخَبَّطُهُ الشَّيْطانُ مِنَ المَسِّ﴾: the meaning is: those who consume usury will not rise in the Hereafter except as the madman rises in the state of his madness. The people of tafsīr held that this is a mark for them at the Standing (al-mawqif), by which the people of the Standing will recognise them, and by which it will be known that they were consumers of usury in this world. One says: ”بِفُلانٍ مَسٌّ“ (so-and-so has a touch [of madness]), and ”هو ألْمَسُ“ and ”أوْلَقُ“, when he is mad.

His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿فَمَن جاءَهُ مَوْعِظَةٌ مِن رَبِّهِ فانْتَهى﴾: the masculine in ”جاءَهُ“ is permissible, while the Exalted said in another place: ﴿قَدْ جاءَتْكم مَوْعِظَةٌ مِن رَبِّكُمْ﴾ [Yūnus: 57], because every feminine that is not real may be treated as masculine. Do you not see that al-waʿẓ and al-mawʿiẓa express one and the same meaning?

His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿فَلَهُ ما سَلَفَ وأمْرُهُ إلى اللَّهِ﴾, i.e. he has been pardoned for what is past; ”وَأمْرُهُ إلى اللَّهِ“, i.e. Allah is his guardian.

The meaning of ﴿وَمَن عادَ فَأُولَئِكَ أصْحابُ النّارِ﴾ is: whoever returns to regarding usury as lawful is a disbeliever, because whoever makes lawful what Allah has forbidden is a disbeliever; and these people said: ﴿إنَّما البَيْعُ مِثْلُ الرِّبا﴾, and whoever believes this is a disbeliever.

zajjaj:278-278.t: His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿وَذَرُوا ما بَقِيَ مِنَ الرِّبا إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾: it was revealed concerning a group of the people of al-Ṭāʾif who had been granted a peace settlement on the terms that whatever usury they owed would be remitted from them, and that they would be allowed to take whatever usury was owed to them. They had money owed to them by a group of Quraysh, so when it fell due they demanded from them the money and the usury. That party said: Why are we the most wretched of people, that usury is taken from us which has been remitted from all other people? So Allah — Mighty and Majestic is He — commanded the abandoning of this remainder.

zajjaj:279-279.t: And He made known that whoever is a believer accepts His command from Allah, and whoever refuses is at war (ḥarb), i.e. a disbeliever. So He said: ﴿فَإنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا فَأْذَنُوا بِحَرْبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ ورَسُولِهِ﴾. Some read: ”فَآذِنُوا“. Whoever reads ”فَأْذَنُوا“, the meaning is: ”أيْقِنُوا“ (be certain); and whoever reads ”فَآذِنُوا“, its meaning is: then inform everyone who has not abandoned usury that he is at war. One says: ”قَدْ آذَنْتُهُ بِكَذا وكَذا، أُوذِنُهُ، إيذانًا“ when I have informed him; and ”قَدْ أذِنَ لَهُ، يَأْذَنُ، إذْنًا“ when he has come to know of it.

zajjaj:280-280.t:
His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿وَإنْ كانَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ فَنَظِرَةٌ إلى مَيْسَرَةٍ﴾, i.e. ”وَإنْ وقَعَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ“ (and if there occurs one in hardship). Had it been read ”وَإنْ كانَ ذا عُسْرَةٍ“, it would have been permissible, i.e. and if the debtor who owes the debt is in hardship; but the Muṣḥaf is not to be contravened. The nominative is on the basis that ”إنْ كانَ“ has the sense of ”إنْ وقَعَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ“. The nominative of ”فَنَظِرَةٌ إلى مَيْسَرَةٍ“ is on [the implied form] ”فَعَلى الَّذِي تُعامِلُونَهُ نَظِرَةٌ“ (then upon the one you deal with there is a deferment), i.e. a postponement; one says: ”بِعْتُهُ بَيْعًا بِنَظِرَةٍ“ (I sold it to him on deferred terms). Whoever read ”فَناظِرَةٌ إلى مَيْسَرَةٍ“, then [the pattern] ”فاعِلَةٌ“ is one of the nouns of maṣdar (verbal noun) [sense], like ﴿لَيْسَ لِوَقْعَتِها كاذِبَةٌ﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 2] and like ﴿تَظُنُّ أنْ يُفْعَلَ بِها فاقِرَةٌ﴾ [al-Qiyāma: 25]. If you wish, you may say: ”إلى مَيْسُرَةٍ“. As for whoever read ”إلى مَيْسُرِهِ“, by way of annexation to the hāʾ, he is mistaken, because ”مَيْسُرٌ“ is [on the pattern] ”مَفْعُلٌ“, and there is no ”مَفْعُلٌ“ in the language; the Basrans held that they do not recognise ”مَفْعُلًا“, but only recognise ”مَفْعُلَةً“.

So Allah commanded them to defer [collection of] the capital after the usury was dropped, if the one from whom it is demanded is in hardship, and He informed them that giving the capital to him in charity is better, so He said: ﴿وَأنْ تَصَدَّقُوا خَيْرٌ لَكم إنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾.

zajjaj:281-281.t: His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿واتَّقُوا يَوْمًا تُرْجَعُونَ فِيهِ إلى اللَّهِ ثُمَّ تُوَفّى كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما كَسَبَتْ وهم لا يُظْلَمُونَ﴾: this is the Day of Resurrection. It is said that it is the last verse revealed of the Book of Allah — Majestic and Mighty is He —; thus it has come in the tafsīr.

zajjaj:114-114.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَمَن أظْلَمُ مِمَّنْ مَنَعَ مَساجِدَ اللَّهِ﴾. The position of "مَن" is nominative (rafʿ), and its wording is the wording of a question; the meaning is: "And what one is more unjust than whoever prevents the mosques of Allah". "أظْلَمُ" is nominative as the khabar (predicate) of the mubtadaʾ (subject). The position of "أنْ" is accusative as a badal (substitute) from "مَساجِدَ اللَّهِ"; the meaning is: "And who is more unjust than whoever prevents His name being mentioned in the mosques of Allah". More than one view has been given in explaining this verse. It has come in the exegesis that by this the Romans (al-Rūm) are meant, because they had entered Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) and ruined it. It has also been said: the polytheists of Mecca are meant, because they strove to prevent the Muslims from remembering Allah in the Sacred Mosque. Some of the people of language said otherwise: it is claimed that all the disbelievers are meant, who joined forces against Islam and obstructed the mosques altogether, because whoever fights the Muslims until he prevents them from praying has obstructed all mosques; and every place in which worship is performed is a masjid. Do you not see that the Prophet ﷺ said: «جُعِلَتْ لِيَ الأرْضُ مَسْجِدًا وطَهُورًا» (The earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification)? So the meaning according to this doctrine is: "And who is more unjust than whoever opposes the religion of Islam?"

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أُولَئِكَ ما كانَ لَهم أنْ يَدْخُلُوها إلا خائِفِينَ﴾. Allah made known in this verse that the cause of the Muslims will prevail over all who oppose them, so that no opponent will be able to enter their mosques except in fear. This is like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿لِيُظْهِرَهُ عَلى الدِّينِ كُلِّهِ ولَوْ كَرِهَ المُشْرِكُونَ﴾ [al-Tawba: 33].

His saying: ﴿لَهم في الدُّنْيا خِزْيٌ ولَهم في الآخِرَةِ عَذابٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾. "خِزْيٌ" is nominative in two ways: one is as mubtadaʾ (ibtidāʾ), and the other is by the verb for which "لَهم" stands in; the meaning is: disgrace has become due to them in this world, and in the Hereafter a mighty punishment. The disgrace they have in this world is that they be killed if they are at war, and be made to pay the jizya (يُجْزَوْا) if they are under protection (dhimma). A mighty punishment was assigned to them because they are the most unjust of all who do wrong, by His saying: ﴿وَمَن أظْلَمُ مِمَّنْ مَنَعَ﴾.

zajjaj:115-115.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلِلَّهِ المَشْرِقُ والمَغْرِبُ﴾. Both are nominative in the two ways we have described. The meaning of "لِلَّهِ" is: He is their Creator.

His saying: ﴿فَأيْنَما تُوَلُّوا فَثَمَّ وجْهُ اللَّهِ﴾. "تُوَلُّوا" is jussive (majzūm) by "أيْنَما", and the answer (jawāb) is "فَثَمَّ وجْهُ اللَّهِ". The sign of the jussive in "تُوَلُّوا" is the dropping of the nūn. "ثَمَّ" is in the position of the accusative, but is indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa; you may not say "ثَمًّا زَيْدٌ". It was built on the fatḥa only because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. "ثَمَّ" is a pointing to place, like "هُنا زَيْدٌ" (Zayd is here): when you mean a near place you say "هُنا زَيْدٌ", and when you mean a place distant from you, you say "ثَمَّ زَيْدٌ" and "هُناكَ زَيْدٌ" (Zayd is there). "ثَمَّ" was denied declension (iʿrāb) only because of its vagueness (ibhām). I know of no one who has given this explanation, because it is not found in their books. As for the meaning of the verse, it has been said that by it the Sacred House is meant, so it was said: "أيْنَما تُوَلُّوا فَثَمَّ وجْهُ اللَّهِ", i.e. aim for the face of Allah by turning towards the qibla. The proof of whoever holds this view is His saying: ﴿وَمِن حَيْثُ خَرَجْتَ فَوَلِّ وجْهَكَ شَطْرَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 149]. It has also been said that some people were on a journey and were overtaken by darkness and rain, and did not know the qibla, so it was said: "فَأيْنَما تُوَلُّوا فَثَمَّ وجْهُ اللَّهِ". Some of the people of language said: the meaning is only the meaning of His saying: ﴿وَهُوَ مَعَكم أيْنَ ما كُنْتُمْ﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 4]; so the meaning according to this view of his is: Allah is with you wherever you turn, as if: "wherever you turn, there is Allah, and He is with you". We have only reported in this what people have said; we hold no definite position on it, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows best its reality. But His saying ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ واسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ points to His making things broad for people in something He has granted them as a concession.

zajjaj:116-116.t:
﴿وَقالُوا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ ولَدًا سُبْحانَهُ﴾. "وَقالُوا" refers to the Christians and the polytheists of the Arabs, because the Christians said: the Messiah is the son of Allah, and the polytheists of the Arabs said: the angels are the daughters of Allah. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿بَلْ لَهُ ما في السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ كُلٌّ لَهُ قانِتُونَ﴾. Al-qānit in the language is the obedient one. Al-Farrāʾ said: "كُلٌّ لَهُ قانِتُونَ" is specific; He means by it only the people of obedience. But the speech points against what he said, because in His saying "ما في السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ كُلٌّ لَهُ قانِتُونَ", "كُلٌّ" is all-encompassing. Its interpretation is only this: everything Allah has created in the heavens and the earth bears the trace of [His] making — so it is qānit to Allah — and is the proof that it is created.

Al-qānit in the language is also the one standing. Do you not see that al-qunūt — whoever supplicates standing in prayer is called by it "qānit"? So the meaning is: everything is qānit to Him, acknowledging that He is its Creator, because most of those who oppose do not deny that they are created; and whatever is otherwise, the trace of [His] making is clear in it, so it is qānit in the general sense. And the qānit is [also] the one who supplicates.

zajjaj:117-117.t:
His saying: ﴿بَدِيعُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ means: He brought them into being without any pattern or model. Whoever brings into being something in which he has not been preceded is told: "أبْدَعْتَ" (you have originated). For this reason everyone who opposes the Sunna and the consensus is called "مُبْتَدِعٌ" (innovator), because he brings into the religion of Islam something in which the Companions and the Successors did not precede him.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذا قَضى أمْرًا فَإنَّما يَقُولُ لَهُ كُنْ فَيَكُونُ﴾. "يَكُونُ" is nominative in two ways: if you wish, by conjunction (ʿaṭf) to "يَقُولُ", and if you wish, as a new beginning (istiʾnāf), the meaning being: "فَهو يَكُونُ" (so it is). As for the meaning of the verse, people have spoken about it with more than one view. Some of them said: "إنَّما يَقُولُ لَهُ كُنْ فَيَكُونُ" means: He only wills, and it comes about — as the poet said:

؎اِمْتَلَأ الحَوْضُ وقالَ قَطْنِي ∗∗∗ مَهْلًا رُوَيْدًا قَدْ مَلَأْتَ بَطْنِي
(The cistern filled and said: "Enough for me! Gently, slowly — you have filled my belly.")

and the cistern did not [actually] speak. Some of the people of language said: "إنَّما يَقُولُ لَهُ كُنْ فَيَكُونُ" means He says to it "Be" even though it is not present, because what is known to Him is like the present. Someone said: "إنَّما يَقُولُ لَهُ كُنْ فَيَكُونُ" — "لَهُ" has the meaning "for its sake", as if He only says, for the sake of His willing it: "Be", i.e. "come into being", and it comes into being. Some said: this may be [said] to known things in which He brought about [new] things, and so they became [so], like His saying: ﴿فَقُلْنا لَهم كُونُوا قِرَدَةً خاسِئِينَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 65]. And Allah knows best.

zajjaj:118-118.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقالَ الَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ لَوْلا يُكَلِّمُنا اللَّهُ أوْ تَأْتِينا آيَةٌ﴾. "لَوْلا" has the meaning of "هَلّا" (why not); the meaning is: why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign come to us? So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made known that their disbelief lay in obstinacy, demanding signs of their own proposing, like the saying of those before them to Moses: "أرِنا اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً" (show us Allah openly), and the like. So Allah made known that their disbelief is alike, and that their hearts have become alike in disbelief.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قَدْ بَيَّنّا الآياتِ لِقَوْمٍ يُوقِنُونَ﴾. The meaning in it is that whoever has certainty and seeks the truth, the clear signs have come to him — such as the Muslims, and those of the Jewish scholars who did not set themselves in hostility — because when he ﷺ brought them signs that cannot be matched, such as informing them of what can be known only by revelation, and such as the splitting of the moon, and his countless signs, peace be upon him, and the Qurʾān, about which it was said to them "فَأْتُوا بِسُورَةٍ مِن مِثْلِهِ" (then bring a sūra like it), and they were unable to do that — in this there is a sufficient proof.

zajjaj:197-197.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الحَجُّ أشْهُرٌ مَعْلُوماتٌ﴾. Most people said: the months of the Hajj are Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda and ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijja; ﴿فَمَن فَرَضَ فِيهِنَّ الحَجَّ فَلا رَفَثَ﴾. Some of them said: if the months that are the months of the Hajj were Shawwāl and Dhū al-Qaʿda, it would not be permissible for one whose dwelling is separated from Mecca by a distance longer than these months to make the Hajj binding upon himself. The real point of this, in my view, is that a person ought not to begin any of the works of the Hajj, such as the iḥrām, before this time, because if he begins before this time he harms himself. So the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, is that Shawwāl be the furthest limit of the times which a person ought not to precede in binding himself to the obligation of the Hajj. Some of the authorities on the language said: the Hajj is only at a specific time in the year, and it is only in the days in which a person engages in the works of the Hajj, because the ʿumra is open to him throughout the year; so at that time he ought not to commit rafath nor fusūq. The interpretation of ﴿فَلا رَفَثَ ولا فُسُوقَ﴾ is: no sexual intercourse, and no word belonging to the means leading to intercourse. The rajaz poet said:
عَنِ اللَّغا ورَفَثِ التَّكَلُّمِ
(…from idle talk and indecency of speech.)
”اَلرَّفَثُ“ is a word comprising everything a man desires from his wife. As for ”وَلا فُسُوقَ“: if intercourse in its entirety has been forbidden, fusūq is included in it; but the meaning — and Allah knows best — of ”وَلا فُسُوقَ“ is: let him not depart from anything of the matter of the Hajj. They gave two views on His saying ﴿وَلا جِدالَ في الحَجِّ﴾. They said: ”وَلا جِدالَ في الحَجِّ“ means there is no doubt about the Hajj; and they said: a man ought not to dispute with his brother so that the dispute leads him to what is improper, out of reverence for the matter of the Hajj. Both are correct. It is permissible to say: ”فَلا رَفَثٌ ولا فُسُوقٌ ولا جِدالٌ في الحَجِّ“, and some recite — namely Abū ʿAmr —: ”فَلا رَفَثٌ ولا فُسُوقَ ولا جِدالَ في الحَجِّ“, and both are correct. We have already explained that ”لا“ puts indefinite nouns in the accusative without tanwīn (nunation), and we have made clear the true nature of its accusative. Sībawayh and al-Khalīl claimed that it may put indefinite nouns in the nominative with tanwīn, and that in the saying of al-ʿAjjāj:
؎تاللَّهِ لَوْلا أنْ يَحُشَّنَّ الطُّبَّخُ ∗∗∗ بِيَ الجَحِيمَ حِينَ لا مُسْتَصْرِخُ
(By Allah, were it not that the stokers would feed Hellfire with me, at a time when there is no one to call for help…)
”مُسْتَصْرِخُ“ must have been put in the nominative by ”لا“; and that his saying:
؎مَن صَدَّ عَنْ نِيرانِها ∗∗∗ فَأنا ابْنُ قَيْسٍ لا بَراحُ
(Whoever turns away from its fires — I am Ibn Qays: there is no leaving!)
«[Translator's note: the sentence is left incomplete in the text as transmitted; the sense is that لا بَراحُ is likewise taken as nominative by لا.]»
The true account of what is nominative after it, according to some of his (Sībawayh's) followers, is that it is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), because when it does not govern the accusative, what follows it is treated just as what follows ”هَلْ“ is treated, i.e. it exerts no government on it at all. So ”فَلا رَفَثٌ“ may be according to what Sībawayh said, or it may be as a mubtadaʾ, as we described, with ”في الحَجِّ“ being the khabar (predicate) of these nominatives. And if you put what precedes the nominative in the accusative without tanwīn and bring what follows it in the nominative, it may be a conjoining onto the position, or its nominative may be as we described. As for conjoining onto the position: when you say ”لا رَجُلَ وغُلامٌ في الدّارِ“, it is as though you said ”ما رَجُلٌ ولا غُلامٌ في الدّارِ“ (there is neither a man nor a boy in the house).
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَتَزَوَّدُوا فَإنَّ خَيْرَ الزّادِ التَّقْوى﴾. It is narrated that some people used to set out on their Hajj living off other people, setting out without provisions; so they were commanded to take provisions, and were told along with that that the best provision one can take is the fear (taqwā) of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واتَّقُونِ يا أُولِي الألْبابِ﴾. The singular of ”اَلْألْبابُ“ is ”لُبٌّ“, and they are the intellects. ”أُولِي“ is accusative because it is a vocative in a genitive construct (munādā muḍāf).

zajjaj:198-198.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لَيْسَ عَلَيْكم جُناحٌ أنْ تَبْتَغُوا فَضْلا مِن رَبِّكُمْ﴾. It is said that they used to claim that there was no Hajj for a porter, a hired worker or a merchant; so Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, made known to them that this is permitted and that there is no junāḥ in it, i.e. no sin in it. ”جُناحٌ“ is the noun (ism) of ”لَيْسَ“ and the khabar (predicate) is ”عَلَيْكم“. The position of ”أنْ“ is accusative, on the implied form ”لَيْسَ عَلَيْكم جُناحٌ في أنْ تَبْتَغُوا“; when ”في“ was dropped, the meaning of ”جُناحٌ“ governed it. The meaning is: "you do not sin in seeking…", i.e. ”في أنْ تَبْتَغُوا...“.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَإذا أفَضْتُمْ مِن عَرَفاتٍ﴾. By this wording He indicated that standing there is obligatory, because pouring forth (ifāḍa) only happens after standing. The meaning of ”أفَضْتُمْ“ is: you pushed onward in great numbers. One says ”أفاضَ القَوْمُ في الحَدِيثِ“ when people launch into talk and range widely in it; ”أفاضَ الرَّجُلُ إناءَهُ“ when a man pours out his vessel; and ”أفاضَ البَعِيرُ بِجَرَّتِهِ“ when the camel throws up its cud scattered and abundant. Al-Rāʿī said:
؎وَأفَضْنَ بَعْدَ كُظُومِهِنَّ بِجَرَّةٍ ∗∗∗ مِن ذِي الأباطِحِ إذْ رَعَيْنَ حَقِيلا
(And after holding back their cud they threw it up — cud from Dhū al-Abāṭiḥ, when they had grazed at Ḥaqīl.)
And ”أفاضَ الرَّجُلُ بِالقِداحِ“ when a man casts the gaming arrows, because they fall springing out and scattered. Abū Dhuʾayb said:
؎وَكَأنَّهُنَّ رِبابَةٌ وكَأنَّهُ ∗∗∗ يَسِرٌ يَفِيضُ عَلى القِداحِ ويَصْدَعُ
(As though they were a bundle of gaming arrows, and he a gambler casting the arrows and calling out.)
Everything in the language belonging to the pattern of ifāḍa comes only from dispersal or abundance. «[Translator's note: in the text this last sentence is marked with the verse sign ؎ as though it were poetry, but it is prose.]»
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿مِن عَرَفاتٍ﴾. The reading and the proper form is with kasra and tanwīn (nunation). ”عَرَفاتٍ“ is the name of a single place whose form is that of a plural, and the proper form in it is to be fully declined (munṣarif) according to all the grammarians, because it is on the same footing as ”اَلزَّيْدِينَ“, its accusative and genitive being the same, and it is not on the footing of the feminine hāʾ. It may be treated as a diptote when it is the name of a single thing, except that it is then only ever with kasra, even if you drop the tanwīn. Imruʾ al-Qays said: تَنَوَّرْتُها مِن أذْرِعاتٍ وأهْلُها ∗∗∗ بِيَثْرِبَ أدْنى دارِها نَظَرٌ عالِ
(I glimpsed her fire from Adhriʿāt while her people were in Yathrib; the nearest of her dwelling is a lofty gaze away.)
This is the majority transmission, and it has also been recited with kasra without tanwīn. As for the fatḥa, it is a mistake, because the accusative of the (sound feminine) plural and its "fatḥa" is a kasra.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ عِنْدَ المَشْعَرِ الحَرامِ﴾. It is Muzdalifa, which is also Jamʿ; the place of worship (al-mashʿar al-mutaʿabbad) is called by both names.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واذْكُرُوهُ كَما هَداكُمْ﴾. The position of the kāf is accusative, and the meaning is: remember Him with a remembrance like His guiding of you, i.e. that it be a recompense for His guiding you; and remember Him by affirming His oneness, by praising Him and by thanking Him.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإنْ كُنْتُمْ مِن قَبْلِهِ لَمِنَ الضّالِّينَ﴾. The meaning of ”مِن قَبْلِهِ“ is: before His guidance. As for the meaning of ”كُنْتُمْ مِن قَبْلِهِ لَمِنَ الضّالِّينَ“: this is by way of emphasising the matter, as though it were said: you were, before it, nothing but astray.

zajjaj:199-199.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ثُمَّ أفِيضُوا مِن حَيْثُ أفاضَ النّاسُ﴾. It is said that the Ḥums of Quraysh and others — and we have explained the Ḥums earlier — would not pour forth with the people from ʿArafa, holding fast to their custom from the Jāhiliyya and doing so out of pride over the people and to set themselves above them. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, commanded them to be equal with the people in the obligation, to stand where they stand and to pour forth from where they pour forth.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واسْتَغْفِرُوا اللَّهَ إنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾, i.e. ask Him to forgive you for your having differed from the people in the pouring forth and the standing.

zajjaj:200-200.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَإذا قَضَيْتُمْ مَناسِكَكُمْ﴾, i.e. your acts of worship which you were commanded to perform in the Hajj; ﴿فاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ كَذِكْرِكم آباءَكُمْ﴾. When the Arabs had completed their rites, they would stand between the mosque at Minā and the mountain, enumerating the merits of their forefathers and recalling the glories of their days. So Allah commanded them to make that remembrance for Him and to exceed that remembrance, remembering Allah by affirming His oneness and enumerating His blessings; for if their forefathers had any blessings, they are from Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and He is the one to be thanked for them.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أوْ أشَدَّ ذِكْرًا﴾. ”أشَدَّ“ is in the position of the genitive (khafḍ), but it is diptote because it is on the pattern of ”أفْعَلُ“ and it is an adjective. If you wish, it is accusative, on the sense ”واذْكُرُوهُ أشَدَّ ذِكْرًا“. ”ذِكْرًا“ is accusative as a tamyīz (specification).
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَمِنَ النّاسِ مَن يَقُولُ رَبَّنا آتِنا في الدُّنْيا﴾. ”آتِنا“ is indeclinable (waqf), because it is a supplication; its meaning is "give us in this world". These are the polytheists of the Arabs, who used to ask for abundance in this world and did not ask for any share of the Hereafter, because they did not believe in the Hereafter.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَما لَهُ في الآخِرَةِ مِن خَلاقٍ﴾ means these people. ”اَلْخَلاقُ“ is the ample share of good.

zajjaj:153-153.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّبْرِ والصَّلاةِ﴾ — "يا أيُّها" is a singular, vague (mubham) vocative (nidāʾ), and "اَلَّذِينَ" is in the position of the nominative (rafʿ), as an adjective (ṣifa) of "أيُّها". This is the doctrine of al-Khalīl and Sībawayh. As for the doctrine of al-Akhfash, "اَلَّذِينَ" is a ṣila (relative clause) of "أيُّ", and the position of "اَلَّذِينَ" is nominative by the implication of the resumptive mention (al-dhikr al-ʿāʾid) referring back to "أيُّ"; it is as though, on al-Akhfash's doctrine, it is equivalent to your saying "يا مَنِ الَّذِينَ", that is: "يا مَن هُمُ الَّذِينَ" ("O you who are those who…"). The "ها" is inseparable from "أيُّ", as a compensation for what was omitted from it of the genitive construct (iḍāfa), and as an addition in alerting (tanbīh). "أيُّ", outside the vocative, does not have "ها" in it, and the resumptive mention referring back to it may be omitted along with it; you say: "اِضْرِبْ أيُّهم أفْضَلُ" and "أيُّهم هو أفْضَلُ" ("strike whichever of them is best"), meaning: "the one who is best".

Al-Māzinī permitted the adjective of "أيُّ" to be accusative (naṣb), and so permitted: "يا أيُّها الرَّجُلَ أقْبِلْ" ("O man, come forward!"). This permission is unknown in the speech of the Arabs; none of the grammarians permitted this doctrine before him, and no one followed him in it after him. So this is discarded and rejected, because it contradicts the speech of the Arabs, the Qurʾān and all the reports.

The meaning of ﴿اسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّبْرِ والصَّلاةِ﴾ is: [seek help] by steadfastness in what you are upon, even if something hateful befalls you in it in this present life, for Allah is with the patient. The interpretation of "Allah is with them" is: He makes His religion prevail over all religions, because whoever Allah is with is the victor, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿فَإنَّ حِزْبَ اللَّهِ هُمُ الغالِبُونَ﴾ [al-Māʾida: 56]. The meaning of "اِسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّلاةِ" ("seek help through prayer") is: when you pray, you recite in your prayer that by which you know the excellence of what you are upon, and that is a help to you.

zajjaj:154-154.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا تَقُولُوا لِمَن يُقْتَلُ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أمْواتٌ﴾ — with the implication (iḍmār) of the pronoun referring to them, that is: do not say: "they are dead". Allah forbade them to call one who was killed in the way of Allah "dead", and commanded them to call them "martyrs" (shuhadāʾ), and said: ﴿بَلْ أحْياءٌ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ يُرْزَقُونَ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 169]; so He informed us that whoever is killed in the way of Allah is alive.

If someone says: then why do we see a corpse that does not move? The proof of that is like what a person sees in his sleep while his body is not moving in accordance with what he sees; Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has taken his soul in his sleep, as He the Exalted said: ﴿اللَّهُ يَتَوَفّى الأنْفُسَ حِينَ مَوْتِها والَّتِي لَمْ تَمُتْ في مَنامِها﴾ [al-Zumar: 42]. The one who wakes from his sleep wakes while he is still in a remnant of that [state]. This is proof that it is possible for the spirits of the martyrs to leave their bodies while they are alive with Allah. So the ruling concerning one killed in the way of Allah is that he must not be called "dead"; rather he is called "martyr", and he is alive with Allah.

Another view than this has been given about it, but the view I have just mentioned is the one I choose. They said: the meaning of "dead" is: do not say: "they are dead in their religion"; rather say: they are alive in their religion. The proponents of this view said: our proof — and Allah knows best — is His saying: ﴿أوَمَن كانَ مَيْتًا فَأحْيَيْناهُ وجَعَلْنا لَهُ نُورًا يَمْشِي بِهِ في النّاسِ كَمَن مَثَلُهُ في الظُّلُماتِ لَيْسَ بِخارِجٍ مِنها﴾ [al-Anʿām: 122]; He made the rightly guided one alive, and [indicated] that when he was in misguidance he was dead. The first view is more consonant with the religion and closer to the exegesis (tafsīr).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلَنَبْلُوَنَّكم بِشَيْءٍ مِنَ الخَوْفِ والجُوعِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 155] — the grammarians differed over the fatḥa of this wāw. Sībawayh said: it takes fatḥa because of the meeting of two quiescent letters (iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn). Others among his followers said: it is indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa. Sībawayh had spoken [likewise] about the lām of "يَفْعَلُ" «[Translator's note: i.e. the final radical of the imperfect verb pattern; the sentence is elliptical in the source]», since with that it may be built on fatḥa; so those of his followers who said "it is indeclinable on fatḥa" are not departing from a view of his. Both views are permissible.

zajjaj:155-155.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿بِشَيْءٍ مِنَ الخَوْفِ والجُوعِ﴾ — and He did not say "بِأشْياءَ" ("with things"); it came only by way of concision, and the meaning indicates that it is: "and something of fear, and something of hunger, and something of loss of wealth and lives". Allah appointed this trial only because it is a greater incentive, for those who came after the Companions and those who were in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, to follow them, because they know that none endures these things patiently except one to whom the truth has become clear and the proof manifest. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gives them [recompense for] the afflictions that befall them in the present and the hereafter, and what is of greater benefit to them. So by this He combined the indication of clear insight, and made reward possible for those patient in that trial; and He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿وَبَشِّرِ الصّابِرِينَ﴾ — with blessings upon them from their Lord, and mercy, and that they are the rightly guided. And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿الَّذِينَ إذا أصابَتْهم مُصِيبَةٌ قالُوا إنّا لِلَّهِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 156], that is: we and our wealth belong to Allah, and we are His servants; He does with us what He wills, and in that there is righteousness and good for us. ﴿وَإنّا إلَيْهِ راجِعُونَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 156], that is: we affirm that we will be resurrected and given the reward for our affirmation and for patience in what He has tried us with.

zajjaj:157-157.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَواتٌ مِن رَبِّهِمْ ورَحْمَةٌ﴾ — ṣalāt in the language is of two kinds: one of them is bowing and prostration, and the other is mercy, praise and supplication. The people's ṣalāt over the dead means only supplication; praise of Allah is ṣalāt; and the ṣalāt of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, upon His prophets and His servants means mercy for them and praise of them. Our ṣalāt is bowing and prostration, as we have described, and supplication is ṣalāt. Al-Aʿshā said:

عَلَيْكِ مِثْلُ الَّذِي صَلَّيْتِ فاغْتَمِضِي ∗∗∗ نَوْمًا فَإنَّ لِجَنْبِ المَرْءِ مُضْطَجَعا
(Upon you be the like of what you prayed for, so close your eyes in sleep, for a man's side must have its resting place.)

It is also narrated: "مِثْلُ الَّذِي صَلَّيْتُ" ("the like of what I prayed"). Whoever says "عَلَيْكِ مِثْلُ الَّذِي صَلَّيْتُ", its meaning is that he commands her to supplicate for him the like of what he supplicated for her, that is, to return the supplication for him. Whoever narrates "عَلَيْكِ مِثْلُ الَّذِي صَلَّيْتِ", it is a reply to her, as though he said: "upon you be the like of your supplication: may there reach you of good the like of what you wished for me by this and supplicated for me". And the poet said:

صَلّى عَلى يَحْيى وأشْياعِهِ ∗∗∗ رَبٌّ كَرِيمٌ وشَفِيعٌ مُطاعْ
(May a generous Lord and an obeyed intercessor bless Yaḥyā and his partisans.)

The meaning is: upon him be mercy from Allah and fine praise.

The origin of all this, in my view, is from [the meaning of] clinging (luzūm). One says "صَلّى", "أصْلى" and "اِصْطَلى" when one clings; and from this is what is roasted (yuṣlā) in the fire, that is, it clings [to it]. The people of language said concerning ṣalāt: it is from al-ṣalawān, which are the two sides flanking the tail of the she-camel, and in the human the beginning of the thigh's junction; it is as though in reality they are what flanks the coccyx.
