So He reported of the believers that they say: we make no distinction between any of His messengers.

His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿وَقالُوا سَمِعْنا وأطَعْنا﴾, i.e. we have heard with the hearing of those who accept, and ”أطَعْنا“: we have accepted what we heard; because whoever hears and does not act is called ”أصَمُّ“ (deaf), as He — Majestic and Mighty is He — said: ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ﴾ [al-Baqara: 18] — not because they do not hear, but because, in failing to accept, they have become like one who does not hear. The poet said:
؎أصَمُّ عَمّا ساءَهُ سَمِيعُ
(Deaf to what displeases him, [yet] keen of hearing.)

The meaning of ﴿غُفْرانَكَ رَبَّنا وإلَيْكَ المَصِيرُ﴾ is: forgive [us] Your forgiveness; ”فُعْلانٌ“ is one of the nouns of maṣdar (verbal noun) [sense], like ”اَلسُّلْوانُ“ and ”اَلْكُفْرانُ“. And the meaning of ﴿وَإلَيْكَ المَصِيرُ﴾ is: we acknowledge the resurrection.

zajjaj:286-286.t:
His saying — Mighty and Majestic is He —: ﴿لا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إلا وُسْعَها﴾, i.e. except to the extent of its capacity: He does not impose on it any of His obligations — fasting, prayer, charity or anything else — except in the measure of its capacity. The meaning of ﴿لَها ما كَسَبَتْ وعَلَيْها ما اكْتَسَبَتْ﴾ is: He does not take anyone to task for another's sin, as He — Majestic and Mighty is He — said: ﴿وَلا تَزِرُ وازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرى﴾ [Fāṭir: 18].

The meaning of ﴿رَبَّنا لا تُؤاخِذْنا إنْ نَسِينا أوْ أخْطَأْنا﴾: two views are given on it. Some said: it accords with what has come from the Prophet ﷺ: ”عُفِيَ لِهَذِهِ الأُمَّةِ عَنْ نِسْيانِها، وما حَدَّثَتْ بِهِ أنْفُسَها“ (This community has been pardoned for its forgetting and for what its souls whisper to it). And it was said: ”﴿إنْ نَسِينا أوْ أخْطَأْنا﴾“, i.e. if we abandoned [something], and ”أوْ أخْطَأْنا“, i.e. we earned a sin — and Allah knows best. However, this supplication is something Allah reported of the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, and He placed it in His Book so that it would be the supplication of those who come after the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions — may Allah have mercy on them. It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ «that Allah — Majestic and Mighty is He — said at each section of this supplication: (I have done so… I have done so)», i.e. I have answered. So it is among the supplications that ought to be memorised and to be made often.

His saying — Majestic and Mighty is He —: ﴿رَبَّنا ولا تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنا إصْرًا كَما حَمَلْتَهُ عَلى الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِنا﴾: every bond, whether of kinship or of covenant, is an iṣr. The Arabs say: ”ما تَأْصِرُنِي عَلى فُلانٍ آصِرَةٌ“, i.e. no kinship nor favour inclines me towards him. Al-Ḥuṭayʾa said:
؎عَطَفُوا عَلَيَّ بِغَيْرِ آ ∗∗∗ صِرَةٍ فَقَدْ عَظُمَ الأواصِرُ
(They inclined towards me without any tie, so the ties [between us] have grown great.)
i.e. they inclined towards me without a bond of kinship. And ”اَلْمَأْصَرُ“ is taken from this: it is a binding by which [something] is held back. The thing with which things are tied is called ”اَلْإصارُ“. So the meaning is: do not lay upon us a heavy matter as You laid upon those before us, like what the Children of Israel were commanded of killing themselves; i.e. also: do not test us with what is heavy, like His saying: ﴿وَلَوْلا أنْ يَكُونَ النّاسُ أُمَّةً واحِدَةً لَجَعَلْنا لِمَن يَكْفُرُ بِالرَّحْمَنِ لِبُيُوتِهِمْ سُقُفًا مِن فِضَّةٍ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 33]. The meaning is: do not test us with a trial that is heavy.

The meaning of ﴿وَلا تُحَمِّلْنا ما لا طاقَةَ لَنا بِهِ﴾ is: what is heavy upon us.
If someone says: is it then possible for Allah to burden anyone with what he cannot bear? It is said to him: if you mean what is utterly outside his ability, this is impossible; but if you mean what is heavy or light, then Allah — Mighty and Majestic is He — may do of that whatever He wishes, because what He imposed on the Children of Israel, the killing of themselves, is heavy. This is like someone's saying: ”ما أُطِيقُ كَلامَ فُلانٍ“ (I cannot bear talking to so-and-so): the meaning is not that it is not within my ability to speak to him; rather, its meaning in the language is that it is heavy upon me.

The meaning of ﴿فانْصُرْنا عَلى القَوْمِ الكافِرِينَ﴾ is: give us victory over them in establishing the proof against them, and in our overcoming them in fighting them and in all their affairs, until You make our religion prevail over all religion, as You promised us.

zajjaj:165-165.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَمِنَ النّاسِ مَن يَتَّخِذُ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ أنْدادًا﴾ — He made known that after this clarification and proof, rivals (andād) are taken besides Him; these are equals (likenesses). So He made clear that among people is one who takes a rival whom he knows neither benefits nor harms, nor brings about anything of what we have mentioned. By this He meant the Arab polytheists.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿يُحِبُّونَهم كَحُبِّ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: they put these idols on a par with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in love. Some grammarian said: [it means] they love them as you love Allah. This view is worth nothing, and the proof of its refutation is His saying: ﴿والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أشَدُّ حُبًّا لِلَّهِ﴾; the meaning is that the sincere, who associate no one else with Allah, are the true lovers.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلَوْ يَرى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا إذْ يَرَوْنَ العَذابَ أنَّ القُوَّةَ لِلَّهِ جَمِيعًا وأنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ العَذابِ﴾ — there is more than one form in this. It is permissible [to read]: "أنَّ القُوَّةَ لِلَّهِ… وأنَّ اللَّهَ", and it is permissible: "أنَّ القُوَّةَ لِلَّهِ… وإنَّ اللَّهَ".

"وَلَوْ يَرى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا" — and "أنَّ" takes fatḥa with "تَرى", and takes kasra; all of that has been read. Al-Ḥasan read: "وَلَوْ يَرى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا إذْ يَرَوْنَ العَذابَ إنَّ القُوَّةَ… وإنَّ اللَّهَ". We shall explain how this must be construed, if Allah wills.

Whoever reads "أنَّ القُوَّةَ", the position of "أنَّ" is accusative (naṣb) by His saying: "وَلَوْ يَرى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا… أنَّ القُوَّةَ لِلَّهِ جَمِيعًا"; likewise the second "أنَّ" is accusative. The meaning is: if those who did wrong saw the severity of Allah's punishment and His power, they would know the harm of their taking rivals; and mention of the rivals has already occurred in His saying: ﴿وَمِنَ النّاسِ مَن يَتَّخِذُ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ أنْدادًا﴾. It is also permissible that the governing word (ʿāmil) in "أنَّ" be the answer (jawāb), according to what came in the exegesis: it is narrated in the exegesis of this that if those who used to associate partners in this world saw the punishment of the Hereafter, they would know, when they see it, that power belongs entirely to Allah. So the fatḥa of "أنَّ" is better and more frequent in reading, and its position is accusative in both these respects, as we have described.

It is also permissible that "إنَّ" be with kasra, beginning a new sentence (mustaʾnafa); then the answer of "وَلَوْ يَرى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا إذْ يَرَوْنَ العَذابَ" would be: "they would see a tremendous matter whose description cannot be reached", because the answer of "لَوْ" is left out only because of the greatness of what is described, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلَوْ أنَّ قُرْآنًا سُيِّرَتْ بِهِ الجِبالُ أوْ قُطِّعَتْ بِهِ الأرْضُ أوْ كُلِّمَ بِهِ المَوْتى﴾ [al-Raʿd: 31], the meaning being: this Qurʾān would be more eloquent than anything described. And "أنَّ القُوَّةَ لِلَّهِ جَمِيعًا" «[Translator's note: so written with fatḥa in the source, though the context is the kasra reading]» would be a new sentence (istiʾnāf), informing by His saying "that power belongs entirely to Allah", and the omitted answer would not be connected with "أنَّ".

Whoever reads "وَلَوْ تَرى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا", the tāʾ is an address to the Prophet ﷺ by which people are meant, as He said: ﴿ألَمْ تَعْلَمْ أنَّ اللَّهَ لَهُ مُلْكُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ وما لَكم مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ مِن ولِيٍّ ولا نَصِيرٍ﴾ [al-Baqara: 107], which is equivalent to "ألَمْ تَعْلَمُوا؟" ("do you [plural] not know?"); likewise "وَلَوْ تَرى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا" is equivalent to "وَلَوْ تَرَوْنَ" ("if you [plural] saw"). Then "أنَّ القُوَّةَ لِلَّهِ جَمِيعًا" would be a new sentence, as we have described, and the answer would be — and Allah knows best —: "you would see a tremendous matter", just as one says: "لَوْ رَأيْتَ فُلانًا والسِّياطُ تَأْخُذُهُ" ("if you had seen so-and-so while the whips were taking him!"), and the answer is dispensed with because the meaning is known. It is also permissible to give "أنَّ" fatḥa with "تَرى", so that it would be: "you would see, O you addressed, that power belongs entirely to Allah", or: "you would see that the rivals did not benefit, but only reached the utmost in harm, because power belongs entirely to Allah".

"جَمِيعًا" is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial); the meaning is that power is established for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in the state of its being all together.

zajjaj:166-166.t:
His saying: ﴿إذْ تَبَرَّأ الَّذِينَ اتُّبِعُوا مِنَ الَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوا﴾ — by it He means the chiefs and the nobles; ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوا﴾ — these are the followers and the lowly. ﴿وَرَأوُا العَذابَ﴾ — by it are meant the followers and the followed. ﴿وَتَقَطَّعَتْ بِهِمُ الأسْبابُ﴾, that is: their bond which had united them was cut off, as He said: ﴿لَقَدْ تَقَطَّعَ بَيْنَكم وضَلَّ عَنْكم ما كُنْتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ﴾ [al-Anʿām: 94]; "بَيْنَهُمْ" is their bond, and what was cut off between them in the Hereafter had joined them in this world.

The alif in His saying "اُتُّبِعُوا" was given ḍamma only because of the ḍamma of the tāʾ, and the tāʾ was given ḍamma as the sign of [the verb] whose agent is not named (i.e. the passive).

If someone says: the [verb] whose agent is not named has ḍamma on its first [letter], while the tāʾ with ḍamma in "اُتُّبِعُوا" is the third — it is said: for [the verb] whose agent is not named, it is the first of the voweled letters of the verb that takes ḍamma. When there is a quiescent letter at the beginning, the connecting alif (alif al-waṣl) is brought in for it, and what was voweled takes ḍamma; the voweled letter in "اُتُّبِعُوا" was the second tāʾ, so it took ḍamma as an indication of the omission of the agent. Also, in "اُتُّبِعُوا" there is a connecting alif, which entered because of the quiescence of the fāʾ of the verb (its first radical), since its pattern among verbs is "اُفْتُعِلُوا". The alif is a connecting alif, and the ḍamma of the first [letter] in a verb whose agent is not named is not built upon it; and the fāʾ is quiescent, and nothing is built upon a quiescent letter. So only the third remained, which is the tāʾ, and it took ḍamma as a mark of the verb whose agent is not named. So, for this reason, the third was [in effect] the first.

zajjaj:167-167.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَقالَ الَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوا لَوْ أنَّ لَنا كَرَّةً فَنَتَبَرَّأ﴾, that is: a return to this world, so that we might disown them. The position of "أنَّ" is nominative (rafʿ); the meaning is: if a return were to happen for us, we would disown them as they disowned us. One says: "تَبَرَّأْتُ مِنهم تَبَرُّؤًا" ("I disowned them"), and "بَرِئْتُ مِنهُ بَراءَةً" ("I was free of him"), and "بَرِئْتُ مِنَ المَرَضِ" ("I recovered from illness") and also "بَرَأْتُ" — two dialects — "أبْرَأُ، بَرْءًا"; and "بَرَيْتُ القَلَمَ، وغَيْرَهُ، وأبْرِيهِ" ("I sharpened the pen and other things"), without hamza; and "بَرَأ اللَّهُ الخَلْقَ بَرْءًا" ("Allah created creation").

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿كَذَلِكَ يُرِيهِمُ اللَّهُ أعْمالَهم حَسَراتٍ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾, that is: like their disowning one another, Allah shows them their deeds as regrets upon them, because what the disbeliever has done does not benefit him along with his disbelief. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وصَدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أضَلَّ أعْمالَهُمْ﴾ [Muḥammad: 1], and He said: "حَبِطَتْ أعْمالُهم" ("their deeds have come to nothing"). The meaning of "أضَلَّ أعْمالَهم" is: He did not reward them for whatever good they did; this is as you say to someone who did a deed from which no benefit returned to him: "لَقَدْ ضَلَّ سَعْيُكَ" ("your effort has gone astray").

zajjaj:168-168.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿يا أيُّها النّاسُ كُلُوا مِمّا في الأرْضِ حَلالا طَيِّبًا﴾ — this is of two kinds. One of them is the permission to eat all things except what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden of carrion and what He mentioned along with it; so "طَيِّبًا" would be a naʿt (adjective) of "the lawful", and "طَيِّبًا" would be a description of what is found wholesome. The better [view] is that "طَيِّبًا" means: from where it is good [lawful] for you, that is: do not eat and spend from what is forbidden to you, like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا تَيَمَّمُوا الخَبِيثَ مِنهُ تُنْفِقُونَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 267].

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا تَتَّبِعُوا خُطُواتِ الشَّيْطانِ﴾ — most of the reading is "خُطُواتِ" with ḍamma on the khāʾ and the ṭāʾ. If you wish, you make the ṭāʾ quiescent, "خُطْواتِ", because of the heaviness of the ḍamma; and if you wish, "خُطَواتِ", which is an anomalous (shādhdha) reading, but it is permissible in Arabic and strong. Al-Khalīl, Sībawayh and all the Basran grammarians recited:

وَلَمّا رَأوْنا بادِيًا رُكَباتُنا ∗∗∗ عَلى مَوْطِنٍ لا نَخْلِطُ الجِدَّ بِالهَزْلِ
(When they saw us with our knees showing, on a battlefield where we do not mix earnest with jest.) «[Translator's note: cited for "رُكَباتُنا" with fatḥa on the middle letter.]»

The meaning of "خُطُواتِ الشَّيْطانِ" is: his paths, that is: do not travel the path to which Satan calls you.

zajjaj:246-246.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ألَمْ تَرَ إلى المَلإ مِن بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ﴾: ”اَلْمَلَأُ“ are the nobles of a people and their leading men. It is narrated «that the Prophet ﷺ heard a man of the Anṣār, when they had returned from Badr, saying: "We killed only bald old men." He ﷺ said: "Those were the notables (al-malaʾ) of Quraysh; had you witnessed their deeds, you would have thought little of your own."» ”اَلْمَلَأُ“ in the language also means character (al-khuluq); one says ”أحْسِنُوا مَلَأكم“, that is, your characters. The poet said:
؎تَنادَوْا يا آلَ بُهْثَةَ إذْ رَأوْنا ∗∗∗ فَقُلْنا أحْسِنِي مَلَأً جُهَيْنا
(They called out "O family of Buhtha!" when they saw us, and we said: "Be of good character (malaʾ), Juhayna!")
that is, in character. One says ”أحْسِنِي مُمالَأةً“, that is, mutual help. And one says ”رَجُلٌ مَلِيءٌ“ — with hamza — that is, "clearly well-off (malāʾ), you there". The origin of all of this in the language is one thing: ”اَلْمَلَأُ“ are the chiefs, and they are called so only because they are full (milʾ) of what is needed from them; and the malaʾ which is in character is only a character full of what is needed. ”اَلْمَلا“ is a wide expanse of land, without hamza; it is written with alif and with yāʾ according to some, while the Basrans write it with alif. The poet said, concerning malā with short final alif, which denotes a wide expanse of land:
؎ألا غَنِّيانِي وارْفَعا الصَّوْتَ بِالمَلا ∗∗∗ فَإنَّ المَلا عِنْدِي يَزِيدُ المَدى بُعْدا
(Come, you two, sing to me and raise your voices in the open plain, for the open plain, to my mind, makes the distance yet farther.)
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ابْعَثْ لَنا مَلِكًا نُقاتِلْ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾: the jussive (jazm) in ”نُقاتِلْ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ“ is the right way, as the answer to the request which is in the form of a command, that is: ”اِبْعَثْ لَنا مَلِكًا نُقاتِلْ“, meaning ”إنْ تَبْعَثْ لَنا مَلِكًا نُقاتِلْ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ“ ("if you send us a king, we will fight in the way of Allah"). Whoever read ”مَلِكًا يُقاتِلُ“, with yāʾ, takes it as a description (ṣifa) of the king. But ”نُقاتِلْ“ is the way followed by the readers. The nominative in it is far-fetched; it is permissible in the sense of ”فَإنّا نُقاتِلُ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ“ ("for we will fight in the way of Allah"), but many grammarians do not permit the nominative in ”نُقاتِلُ“.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿هَلْ عَسَيْتُمْ إنْ كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ القِتالُ ألا تُقاتِلُوا﴾ means: perhaps you will be too cowardly to fight. Some read ”هَلْ عَسِيتُمْ“ — with kasra on the sīn — ”إنْ كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ القِتالُ“, and this is the reading of Nāfiʿ; but all the philologists say ”عَسَيْتُ أنْ أفْعَلَ“ and prefer it. The position of ”ألّا تُقاتِلُوا“ is accusative — I mean the position of ”أنْ“ — because ”أنْ“ and what it governs are like a maṣdar (verbal noun): when you say ”عَسَيْتُ أنْ أفْعَلَ ذاكَ“, it is as though you said ”عَسَيْتُ فِعْلَ ذَلِكَ“.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قالُوا وما لَنا ألا نُقاتِلَ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾: Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash held that ”أنْ“ here is redundant (zāʾida); he said: the meaning is "and why should we not fight in the way of Allah". Others said: ”وَما لَنا في ألّا نُقاتِلَ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ“, with ”في“ dropped. Some grammarians said: ”أنْ“ only entered because ”ما“ means ”ما يَمْنَعُنا؟“ ("what prevents us?"), and that is why ”أنْ“ entered, since the [usual] expression is "what is the matter with you that you do such-and-such". The correct view in my opinion is that ”أنْ“ is not to be treated as void here, and that the meaning is: "and what [benefit] is there for us in not fighting in the way of Allah?", that is: "what is there for us in abandoning fighting?" ﴿وَقَدْ أُخْرِجْنا مِن دِيارِنا وأبْنائِنا﴾: the meaning of ”وأبْنائِنا“ is: our offspring have been taken captive. But ”في“ dropped together with ”أنْ“, because the verb used with ”أنْ“ indicates a known time, so with ”أنْ“ the preposition may be omitted, as you say ”هَرَبْتُ أنْ أقُولَ كَ كَذا وكَذا“ «[Translator's note: so in the source, «أقُولَ كَ», apparently a slip for «أقُولَ لَكَ».]», meaning ”هَرَبْتُ أنْ أقُولَ لَكَ كَذا وكَذا“ ("I fled from saying such-and-such to you").
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿تَوَلَّوْا إلا قَلِيلا مِنهُمْ﴾: ”قَلِيلًا“ is accusative as the excepted (mustathnā). As for whoever transmitted ”تَوَلَّوْا إلّا قَلِيلٌ مِنهم“, I do not know this reading, nor does it have any justification in my view, because the muṣḥaf has the accusative and grammar requires it: when the beginning of the sentence in an exception is affirmative, as in your saying ”جاءَنِي القَوْمُ إلّا زَيْدًا“ ("the people came to me except Zayd"), the excepted ”زَيْدٌ“ can only be accusative. The meaning is: "they turned away — I except a few of them". I mentioned this only because some transmitted ”فَشَرِبُوا مِنهُ إلّا قَلِيلٌ مِنهم“, and this in my view has no justification.

zajjaj:247-247.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقالَ لَهم نَبِيُّهم إنَّ اللَّهَ قَدْ بَعَثَ لَكم طالُوتَ مَلِكًا﴾ means: He has granted you what you asked for — the sending of a king who will fight, and you will fight with him. ”طالُوتُ“, ”جالُوتُ“ and ”داوُدُ“ are diptotes (lā tanṣarif), because they are foreign names and they are definite, so two things are combined in them: definiteness and foreignness. As for ”جامُوسٌ“ (buffalo), if you named a man with it, it would be fully declined even though it is foreign, because it has become established in Arabic, since you put the article on it and say ”اَلْجامُوسُ“, and likewise ”اَلرّاقُودُ“ (a large wine-jar). On this basis is the analogy for the whole chapter.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أنّى يَكُونُ لَهُ المُلْكُ عَلَيْنا﴾ means: from what direction could that be? ﴿وَلَمْ يُؤْتَ سَعَةً مِنَ المالِ﴾ means: he has not been given that by which kings acquire kingship. So Allah informed them that He ﴿اصْطَفاهُ﴾, meaning: chose him. It is the form ”اِفْتَعَلَ“ from ”اَلصَّفْوَةُ“, and the original is ”اِصْتَفاهُ“. When tāʾ comes after ṣād it is changed into ṭāʾ, because tāʾ is from the point of articulation of ṭāʾ, and ṭāʾ is a covered (muṭbaqa, velarised) letter just as ṣād is; so they substituted ṭāʾ for tāʾ to make pronouncing what comes after the ṣād easier. Likewise ”اِفْتَعَلَ“ from ”اَلضَّرْبُ“ is ”اِضْطَرَبَ“, and from ”اَلظُّلْمُ“ is ”اِظْطَلَمَ“. In ”اِظْطَلَمَ“ two other forms are permissible: ”اِطَّلَمَ“, with a doubled undotted ṭāʾ, and ”اِظَّلَمَ“, with a doubled ẓāʾ. Zuhayr said:
؎هُوَ الجَوادُ الَّذِي يُعْطِيكَ نائِلَهُ ∗∗∗ عَفْوًا ويَظْلِمُ أحْيانًا فَيَظْطَلِمُ
(He is the generous one who gives you his bounty unasked, and is sometimes imposed upon, and bears the imposition.)
— and ”فَيَطَّلِمُ“ and ”فَيَظَّلِمُ“. Allah informed them that He had chosen him and that he had been given increase of abundance in knowledge and in body, and He informed them that knowledge is that by which the choice ought to be made — it is not that Allah, Majestic and Mighty is He, makes only a man of wealth a king. And He made known that increase in body is among the things by which the enemy is awed «[Translator's note: the source has «يَهَبُ بِهِ العَدُوُّ»; translated as if «يَهابُهُ», "is awed by".]». And He informed them that He gives His kingship to whom He wills, and He, Majestic and Mighty is He, wills only what is wisdom and justice.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واللَّهُ واسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ means: He gives abundance to whom He wills, and knows where abundance ought to be.

zajjaj:248-248.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقالَ لَهم نَبِيُّهم إنَّ آيَةَ مُلْكِهِ﴾ means: the sign of Allah's granting him kingship ﴿أنْ يَأْتِيَكُمُ التّابُوتُ﴾. The position of ”أنْ“ is nominative; the meaning is: the sign of his kingship is the Ark's coming to you.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فِيهِ سَكِينَةٌ مِن رَبِّكُمْ﴾ means: in it is that by which you will find tranquillity when it comes to you. It has been said in the exegesis that the sakīna had a head like the head of a cat, of chrysolite or ruby, and it had two wings.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَبَقِيَّةٌ مِمّا تَرَكَ آلُ مُوسى وآلُ هارُونَ﴾: it has been said in its exegesis that ”اَلْبَقِيَّةُ“ (the remnant) is the fragments of the Tablets, and that the Torah was in it, and another book which collected the Torah, and the staff of Moses; this is what has been narrated of its contents. The apparent sense is that ”فِيهِ بَقِيَّةٌ“ may be a remnant of some of the signs of the prophets, or the remnant may be of knowledge, or it may include both together. The benefit of this Ark was that the prophets, the blessings of Allah be upon them, used to seek victory through it in wars: the Ark would be in front of them, and when a moaning was heard from inside it, the Ark would move off (duffa), that is, travel, with all of them behind it. And Allah knows best the reality of that.
It is narrated in the exegesis that it was made of boxwood (al-shamshār), and Goliath and his companions had seized it, and on account of it a disease befell them — it is said to have been the fistula (al-nāsūr) that occurs in the ʿinab «[Translator's note: so in the source, «في العِنَبِ», literally "in the grapes"; the intended word is uncertain.]». They knew that the affliction had befallen them because of it, so they placed it on two oxen, so it is said. It has been said that the meaning of ﴿تَحْمِلُهُ المَلائِكَةُ﴾ is that they were driving the two oxen; and it is permissible in the language to say ”تَحْمِلُهُ المَلائِكَةُ“ ("the angels carry it") when they were only driving what carried it, as you say ”حَمَلْتُ مَتاعِي إلى مَكَّةَ“ ("I carried my goods to Mecca"), that is, I was the cause of its being carried to Mecca. The meaning of ﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لآيَةً لَكُمْ﴾ is: in the return of the Ark to you is a sign that Allah has made Ṭālūt king over you, since He informed you of something unseen in his story. ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ means: if you are believers (muṣaddiqīn).

zajjaj:128-128.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واجْعَلْنا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ ومِن ذُرِّيَّتِنا أُمَّةً مُسْلِمَةً لَكَ﴾. The explanation of al-muslim in the language: the one who has surrendered to the whole of Allah's command and submitted to it. The true muslim is the one who has outwardly shown acceptance of the whole of Allah's command and inwardly holds the same. Likewise His saying: ﴿قالَتِ الأعْرابُ آمَنّا قُلْ لَمْ تُؤْمِنُوا ولَكِنْ قُولُوا أسْلَمْنا﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 14]; the meaning is: say, all of you, "We have submitted and shown Islam outwardly", while their inner state was other than their outward one, because these were hypocrites; so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed the Prophet of their secrets. So the muslim is of two kinds: one who shows acceptance outwardly and holds inwardly the same as he shows — this one is called "مُؤْمِنٌ" (believer); and a muslim who shows outwardly other than what he hides — this one is not a believer, because assent and faith consist in outward display together with [inner] acceptance. Do you not see that it was said to them: ﴿وَلَمّا يَدْخُلِ الإيمانُ في قُلُوبِكُمْ﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 14]? I.e. you displayed faith out of fear.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَأرِنا مَناسِكَنا﴾. Its meaning is: make known to us our places and acts of worship. Every place or act of worship is a "مَنسَكٌ" or "مَنسِكٌ"; from this the worshipper is called "ناسِكٌ", and the sacrificial animal offered to draw near to Allah, Exalted is He, is called "اَلنَّسِيكَةُ" — as though the origin of al-nusuk were from sacrifice to Allah, Majestic and Mighty. "وَأرِنا" is also read in two ways: with kasra on the rāʾ and with it quiescent; the better is the kasra. Abū ʿAmr made it quiescent only because he treated it like "فَخِذٌ" (fakhidh → fakhdh) and "عَضُدٌ" (ʿaḍud → ʿaḍd). But this is not like "فَخِذٌ" nor "عَضُدٌ", because the base of this is "أرْئِنا"; the kasra is the kasra of a hamza that was dropped and whose vowel was cast onto the rāʾ, so the kasra is the indication of the hamza, and deleting it is ugly. It is permissible, though far-fetched, because kasra and ḍamma are deleted only by way of [avoiding] heaviness, and pronouncing the kasra of the hamza and the kasra that is part of the word's structure is one and the same in pronunciation. But the preferred choice is what we described first.

zajjaj:130-130.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَمَن يَرْغَبُ عَنْ مِلَّةِ إبْراهِيمَ إلا مَن سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾. The meaning of "مَن" is affirmation-seeking (taqrīr) and rebuke (tawbīkh), while its wording is the wording of a question; its position is nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject). The meaning is: none turns away from the religion of Abraham except one who سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ. We have explained "اَلْمِلَّةُ": it is the way of life and the doctrine. The grammarians have said much and differed over the explanation of سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ, and likewise the people of language. Al-Akhfash said: the people of interpretation claim that the meaning is "سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ" [Translator's note: so in the text; probably intended as سَفَّهَ نَفْسَهُ, "made a fool of himself"]. Yūnus the grammarian said: I consider it a dialectal usage. Yūnus held that "فَعِلَ" is for intensiveness, as "فَعُلَ" is for intensiveness, so in this he followed the approach of the interpreters; on this view one may say "سَفِهْتُ زَيْدًا" in the sense of "سَفَّهْتُ زَيْدًا" (I declared Zayd foolish). Abū ʿUbayda said: its meaning is: he destroyed himself and ruined himself; this does not depart from the approach of the interpreters and the approach of Yūnus. One of the grammarians said that "نَفْسَهُ" is accusative as tafsīr (specification, i.e. tamyīz), and said: specification is more common with indefinite nouns, as in "طابَ زَيْدٌ بِأمْرِهِ نَفْسًا، وقَرَّ بِهِ عَيْنًا" (Zayd was content with his affair in soul and delighted with it in eye). He claimed that with these definite specifiers the verb originally belongs to them and was then transferred to the agent, as in "وَجِعَ زَيْدٌ رَأسَهُ" (Zayd ached in his head), claiming that the verb originally belongs to the head and the like; that he does not permit any of these accusatives to be placed first; and he put "سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ" in this category. Abū Isḥāq [al-Zajjāj] said: In my view the meaning of tamyīz (specification) does not admit definiteness, because tamyīz is only a single item indicating a genus, or one quality singled out from among qualities; if one makes it definite it becomes something specifically intended. None of the earlier grammarians said this. Abū Isḥāq said: "سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ" means "سَفُهَ في نَفْسِهِ" (he was foolish in himself), except that "في" was deleted, as prepositions have been deleted in more than one place. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "وَلا جُناحَ عَلَيْكم أن تَسْتَرْضِعُوا أوْلادَكم", the meaning being: that you seek wet-nurses for your children; so the preposition was deleted outside an adverbial (ẓarf). Its like is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا تَعْزِمُوا عُقْدَةَ النِّكاحِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 235], i.e. "عَلى عُقْدَةِ النِّكاحِ". Its like is the poet's saying:

؎نُغالِي اللَّحْمَ لِلْأضْيافِ نَيْئًا ∗∗∗ ونَبْذُلُهُ إذا نَضِجَ القُدُورُ
(We pay a high price for meat for our guests while it is raw, and give it freely when the pots have cooked.)

The meaning is "نُغالِي بِاللَّحْمِ". Its like is the Arabs' saying "ضَرَبَ فُلانٌ الظَّهْرَ والبَطْنَ" (so-and-so struck the back and the belly), meaning "on the back and the belly". This usage of deleting the preposition is found in the Book of Allah, in the poetry of the Arabs and in their prose expressions, and in my view it is a sound approach. But the good view in my opinion on this is that "سَفِهَ" stands in place of "جَهِلَ" (was ignorant of); so the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: "except one who is ignorant of himself", i.e. did not reflect on himself, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَفِي أنْفُسِكم أفَلا تُبْصِرُونَ﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 21]. So it was put in the place of "جَهِلَ" and made transitive as it is transitive. This is all that people have said on this, and what we have at hand of views on it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَقَدِ اصْطَفَيْناهُ في الدُّنْيا﴾. Its meaning is: We chose him; its wording is derived from "اَلصَّفْوَةُ" (the choicest part). ﴿وَإنَّهُ في الآخِرَةِ لَمِنَ الصّالِحِينَ﴾: the righteous one in the Hereafter is the one who attains success.

zajjaj:131-131.t: His saying: ﴿إذْ قالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أسْلِمْ﴾. Its meaning is: "He chose him when his Lord said to him: Submit", i.e. at that time. ﴿قالَ أسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾.

zajjaj:132-132.t:
His saying: ﴿وَوَصّى بِها إبْراهِيمُ بَنِيهِ ويَعْقُوبُ﴾. His saying "بِها": this hāʾ refers back to the religion (al-milla), because his submission is the manifesting of his path and his way of life; and what points to His saying ﴿وَمَن يَرْغَبُ عَنْ مِلَّةِ إبْراهِيمَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 130] is His saying: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفى لَكُمُ الدِّينَ﴾. "إنَّ" has kasra only because the meaning of "وَصّى" and "أوْصى" is saying; the meaning is: he said to them: Allah has chosen the religion for you. "وَصّى" is more emphatic than "أوْصى", because "أوْصى" may be that he said it to them once, whereas "وَصّى" is only for many times.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَلا تَمُوتُنَّ إلا وأنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾. If someone asks: how does He forbid them to die, when they are only made to die? This occurred only by the latitude of speech and what the Arabs use much, like their saying "لا أرَيَنَّكَ هَهُنا" (let me not see you here): the wording of the prohibition is for the speaker, but in reality it is for the one addressed; the meaning is: "do not be here, for whoever is here I will see". The meaning in the verse is: "Hold fast to Islam, so that when death overtakes you it finds you muslims."

zajjaj:133-133.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أمْ كُنْتُمْ شُهَداءَ إذْ حَضَرَ يَعْقُوبَ المَوْتُ﴾. The meaning is: rather, were you witnesses when death came to Jacob, when he said to his sons...? The position of the second "إذْ" is accusative, like the position of the first; this is an emphasising badal (substitute).

His saying: ﴿قالُوا نَعْبُدُ إلَهَكَ وإلَهَ آبائِكَ﴾. The reading is with the plural. Some read "وَإلَهَ أبِيكَ", as if disliking to make the paternal uncle [Ishmael] his father, and made "إبْراهِيمَ" a badal from "أبِيكَ", explaining it. With "إسْماعِيلَ" and "إسْحاقَ" in the genitive, the meaning would be: "your God, and the God of your father, and the God of Ishmael", as you say "رَأيْتُ غُلامَ زَيْدٍ وعَمْرٍو" (I saw the servant of Zayd and ʿAmr), i.e. the servant of both. Whoever says "وَإلَهَ آبائِكَ" in the plural — which is the agreed reading — makes "إبْراهِيمَ وإسْماعِيلَ وإسْحاقَ" a badal, and their position is genitive as an explanatory badal from "آبائِكَ".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إلَهًا واحِدًا﴾ is accusative in two ways. If you wish, as ḥāl (circumstantial), as if they said: "we worship your God in the state of His being one"; and if you wish, as badal, the benefit of this badal being the mention of the divine oneness (tawḥīd), so that the meaning is: "we worship one God".

zajjaj:134-134.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿تِلْكَ أُمَّةٌ قَدْ خَلَتْ﴾. The meaning of "خَلَتْ" is: passed away, as you say "لِثَلاثٍ خَلَوْنَ مِنَ الشَّهْرِ" (when three [nights] of the month had passed), i.e. had gone by.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تُسْألُونَ عَمّا كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾. The meaning is: "You will be asked only about your own deeds."

zajjaj:213-213.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿كانَ النّاسُ أُمَّةً واحِدَةً﴾, i.e. upon one religion. ”اَلْأُمَّةُ“ in the language means several things. Among them: ”اَلْأُمَّةُ“ is religion, and that is the sense here. ”اَلْأُمَّةُ“ is stature: one says ”فُلانٌ حَسَنُ الأُمَّةِ“, i.e. of fine stature. The poet said:
؎وَأنَّ مُعاوِيَةَ الأكْرَمِينَ حِسانُ الوُجُوهِ طِوالُ الأُمَمْ
(…and that Muʿāwiya, the most noble, are fair of face and tall of stature.)
i.e. tall of statures. ”اَلْأُمَّةُ“ is a generation of people: they say ”قَدْ مَضَتْ أُمَمٌ“, i.e. generations. ”اَلْأُمَّةُ“ is the man who has no equal, and from this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ إبْراهِيمَ كانَ أُمَّةً قانِتًا لِلَّهِ حَنِيفًا﴾ [al-Naḥl: 120]; Abū ʿUbayda said: the meaning of ”كانَ أُمَّةً“ is "he was an imam (a leader)". ”اَلْأُمَّةُ“ in the language is also blessing and good fortune. ʿAdī ibn Zayd said: ”ثُمَّ بَعْدَ الفَلاحِ والرُّشْدِ والأُمَّةِ، وارَتْهم هُناكَ القُبُورُ“ (then, after prosperity, right guidance and good fortune, the graves there concealed them), i.e. after blessing and good fortune. Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī mentioned that the Arabs say of an old man, when his strength remains: ”فُلانٌ بِأُمَّةٍ“, and its meaning goes back to good fortune and blessing, because the remaining of his strength is among the greatest of blessings. The origin of all this is from "aiming at" (qaṣd): one says ”أمَمْتُ الشَّيْءَ“ when I aim at a thing. So the meaning of ”اَلْأُمَّةُ“ in religion is that their aim is a single aim; and the meaning of ”اَلْأُمَّةُ“ for the solitary man who has no equal is that his aim is solitary, apart from the aim of all other people. It is narrated that Zayd ibn ʿAdī ibn Nufayl «[Translator's note: so in the text; the well-known figure is Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl.]» will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as a community (umma) by himself; that is only because he submitted (to the one God) in the Jāhiliyya before the mission of the Prophet ﷺ and died a monotheist, so he was an umma in his time because of his solitariness. And the verse of al-Nābigha:
؎حَلَفْتُ فَلَمْ أتْرُكْ لِنَفْسِكَ رِيبَةً ∗∗∗ وهَلْ يَأْثَمَن ذُو أُمَّةٍ وهْوَ طائِعُ
(I swore, and left no doubt for your soul — and would a man of umma commit perjury when acting of his own will?)
It is transmitted as ”ذُو أمَّةٍ“ and ”ذُو إمَّةٍ“, and it admits two kinds of interpretation: ”ذُو أُمَّةٍ“ = a man of religion, and ”ذُو أُمَّةٍ“ = a man to whom a blessing has been granted. The meaning of ”اَلْأُمَّةُ“ as stature is: the whole aim (extent) of the body. So nothing in this chapter departs from the meaning of ”أمَمْتُ“, i.e. "I aimed at". One says ”إمامُنا هَذا حَسَنُ الأمَّةِ“, i.e. he performs his leading of us in his prayer and does it well.
They gave more than one view on the meaning of the verse. They said: the people between Ādam and Nūḥ, peace be upon them both, were unbelievers, so Allah sent the prophets to give those who obeyed glad tidings of Paradise and to warn those who disobeyed of the Fire. Some said: the meaning of ”كانَ النّاسُ أُمَّةً واحِدَةً“ is: all those to whom the prophets were sent were unbelievers.
﴿فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ النَّبِيِّينَ مُبَشِّرِينَ ومُنْذِرِينَ﴾: ”مُبَشِّرِينَ ومُنْذِرِينَ“ is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial). The meaning is that the nations of the prophets, to whom the prophets were sent, were unbelievers, just as this nation was before the mission of the Prophet ﷺ.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لِيَحْكُمَ بَيْنَ النّاسِ فِيما اخْتَلَفُوا فِيهِ﴾, i.e. so that He may decide between them with wisdom.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَما اخْتَلَفَ فِيهِ إلا الَّذِينَ أُوتُوهُ﴾, i.e. none differed about the affair of the Prophet ﷺ except those who had been given knowledge of its reality.
His saying: ﴿بَغْيًا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾: ”بَغْيًا“ is accusative in the sense of a mafʿūl lahu (object of purpose). The meaning is: they brought about the disagreement only out of transgression, because they knew the reality of his affair from their scriptures.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَهَدى اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لِما اخْتَلَفُوا فِيهِ مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾, i.e. to the truth about which the people of deviation differed.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بِإذْنِهِ﴾, i.e. by His knowledge, i.e. of the truth which He commanded.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يَهْدِي مَن يَشاءُ إلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾, i.e. to the path of the clear religion. The meaning of ”يَهْدِي مَن يَشاءُ“ is: He directs him to the path of guidance, when he seeks it without being obstinate or transgressing.

zajjaj:214-214.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أمْ حَسِبْتُمْ أنْ تَدْخُلُوا الجَنَّةَ﴾. Its meaning is: "nay, did you suppose that you would enter Paradise?"
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَمّا يَأْتِكم مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ خَلَوْا مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾. The meaning of ”مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ“ is: the description of those who…, i.e. and there has not yet befallen you the like of what befell those who passed away before you. ”خَلَوْا“ means: passed away. ﴿مَسَّتْهُمُ البَأْساءُ والضَّرّاءُ﴾: al-baʾsāʾ and al-ḍarrāʾ are killing and poverty. ﴿وَزُلْزِلُوا﴾: the meaning of ”زُلْزِلُوا“ is: they were made to fear and were shaken with what hurts. The origin of zalzala in the language is from ”زَلَّ الشَّيْءَ عَنْ مَكانِهِ“ (a thing slipped from its place); so when you say ”زَلْزَلْتُهُ“, its interpretation is: I repeated its slipping from its place. Everything that involves repetition, you repeat in it the fāʾ (first radical) of the verb form: you say ”أقَلَّ فُلانٌ الشَّيْءَ“ when he lifts a thing from its place, and when he repeats lifting it and putting it back it is said ”قَلْقَلَهُ“; likewise ”صَلَّ“ and ”صَلْصَلَ“, ”صَرَّ“ and ”صَرْصَرَ“. This is the analogy of this chapter. So the meaning is that He repeatedly shook them with fear.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿حَتّى يَقُولَ الرَّسُولُ﴾. It has been recited ”حَتّى يَقُولَ الرَّسُولُ“ in the accusative and ”يَقُولُ“ in the nominative. When you use the accusative with ”حَتّى“ and say ”سِرْتُ حَتّى أدْخُلَها“, Sībawayh, al-Khalīl and all the grammarians whose knowledge is trusted claimed that this is accusative in two ways. One of the two ways is that the entering is the end-point of the journeying, with the journeying and the entering both having been put in the accusative «[Translator's note: so in the text (نُصِبا); the context suggests "having both already taken place" (مَضَيا).]», so the meaning is "I journeyed until my entering it", the entering having already taken place. On this the verse is in the accusative; the meaning is: "and they were shaken until the Messenger said", as though it were ”حَتّى قَوْلِ الرَّسُولِ“ (until the saying of the Messenger). Its other way in the accusative — I mean ”سِرْتُ حَتّى أدْخُلَها“ — is that the journeying has occurred and the entering has not occurred, the meaning being ”سِرْتُ كَيْ أدْخُلَها“ (I journeyed so that I might enter it); and this is not the way of the accusative in the verse.
The nominative after ”حَتّى“ is in two ways. One of the two is the way of the nominative in the verse, the meaning being ”سِرْتُ حَتّى أدْخُلُها“ when both the journeying and the entering have taken place; it is as if it were equivalent to your saying ”سِرْتُ فَأدْخُلُها“, i.e. equivalent to ”سِرْتُ فَدَخَلْتُها“ (I journeyed and entered it). Here ”حَتّى“ has become one of the things that exert no government at all on the verb, because it is followed by clauses: you say ”سِرْتُ حَتّى أنِّي داخِلٌ“, and the poet's saying:
؎فَيا عَجَبًا حَتّى كُلَيْبٌ تَسُبُّنِي ∗∗∗ كَأنَّ أباها نَهْشَلٌ أوْ مُجاشِعُ
(How strange! Even Kulayb insults me, as though its father were Nahshal or Mujāshiʿ!)
So its effect on clauses is in their meaning, not in their wording; the interpretation is ”سِرْتُ حَتّى دُخُولِها“ (I journeyed until my entering it), and on this is the way of the verse. It may also be that the journeying is past and the entering is occurring now, the journeying having ceased: you say ”سِرْتُ حَتّى أدْخُلُها الآنَ، ما أمْنَعُ“ (I journeyed so that I am entering it now, I am not prevented). This is the sum of the chapter on ”حَتّى“.
The meaning of the verse is that hardship reached such a degree with the nations before this nation that they thought the help slow in coming; so Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿ألا إنَّ نَصْرَ اللَّهِ قَرِيبٌ﴾, thereby informing His friends that He will help them without doubt and that this is near to them, as He said: ﴿فَإنَّ حِزْبَ اللَّهِ هُمُ الغالِبُونَ﴾ [al-Māʾida: 56].

zajjaj:170-170.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَإذا قِيلَ لَهُمُ اتَّبِعُوا ما أنْـزَلَ اللَّهُ قالُوا بَلْ نَتَّبِعُ ما ألْفَيْنا عَلَيْهِ آباءَنا﴾ — the meaning of "ألْفَيْنا" is: we found. So Allah reproached them and censured their blind imitation (taqlīd) of their fathers, and said: ﴿أوَلَوْ كانَ آباؤُهم لا يَعْقِلُونَ شَيْئًا ولا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾; the meaning is: would they follow their fathers even if they were ignorant?! This wāw takes fatḥa because it is a wāw of conjunction upon which the alif of rebuke (tawbīkh) — which is the alif of interrogation (istifhām) — has entered; so the wāw remained with fatḥa, as is its due.

zajjaj:215-215.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يَسْألُونَكَ ماذا يُنْفِقُونَ﴾. It is said that they had asked on whom they ought to bestow their bounty; so Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, made known that the first to receive bounty are the parents and the nearest relatives, and said: ﴿قُلْ ما أنْفَقْتُمْ مِن خَيْرٍ﴾, i.e. of wealth, ﴿فَلِلْوالِدَيْنِ والأقْرَبِينَ واليَتامى والمَساكِينِ وابْنِ السَّبِيلِ وما تَفْعَلُوا مِن خَيْرٍ فَإنَّ اللَّهَ بِهِ عَلِيمٌ﴾, i.e. He records it, and when He has recorded it He recompenses it, as He said: ﴿فَمَن يَعْمَلْ مِثْقالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًا يَرَهُ﴾ [al-Zalzala: 7], i.e. he will see the recompense for it, because seeing his past deed has no benefit in it, and it is not seen, since it is past.
The meaning of ”ماذا“ in the language is of two kinds. One of them is that ”ذا“ is in the sense of ”اَلَّذِي“ (the relative "which"), with ”يُنفِقُونَ“ belonging to its ṣila (relative clause); the meaning is: they ask you, what is the thing which they spend? — as though: what is the proper way of that which they spend? — because they know what is spent, but they wanted to know Allah's (ruling on) its proper way. Like their making ”ذا“ in the sense of ”اَلَّذِي“ is the poet's saying:
؎عَدَسْ ما لِعَبّادٍ عَلَيْكِ إمارَةٌ ∗∗∗ أمِنتِ وهَذا تَحْمِلِينَ طَلِيقُ
(Hush, mule! ʿAbbād has no authority over you; you are safe, and the one you are carrying is set free.)
The meaning is: "and the one whom you are carrying is set free". So ”ما“ is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject) and ”ذا“ is its khabar (predicate). It is also permissible that ”ما“ together with ”ذا“ be equivalent to a single noun, with the position being accusative through ”يُنْفِقُونَ“; the meaning is: they ask you, what thing do they spend? This is the consensus of the grammarians, and likewise the first way is also agreed upon. Like their making ”ماذا“ equivalent to a single noun is the poet's saying:
؎دَعِي ماذا عَلِمْتُ سَأتَّقِيهِ ∗∗∗ ولَكِنْ بِالمَغِيبِ فَنَبِّئِينِي
(Leave what I know — I shall guard against it; but tell me rather of the unseen.)
as though it were equivalent to: leave that which I know. ”وَما تَفْعَلُوا“ is jussive by the condition: the conditional noun is ”ما“, and the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is ”فَإنَّ اللَّهَ بِهِ عَلِيمٌ“; the position of ”ما“ is accusative through His saying ”تَفْعَلُوا“.

zajjaj:171-171.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَمَثَلُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي يَنْعِقُ بِما لا يَسْمَعُ إلا دُعاءً ونِداءً﴾ — Allah, Mighty and Majestic, struck this parable for them and likened them to sheep that are shouted at by one of whom they hear nothing but the sound. So the meaning is: your likeness, O Muḥammad, and their likeness is as the likeness of the one who shouts and the one shouted at, with what does not hear; because their hearing did not benefit them, so in their polytheism and their non-acceptance of what they heard they were in the position of one who has not heard. The Arabs say of one who hears and does not act on what he hears: "أصَمُّ" (deaf). The poet said:

أصَمُّ عَمّا ساءَهُ سَمِيعُ
(Deaf to what displeases him, [yet] hearing.)

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ﴾ — He described them with bakam, which is muteness, and with blindness, because in their abandoning the guidance they see they are in the position of the blind. We have explained this at the beginning of the sūra sufficiently, if Allah wills.

zajjaj:173-173.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿إنَّما حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمُ المَيْتَةَ﴾ — the accusative in "اَلْمَيْتَةَ" and what is conjoined to it is the reading. It is accusative because it is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object); "ما" has entered, preventing "إنَّ" from governing, and the verb follows it. We have already explained the entry of "ما" with "إنَّ". It is [also] permissible [to say]: "إنَّما حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمُ المَيْتَةُ" (with the nominative). What I choose is that "ما" prevents "إنَّ" from governing, and that the meaning is: "He has forbidden you nothing but carrion, blood and the flesh of swine", because "إنَّما" comes as an affirmation of what is mentioned after it, [and a negation] of what is other than it «[Translator's note: the bracketed words are supplied; the source reads literally "an affirmation of what is mentioned after it, of what is other than it"]». The poet said:

أنا الذّائِدُ الحامِي الذِّمارَ وإنَّما ∗∗∗ يُدافِعُ عَنْ أحْسابِهِمْ أنا أوْ مِثْلِي
(I am the defender, the protector of what must be guarded; and none defends their honour but I or one like me.)

The meaning is: none defends their honour except me or one like me. So the choice is what the body of readers (qurrāʾ) follow, for following the Sunna and for its soundness in meaning.

The meaning of ﴿وَما أُهِلَّ بِهِ لِغَيْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ is: that over which the voice was raised in naming other than Allah upon it. This is found in the language; from it is al-ihlāl with the ḥajj, which is only raising the voice with the talbiya. "اَلْمَيْتَةَ" — its origin is "اَلْمَيِّتَةَ"; the second yāʾ was omitted for lightness because of the heaviness of the two yāʾs and the kasra. The better reading is "اَلْمَيْتَةَ" with the lightened form; likewise in His saying: ﴿أوَمَن كانَ مَيْتًا فَأحْيَيْناهُ﴾ [al-Anʿām: 122], its origin is "أوَمَن كانَ مَيِّتًا" with doubling (tashdīd), and the explanation of the omission and lightening in it is like its explanation in "اَلْمَيْتَةَ".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ غَيْرَ باغٍ ولا عادٍ﴾ — concerning its interpretation and meaning there are three views. Some said: "فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ غَيْرَ باغٍ ولا عادٍ", that is: whoever is compelled, being hungry, "غَيْرَ باغٍ", not eating it for pleasure, "ولا عادٍ", and not exceeding what wards off hunger from himself, there is no sin upon him.

And they said: "غَيْرَ باغٍ": not exceeding the measure of his need, and not falling short of what keeps him alive. They also said: the meaning of "غَيْرَ باغٍ" is: [not rebelling] against an imam, and not transgressing against his community. The meaning of "اَلْبَغْيُ" in the language is: intending corruption; one says: "بَغى الجُرْحُ، يَبْغِي، بَغْيًا" when a wound tends towards festering. This is the consensus of the people of language. And one says: "بَغى الرَّجُلُ حاجَتَهُ، يَبْغِيها، بِغاءً" ("the man sought his need"), and the Arabs say: "خَرَجَ في بِغاءِ إبِلِهِ" ("he went out in search of his camels"). The poet said:

لا يَمْنَعَنَّكَ مِن بِغاءِ الخَيْرِ تَعْقادُ التَّمائِمْ
إنَّ الأشائِمَ كالأيامِنِ والأيامِنَ كالأشائِمْ
(Let not the tying of amulets keep you from seeking good; the ill-omened are like the auspicious, and the auspicious like the ill-omened.)

And one says: "بَغَتِ المَرْأةُ، تَبْغِي، بِغاءً" when a woman commits fornication. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿وَلا تُكْرِهُوا فَتَياتِكم عَلى البِغاءِ إنْ أرَدْنَ تَحَصُّنًا﴾ [al-Nūr: 33], that is: to fornication. And one says: "اِبْتَغى لِفُلانٍ أنْ يَفْعَلَ كَذا", that is: it became fitting for him to do such-and-such; it is as though he said: "doing such-and-such was sought, and it was compliant for him", that is, it yielded to him; but they made do with their saying "اِبْتَغى". "اَلْبَغايا" in the language is two things: "اَلْبَغايا" are fornicating women, and "اَلْبَغايا" are slave-women. Al-Aʿshā said:

والبَغايا يَرْكُضْنَ أكْسِيَةَ الأ ∗∗∗ ضْرِيجِ والشَّرْعَبِيَّ ذا الأذْيالِ
(And the slave-girls kick along the hems of red-dyed garments and long-trailing Sharʿabī cloth.)

"غَيْرَ باغٍ" is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial).

zajjaj:174-174.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ يَكْتُمُونَ ما أنْـزَلَ اللَّهُ مِنَ الكِتابِ﴾ — He means the scholars of the Jews who concealed the matter of the Prophet ﷺ.

His saying: ﴿وَيَشْتَرُونَ بِهِ ثَمَنًا قَلِيلا﴾, that is: they concealed it because they took bribes for concealing it.

﴿أُولَئِكَ ما يَأْكُلُونَ في بُطُونِهِمْ إلا النّارَ﴾ — the meaning is that those who consume it will be punished by it, so it is as though they ate only fire. Likewise His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿الَّذِينَ يَأْكُلُونَ الرِّبا لا يَقُومُونَ إلا كَما يَقُومُ الَّذِي يَتَخَبَّطُهُ الشَّيْطانُ مِنَ المَسِّ﴾ [al-Baqara: 275], that is: consuming it brings them in the Hereafter to the like of this state. "اَلَّذِينَ" is accusative by "إنَّ", and the khabar (predicate) of "إنَّ" is the whole clause, namely "أُولَئِكَ ما يَأْكُلُونَ في بُطُونِهِمْ إلّا النّارَ". "أُولَئِكَ" is nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject), and the khabar of "أُولَئِكَ" is "ما يَأْكُلُونَ في بُطُونِهِمْ إلّا النّارَ".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا يُكَلِّمُهُمُ اللَّهُ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ — there is more than one view on it. Some said: its meaning is: He will be angry with them, just as you say: "فُلانٌ لا يُكَلِّمُ فُلانًا" ("so-and-so does not speak to so-and-so"), meaning: he is angry with him. Some said: the meaning of "لا يُكَلِّمُهُمُ اللَّهُ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ" is: He will not send the angels to them with greeting. It is also possible that "لا يُكَلِّمُهُمُ اللَّهُ" means: Allah will not let them hear His speech, while the righteous and the people of rank, with whom Allah is pleased, will hear His speech.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا يُزَكِّيهِمْ﴾, that is: He will not praise them; and whoever Allah does not praise is punished.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلَهم عَذابٌ ألِيمٌ﴾ — the meaning of "ألِيمٌ" is "مُؤْلِمٌ" (painful), and the meaning of "مُؤْلِمٌ" is: extreme in pain.

zajjaj:175-175.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فَما أصْبَرَهم عَلى النّارِ﴾ — there is more than one view on it. Some said: what thing has made them endure the Fire?! Others said: how patient they are in doing what leads to the Fire! Because these people knew that whoever stubbornly opposed the Prophet ﷺ would end up in the Fire. It is as you say: "ما أصْبَرَ فُلانًا عَلى الجِنْسِ!", that is: "how much he remains in it!" «[Translator's note: "الجِنْسِ" is as printed; it may be a corruption of "الحَبْسِ" (imprisonment)]».

zajjaj:176-176.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿ذَلِكَ بِأنَّ اللَّهَ نَـزَّلَ الكِتابَ بِالحَقِّ﴾ — the meaning is: "the matter is that", or: "that is the matter". So "ذَلِكَ" is nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject), or as the khabar (predicate) of a mubtadaʾ.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَإنَّ الَّذِينَ اخْتَلَفُوا في الكِتابِ لَفي شِقاقٍ بَعِيدٍ﴾ — by the distance of some of them from others in their mutual hostility, because the Jews and the Christians are those who differed concerning the Book, and their hostility is far-reaching.

zajjaj:249-249.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ مُبْتَلِيكم بِنَهَرٍ﴾ means: He is testing you and trying you with a river. None but a prophet could say this, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿عالِمُ الغَيْبِ فَلا يُظْهِرُ عَلى غَيْبِهِ أحَدًا﴾ [al-Jinn: 26] ﴿إلا مَنِ ارْتَضى مِن رَسُولٍ﴾ [al-Jinn: 27]. The point of the test by this river was so that Ṭālūt would know who had the intention of fighting with him and who did not. So he said: ﴿فَمَن شَرِبَ مِنهُ فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي﴾, that is, he is not of my companions nor of those who follow me; and whoever does not taste it — ﴿وَمَن لَمْ يَطْعَمْهُ فَإنَّهُ مِنِّي﴾, that is, does not taste of it — ﴿إلا مَنِ اغْتَرَفَ غُرْفَةً بِيَدِهِ﴾. ”غُرْفَةً“ and ”غَرْفَةً“ have both been read. Whoever says ”غَرْفَةً“, its meaning is a single scoop with the hand; and whoever says ”غُرْفَةً“, its meaning is the amount of a handful. The meaning of ﴿فَشَرِبُوا مِنهُ إلا قَلِيلا مِنهُمْ﴾ is: they drank from it in order to turn back from the war, because he had informed them of that. It is mentioned in the exegesis that the few who did not drink numbered three hundred and some ten-odd men, like the number of the people of Badr.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَلَمّا جاوَزَهُ﴾ means: he crossed the river, he and those with him. It has been said that when they saw how few they were, some of them said to others: ﴿لا طاقَةَ لَنا اليَوْمَ بِجالُوتَ وجُنُودِهِ﴾, that is, no strength. One says ”أطَقْتُ الشَّيْءَ، إطاقَةً، وطَوْقًا“, like ”أطَعْتُ، طاعَةً، وإطاعَةً، وطَوْعًا“.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قالَ الَّذِينَ يَظُنُّونَ أنَّهم مُلاقُو اللَّهِ﴾: two views have been given on it. Some said — and it is the doctrine of the philologists —: those who were certain that they would meet Allah said; they said: had they been doubting, they would have been astray and unbelievers. ”ظَنَنْتُ“ in the sense of ”أيْقَنْتُ“ (I was certain) is found in the language. The poet — he is Durayd — said:
؎فَقُلْتُ لَهم ظُنُّوا بِألْفَيْ مُدَجَّجٍ ∗∗∗ سَراتُهم في الفارِسِيِّ المُسَرَّدِ
(I said to them: be certain of two thousand fully-armed men, their chiefs clad in close-knit Persian mail.)
that is, be certain. The exegetes said: the meaning of ”يَظُنُّونَ أنَّهم مُلاقُو اللَّهِ“ is that they supposed that in this battle they would be killed in the way of Allah, because of the smallness of their number and the great number of their enemy, who were the companions of Goliath.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿كَمْ مِن فِئَةٍ قَلِيلَةٍ غَلَبَتْ فِئَةً كَثِيرَةً بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾ means: how many a group! A group is called ”فِئَةٌ“ from their saying ”فَأوْتُ رَأْسَهُ بِالعَصا“ and ”فَأيْتُ“, when you split it; so ”اَلْفِئَةُ“, the group, is from this.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واللَّهُ مَعَ الصّابِرِينَ﴾ means: Allah helps the patient, when they are patient in obeying Him and in what brings them near to Him.

zajjaj:250-250.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿رَبَّنا أفْرِغْ عَلَيْنا صَبْرًا﴾ means: pour patience upon us abundantly, as you say ”أفْرَغْتُ الإناءَ“ ("I emptied the vessel"), when you have poured out what is in it.

zajjaj:251-251.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَهَزَمُوهم بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾ means: they broke them and drove them back. The root of ”اَلْهَزْمُ“ in the language is breaking a thing and folding part of it over another part. One says ”سِقاءٌ مَهْزُومٌ“ (a creased water-skin) when part of it has been folded over another part through dryness; and ”قَصَبٌ مُتَهَزِّمٌ، ومَهْزُومٌ“ is reed that has been broken and split. The Arabs say ”هَزَمْتُ عَلى زَيْدٍ“, that is, I inclined towards him (with kindness). The poet said:
؎هَزَمْتُ عَلَيْكِ اليَوْمَ يا بِنْتَ مالِكٍ ∗∗∗ فَجُودِي عَلَيْنا بِالنَّوالِ وأنْعِمِي
(I have turned to you today, O daughter of Mālik, so be generous to us with your bounty and be kind.)
One says ”سَمِعْتُ هَزْمَةَ الرَّعْدِ“ ("I heard the crash of the thunder"); al-Aṣmaʿī said: it is as though it is a sound with a splitting in it.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَآتاهُ اللَّهُ المُلْكَ والحِكْمَةَ﴾ means: He gave David, peace be upon him, kingship, because he was made king after his killing of Goliath, and he was given knowledge. As for the meaning of ﴿وَعَلَّمَهُ مِمّا يَشاءُ﴾, it has been said: among what He taught him was the making of coats of mail and the speech of birds.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَوْلا دَفْعُ اللَّهِ النّاسَ بَعْضَهم بِبَعْضٍ لَفَسَدَتِ الأرْضُ﴾ means: were it not for what Allah commanded the Muslims of fighting the unbelievers, the earth would have been corrupted. It has also been said: were it not for Allah's repelling the unbelievers by means of the Muslims, unbelief would have multiplied, wrath would have descended upon people and the inhabitants of the earth would have been uprooted. Both ”وَلَوْلا دَفْعُ اللَّهِ“ and ”وَلَوْلا دِفاعُ اللَّهِ“ are permissible. ”بَعْضَهم“ is accusative as a badal (substitute) for ”اَلنّاسَ“; the meaning is ”وَلَوْلا دَفْعُ اللَّهِ بَعْضَ النّاسِ بِبَعْضٍ“. ”دَفْعُ“ is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject); we have explained this earlier.

zajjaj:252-252.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿تِلْكَ آياتُ اللَّهِ نَتْلُوها عَلَيْكَ بِالحَقِّ﴾ means: these signs which you have told of and been told of are the signs of Allah, that is, His marks which point to His oneness and confirm the messages of His prophets, since created beings are incapable of producing the like of them.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإنَّكَ لَمِنَ المُرْسَلِينَ﴾ means: and you are among those whose signs I have related, because you have been given signs like those they were given, and more than what they were given. We shall explain that in the verse that follows, if Allah wills.

zajjaj:253-253.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿تِلْكَ الرُّسُلُ فَضَّلْنا بَعْضَهم عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾: ”اَلرُّسُلُ“ is a ṣifa (description) of ”تِلْكَ“, as in your saying ”أُولَئِكَ الرُّسُلُ فَضَّلْنا بَعْضَهم عَلى بَعْضٍ“, except that ”تِلْكَ“ is said for the group. The khabar (predicate) of the subject is ”فَضَّلْنا بَعْضَهم عَلى بَعْضٍ“. The meaning of ﴿مِنهم مَن كَلَّمَ اللَّهُ﴾ is: one whom Allah spoke to (man kallamahu Allāh).
The hāʾ has been omitted from the ṣila (relative clause) because of the length of the noun. He is Moses ﷺ: Allah made him hear His speech without a revelation brought to him from Allah by an angel.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَآتَيْنا عِيسى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ البَيِّناتِ﴾ means: We gave him; and ”اَلْبَيِّناتُ“ are the proofs which establish his prophethood ﷺ: healing the one born blind and the leper, bringing the dead to life, and telling of what was hidden from him.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَرَفَعَ بَعْضَهم دَرَجاتٍ﴾: it has come in the exegesis that Muḥammad ﷺ is meant by it. He was sent to all mankind, and there is no sign that the prophets were given but what Muḥammad ﷺ was given is more than it: the tree spoke to him ﷺ; he fed a great multitude from a handful of dates; he passed his hand over the ewe of Umm Maʿbad and she gave milk abundantly, yielding milk after having been dry; and among them is the splitting of the moon — for the Prophet ﷺ saw signs on earth and saw them in the sky. What has come concerning the signs of the Prophet is much. As for the splitting of the moon and its authenticity, we have narrated ḥadīths about it: Ismāʿīl ibn Isḥāq narrated to me, saying: Muḥammad ibn al-Minhāl narrated to us, saying: Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, from Saʿīd, from Qatāda, from Anas, who said: «The people of Mecca asked the Prophet ﷺ for a sign, so he showed them the splitting of the moon into two parts.» And Musaddad narrated to me the like of that, tracing it back to Anas as well. We shall mention everything that has been narrated in this chapter in its place, if Allah wills; but we have mentioned here a selection of the signs in order to show by them the excellence of the Prophet ﷺ in the signs he brought. Among the greatest of signs is the Qurʾān, which he brought to the Arabs, who were the most knowledgeable of peoples in speech: they had poetry, rhymed prose (sajʿ) and oratory, and all of that is well known in their speech. They were told: "Bring ten sūras", and they were unable to do so; and they were told: "Bring a sūra", with no condition imposed on them that it be like al-Baqara or Āl ʿImrān — they were only told "Bring a sūra" — and they were unable to do so. This is the meaning of ”وَرَفَعَ بَعْضَهم دَرَجاتٍ“.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ ما اقْتَتَلَ الَّذِينَ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ﴾ means: after the messengers. ﴿مِن بَعْدِ ما جاءَتْهُمُ البَيِّناتُ﴾ means: after the proofs had become clear to them. So had Allah willed, He would not have commanded fighting after the proof had become clear. It may also be: had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another, that is, had Allah willed to compel them to be believers without disagreement, He would have done so, as He said: ﴿وَلَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَمَعَهم عَلى الهُدى﴾ [al-Anʿām: 35]

zajjaj:135-135.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقالُوا كُونُوا هُودًا أوْ نَصارى تَهْتَدُوا﴾. The meaning is: "The Jews said: Be Jews; and the Christians said: Be Christians." "تَهْتَدُوا" is jussive (majzūm) as the answer to the command; the meaning of a condition is present in the expression, the meaning being: if you are on this religion you will be guided. So the jussive of "تَهْتَدُوا" is in reality [that of] the apodosis (jawāb al-jazāʾ).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بَلْ مِلَّةَ إبْراهِيمَ حَنِيفًا﴾. "اَلْمِلَّةُ" is accusative on the implied construction: "rather we follow the religion of Abraham". It may also be accusative in the sense: "rather we are the people of the religion of Abraham", with "people" omitted, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿واسْألِ القَرْيَةَ الَّتِي كُنّا فِيها﴾ [Yūsuf: 82], since a town is not asked and does not answer. The nominative is also permissible: "بَلْ مِلَّةُ إبْراهِيمَ حَنِيفًا"; but the accusative is better and more common. The nominative is allowed in the sense: "Say: our religion and our creed is the religion of Abraham". "حَنِيفًا" is accusative as ḥāl (circumstantial); the meaning is: rather we follow the religion of Abraham in the state of his ḥanīf-ness. The meaning of al-ḥanīfa in the language is inclining; so the meaning is that Abraham inclines towards the religion of Allah, the religion of Islam, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿إنَّ الدِّينَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ الإسْلامُ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 19]. No prophet was sent except with it, even though their laws differed: the binding creed is the oneness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and faith in His messengers, even though the laws differ — except that it is not permissible to abandon the law of a prophet, or to act upon the law of a prophet before him that contradicts the law of the prophet of the community in which one is. Al-ḥanaf was taken from their saying "اِمْرَأةٌ حَنْفاءُ" and "رَجُلٌ أحْنَفُ": the one whose feet each incline, with their toes, towards the other. The mother of al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays said, while dandling him — and he grew up to be the chief of Banū Tamīm:

؎واللَّهِ لَوْلا حَنَفٌ في رِجْلِهِ ∗∗∗ ودِقَّةٌ في ساقِهِ مِن هُزْلِهِ
ما كانَ في فِتْيانِكم مِن مِثْلِهِ
(By Allah, were it not for a crookedness in his foot and a thinness in his shank from his leanness, there would be none like him among your young men.)

zajjaj:136-136.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أحَدٍ مِنهُمْ﴾. The meaning is: we do not disbelieve in some and believe in others.

zajjaj:137-137.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَإنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ ما آمَنتُمْ بِهِ فَقَدِ اهْتَدَوْا﴾.

If someone asks: does faith have a "like" that is other than faith? He is told: the meaning is plain and clear; its interpretation is: "If they bring assent like your assent and your faith in the prophets, and affirm the oneness [of Allah] as you affirm it, then they are guided", i.e. they have become muslims like you. ﴿وَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَإنَّما هم في شِقاقٍ﴾, i.e. in hostility (mushāqqa) and enmity. From this is people's saying: "so-and-so has split the staff of the Muslims"; it only means he has separated from what they agreed upon in following their imam, and has come to be in a side (shiqq) other than the side of the Muslims.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَسَيَكْفِيكَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾. This is a guarantee from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, of help for His Prophet ﷺ, because He suffices him against them only by making what He sent him with prevail over every other religion. This is like His saying: ﴿لِيُظْهِرَهُ عَلى الدِّينِ كُلِّهِ﴾ [al-Tawba: 33]. This is its interpretation, and Allah knows best.

Likewise His saying: ﴿كَتَبَ اللَّهُ لأغْلِبَنَّ أنا ورُسُلِي﴾ [al-Mujādila: 21].

If someone says: but among the messengers there are some who were killed — the interpretation of that, and Allah knows best, is that Allah and His messengers prevail by clear argument and evident sign. It may also be the victory of the Hereafter, because the matter is according to what it finally settles upon in the end. It has also been said: Allah never commanded a messenger to fight and he followed what Allah commanded him in his fighting except that he prevailed; so on this interpretation it may be that "no messenger was ever killed while fighting".

zajjaj:138-138.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللَّهِ ومَن أحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ صِبْغَةً﴾. "صِبْغَةً" may be accusative according to His saying "rather we follow the religion of Abraham", i.e. "rather we follow the ṣibgha (dye) of Allah". Its accusative may also be on: "rather we are the people of the ṣibgha of Allah", as we said for "مِلَّةَ إبْراهِيمَ". Al-ṣibgha may also be nominative with "هي" implied (iḍmār), as if they said: "it is the ṣibgha of Allah", i.e. "it — the religion of Abraham — is the ṣibgha of Allah". It has been said that the ṣibgha was mentioned only because a group of Christians used to dip their children in a water of theirs and say: "This is a purification, just as circumcision is a purification for you." So it was said to them: "صِبْغَةَ اللَّهِ ومَن أحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ صِبْغَةً", i.e. the purification He commanded is the utmost in cleanness. It may also be — and Allah knows best — that "صِبْغَةَ اللَّهِ" means "Allah's, Majestic and Mighty, creating of creation", so that the meaning is that Allah began creation upon Islam. The proof of this view would be the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَإذْ أخَذَ رَبُّكَ مِن بَنِي آدَمَ مِن ظُهُورِهِمْ ذُرِّيَّتَهم وأشْهَدَهم عَلى أنْفُسِهِمْ ألَسْتُ بِرَبِّكم قالُوا بَلى﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 172]; and it has come in the ḥadīth that He brought them out like tiny particles (al-dharr). A proof of this interpretation is also His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فِطْرَتَ اللَّهِ الَّتِي فَطَرَ النّاسَ عَلَيْها﴾ [al-Rūm: 30]. The report may also belong to this: "«كُلُّ مَوْلُودٍ يُولَدُ عَلى الفِطْرَةِ حَتّى يَكُونَ أبَواهُ هُما اللَّذانِ يُهَوِّدانِهِ، أوْ يُنَصِّرانِهِ»" (Every child is born upon the fiṭra until his parents are the ones who make him a Jew or a Christian). And "صَبَغْتُ الثَّوْبَ" (I dyed the garment) only means: I changed its colour and its make.

zajjaj:139-139.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قُلْ أتُحاجُّونَنا في اللَّهِ﴾. In "أتُحاجُّونَنا في اللَّهِ" there are several forms. The best of them is "أتُحاجُّونَنا" with two nūns. If you wish, with one nūn: "أتُحاجُّونّا", by assimilating (idghām) the first into the second; this is a good way. Some of them, when assimilating, hint at the fatḥa, as they read: ﴿ما لَكَ لا تَأْمَنّا عَلى يُوسُفَ﴾ [Yūsuf: 11] with assimilation and a hint at the ḍamma. If you wish you may delete one of the two nūns and say "أتُحاجُّونا", deleting because two nūns come together. The poet said:

؎تَراهُ كالثِّغامِ يُعَلُّ مِسْكًا ∗∗∗ يَسُوءُ الغانِياتِ إذا فَلْيَنِي
(You see it [my hair], like the white thaghām plant, drenched again and again with musk; it grieves the fair women when they search my head [for lice].)

He means "فَلَيْنَنِي". I have seen that the position of al-Māzinī and others is to reject this reading, and likewise they rejected ﴿فَبِمَ تُبَشِّرُونَ﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 54] [read with a single kasra-nūn]. Abū Isḥāq [al-Zajjāj] said: Venturing to reject this reading is an error, because Nāfiʿ, may Allah have mercy on him, read it. Ismāʿīl ibn Isḥāq informed me that Nāfiʿ, may Allah have mercy on him, did not read any letter unless at least two of the readers of Medina had read it; and it has a basis in Arabic, so it should not be rejected. But the fatḥa in His saying "فَبِمَ تُبَشِّرُونَ" is stronger in Arabic.

The meaning of His saying "﴿قُلْ أتُحاجُّونَنا في اللَّهِ﴾" is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded the Muslims to speak to the Jews who had supported those who do not affirm the oneness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic — the Christians and idol-worshippers. Allah commanded that the argument against them be: "You claim that you affirm the oneness [of Allah], and we affirm His oneness; so why have you supported those who do not affirm the oneness of Allah, Majestic and Mighty, while He is our Lord and your Lord, and to us belong our deeds and to you your deeds?" Then they informed them that they are sincere (mukhliṣūn), and their sincerity is their faith that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is One, and their assent to all His messengers. So they made known that they are sincere, unlike those who opposed them.

zajjaj:177-177.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿لَيْسَ البِرَّ أنْ تُوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكم قِبَلَ المَشْرِقِ والمَغْرِبِ﴾ — the meaning is: "righteousness is not all in prayer; rather righteousness is whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day… and establishes prayer…" to the end of the verse. It was said: this is specific to the prophets alone, because these things that have been described are not performed in their entirety as duly required except by the prophets, peace be upon them. And it is possible that it applies to all people, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has commanded creation with everything in this verse.

You have two options in "اَلْبِرَّ": you may read "لَيْسَ البِرَّ أنْ تُوَلُّوا" and "لَيْسَ البِرُّ أنْ تُوَلُّوا". Whoever reads it accusative makes "أنْ" together with its ṣila the noun (ism) [of لَيْسَ], so the meaning is: "your turning your faces is not all of righteousness". Whoever reads "اَلْبِرَّ" nominative, the meaning is: "all righteousness is not your turning"; so "اَلْبِرُّ" is the ism of "لَيْسَ", and "أنْ تُوَلُّوا" is the khabar (predicate).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ البِرَّ مَن آمَنَ بِاللَّهِ واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ﴾ — if you double the nūn of "لَكِنَّ", you make "اَلْبِرَّ" accusative; if you lighten it, you make "اَلْبِرَّ" nominative and say: "وَلَكِنِ البِرُّ مَن آمَنَ بِاللَّهِ", giving the nūn of the lightened form kasra because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. The meaning is: "but the one possessing righteousness is whoever believes in Allah". It may also be: "but righteousness is the righteousness of whoever believes in Allah", as the poet said:

وَكَيْفَ تُواصِلُ مَن أصْبَحَتْ ∗∗∗ خِلالَتُهُ كَأبِي مَرْحَبِ
(How can you keep ties with one whose friendship has become like Abū Marḥab?)

The meaning is: "like the friendship of Abū Marḥab". Similar to it is: ﴿واسْألِ القَرْيَةَ الَّتِي كُنّا فِيها﴾ [Yūsuf: 82], the meaning being: "and ask the people of the town".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿والمُوفُونَ بِعَهْدِهِمْ إذا عاهَدُوا﴾ — there are two views on its nominative. The better is that it is nominative by way of praise (madḥ), because when a description (naʿt) becomes long and extensive, some of it is put in the nominative and [some] in the accusative by way of praise; the meaning is: "they are those who fulfil their covenant". It is also possible that it is conjoined to "مَن"; the meaning is: "but righteousness — and the people of righteousness — are the believers and those who fulfil their covenant".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿والصّابِرِينَ﴾ — there are two views on its accusative. The better of them is praise, as we described concerning a description when it becomes long; the meaning is: "I mean the patient". Some grammarian said: it is conjoined to "ذَوِي القُرْبى", as though He said: "and gave wealth, despite love of it, to relatives… and to the patient". This is not sound unless "والمُوفُونَ" is nominative by way of praise for implied [subjects] (i.e. "they are…"), because what is inside the ṣila cannot be conjoined to after something has been conjoined to the relative noun (mawṣūl) itself.

The meaning of "وَحِينَ البَأْسِ" is: [in time of] the severity of war. One says: "قَدْ بَأسَ الرَّجُلُ يَبْأسُ، بَأْسًا، وباسًا، وبُؤْسًا يا هَذا" when a man becomes poor; and "قَدْ بَؤُسَ الرَّجُلَ، يَبْؤُسُ، فَهو بَئِيسٌ" when his courage becomes intense «[Translator's note: "الرَّجُلَ" is printed in the accusative in the source; the subject would be expected in the nominative]».

zajjaj:178-178.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ القِصاصُ في القَتْلى الحُرُّ بِالحُرِّ والعَبْدُ بِالعَبْدِ والأُنْثى بِالأُنْثى﴾ — the meaning of "كُتِبَ عَلَيْكم" is "it has been made obligatory upon you". His saying: "اَلْحُرُّ بِالحُرِّ والعَبْدُ بِالعَبْدِ والأُنْثى بِالأُنْثى" — it is said that a tribe of the Arabs had superiority over others; they used to marry among them without dowries, and to demand for blood more than its measure, killing, for a slave of their slaves, a free man of those over whom they had superiority. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down: ﴿فَمَن عُفِيَ لَهُ مِن أخِيهِ شَيْءٌ فاتِّباعٌ بِالمَعْرُوفِ وأداءٌ إلَيْهِ بِإحْسانٍ﴾, that is: whoever has the killing [in retaliation] waived for him and blood-money (diya) is accepted from him, while he is a killer who intended the killing, he is pardoned in that his blood is waived for him and blood-money is accepted from him. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿ذَلِكَ تَخْفِيفٌ مِن رَبِّكم ورَحْمَةٌ﴾. It has been mentioned that for those before us nothing but a life [for a life] was prescribed, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿وَكَتَبْنا عَلَيْهِمْ فِيها أنَّ النَّفْسَ بِالنَّفْسِ﴾ [al-Māʾida: 45], that is: in the Torah. So Allah favoured this community with the lightening and with blood-money, when the next of kin of the slain (walī al-dam) accepts it.

The meaning of "فاتِّباعٌ بِالمَعْرُوفِ" is of two kinds. It may be: "upon the owner of the blood [claim] is pursuit in fairness — that is, claiming the blood-money — and upon the killer is payment with excellence". And it may be that both pursuit in fairness and payment with excellence are upon the killer — and Allah knows best.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فَمَنِ اعْتَدى بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ فَلَهُ عَذابٌ ألِيمٌ﴾, that is: after taking the blood-money. The meaning of "اِعْتَدى" is: he did wrong, leapt up and killed the killer of his kinsman after taking the blood-money; "فَلَهُ عَذابٌ ألِيمٌ", that is: painful.

"فاتِّباعٌ بِالمَعْرُوفِ" is nominative in the sense of "then upon him is pursuit". Were it outside the Qurʾān, "فاتِّباعًا بِالمَعْرُوفِ وأداءً…" would be permissible, in the sense of "let him pursue a pursuit… and pay a payment…" (as mafʿūl muṭlaq, absolute object); but the nominative is better in Arabic, and it is what is in the Muṣḥaf and the consensus of the readers, so there is no way to anything else.

zajjaj:179-179.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلَكم في القِصاصِ حَياةٌ﴾ — "حَياةٌ" is nominative in two ways: as mubtadaʾ (subject), and by "لَكم", as though He said: "and life is established for you in retaliation". ﴿يا أُولِي الألْبابِ﴾, that is: "O possessors of minds". The meaning of life in retaliation is that when a man knows that he will be killed if he kills, he refrains from killing; so in his refraining from killing there is life for the one he intended to kill, and life for himself, because it was on account of retaliation that he refrained from killing, and so he was safe from being killed.

zajjaj:216-216.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ القِتالُ وهو كُرْهٌ لَكُمْ﴾. The meaning of ”كُتِبَ عَلَيْكم“ is: it has been made obligatory for you. Regarding ”اَلْكُرْهُ“ one says: ”كَرِهْتُ الشَّيْءَ كُرْهًا، وكَرْهًا، وكَراهَةً، وكَراهِيَةً“ (I disliked the thing). Everywhere in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, where ”اَلْكُرْهُ“ occurs, the fatḥa is permissible in it: you say ”اَلْكُرْهُ“ and ”اَلْكَرْهُ“; except that, regarding this word in this verse, Abū ʿUbayda mentioned that people agree on its ḍamma. Thus is the reading of the people of the Ḥijāz and of the people of Kufa alike: ”وَهو كُرْهٌ لَكم“ — they put this word with ḍamma.
”كُرْهٌ“ is nominative because it is the khabar (predicate) of the mubtadaʾ (subject); its interpretation is: "a thing of dislike". The meaning of their disliking fighting is that they disliked it only in respect of the nature of its harshness upon them and its hardship, not that the believers dislike the obligation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, does only what contains wisdom and benefit.
His saying: ﴿وَعَسى أنْ تَكْرَهُوا شَيْئًا وهو خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾: by ”﴿وَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾“ He means here the fighting. The meaning of the good in it is that whoever is killed is a martyr, and this is the utmost good; and if he kills, he is also rewarded and is demolishing the cause of unbelief, and along with that he takes spoils. It may also bring about the entry of the one he fights into Islam, because the whole matter of the fighting of the people of Islam was among the indications that establish the matter of prophethood and of Islam: Allah announced that He would help His religion, and then He made the help manifest in that the small number overcame the large number. This is what fighting contains of the good which they had disliked. The meaning of ﴿وَعَسى أنْ تُحِبُّوا شَيْئًا وهو شَرٌّ لَكُمْ﴾ is: it may be that you love staying back from fighting, and so are deprived of the good He described as being in fighting.

zajjaj:217-217.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الشَّهْرِ الحَرامِ قِتالٍ فِيهِ﴾. ”قِتالٍ“ is genitive as a badal (substitute) from ”اَلشَّهْرِ الحَرامِ“; the meaning is: they ask you about fighting in the sacred month. We have explained what is in this verse earlier in the book. As for ﴿قُلْ قِتالٌ فِيهِ كَبِيرٌ﴾: ”قِتالٌ“ is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and ”كَبِيرٌ“ is its khabar (predicate).
﴿وَصَدٌّ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ وكُفْرٌ بِهِ﴾ is nominative as a mubtadaʾ, and the khabar of these things is ﴿أكْبَرُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾. The meaning is: and turning (people) away from the way of Allah, and disbelief in Him, and expelling the people of the Sacred Mosque from it, are greater with Allah, i.e. greater in sin.
