﴿والفِتْنَةُ أكْبَرُ مِنَ القَتْلِ﴾, i.e. and unbelief is greater than killing; the meaning is: these things are unbelief, and unbelief is greater than killing.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَمَن يَرْتَدِدْ مِنكم عَنْ دِينِهِ فَيَمُتْ وهو كافِرٌ﴾. ”يَرْتَدِدْ“ is jussive by the condition, and the doubled consonant appears (unassimilated) with the jussive because the second letter is vowelless; this is more frequent in the language. It has been recited: ”يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَن يَرْتَدَّ“ «[Translator's note: i.e. in al-Māʾida: 54.]» with assimilation (idghām) and fatḥa; and this is the reading of people generally except the people of Medina, for in their muṣḥaf it is ”مَن يَرْتَدِدْ“; and both are correct. As for the one in Sūrat al-Baqara, nothing is permissible in it except ”مَن يَرْتَدِدْ“, because the people of the garrison cities agree on showing the doubled consonant, and so it is in their copies. Recitation is a sunna that is not to be contravened: if a word is in one form in every copy, reciting it otherwise is not permissible. (In the language) you may say ”مَن يَرْتَدِّ مِنكم“, using kasra because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, except that the fatḥa is better because of the fatḥa on the tāʾ and the readers' agreement on it.

zajjaj:218-218.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا والَّذِينَ هاجَرُوا وجاهَدُوا في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أُولَئِكَ يَرْجُونَ رَحْمَتَ اللَّهِ﴾. ”اَلَّذِينَ“ is accusative by ”إنَّ“; ”أُولَئِكَ“ is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject); ”يَرْجُونَ“ is the khabar (predicate) of ”أُولَئِكَ“; and ”أُولَئِكَ يَرْجُونَ“ is the khabar of ”إنَّ اَلَّذِينَ“. It was said of the striving believers here only that they hope for Allah's mercy because, in their own estimation, they have not attained what is due to Allah from them, and they do not know with what they will seal their affair. The sum of what Allah has told about the believers who do righteous deeds is that they will be recompensed with Paradise. Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ أُولَئِكَ هم خَيْرُ البَرِيَّةِ﴾ [al-Bayyina: 7] ﴿جَزاؤُهم عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ جَنّاتُ عَدْنٍ﴾ [al-Bayyina: 8].

zajjaj:219-219.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الخَمْرِ والمَيْسِرِ﴾. ”اَلْخَمْرِ“ is the (drink) agreed upon; and the analogy for everything that has its effect is that it be called khamr and be on the same footing with it in prohibition. The interpretation of ”اَلْخَمْرِ“ in the language is: everything that covers the intellect. Everything that covers a person, of trees and other things, is called ”خَمْرٌ“, and what covers him specifically of trees is ”ضَرى“ — with a shortened final alif (maqṣūr). One says ”دَخَلَ فُلانٌ في خِمارٍ“, i.e. into the great mass in which he hides. ”خِمارُ المَرْأةِ“ is a woman's head-covering; it is called ”خِمارٌ“ only because it covers. ”اَلْخُمْرَةُ“ is the (mat) on which one prostrates; it is called so only because it screens the face from the ground. It is said of dough ”قَدِ اخْتَمَرَ“ (it has fermented), because its unleavened state has been covered by khamr, I mean by fermentation: one says ”قَدِ اخْتَمَرَ العَجِينُ، وخَمَّرْتُهُ، وفَطَرْتُهُ وأفْطَرْتُهُ“. All of this shows that every intoxicant is khamr, and every intoxicant mingles with the intellect and covers it. No one says of the drinker, from any intoxication, anything but ”مَخْمُورٌ“ and ”بِهِ خُمارٌ“ (he has a hangover). This is clear and evident. Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī was misled: it was said to him that this intoxicant which they called by a name other than khamr is lawful, and he thought it was as he had been told; then his natural sense led him to judge that the two are one, and he said:
؎دَعِ الخَمْرَ يَشْرَبْها الغُواةُ فَإنَّنِي ∗∗∗ رَأيْتُ أخاها مُجْزِيًا لِمَكانِها
؎فَإنْ لا يَكُنْها أوْ تَكُنْهُ فَإنَّهُ ∗∗∗ أخُوها غَذَتْهُ أُمُّها بِلَبانِها
(Leave wine for the misguided to drink, for I have found its brother a sufficient substitute in its place; / if it is not she, or she not it, then it is her brother, whom her mother nursed with her own milk.)
The exegetes said regarding His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قُلْ فِيهِما إثْمٌ كَبِيرٌ﴾ — and it has also been recited ”كَثِيرٌ“ — some people said: in this place He urged abstention from it, and He made its prohibition clear in Sūrat al-Māʾida in His saying: ﴿إنَّما الخَمْرُ والمَيْسِرُ والأنْصابُ والأزْلامُ رِجْسٌ مِن عَمَلِ الشَّيْطانِ فاجْتَنِبُوهُ لَعَلَّكم تُفْلِحُونَ﴾ [al-Māʾida: 90] ﴿إنَّما يُرِيدُ الشَّيْطانُ أنْ يُوقِعَ بَيْنَكُمُ العَداوَةَ والبَغْضاءَ في الخَمْرِ والمَيْسِرِ ويَصُدَّكم عَنْ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وعَنِ الصَّلاةِ فَهَلْ أنْتُمْ مُنْتَهُونَ﴾ [al-Māʾida: 91]. The meaning of ”﴿فَهَلْ أنْتُمْ مُنْتَهُونَ﴾“ [al-Māʾida: 91] is urging to desist and threatening against failing to desist. Other people said: no, rather it is forbidden by what He made clear here, as the Book indicates in another place, because He said ﴿إثْمٌ كَبِيرٌ﴾, and Allah has explicitly forbidden sin (ithm), saying: ﴿قُلْ إنَّما حَرَّمَ رَبِّيَ الفَواحِشَ ما ظَهَرَ مِنها وما بَطَنَ والإثْمَ والبَغْيَ بِغَيْرِ الحَقِّ﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 33]. We have made clear the prohibition of khamr — though it is agreed upon — only so that it may be known that the explicit text of it is in the Book. As for the great sin that is in khamr, it is clear, because it brings about enmity and hatred and comes between a man and his intellect, by which he discerns and knows what is due to his Creator. Gambling breeds enmity and hatred, since a person's wealth passes to someone else without any compensation being taken for it. As for the benefits in it for people: there is the pleasure in khamr and the profit in trading in it; and likewise the benefit in gambling is that a thing comes to a person without toil or effort. So Allah made known that the sin in both is a sin greater than their benefit.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَيَسْألُونَكَ ماذا يُنْفِقُونَ قُلِ العَفْوَ﴾. Both the accusative and the nominative are possible in ”اَلْعَفْوَ“. Whoever makes ”ماذا“ a single noun refers ”اَلْعَفْوَ“ back to it (in the accusative); and whoever makes ”ما“ a noun and ”ذا“ its khabar (predicate), in the sense of ”اَلَّذِي“, refers ”اَلْعَفْوُ“ back to it and puts it in the nominative, as though one said: ”ما الَّذِي يُنْفِقُونَ؟“ (what is it that they spend?), and He said: ”اَلْعَفْوُ“. It is also permissible to put ”اَلْعَفْوَ“ in the accusative even when ”ما“ alone is a noun, construing ”اَلْعَفْوَ“ with ”يُنْفِقُونَ“, as though it were said: ”أنْفِقُوا العَفْوَ“ (spend the surplus). It is also permissible to put it in the nominative even when ”ماذا“ is treated as a single thing, on the sense ”قُلْ هو العَفْوُ“ (say: it is the surplus). ”اَلْعَفْوُ“ in the language is surplus and abundance: one says ”عَفا القَوْمُ“ when the people become numerous. So they were commanded to spend the surplus, until the zakāt was made obligatory. The people of earnings would each take from his earnings what sufficed him and give the rest in charity, and the people of gold and silver would take what sufficed them for their year and spend the rest. This has been narrated in exegesis; and what there is consensus upon is that for zakāt in all things what is due in them has been made clear.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿كَذَلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمُ الآياتِ﴾, i.e. with the like of this explanation concerning khamr and gambling, Allah makes the signs clear to you. (The singular ”كَذَلِكَ“ is used) because the address to the Prophet ﷺ includes the address to his community, as He said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يا أيُّها النَّبِيُّ إذا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّساءَ﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]; and the like of this in the Quran is frequent — it renders the address to the whole group (al-ijmāʿ) with ”ذَلِكَ“, though ”ذَلِكم“ is more frequent in the language. ”ذَلِكَ“ has been used in the Quran for a group elsewhere too; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿يا نِساءَ النَّبِيِّ مَن يَأْتِ مِنكُنَّ بِفاحِشَةٍ مُبَيِّنَةٍ يُضاعَفْ لَها العَذابُ ضِعْفَيْنِ وكانَ ذَلِكَ عَلى اللَّهِ يَسِيرًا﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 30], where the original would be ”ذَلِكُنَّ“; but the group is in the sense of a single body (al-qabīl).

zajjaj:180-180.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ — the meaning is "and it has been prescribed for you", except that when speech becomes long, conjunction by wāw is dispensed with, and it is known that its meaning is the meaning of the wāw; and because the first account had been completed and the sense of obligation in it had come to an end, it is known that the meaning is: "retaliation has been made obligatory upon you, and the bequest has been made obligatory upon you".

The meaning of ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكم إذا حَضَرَ أحَدَكُمُ المَوْتُ إنْ تَرَكَ خَيْرًا الوَصِيَّةُ لِلْوالِدَيْنِ والأقْرَبِينَ﴾: this obligation was, by consensus, abrogated by the verses of inheritance in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ; this is agreed upon. But it must still be explained, so that it may be known what the aspect of wisdom in it was, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not impose worship at any time except with what contains consummate wisdom. So the meaning of "كُتِبَ عَلَيْكم" is: "it is made obligatory upon you, if one of you leaves wealth, [to make] the bequest to parents and relatives in fairness".

The nominative of "اَلْوَصِيَّةُ" is of two kinds. One of them is as [the subject of a verb] whose agent is not named, as though He said: "the bequest to parents has been prescribed for you", that is: "made obligatory upon you". It is also possible that the nominative of al-waṣiyya is as mubtadaʾ (subject), and that "لِلْوالِدَيْنِ" is the khabar (predicate), in the manner of quotation (ḥikāya), because the meaning of "كُتِبَ عَلَيْكم" is: "it has been said to you: the bequest is for parents and relatives".

They were commanded to make the bequest at that time only because they would sometimes go beyond [their kin] by giving wealth to distant people, seeking show and reputation. The meaning of ﴿حَضَرَ أحَدَكُمُ المَوْتُ﴾ is not that it is prescribed for him to make a bequest when death is present to him, because when he beholds death he is occupied away from bequests and other matters. Rather the meaning is: "it is prescribed for you to make bequests while you are capable of making a bequest, so that a man says: when death comes to me — that is, when I die — so-and-so shall have such-and-such", according to the measure of what he was commanded. What he was commanded is to strive for justice in the time of respite, and bequeath in fairness, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, to his parents and his relatives. The meaning of "بِالمَعْرُوفِ" is: with that which a person of discernment knows contains no deviation (janaf) and no injustice.

Some people said: what is abrogated of this is what inheritance abrogated, while the matter of bequest within the third [of the estate] remains. This view is worth nothing, because the consensus of the Muslims is that a man's third is his: if he wishes to bequeath something, it is his right, and if he refrains, that is permissible. So the verse, in His saying "كُتِبَ عَلَيْكم… اَلْوَصِيَّةُ", is abrogated by consensus, as we have described.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿حَقًّا عَلى المُتَّقِينَ﴾ is accusative on [the sense of]: "that has become due upon you as a due" (as mafʿūl muṭlaq, absolute object). Were it outside the Qurʾān and put in the nominative, it would be permissible, in the sense of: "that is a duty upon the God-fearing".

zajjaj:181-181.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فَمَن بَدَّلَهُ بَعْدَما سَمِعَهُ﴾ — meaning: whoever alters the matter of the bequest after hearing it, its sin is only upon the one who alters it. There is no sin upon the testator — if he took precaution, or strove [in choosing] the one he appoints as executor — nor is there sin upon the beneficiary; the sin is only upon the testator if he alters «[Translator's note: so in the source ("المُوصِي"); the context suggests the one who alters, e.g. the executor, is meant]».

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾, that is: He has heard what the testator said, and knows what the executor does, because He, Mighty and Majestic, is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed.

zajjaj:182-182.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فَمَن خافَ مِن مُوصٍ جَنَفًا أوْ إثْمًا﴾, that is: an inclination [from justice], or a sin, or an intention towards sin; ﴿فَأصْلَحَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾, that is: he acted to set things right between the beneficiaries, then there is no sin upon him; that is, because he only intends to set things right, after the testator has made the bequest not in fairness, contrary to Allah's command. So when the executor returns it to fairness, he has returned it to what Allah commanded.

zajjaj:183-183.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الصِّيامُ﴾ — the meaning is: fasting has been made obligatory upon you as an obligation, like that which was made obligatory upon those before you. It was said that the fast of Ramaḍān had been made obligatory upon the Christians, and they moved it from its time and added to it. I do not know what the basis of this report is, nor the reliability of its transmitters; but the sum of it is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has informed us that He made fasting obligatory upon those before us, and that it has been made obligatory upon us as He made it obligatory upon those before us.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿لَعَلَّكم تَتَّقُونَ﴾ — the meaning is that fasting is a means of reaching piety (tuqā), because it is of the righteousness that restrains a person from much of the disobedience the soul longs for; therefore it was said: "لَعَلَّكم تَتَّقُونَ". "لَعَلَّ" here is according to the hope of the servants, while Allah, Mighty and Majestic, encompasses the knowledge of whether you will be pious or not; rather the meaning is that through fasting your hope of piety ought to grow strong.

zajjaj:184-184.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿أيّامًا مَعْدُوداتٍ﴾ — the accusative of "أيّامًا" is of two kinds. The better of them is that it is as an adverb (ẓarf), as though: "fasting has been prescribed for you in these days", the governing word (ʿāmil) in it being "اَلصِّيامُ"; it is as though the meaning were: "it has been prescribed for you that you fast numbered days". Some grammarian said: it is accusative as the object of [a verb] whose agent is not named, like "أُعْطِيَ زَيْدٌ المالَ" ("Zayd was given the money"). This is worth nothing, because the days here are attached to the fasting, whereas "زَيْدٌ" and "اَلْمالَ" are two objects of "أُعْطِيَ", so you may put whichever of them you wish in the place of the agent; and there is nothing here but the accusative of the days by the fasting.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فَمَن كانَ مِنكم مَرِيضًا أوْ عَلى سَفَرٍ فَعِدَّةٌ مِن أيّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾, that is: upon him is a number, or: what substitutes for his fasting in the time of fasting is a number of other days. "أُخَرَ" is in the position of the genitive (jarr), except that it is a diptote (lā tanṣarif), so the genitive in it takes fatḥa.

The meaning of ﴿وَعَلى الَّذِينَ يُطِيقُونَهُ﴾ is: [those who] are able to fast; ﴿فِدْيَةٌ طَعامُ مِسْكِينٍ﴾, that is: if he breaks the fast and leaves fasting, the ransom (fidya) for leaving it is the feeding of a poor person. It has also been read: "طَعامُ مَساكِينَ" ("the feeding of poor persons"); the meaning of "طَعامُ مَساكِينَ" is: the ransom for days in which he breaks the fast. This, by consensus and by the text of the Qurʾān, is abrogated; the verse that follows this one abrogated it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَأنْ تَصُومُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾ — "خَيْرٌ" is nominative as the khabar of the mubtadaʾ; the meaning is: "your fasting is better for you". This was better for them while the ransom was permissible. As for after the abrogation, it is not permissible to say: "fasting is better than the ransom and breaking the fast at this time", because what is not permissible at all cannot have something preferred over it, which would give the impression that it is permissible. It has been said that the fasting made obligatory at the beginning of Islam was the fast of three days in every month and the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ; but the month of Ramaḍān abrogated the obligation in all of that fasting.

zajjaj:254-254.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أنْفِقُوا مِمّا رَزَقْناكُمْ﴾ means: spend in jihad, and let some of you help others in it.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿مِن قَبْلِ أنْ يَأْتِيَ يَوْمٌ لا بَيْعٌ فِيهِ ولا خُلَّةٌ﴾ means the Day of Resurrection; ”اَلْخُلَّةُ“ is friendship. It is permissible to say ”لا بَيْعَ فِيهِ ولا خُلَّةٌ ولا شَفاعَةٌ“ «[Translator's note: so in the source; the sentence goes on to describe the forms with nunation in the nominative and the forms without nunation in the accusative, which suggests the intended pair is «لا بَيْعٌ فِيهِ ولا خُلَّةٌ ولا شَفاعَةٌ» and «لا بَيْعَ فِيهِ ولا خُلَّةَ ولا شَفاعَةَ».]» and ”لا بَيْعٌ فِيهِ ولا خُلَّةَ ولا شَفاعَةَ“, with the nominative with nunation and the accusative without nunation. It is also permissible to say ”لا بَيْعَ فِيهِ ولا خُلَّةٌ ولا شَفاعَةَ“, with the first in the accusative without nunation and the second conjoined to the position of the first, since its position is accusative, except that the nunation has been dropped for a reason we have already mentioned «[Translator's note: so in the source; conjoining to the position would normally give «خُلَّةً» with accusative nunation, as the example that follows shows.]». The entry of ”لا“ along with the conjunctions is then for emphasis, because when you conjoin to the position of what follows ”لا“, you conjoin it with nunation; you say ”لا رَجُلَ وغُلامًا لَكَ“ ("you have no man and no boy"). The poet said:
؎فَلا أبَ وابْنًا مِثْلُ مَرْوانَ وابْنِهِ ∗∗∗ إذا هو بِالمَجْدِ ارْتَدى أوْ تَأزَّرا
(There is no father and son like Marwān and his son, when he puts on glory as a cloak or wraps it round as a waist-wrapper.)
The meaning of ﴿والكافِرُونَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾ is: they are the ones who put the matter in other than its proper place; and this is the root meaning of ”اَلظُّلْمُ“ in the language.

zajjaj:255-255.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿اللَّهُ لا إلَهَ إلا هو الحَيُّ القَيُّومُ﴾: it is narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The noblest verse in the Qurʾān is the Verse of the Throne (āyat al-kursī)." The i'rab of ”لا إلَهَ إلّا هو“: the accusative without nunation in ”إلَهَ“; the meaning is "there is no god for any created being except He". It [the pronoun هو] is construed on the position of the subject (ibtidāʾ); the meaning is "there is no god for creation except He". If you say in ordinary speech ”لا إلَهٌ إلّا اللَّهُ“, it is permissible; but as for the Qurʾān, it is read only as the readers have read it and as sound transmission has established. If in ordinary speech one said ”لا رَجُلَ عِنْدَكَ إلّا زَيْدًا“ ("there is no man with you except Zayd"), it would be permissible, and ”لا إلَهَ إلّا اللَّهَ“ would be permissible; but the best is what is in the Qurʾān, and it is also the best in ordinary speech. Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿إنَّهم كانُوا إذا قِيلَ لَهم لا إلَهَ إلا اللَّهُ يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 35]. If you put what follows ”إلّا“ in the accusative, you do so only as an exception.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الحَيُّ القَيُّومُ﴾: the meaning of ”اَلْحَيُّ“ is the Everlasting, and the meaning of ”اَلْقَيُّومُ“ is the One who undertakes the management of every affair of His creation. ”اَلْقَيّامُ“ is also permissible, and the meaning of both is the same. He is Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, who undertakes the management of the affair of creation in originating them, providing for them, and His knowledge of their places; this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَما مِن دابَّةٍ في الأرْضِ إلا عَلى اللَّهِ رِزْقُها ويَعْلَمُ مُسْتَقَرَّها ومُسْتَوْدَعَها﴾ [Hūd: 6]. The meaning of ﴿لا تَأْخُذُهُ سِنَةٌ﴾ is: no drowsiness overtakes Him, ﴿وَلا نَوْمٌ﴾; and its interpretation is that He is never heedless of managing the affair of creation. The meaning of ﴿مَن ذا الَّذِي يَشْفَعُ عِنْدَهُ إلا بِإذْنِهِ﴾ is: there is no intercession with Him except by what He has commanded — the Muslims' praying for one another, the Muslims' honouring the prophets and praying for them, and what we know of the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ. The polytheists used to claim that the idols would intercede for them; the proof of that is their saying: ﴿ما نَعْبُدُهم إلا لِيُقَرِّبُونا إلى اللَّهِ زُلْفى﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and that is their saying: ﴿وَيَقُولُونَ هَؤُلاءِ شُفَعاؤُنا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾ [Yūnus: 18]. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, made known that intercession is only what He has made known of the intercession of some believers for others in supplication, and the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ. The meaning of ﴿يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وما خَلْفَهُمْ﴾ is: He knows the unseen that preceded them and the unseen that will come after them. The meaning of ﴿وَلا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَيْءٍ مِن عِلْمِهِ إلا بِما شاءَ﴾ is: they do not know the unseen, neither of what preceded them nor of what will be after them; and the meaning of ﴿إلا بِما شاءَ﴾ is: except what He has told of, so that it may be a proof establishing their prophethood.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضَ﴾: more than one view has been given on it. Ibn ʿAbbās said: ”كُرْسِيُّهُ“ is His knowledge. It is narrated from ʿAṭāʾ that he said: "The heavens and the earth are, in relation to the Kursī, nothing but a ring in a desert." This view is clear, because what we know of the kursī in the language is the thing on which one leans and sits; so this shows that the Kursī is immense, the heavens and the earths being upon it. ”اَلْكُرْسِيُّ“ in the language, and ”اَلْكُرّاسَةُ“ (a quire), is only something that is firm and whose parts cling to one another; and ”اَلْكُرْسِيُّ“ is what has become matted together in the ears of sheep and in the resting places of camels. Some said: ”كُرْسِيُّهُ“ is His power by which He holds the heavens and the earth; they said: this is like your saying ”اِجْعَلْ لِهَذا الحائِطِ كُرْسِيًّا“ ("make a support for this wall"), that is, make for it something that props it and holds it up. This is close to the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah have mercy on him, because His knowledge which encompasses the heavens and the earth does not fall outside this. And Allah knows best the reality of the Kursī, except that, in sum, it is a mighty matter of His affair, Majestic and Mighty is He.
The meaning of ﴿وَلا يَئُودُهُ حِفْظُهُما﴾ is: it does not weigh Him down. The hāʾ may refer to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and it may refer to the Kursī; and if it refers to the Kursī, it [the Kursī] is of the affair of Allah.

zajjaj:256-256.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لا إكْراهَ في الدِّينِ﴾: ”إكْراهَ“ is accusative without nunation. The nominative ”لا إكْراهٌ“ is permissible, but it is not to be read so unless a sound transmission is established. They have given three views on ”﴿لا إكْراهَ في الدِّينِ﴾“. Some said: this was abrogated by the command to fight in His saying, Majestic and Mighty is He: ﴿واقْتُلُوهم حَيْثُ ثَقِفْتُمُوهُمْ﴾ [al-Baqara: 191]. It has been said that this verse was revealed on account of the People of the Book, that they should not be compelled after they pay the jizya; as for the polytheists of the Arabs, jizya is not accepted from them, and there is nothing in their case but being fought or Islam. And it has been said that the meaning of ”لا إكْراهَ في الدِّينِ“ is: do not say of one who entered it after war that he entered it under compulsion, because if he became content after the war and his Islam is sound, he is not one under compulsion.
The meaning of ﴿فَمَن يَكْفُرْ بِالطّاغُوتِ﴾: it has been said that ”اَلطّاغُوتُ“ are the rebellious ones among the People of the Book, and it has been said that the ṭāghūt is Satan. In sum, whoever disbelieves in it and believes in Allah and what He has commanded ﴿فَقَدِ اسْتَمْسَكَ بِالعُرْوَةِ الوُثْقى﴾, that is, he has tied for himself a firm knot which no argument can undo.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لا انْفِصامَ لَها﴾: there is no breaking for it. One says ”فَصَمْتُ الشَّيْءَ، أفْصُمُهُ، فَصْمًا“, that is, I cut it. The meaning of ﴿واللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ is: He hears what a person binds himself to in the matter of faith, and knows his intention in that.

zajjaj:257-257.t:
His saying, Majestic and Mighty is He: ﴿اللَّهُ ولِيُّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: one says ”قَدْ تَوَلَّيْتُ فُلانًا“ and ”وَلَّيْتُ فُلانًا وِلايَةً“; ”اَلْوِلايَةُ“, with kasra, is a noun for everything that is taken charge of. The meaning of ”وَلِيُّ“ is of various kinds: Allah is the walī (protector) of the believers in their arguments and their guidance and establishing the proof for them, because He increases them in guidance by their faith, as He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿والَّذِينَ اهْتَدَوْا زادَهم هُدًى﴾ [Muḥammad: 17]. He is also their walī in helping them and making their religion prevail over the religion of their opponents; and He is also their walī in taking charge of their words and rewarding them for the goodness of their deeds.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يُخْرِجُهم مِنَ الظُّلُماتِ إلى النُّورِ﴾ means: He brings them out of the darknesses of ignorance into the light of guidance, because the matter of error is dark and unclear, while the matter of guidance is plain, like the clarity of light. Some said: ”يُخْرِجُهم مِنَ الظُّلُماتِ إلى النُّورِ“ means He judges them to be coming out of the darknesses into the light; but this is not the view of the exegetes, nor the view of most philologists — al-Akhfash alone said it.
The proof that He increases them in guidance is the verse we have mentioned,
and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَأمّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا فَزادَتْهم إيمانًا﴾ [al-Tawba: 124].
The meaning of ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا أوْلِياؤُهُمُ الطّاغُوتُ﴾ is: those who take charge of their affair are the ṭāghūt. We have already explained ”اَلطّاغُوتُ“. ”اَلطّاغُوتُ“ here is singular with the meaning of a plural, and this is permissible in the language when there is an indication of plurality in the speech. The poet said:
؎بِها جِيَفُ الحَسْرى فَأمّا عِظامُها ∗∗∗ فَبِيضٌ وأمّا جِلْدُها فَصَلِيبُ
(In it are the carcasses of the exhausted camels: as for their bones, they are white, and as for their skin, it is hard and dry.)
”جِلْدُها“ (their skin) is in the sense of ”جُلُودُها“ (their skins).

zajjaj:140-140.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أمْ تَقُولُونَ إنَّ إبْراهِيمَ وإسْماعِيلَ وإسْحاقَ ويَعْقُوبَ والأسْباطَ كانُوا هُودًا أوْ نَصارى﴾. It is as if they said to them: by which of the two arguments do you hold on in our matter? By the affirmation of oneness? Then we affirm the oneness [of Allah]. Or by following the religion of the prophets? Then we are followers [of it].

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قُلْ أأنْتُمْ أعْلَمُ أمِ اللَّهُ﴾. Its interpretation is that the Prophet who brought us the miraculous signs, and brought them to you, has informed you and informed us that Islam is the religion of these prophets.

"اَلْأسْباطُ" are those of the offspring of the prophets. The asbāṭ are twelve tribes, and they are the children of Jacob, peace be upon him. The meaning of al-sibṭ in the language is the group who trace back to one father; and al-sibṭ in the language is [also] the tree; so the sibṭ are those who are from one tree.

His saying: ﴿وَمَن أظْلَمُ مِمَّنْ كَتَمَ شَهادَةً عِنْدَهُ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾. By them He means these who are the scholars of the Jews, because they knew that the messengership of the Prophet is true, and they disbelieved only out of envy, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, and seeking the continuance of their leadership and their earnings, because they used to make a living by their remaining on their religion. So it was said: and who is more unjust than whoever concealed the matter of the Prophet ﷺ?! No one is more unjust than he.

His saying: ﴿وَما اللَّهُ بِغافِلٍ عَمّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ means: of your concealing what you knew of the truth of the Prophet's ﷺ matter.

zajjaj:141-141.t: His saying: ﴿تِلْكَ أُمَّةٌ قَدْ خَلَتْ لَها ما كَسَبَتْ﴾. The meaning is: theirs is the reward of what they earned, and yours is the reward of what you earned.

zajjaj:142-142.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿سَيَقُولُ السُّفَهاءُ مِنَ النّاسِ﴾. There are two views on it: it has been said that it means the disbelievers of the people of Mecca, and it has been said that it means the Jews.

"اَلسُّفَهاءُ": its singular is "سَفِيهٌ", like "شَهِيدٌ" and "شُهَداءُ", and "عَلِيمٌ" and "عُلَماءُ".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ما ولاهم عَنْ قِبْلَتِهِمُ الَّتِي كانُوا عَلَيْها﴾. The meaning of "ما ولّاهم" is: what turned them away from it? He means the qibla of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), because the Prophet ﷺ had been commanded to pray towards Jerusalem — because the Arabs were accustomed to making pilgrimage to Mecca and the Sacred House of Allah, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, wished to test the people with something other than what they were accustomed to, so that it would become manifest who follows the Messenger ﷺ as distinct from who does not follow him, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿وَما جَعَلْنا القِبْلَةَ الَّتِي كُنْتَ عَلَيْها إلا لِنَعْلَمَ مَن يَتَّبِعُ الرَّسُولَ مِمَّنْ يَنْقَلِبُ عَلى عَقِبَيْهِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 143]. So Allah tested [them] with Jerusalem, according to what is transmitted, for this reason; and Allah knows best.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قُلْ لِلَّهِ المَشْرِقُ والمَغْرِبُ يَهْدِي مَن يَشاءُ إلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾. Its meaning is: wherever Allah has commanded that prayer and worship be performed, it belongs to Him, He knows it, and He is in it, as He said: ﴿وَهُوَ اللَّهُ في السَّماواتِ وفي الأرْضِ يَعْلَمُ سِرَّكم وجَهْرَكُمْ﴾ [al-Anʿām: 3], and as He said: ﴿وَهُوَ مَعَكم أيْنَ ما كُنْتُمْ﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 4], and as He said: ﴿ما يَكُونُ مِن نَجْوى ثَلاثَةٍ إلا هو رابِعُهُمْ﴾ [al-Mujādila: 7]. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿إلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ means "to a straight way", as Allah loves.

zajjaj:143-143.t:
His saying: ﴿وَكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْناكم أُمَّةً وسَطًا﴾. The meaning of al-umma is a group, any group whatever, except that this group has been described as being wasaṭ. On "أُمَّةً وسَطًا" there are two views. Some said: "وَسَطًا" means just (ʿadl); others said: the best (akhyār). The two words differ but the meaning is one, because the just is good and the good is just. It has been said in describing the Prophet ﷺ: "He is of the most central (awsaṭ) of his people in lineage", i.e. of the best of them. The Arabs describe a person of excellent lineage as being "of the most central of his people". The people of language know the reality of this, because the Arabs use comparison a great deal, likening the tribe to a valley, a plain and the like; the best of a valley is its middle. So it is said: "هَذا مِن وسَطِ قَوْمِهِ" (he is from the middle of his people), "مِن وسَطِ الوادِي" (from the middle of the valley), "سَرَرِ الوادِي", "سِرارَةُ الوادِي" and "سِرُّ الوادِي"; the meaning of all of it is: from the best place in it. Likewise the Prophet ﷺ is from the best place in the lineage of the Arabs. "وَكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْناكم أُمَّةً وسَطًا", i.e. the best.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لِتَكُونُوا شُهَداءَ عَلى النّاسِ﴾. "تَكُونُوا" is in the position of the accusative; the meaning is: "We made you the best, in order that you be witnesses". "تَكُونُوا" is accusative by "أنْ", and "شُهَداءَ" is accusative as the khabar (predicate) of "تَكُونُوا", except that "شُهَداءَ" does not take tanwīn because it is a diptote, as it contains the feminine alif; the noun is built together with the feminine alif, which was not appended after the noun was complete. That is why "شُهَداءَ" is diptote.

If someone asks: why was the plural made with the feminine alif? It is said: just as the feminine was used in the like of your saying "جَرِيبٌ" and "أجْرِبَةٌ", "غُرابٌ" and "أغْرِبَةٌ", "ضارِبٌ" and "ضَرَبَةٌ", "كاتِبٌ" and "كَتَبَةٌ". On the interpretation of "﴿لِتَكُونُوا شُهَداءَ عَلى النّاسِ﴾" there are two views. It has come in the exegesis that the communities of the prophets will lie in the Hereafter when they are asked about who was sent to them, and will deny their prophets — this concerns those among them who denied in this world — so this community will testify to the truthfulness of the prophets and testify against them that they gave the lie [to them], and the Prophet ﷺ will testify for this community to their truthfulness. This testimony is valid, even though they did not see those communities, because of what the Prophet ﷺ told them. This is one view. Others said: "﴿لِتَكُونُوا شُهَداءَ عَلى النّاسِ﴾" means: presenting the argument against all who oppose you, while the Messenger presents the argument against you and makes things clear to you. The first view is closer to the exegesis and closer to His saying "وَسَطًا", because the Prophet ﷺ presents the argument against the Muslims and others.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإنْ كانَتْ لَكَبِيرَةً إلا عَلى الَّذِينَ هَدى اللَّهُ﴾. He means the qibla of Jerusalem, i.e. "though following it was indeed a great [burden]". The meaning is: it is heavy for those who are not sincere; as for whoever is sincere, it is not heavy for him, as He said: ﴿إلا عَلى الَّذِينَ هَدى اللَّهُ﴾, i.e. it is not heavy for them. This lām came in with "إنْ" because, if the lām does not come with the light "إنْ", the speech is a negation (jaḥd); without the lām, the meaning would be "it was not heavy". When "إنْ" and the lām come, its meaning is emphasis (tawkīd) of the statement, and the lām enters the khabar (predicate). We shall explain its entry with the light [إنْ] in its place, if Allah wills.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إيمانَكُمْ﴾. This lām is the one the grammarians call "the lām of denial" (lām al-juḥūd); it puts the following verb in the accusative. We have explained it thoroughly before this place. The meaning of "﴿وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إيمانَكُمْ﴾" is: whoever prayed towards Jerusalem before the qibla was turned to the Sacred House in Mecca, his prayer is not lost and his reward stands. It has been said that some people said: what are we to do about our prayers that we prayed towards Jerusalem? So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down: ﴿وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إيمانَكُمْ﴾, i.e. your assent to the matter of that qibla. It has also been said that a group of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ died while praying towards Jerusalem, before the qibla was moved to the Sacred House of Allah, and the Prophet ﷺ was asked about their prayer, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down: ﴿وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إيمانَكم إنَّ اللَّهَ بِالنّاسِ لَرَءُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾. If you wish you say "لَرَؤُوفٌ", and if you wish "لَرَوُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ", pronouncing the hamza or lightening it. The meaning of raʾfa (tenderness) is like the meaning of raḥma (mercy).

zajjaj:144-144.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قَدْ نَرى تَقَلُّبَ وجْهِكَ في السَّماءِ﴾. The meaning is: in looking towards the sky. It has also been said: "the turning of your eye", and the meaning is one, because the turning was only because the Prophet ﷺ had been commanded to stop praying towards Jerusalem, and he was waiting for revelation to come down to him [telling him] towards which qibla to pray. "تَقَلُّبَ" is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of "تَقَلَّبَ، تَقَلُّبًا"; in [ordinary] speech "تِقْلابًا" is permissible, but not in the Qurʾān, because it would be a change to the muṣḥaf.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ قِبْلَةً تَرْضاها﴾. The Prophet ﷺ was in Medina when he was commanded to move away from praying towards Jerusalem, and he was commanded to pray towards the Sacred House of Allah. Two views have been given on His saying "تَرْضاها". Some said: its meaning is "that you love" — not that the Prophet ﷺ was not content with that [earlier] qibla, because everything Allah commands the prophets, peace be upon them, they are content with. The Prophet ﷺ loved it only because it was — according to what is transmitted — the qibla of the prophets; and it has been said: because in his view it was more inviting for his people to faith.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَوَلِّ وجْهَكَ شَطْرَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾, i.e. the Sacred Mosque. So he was commanded, while in Medina, to face Mecca and the Sacred House, and he was commanded to face the House wherever people are. The meaning of al-shaṭr is direction (al-naḥw), and "شَطْرَ" is accusative as an adverbial (ẓarf). The poet said:

؎إنَّ العَسِيرَ بِها داءٌ يُخامِرُها ∗∗∗ فَشَطْرَها نَظَرُ العَيْنَيْنِ مَحْسُورُ
(The unbroken she-camel has an ailment that afflicts her, so towards her [direction] the gaze of the eyes is wearied.)

i.e. towards her. There is no disagreement among the people of language that al-shaṭr is direction. People's saying "فُلانٌ شاطِرٌ" means: he has taken a direction other than the straight one; that is why he is called "شاطِرٌ", for his deviating from straightness. One says: "قَدْ شَطَرَ الرَّجُلُ، يَشْطُرُ، شِطارَةً، وشَطارَةً". And one says: "هَؤُلاءِ قَوْمٌ مُشاطِرُونا", i.e. their houses adjoin our houses, as you say "هَؤُلاءِ يُناحُونَنا", i.e. "we are in their direction and they are in ours"; that is why they are "شاطَرُونا".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إلا لِنَعْلَمَ مَن يَتَّبِعُ الرَّسُولَ مِمَّنْ يَنْقَلِبُ عَلى عَقِبَيْهِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 143]. If someone asks: what is the meaning of "﴿إلا لِنَعْلَمَ مَن يَتَّبِعُ الرَّسُولَ مِمَّنْ يَنْقَلِبُ عَلى عَقِبَيْهِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 143]", when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knew what would be before it came to be? The answer to that is that Allah knows who follows the Messenger, as distinct from who does not follow him, before it occurs; but that knowledge does not entail requital in reward or punishment. Rather the meaning is: that He may know that from them as witnessed knowledge (shahāda), so that by that knowledge the name "obedient" and the name "disobedient" applies to them, and their reward becomes due according to the measure of their deeds; and what is known at the time the act occurs from them is knowledge of the witnessed, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿عالِمُ الغَيْبِ والشَّهادَةِ﴾ [al-Raʿd: 9]. His knowledge of it before it occurs is knowledge of the unseen (ghayb), and His knowledge of it at the time it occurs is [knowledge of the] witnessed; and everything Allah knows as witnessed was already known to Him as unseen, because He knows it before it comes to be. This clarifies everything like it in the Qurʾān, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَلَنَبْلُوَنَّكم حَتّى نَعْلَمَ المُجاهِدِينَ مِنكم والصّابِرِينَ ونَبْلُوَ أخْبارَكُمْ﴾ [Muḥammad: 31].

zajjaj:220-220.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لَعَلَّكم تَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 219] ﴿فِي الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ﴾. It may be that ”في الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ“ in ”تَتَفَكَّرُونَ في الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ“ belongs to the complement (ṣila) of ”تَتَفَكَّرُونَ“; the meaning is: so that you may reflect on the affair of this world and the affair of the Hereafter. It may also be that ”في الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ“ belongs to the complement of ”كَذَلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمُ الآياتِ“, i.e. He makes the signs clear to you concerning the affair of this world and the affair of the Hereafter, so that you may reflect.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَيَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ اليَتامى﴾. This is among the things whose exegesis we will set out thoroughly in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, if Allah wills; but its sum is that they used to wrong the orphans: they would marry ten wives and consume the orphans' wealth along with their own wealth. So they were dealt with severely in the matter of the orphans, with a severity that made them fear marrying the orphan women and mixing with them. Then Allah made known to them that setting things right for them is the best of things, and that mixing with them, in marriage and otherwise, is permissible provided one strives to set things right. So He said: ﴿وَإنْ تُخالِطُوهم فَإخْوانُكُمْ﴾, i.e. then they are your brothers; the nominative is on this sense. The accusative is permissible — ”وَإنْ تُخالِطُوهم فَإخْوانَكم“, i.e. then it is your brothers that you mix with — but I know of no one who recited it so, so you must not recite it so unless a sound transmission is established.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لأعْنَتَكُمْ﴾. Abū ʿUbayda said: its meaning is "He would have destroyed you". Its real sense is: had Allah willed, He would have charged you with what is hard upon you, so that you would be put in distress. The origin of ”اَلْعَنَتُ“ in the language is from their saying ”عَنِتَ البَعِيرُ، يَعْنِتُ“ when a fracture occurs in a camel's leg after it has been set, such that it cannot move it. One says ”أكَمَةٌ عَنُوتٌ“ (a ʿanūt hillock) when one cannot cross it except with severe hardship.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ﴾, i.e. by His might He does what He loves, and no repeller can repel it from Him; ”حَكِيمٌ“, i.e. possessed of wisdom in what He commanded you concerning the orphans and other matters.

zajjaj:221-221.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تَنْكِحُوا المُشْرِكاتِ حَتّى يُؤْمِنَّ﴾. The meaning of ”لا تَنْكِحُوا“ is: do not marry the polytheist women. Had it been recited ”وَلا تُنْكِحُوا المُشْرِكاتِ“ it would be a valid way, but I know of no one who recited it so. The meaning in this is: do not marry the polytheist women until they believe. The meaning of ”اَلْمُشْرِكاتِ“ here: (it applies) to everyone who disbelieves in the Prophet ﷺ; and the language applies it to every unbeliever — he is simply called ”مُشْرِكٌ“. The prohibition had come down concerning all the unbelievers, regarding the marriage of their women to Muslims; then He made lawful, from among them, marrying the women of the People of the Book. Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿اليَوْمَ أُحِلَّ لَكُمُ الطَّيِّباتُ وطَعامُ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ حِلٌّ لَكم وطَعامُكم حِلٌّ لَهم والمُحْصَناتُ مِنَ المُؤْمِناتِ والمُحْصَناتُ مِنَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ [al-Māʾida: 5].
If someone says: on what basis is one who disbelieves in the Prophet ﷺ called a mushrik (associator), even if he says that Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, is One? The answer to that is that when he disbelieves in the Prophet ﷺ, he has claimed that the Quran he brought is from other than Allah, exalted be His praise; yet the Quran is only from Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, because created beings are incapable of producing its like. So he has claimed that someone other than Allah has brought what none but Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, can bring; and thus he has associated another with Him.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تُنْكِحُوا المُشْرِكِينَ حَتّى يُؤْمِنُوا﴾, i.e. do not give a Muslim woman to them in marriage.
His saying: ﴿وَلَعَبْدٌ مُؤْمِنٌ خَيْرٌ مِن مُشْرِكٍ ولَوْ أعْجَبَكُمْ﴾. Its meaning is: even if he pleases you; except that ”لَوْ“ comes and stands in for ”إنْ“ with the past verb. The meaning of the statement is that the unbeliever is worse for you than the believer, even if he pleases you, i.e. his affair pleases you in respect of worldly matters; because the unbelieving man and the unbelieving woman call to the Fire, i.e. they do the deeds of the people of the Fire, so it would be as though your offspring were raised with one whose state is this.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واللَّهُ يَدْعُو إلى الجَنَّةِ والمَغْفِرَةِ بِإذْنِهِ﴾, i.e. He calls you to intermixing with the believers, because that is more conducive for you to reaching Paradise. The meaning of ”بِإذْنِهِ“ is: by His knowledge, by which He made known that it is a means for you to reach it. ﴿وَيُبَيِّنُ آياتِهِ﴾, i.e. His signs: one says ”آيَةٌ“, (plural) ”آيٌ“ and ”آياتٌ“, the latter being more frequent, and the Noble Quran came with it.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لَعَلَّهم يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾. The meaning of ”لَعَلَّ“ here is hope on their part, i.e. so that they themselves may be hoping; Allah knows whether they will take heed or not, but they were addressed according to their own manner of expression and usage.

zajjaj:222-222.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَيَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ المَحِيضِ قُلْ هو أذًى﴾. One says ”حاضَتِ المَرْأةُ، تَحِيضُ، حَيْضًا، ومَحاضًا، ومَحِيضًا“ (the woman menstruated). According to the grammarians, the maṣdar (verbal noun) in this class is mafʿil, while mafʿal is good and in full use in it: one says ”ما في بُرِّكَ مَكالٌ“, i.e. measuring, and ”ما فِيهِ مَكِيلٌ“ is also permissible.
The poet — al-Rāʿī — said:
؎بُنِيَتْ مَرافِقُهُنَّ فَوْقَ مَزَلَّةٍ ∗∗∗ لا يَسْتَطِيعُ بِها القُرادُ مَقِيلا
(Their elbows were built upon a slippery surface on which the tick cannot find a midday resting-place.)
i.e. a midday rest (qaylūla). The meaning of the verse is that the Arabs used to do regarding the menstruating woman what the Magians used to do: they would avoid charging her with doing any work, and she would be avoided in intercourse and in everything else women are charged with, meaning that she was impure. So Allah made known that what ought to be avoided of her is the private part only, and that she does not make anything impure. He made known that menstruation is adhan, i.e. something loathsome, and He forbade approaching the woman until she purifies herself from her menstruation with water after she has become clean of the blood, i.e. is cleansed of it. So He said: ﴿وَلا تَقْرَبُوهُنَّ حَتّى يَطْهُرْنَ﴾; the meaning is: until they purify themselves, i.e. wash with water after the blood has stopped. It has also been recited ”حَتّى يَطَّهَّرْنَ“; but ﴿فَإذا تَطَهَّرْنَ﴾ points to ”وَلا تَقْرَبُوهُنَّ حَتّى يَطْهُرْنَ“. Both — ”يَطْهُرْنَ“ and ”يَطَّهَّرْنَ“, both having been recited — are good. One says both ”طَهَرَتْ“ and ”طَهُرَتْ“, and ”طَهُرَتْ“ is more frequent.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَأْتُوهُنَّ مِن حَيْثُ أمَرَكُمُ اللَّهُ﴾, i.e. from the aspects in which it is lawful to approach the woman; and do not approach them in a way that is not proper — I mean, do not approach them as companions or mistresses «[Translator's note: so in the text (صاحِباتٍ ولا عَشِيقاتٍ); the intended words are uncertain.]». It has been said in exegesis: ”﴿مِن حَيْثُ أمَرَكُمُ اللَّهُ﴾“ means in the vagina, and it is not permissible that they be approached in the anus. What is narrated from Mālik is not sound, because the consensus of the Muslims is that intercourse is where offspring is sought, and that the matter of the anus is an abomination. The ḥadīth has come: «أنَّ مَحاشَّ النِّساءِ حَرامٌ» (the maḥāshsh of women are forbidden), which is used as a euphemism for the anus.

zajjaj:223-223.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿نِساؤُكم حَرْثٌ لَكُمْ﴾. Abū ʿUbayda claimed that it is a metonymy (kināya). My view on it is that its meaning is: your women are a tillage for you; from them you cultivate offspring and pleasure.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَأْتُوا حَرْثَكم أنّى شِئْتُمْ﴾, i.e. however you wish, i.e. come to the place of your tillage however you wish. It was said to them "however you wish" only because the Jews used to say: if a man has intercourse with a woman from behind, the child comes out squint-eyed. So Allah made known that intercourse, when it is in the vagina, is lawful from every direction.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَقَدِّمُوا لأنْفُسِكم واتَّقُوا اللَّهَ﴾, i.e. fear Allah in what He has set as limits for you regarding intercourse and the matter of menstruation. ”وَقَدِّمُوا لِأنْفُسِكم“, i.e. send ahead obedience to Him and following His command; for whoever follows what Allah has commanded has sent ahead good for himself.

zajjaj:185-185.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿شَهْرُ رَمَضانَ الَّذِي أُنْـزِلَ فِيهِ القُرْآنُ﴾ — the reading is with the nominative, and the accusative is permissible; it is a reading that is not widespread. Its nominative is of three kinds. One of them is a new sentence (istiʾnāf); the meaning is: "the fasting that has been prescribed for you — or the days that have been prescribed for you — is the month of Ramaḍān". It may also be nominative as a badal (substitute) for "اَلصِّيامُ", so that it is nominative as [the subject of a verb] whose agent is not named; the meaning is: "the month of Ramaḍān has been prescribed for you". And it may be nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject), with the khabar (predicate) being "اَلَّذِي أُنْزِلَ فِيهِ القُرْآنُ". In the two [other] ways we have explained, "اَلَّذِي" is nominative as an adjective (ṣifa) of "the month", and the command of obligation concerning it is: ﴿فَمَن شَهِدَ مِنكُمُ الشَّهْرَ فَلْيَصُمْهُ﴾.

The meaning of "مَن شَهِدَ" is: whoever is present (resident), not travelling, let him fast; and whoever is travelling or ill, it has been granted to him to fast the number of the days of illness and the days of travel from other days.

Whoever reads "شَهْرَ رَمَضانَ" in the accusative takes it in two ways. One of them is that it is a badal from ﴿أيّامًا مَعْدُوداتٍ﴾ [al-Baqara: 184]. The second way is as a command, as though He said: "عَلَيْكم شَهْرَ رَمَضانَ" ("[keep to] the month of Ramaḍān"), by way of incitement (ighrāʾ).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ بِكُمُ اليُسْرَ﴾, that is: to make it easy for you by lifting fasting from you in travel and illness.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلِتُكْمِلُوا العِدَّةَ﴾ — it has been read with doubling, "وَلِتُكَمِّلُوا", and with the light form — from "كَمَّلَ، يُكَمِّلُ" and "أكْمَلَ، يُكْمِلُ" «[Translator's note: the source text runs the two together as "with doubling: وَلِتُكَمِّلُوا, with the light form"; the sense is that both readings exist]». The meaning of the lām and the conjunction here is a subtle meaning: this speech is conjoined and construed according to the sense; the meaning is: Allah did that to make it easy for you, and so that you may complete the number. The poet said:

بادَتْ وغَيَّرَ آيَهُنَّ مَعَ البِلى ∗∗∗ إلّا رَواكِدَ جَمْرُهُنَّ هَباءُ
وَمُشَجَّجٌ أمّا سَواءُ قَذالِهِ ∗∗∗ فَبَدا وغَيَّرَ سارَهُ المَعْزاءُ
(They perished, and decay altered their traces, except for fixed hearth-stones whose embers are dust; and a battered tent-peg, whose top has become exposed while the stony ground has altered the rest of it.)

He conjoined "مُشَجَّجٌ" (nominative) according to the sense of "there are in it fixed [stones] and a battered [peg]", because when he said "they perished, except fixed [stones]", it was known that the meaning is: "there remained fixed [stones] and a battered [peg]".

zajjaj:186-186.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَإذا سَألَكَ عِبادِي عَنِّي فَإنِّي قَرِيبٌ﴾ — the meaning is: if someone says: "where is Allah?", then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is near; no place is devoid of Him, as He said: ﴿ما يَكُونُ مِن نَجْوى ثَلاثَةٍ إلا هو رابِعُهُمْ﴾ [al-Mujādila: 7], and as He said: ﴿وَهُوَ مَعَكم أيْنَ ما كُنْتُمْ﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 4].

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الدّاعِ إذا دَعانِ﴾ — if you wish, you say "إذا دَعانِي" with a yāʾ, and if you wish, without a yāʾ; except that the Muṣḥaf is followed, so one pauses on the word as it is in it.

The meaning of supplication (duʿāʾ) to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is of three kinds. One kind is affirming His oneness and praising Him, as in your saying: "O Allah, there is no god but You", and your saying: "Our Lord, to You belongs praise"; you have called upon Him by your saying "Our Lord", then brought praise and affirmation of oneness. Similar is: ﴿وَقالَ رَبُّكُمُ ادْعُونِي أسْتَجِبْ لَكم إنَّ الَّذِينَ يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ عَنْ عِبادَتِي سَيَدْخُلُونَ جَهَنَّمَ داخِرِينَ﴾ [Ghāfir: 60], that is: they are too proud to affirm My oneness and praise Me. This is one kind of supplication. A second kind is asking Allah for pardon, mercy and what brings near to Him, as in your saying: "O Allah, forgive us". A third kind is asking Him for [things] of this world, as in your saying: "O Allah, provide me with wealth and children", and the like. All of this was called "duʿāʾ" (calling) only because a person begins these things with his saying "O Allah", "O Lord", "O Living One"; hence it was called "duʿāʾ".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِي﴾, that is: let them answer Me. The poet said:

وَداعٍ دَعا يا مَن يُجِيبُ إلى النِّدا ∗∗∗ فَلَمْ يَسْتَجِبْهُ عِنْدَ ذاكَ مُجِيبُ
(And a caller called out: "O who will answer the call?", but no answerer answered him then.)

That is: no one answered him.

zajjaj:187-187.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿أُحِلَّ لَكم لَيْلَةَ الصِّيامِ الرَّفَثُ إلى نِسائِكُمْ﴾ — "اَلرَّفَثُ" is a word comprising everything a man wants from a woman; the meaning here is a euphemism (kināya) for intercourse, that is: intercourse has been made lawful for you on the night of fasting. For at the beginning of the obligation of fasting, intercourse on the night of fasting was forbidden, as was eating and drinking after the last ʿishāʾ [prayer] and [after] sleep. So Allah made intercourse, eating and drinking lawful until the time of the rising of dawn.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿هُنَّ لِباسٌ لَكم وأنْتُمْ لِباسٌ لَهُنَّ﴾ — more than one view has been given about it. It was said: the meaning is: so you embrace them and they embrace you. And it was said: each party of you finds repose in the other and is in close contact with him, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿وَجَعَلَ مِنها زَوْجَها لِيَسْكُنَ إلَيْها﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 189]. The Arabs call a woman "لِباسًا" (garment) and "إزارًا" (wrapper). The poet said:

إذا ما الضَّجِيعُ ثَنى عِطْفَهُ ∗∗∗ تَثَنَّتْ فَكانَتْ عَلَيْهِ لِباسا
(When her bedfellow turns his side, she bends towards him and becomes a garment over him.)

And he also said:

ألا أبْلِغْ أبا حَفْصٍ رَسُولًا ∗∗∗ فِدًى لَكَ مِن أخِي ثِقَةٍ إزارِي
(Convey to Abū Ḥafṣ a message: may my wrapper be a ransom for you, from a trusted brother.)

The people of language said: [it means] "may my wife be a ransom for you".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وابْتَغُوا ما كَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ﴾ — they said: its meaning is: children. It may also be — and it is the correct view in my opinion, and Allah knows best — that "وابْتَغُوا ما كَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَكم" means: follow the Qurʾān in what has been made permissible for you in it and what you have been commanded; that is what is to be sought.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿حَتّى يَتَبَيَّنَ لَكُمُ الخَيْطُ الأبْيَضُ مِنَ الخَيْطِ الأسْوَدِ مِنَ الفَجْرِ﴾ — they are two dawns: one of them appears black, lying across [the horizon], and that is the black thread; and the white one rises radiant, filling the horizon. Its reality is: "until night becomes distinct to you from day". Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made the limits of fasting the rising of the clear dawn; but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made clear in His obligation what most people are equal in knowing.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا تُباشِرُوهُنَّ وأنْتُمْ عاكِفُونَ في المَساجِدِ﴾ — the meaning of mubāshara here is intercourse. A man used to leave the mosque while in iʿtikāf, have intercourse, then return to the mosque. Iʿtikāf is that a man confines himself in a congregational mosque, worshipping in it; when he does that, he must not have intercourse, nor occupy himself except with what he cannot do without of his needs.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿تِلْكَ حُدُودُ اللَّهِ فَلا تَقْرَبُوها﴾ — the meaning of "اَلْحُدُودُ" (limits) is: what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has prevented from being contravened. The meaning of "اَلْحَدّادُ" in the language is the doorkeeper; everyone who prevents something is a "حَدّادٌ". Their saying "أحَدَّتِ المَرْأةُ عَلى زَوْجِها" means: she cut off adornment and refrained from it [in mourning for her husband]. "اَلْحَدِيدُ" (iron) was called "حَدِيدًا" only because by it one is protected from enemies. "حَدُّ الدّارِ" (the boundary of the house) is what prevents anything else from entering it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿كَذَلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ آياتِهِ لِلنّاسِ﴾, that is: like the explanation that has been mentioned; the meaning is: He makes clear to them what He has commanded them.

zajjaj:258-258.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ألَمْ تَرَ إلى الَّذِي حاجَّ إبْراهِيمَ في رَبِّهِ﴾: this is an expression by which the person addressed is brought to attend to something to be wondered at; its wording is that of a question. You say in ordinary speech: ”ألَمْ تَرَ إلى فُلانٍ صَنَعَ كَذا، وصَنَعَ كَذا؟“ ("have you not seen so-and-so, how he did this and did that?"). This is among the things made known to the Prophet ﷺ as a proof against the People of the Book and the polytheists of the Arabs, because it is a report that no one could know except one who came upon it by reading a book, or by the teaching of a teacher, or by revelation from Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. The Arabs among whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ grew up knew that he was unlettered (ummī), and that he had not been taught the Torah, the Gospel, or the reports of the prophets who had passed away; so no way remained by which these accounts could be known except revelation.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أنْ آتاهُ اللَّهُ المُلْكَ﴾ means: He gave the unbeliever kingship. This is what the exegetes hold, and on it the meaning is sound. Some said that the one to whom Allah gave kingship was Abraham, peace be upon him; they said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, does not give kingship to unbelievers. They said this only because of His mention, Mighty and Majestic is He, of ”آتاهُ المُلْكَ“; but Allah said: ﴿تُؤْتِي المُلْكَ مَن تَشاءُ وتَنْـزِعُ المُلْكَ مِمَّنْ تَشاءُ وتُعِزُّ مَن تَشاءُ وتُذِلُّ مَن تَشاءُ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 26]. So the interpretation of Allah's giving the unbeliever kingship is that it is a kind of the trial by which Allah tries His creation, and He knows best the aspect of wisdom in it. The proof that it was the unbeliever who had been made king is that he said ﴿أنا أُحْيِي وأُمِيتُ﴾, and that he summoned two men, killed one of them and released the other. Had he not been a king, and Abraham, peace be upon him, not a king, it would not have been possible for him to kill while Abraham was the king — he being the prophet, peace be upon him. As for the sense of his arguing against Abraham that he gives life and causes death, and Abraham's leaving off contradicting him on giving life and causing death: among the most effective ways of silencing opponents is to avoid prolixity and to argue with the silencing proof. For when Abraham said to him ﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْتِي بِالشَّمْسِ مِنَ المَشْرِقِ فَأْتِ بِها مِنَ المَغْرِبِ﴾, his answer, on the pattern of how he had answered the first question, would have been to say "then I will do that", and so his incapacity became evident; and in this was the silencing of the unbeliever. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿فَبُهِتَ الَّذِي كَفَرَ﴾, and its interpretation is: he was cut short and fell silent, bewildered. One says ”بُهِتَ الرَّجُلُ، يُبْهَتُ، بُهْتًا“ when he is cut short and bewildered; with this meaning one also says ”بَهِتَ الرَّجُلُ يَبْهَتُ“. And one says ”بَهَتُّ الرَّجُلَ، أبْهَتُهُ، بُهْتانًا“ when you confront him with a lie.

zajjaj:259-259.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أوْ كالَّذِي مَرَّ عَلى قَرْيَةٍ﴾: this speech is conjoined to the sense of the first speech, and the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: ”أرَأيْتَ كالَّذِي مَرَّ عَلى قَرْيَةٍ؟“ ("have you seen the like of the one who passed by a town?"). In the language a town is called ”قَرْيَةٌ“ because people gather in it; one says ”قَرَيْتُ الماءَ في الحَوْضِ“ when you have collected the water in the basin.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَهِيَ خاوِيَةٌ عَلى عُرُوشِها﴾: the meaning of ”خاوِيَةٌ“ is empty. As for ”عُرُوشِها“, Abū ʿUbayda said: they are the tents, that is, the dwellings of the Bedouin. Others than Abū ʿUbayda said: the meaning of ”وَهي خاوِيَةٌ عَلى عُرُوشِها“ is that its walls remained without roofs. One says ”خَوَتِ الدّارُ والمَدِينَةُ، تَخْوِي، خَواءً“ — with long final alif (mamdūd) — when it is empty of its inhabitants; one also says ”خَوِيَتْ“, but the [usual] speech is the first. Of a woman whose belly is empty after giving birth, and of a man whose belly is empty of food, one says ”قَدْ خَوِيَ، ويَخْوى، خَوًى“ — with short final alif (maqṣūr); and one may also say ”خَوى يَخْوِي“, but the first is better here.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أنّى يُحْيِي هَذِهِ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ مَوْتِها﴾ means: from where will Allah bring this to life after its death?! It has been said in the exegesis that he was a believer, and it has been said that he was an unbeliever. It cannot be denied that he may have been a believer who wished to increase in insight in his faith, so that he says: "I wish I knew how the dead will be raised!" — as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿رَبِّ أرِنِي كَيْفَ تُحْيِ المَوْتى﴾ [al-Baqara: 260]. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَأماتَهُ اللَّهُ مِائَةَ عامٍ ثُمَّ بَعَثَهُ﴾ means: then He brought him to life, because he is not raised up and does not move about except when he is alive.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿كَمْ لَبِثْتَ﴾ is read with the thāʾ pronounced distinctly and with the thāʾ assimilated into the tāʾ; it is assimilated only because the two points of articulation are close. The meaning of ﴿قالَ لَبِثْتُ يَوْمًا أوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ﴾ is that he had been made to die at the beginning of the day and was then raised a hundred years later at the end of the day, so he thought that the length of his stay was what lies between the beginning of the day and its end. So Allah informed him that he had stayed a hundred years, and showed him a sign of that in the decay of the bones of his donkey, showed him his food and drink unchanged, and showed him how He raises the bones and how they are clothed with flesh. So He said: ﴿فانْظُرْ إلى طَعامِكَ وشَرابِكَ لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ﴾. In ordinary speech it is permissible with the hāʾ retained and with the hāʾ dropped; its meaning is: the years have not changed it. Whoever says, regarding ”اَلسَّنَةُ“ (year), ”سانَهْتُ“, the hāʾ is part of the root of the word; and whoever says, regarding ”اَلسَّنَةُ“, ”سانَيْتُ“, the hāʾ has been added to show the vowel. The proper way of reading in any case is to retain it and to pause on it without continuing. So whoever makes it from ”سانَيْتُ“ may continue it if he wishes, or pause on it, according to whoever makes it from ”سانَهْتُ“ «[Translator's note: the sentence is so in the source and its wording is unclear; the sense appears to be that on the سانَيْتُ derivation one may read on without the hāʾ or pause with it, while on the سانَهْتُ derivation the hāʾ belongs to the root.]». As for whoever said that it is from ”تَغَيَّرَ“ (to change), from ”أسِنَ الطَّعامُ، يَأْسَنُ“ (the food went stale), that is a mistake. One of the grammarians said that it may be from the sense of changing, from your saying ”مِن حَمَإٍ مَسْنُونٍ“; the original according to him was ”لَمْ يَتَسَنَّنْ“, but he substituted yāʾ for the nūn, as [the poet] said:
تَقَضّى البازِي إذا البازِي كَشَرْ
(The falcon swooped down, when the falcon bared its beak.)
meaning ”تَقَضَّضَ“. But this is not of that kind, because ”مَسْنُونٍ“ means only "poured out along the course (sunna) of the way".
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وانْظُرْ إلى العِظامِ كَيْفَ نُنْشِزُها﴾ is read ”نُنْشِزُها“ with zāy, and ”نُنْشِرُها“ and ”نَنْشُرُها“ with rāʾ. Whoever reads ”نُنْشِزُها“, its meaning is: We make them, after their decay and lying still, rise up (nāshiza), one part rising towards another, that is, lifting up; ”اَلنَّشَزُ“ in the language is what is raised above the ground. Whoever reads ”نُنْشِرُها“ and ”نَنْشُرُها“, it is from ”أنْشَرَ اللَّهُ المَوْتى، ونَشَرَهم“ ("Allah raised the dead"); one may also say ”نَشَرَهُمُ اللَّهُ“, that is, He resurrected them, as He said: ﴿وَإلَيْهِ النُّشُورُ﴾ [al-Mulk: 15].
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَلَمّا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ قالَ أعْلَمُ أنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ means: when it became clear to him how the dead are brought to life, he said: I know that Allah has power over all things. If it is as has been said, that he was a believer, then the interpretation of his saying "I know that Allah has power over all things" is not that he did not know before he witnessed it; rather its interpretation is: I now know by witnessing what I used to know as something unseen. Whoever reads ”اِعْلَمْ أنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ“, its interpretation, when he reads it with jazm (as an imperative), is that he turns to himself and says: ”اِعْلَمْ أيُّها الإنْسانُ أنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ“ ("know, O man, that Allah has power over all things"). The nominative [أعْلَمُ] is as a statement.

zajjaj:224-224.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تَجْعَلُوا اللَّهَ عُرْضَةً لأيْمانِكم أنْ تَبَرُّوا وتَتَّقُوا﴾. The position of ”أنْ“ is accusative by the meaning of ”عُرْضَةً“. The meaning is: do not put forward the oath by Allah as an obstacle to your doing good. When ”في“ dropped, (the verb) passed through to the sense of obstruction (iʿtirāḍ), and so ”أنْ“ became accusative (manṣūb bi-nazʿ al-khāfiḍ, accusative by removal of the preposition). More than one of the grammarians said: its position may be genitive even though ”في“ has dropped, because omission (of the preposition) is customary with ”أنْ“: you say ”جِئْتُ لِأنْ تَضْرِبَ زَيْدًا“ and ”جِئْتُ أنْ تَضْرِبَ زَيْدًا“ (I came in order that you strike Zayd), the lām being omitted with ”أنْ“. But if you said ”جِئْتُ ضَرْبِ زَيْدٍ“, meaning ”لِضَرْبِ زَيْدٍ“, it would not be permissible as it is with ”أنْ“, because when ”أنْ“ is connected (with its verb) what follows it indicates the future; and the meaning is just as when you say ”جِئْتُكَ أنْ ضَرَبْتَ زَيْدًا“ and ”جِئْتُكَ أنْ تَضْرِبَ زَيْدًا“; therefore omission of the lām is permissible. Whereas when you say ”جِئْتُكَ ضَرْبَ زَيْدٍ“, the (word) ”ضَرْب“ does not indicate the sense of the future. The accusative for ”أنْ“ in this place is the choice of all the grammarians.
The meaning of the verse is that they used to excuse themselves from doing good on the grounds that they had sworn; so Allah made known that the sin lies only in persisting in abandoning goodness and piety, and that when an oath has been expiated, the wrongdoing in it is forgiven. So He said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لا يُؤاخِذُكُمُ اللَّهُ بِاللَّغْوِ في أيْمانِكم ولَكِنْ يُؤاخِذُكم بِما كَسَبَتْ قُلُوبُكم واللَّهُ غَفُورٌ حَلِيمٌ﴾ [al-Baqara: 225]. More than one view has been given on the meaning of ”اَللَّغْوِ“. Some of them said: its meaning is (saying) ”لا واللَّهِ“ (no, by Allah) and ”بَلى واللَّهِ“ (yes indeed, by Allah). It has also been said: the meaning of ”اَللَّغْوِ“ is ”اَلْإثْمِ“ (sin), so the meaning is: Allah will not take you to task for the sin in swearing if you expiate; it was called ”لَغْوٌ“ only because the sin falls away in it (becomes void) when the expiation takes place.

zajjaj:225-225.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَكِنْ يُؤاخِذُكم بِما كَسَبَتْ قُلُوبُكُمْ﴾, i.e. for your resolve not to do good and not to be pious, and to excuse yourselves in that by the fact that you have sworn. One says ”لَغَوْتُ، ألْغُو، لَغْوًا“, and ”لَغَوْتُ ألْغى، لَغْوًا“, like ”مَحَوْتُ، أمْحُو، مَحْوًا“ and ”أمْحى“; and one says ”لَغَيْتُ في الكَلامِ، ألْغى، لَغًى“ when I utter idle talk (laghw). Everything in speech in which there is no good, whether something in which one sins or something not needed, is laghw and laghan. Al-ʿAjjāj said:
عَنِ اللَّغا ورَفَثِ التَّكَلُّمِ
(…from idle talk and indecency of speech.)
The sum of oath-taking is that it is of four kinds. Two of them are those in which the jurists agree that expiation is obligatory, namely your saying ”واللَّهِ لا أفْعَلُ“ (by Allah, I will not do) or ”واللَّهِ لَأفْعَلَنَّ“ (by Allah, I will certainly do): in these two there is expiation when one prefers to go against what he swore upon, seeing something else better than it; in this there is expiation without doubt. And two in which most of the jurists see no expiation, namely your saying ”واللَّهِ ما قَدْ فَعَلْتُ“ (by Allah, I did not do it) when he did, or ”واللَّهِ لَقَدْ فَعَلْتُ“ (by Allah, I did it) when he did not. This is a lie he has reinforced with an oath, so he ought to seek Allah's forgiveness for it. This is the sum of what there is regarding the oath.
(Returning to ﴿أنْ تَبَرُّوا﴾:) it is also permissible that the position of ”أنْ“ be nominative, the meaning being: ”وَلا تَجْعَلُوا اللَّهَ عُرْضَةً لِأيْمانِكم أنْ تَبَرُّوا وتَتَّقُوا وتُصْلِحُوا أوْلى“, i.e. goodness and piety are more fitting, with ”أوْلى“ omitted, just as the omission of things occurs in the Quran because there is an indication of them in the speech. Resembling this is: ﴿طاعَةٌ وقَوْلٌ مَعْرُوفٌ﴾ [Muḥammad: 21], i.e. obedience and an honourable word are better. The accusative and the genitive for ”أنْ“ are the doctrine of the grammarians, and I know of none of them who mentioned this (nominative) view. We choose what they said, because it is good and because following (them) is preferable, even if something else is permissible.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ [al-Baqara: 224]. Its meaning in this place is: He hears your oaths and knows what you intend by them.

zajjaj:226-226.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِن نِسائِهِمْ تَرَبُّصُ أرْبَعَةِ أشْهُرٍ﴾. The meaning of ”يُؤْلُونَ“ is: they swear. Its meaning in this place is that a man would not want his wife, so he would swear never to approach her, yet would not like another man to marry her; so he would leave her neither unmarried nor having a husband. They used to do this in the Jāhiliyya and in Islam. So Allah made the term by which the man's intention regarding the woman becomes known — its furthest extent — the end of four months. When four months are completed and the man has not "returned" (yafiʾ) to his wife, i.e. has not come back to her, then his wife after the four months — according to the view of some of them — is separated from him irrevocably, whether he pronounced divorce with his tongue or not. Others said: after the four months he is required either to divorce or to return. One says ”آلَيْتُ، أُولِي، إيلاءً، وألِيَّةً، وأُلُوَّةً، وإلِوَّةً، وإيَلًا“ (I swore), and the kasra form is the least frequent of the dialectal forms. The meaning of tarabbuṣ in the language is waiting.
Those who argued that he must pronounce divorce argued from His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلاقَ فَإنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ [al-Baqara: 227], and they said: ”سَمِيعٌ“ indicates that it is the hearing of the divorce in this place. This is not impossible in the language; yet it may be that ”سَمِيعٌ“ is mentioned here only because of his oath, i.e. Allah has heard his oath and knows what he intended. Both ways are possible in the language.

zajjaj:260-260.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإذْ قالَ إبْراهِيمُ رَبِّ أرِنِي كَيْفَ تُحْيِ المَوْتى﴾: the position of ”إذْ“ is accusative; the meaning is: remember this story. His saying ”رَبِّ أرِنِي“: its original is ”أرْئِنِي“, but what is agreed upon in the speech of the Arabs and in the reading is dropping the hamza. ”أرْنِي“ is also permissible, and we have explained the dropping of this kasra earlier in the book. The position of ”كَيْفَ“ is accusative by His saying ﴿تُحْيِ المَوْتى﴾, that is: in what manner do You give life to the dead. Abraham, peace be upon him, was not doubting; but he had not witnessed the bringing to life of a dead person, and did not know how scattered, decayed and transformed bones are gathered together from widely separated places, so he wanted to know that by witnessing it. It is narrated in the exegesis that he passed by a carcass on the seashore: the fish were coming out of the sea and plucking at the flesh of the carcass, the birds were alighting on it and tearing at it, and the beasts of the land were eating from it. So he reflected on how what had been scattered of that carcass — having passed into the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky and the beasts of the land — would be gathered together and then return alive. So he asked Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, to show him how He gives life to the dead. Allah commanded him to take four birds; this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَصُرْهُنَّ إلَيْكَ﴾, which is also read ”فَصِرْهُنَّ إلَيْكَ“ — with ḍamma and with kasra. The philologists said: the meaning of ”صُرْهُنَّ“ is: incline them to you and gather them to you; most of them said this. Some of them said: ”صُرْهُنَّ إلَيْكَ“ means: cut them up. As for a parallel to ”صُرْهُنَّ“ meaning "incline them and gather them", it is the poet's saying:
؎وَجاءَتْ خِلْعَةٌ دَهْسٌ صَفايا ∗∗∗ يَصُورُ عُنُوقَها أحْوى زَنِيمُ
(There came choice ewes, dun-coloured and rich in milk, their young kids herded together by a dark ram with dewlaps.)
The meaning is that this dark ram turns the young of these sheep towards him. Whoever says ”صِرْتُ“ means "I cut", so the meaning is: "take four birds and ”صُرْهُنَّ“", that is, cut them up. ﴿ثُمَّ اجْعَلْ عَلى كُلِّ جَبَلٍ مِنهُنَّ جُزْءًا﴾: the meaning is: put on every mountain a part of each one of them. Abraham, peace be upon him, did that, then called them, and he saw the feathers hastening towards one another, and likewise the bones and the flesh.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واعْلَمْ أنَّ اللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ﴾: ”عَزِيزٌ“ means: nothing He wills is beyond Him; ”حَكِيمٌ“ in what He manages: He does nothing but what contains wisdom. So Abraham, peace be upon him, witnessed with his own eyes what he had known as something unseen, and learned how Allah does that. When Allah had related what contains the proof and the indication of His oneness and the clear proofs He gave the messengers, He urged to jihad, and declared that whoever opposes Him after these proofs has embarked on a grave error, and that whoever fights those who disbelieve after this proof has a great reward in his jihad and his spending in it; and that Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, has promised in Paradise ten times its like from jihad «[Translator's note: so in the source, «وَعَدَ في الجَنَّةِ عَشْرَ أمْثالِها مِنَ الجِهادِ»; the sense is perhaps that a good deed is generally rewarded tenfold, while spending in jihad is multiplied seven hundredfold.]», and has promised in jihad to multiply one by seven hundred times, because of the establishment of truth through tawḥīd that lies in it, and the great corruption that lies in unbelief. So He said: ﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ حَبَّةٍ أنْبَتَتْ سَبْعَ سَنابِلَ في كُلِّ سُنْبُلَةٍ مِائَةُ حَبَّةٍ واللَّهُ يُضاعِفُ لِمَن يَشاءُ واللَّهُ واسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ [al-Baqara: 261], that is: generous, His bounty of abundance not diminishing Him, knowing where He places it.

zajjaj:264-264.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تُبْطِلُوا صَدَقاتِكم بِالمَنِّ والأذى﴾: ”اَلْمَنُّ“ is that you remind [the recipient] of what you have given and count it [against him], as though you intended by it only to have it counted; and ”الأذى“ (injury) is that you reproach the one given to. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, made known that reminders of generosity and injury nullify charity, just as the spending of the hypocrite is nullified — he who gives without intending by that giving what is with Allah, but gives only to create the impression that he is a believer. And He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿فَمَثَلُهُ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوانٍ﴾; ”اَلصَّفْوانُ“ is the smooth rock, and likewise al-ṣafā.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿عَلَيْهِ تُرابٌ فَأصابَهُ وابِلٌ﴾: ”اَلْوابِلُ“ is rain with large drops. When this rain strikes the rock on which there is soil, none of the soil remains on it; and likewise the spending of the hypocrite and the spending of the one who reminds of his generosity and causes injury are nullified.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واللَّهُ لا يَهْدِي القَوْمَ الكافِرِينَ﴾ means: He does not make them rightly guided in their unbelief. It has also been said: He does not make their recompense for unbelief that He should guide them.

zajjaj:265-265.t:
Then Allah struck a parable for one who spends seeking what is with Allah and does not remind of his generosity or cause injury, saying: ﴿وَمَثَلُ الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهُمُ ابْتِغاءَ مَرْضاتِ اللَّهِ وتَثْبِيتًا مِن أنْفُسِهِمْ﴾, that is: in order to seek the pleasure of Allah. ”وَتَثْبِيتًا مِن أنْفُسِهِمْ“ means: they spend it affirming that it is among the things for which Allah rewards.
﴿كَمَثَلِ جَنَّةٍ بِرَبْوَةٍ﴾ — with fatḥa on the rāʾ; and ”بِرُبْوَةٍ“ with ḍamma, and ”بِرِبْوَةٍ“ with kasra, and ”بِرِباوَةٍ“, which is a fourth form. ”اَلرَّبْوَةُ“ is raised ground. ”اَلْجَنَّةُ“ is the garden; everything that grows, becomes dense and abundant, and whose parts cover one another, is a jannah. A raised place, when it has water to irrigate it, is more productive than low-lying ground. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, made known that the spending of these believers grows, just as the vegetation of this garden which is in a raised place grows. ﴿أصابَها وابِلٌ﴾: it is rain with large drops. ﴿فَآتَتْ أُكُلَها﴾ means: its fruit; it is also read ”أُكْلَها“, and the meaning is the same. ﴿ضِعْفَيْنِ﴾ means: twofold. ﴿فَإنْ لَمْ يُصِبْها وابِلٌ فَطَلٌّ﴾: ”اَلطَّلُّ“ is persistent rain with small drops, from which the gutters hardly run. The meaning of ﴿واللَّهُ بِما تَعْمَلُونَ بَصِيرٌ﴾ is: knowing; and when He knows it, He requites it. What ”فَطَلٌّ“ is in the nominative by is that it is in the sense of ”فَإنْ لَمْ يُصِبْها وابِلٌ فالَّذِي يُصِيبُها طَلٌّ“ ("if a downpour does not strike it, then what strikes it is a drizzle").

zajjaj:188-188.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا تَأْكُلُوا أمْوالَكم بَيْنَكم بِالباطِلِ﴾ — "تَأْكُلُوا" is jussive (majzūm) by "لا", because the prohibitive "لا" belongs exclusively to verbs, not nouns, and its effect on them is the jussive; for the nominative enters [imperfect verbs] through their occurring in the position of nouns, and the accusative enters them because the particle that makes them accusative resembles the one that makes nouns accusative, and after these two domains nothing remains in them except the jussive. The meaning of "بِالباطِلِ" is: through injustice.

﴿وَتُدْلُوا بِها إلى الحُكّامِ﴾, that is: you act according to what the outward judgement requires, and leave what you know to be the truth. The meaning of "تُدْلُوا" in the language: its origin is from "أدْلَيْتُ الدَّلْوَ" ("I let down the bucket") when you send it down to be filled, and "دَلَوْتُها" when you draw it up. The meaning of "أدْلى لِي فُلانٌ بِحُجَّتِهِ" is: he sent forth his argument and presented it as sound. So the meaning of "وَتُدْلُوا بِها إلى الحُكّامِ" is: you act according to what the presenting of the argument requires, and you betray the trust.

﴿لِتَأْكُلُوا فَرِيقًا مِن أمْوالِ النّاسِ بِالإثْمِ وأنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, that is: while you know that the argument is against you inwardly, even if the contrary appears outwardly.

The position of "وَتُدْلُوا" may be jussive or accusative. As for the jussive, it is by the prohibition, conjoined to "وَلا تَأْكُلُوا".
