It may be accusative in the way the wāw makes [a verb] accusative — which is what some grammarians call "al-ṣarf" (diversion) — its accusative being by an implied "أنْ"; the meaning is: do not combine consuming [wealth] unjustly with presenting [it] to the judges. We have explained this before this place.

zajjaj:189-189.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿يَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الأهِلَّةِ﴾ — the Prophet ﷺ had been asked about the crescent moon: about its being thin at its beginning, its growing large afterwards, and its returning thin like the old date-stalk. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made known that He made that so that people would know their times for their ḥajj, the waiting periods (ʿidad) of their women, and everything they want to know by the month, because this is easier for people than keeping count of days, and the one who calculates and the one who does not are equal in it.

The meaning of "اَلْهِلالُ" and its derivation is from their saying "اِسْتَهَلَّ الصَّبِيُّ" when the infant cries or shouts at birth; and it is as in their saying "أهَلَّ القَوْمُ بِالحَجِّ والعُمْرَةِ", that is: they raised their voices with the talbiya. It was called "هِلالٌ" only because when it is seen people raise their voices in mentioning it. One says "أُهِلَّ الهِلالُ" and "اسْتَهَلَّ" ("the crescent appeared"), but one does not say "أهَلَّ". One says "أهَلَلْنا", that is: we saw the crescent, and "أهْلَلْنا شَهْرَ كَذا وكَذا" when we have entered such-and-such a month.

Someone I trust among the transmitters of both the Basrans and the Kufans informed me of what I [now] mention concerning the names of the crescent and the descriptions of the nights in each month. First of all, the month was called "شَهْرٌ" only because of its being well known (shuhra) and clear; and it was called "هِلالٌ" for what we described of raising the voice in announcing it. People differed over its being called hilāl, for how many nights it is so called, and when it is called qamar (moon). Some said: it is called "هِلالٌ" for two nights of the month, and then it is not called "هِلالٌ" until it returns in the following month. Some said: it is called "هِلالٌ" for three nights, then it is called "قَمَرٌ". Some said: it is called "هِلالٌ" until it is "taḥjīr-ed", its taḥjīr being that it becomes rounded by a fine line; this is the view of al-Aṣmaʿī. Some said: it is called "هِلالٌ" until its light overpowers the blackness of the night; when its light overcomes the blackness of the night it is called "قَمَرٌ", and this happens only on the seventh night. My own view, and that of the majority, is that it is called "هِلالٌ" when two nights old, for on the third its light becomes evident.

The name of the moon is "اَلزِّبْرِقانُ", the name of its halo is "اَلْهالَةُ", and the name of its light is "اَلْفَخْتُ". Some of the people of language said: I do not know whether "اَلْفَخْتَ" is the name of its light or of its darkness, and [whether it is] the name of its darkness in reality. The name of its shade is "اَلسَّمَرُ", and for this reason those who converse at night are called "سُمّارٌ". One says "ضاءَ القَمَرُ" and "أضاءَ" ("the moon shone"), and one says "طَلَعَ القَمَرُ" ("the moon rose"), but one does not say "أضاءَتِ القَمَرُ" or "ضاءَتْ" (with the feminine).

Abū Isḥāq [al-Zajjāj] said: someone I trust related to me from al-Riyāshī, from Abū Zayd, and someone I trust also informed me from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, of what I mention in this section. Abū Zayd al-Anṣārī said: of the moon one night old it is said: "عَتَمَةٌ سُخَيْلَةٌ حَلَّ أهْلُها بِرُمَيْلَةٍ" (a little kid's evening-milking time; its people have alighted at a little sand-patch); two nights old: "حَدِيثُ أمَتَيْنِ، كَذِبٌ ومَيْنٌ" (the talk of two slave-girls: lies and falsehood) — Ibn al-Aʿrābī narrated it: "بِكَذِبٍ ومَيْنٍ" (with lies and falsehood); three nights old: "حَدِيثُ فَتَياتٍ غَيْرِ جَدِّ مُؤْتَلِفاتٍ" (the talk of girls not much in agreement). And it was said: "اِبْنُ ثَلاثٍ: قَلِيلُ اللِّباثِ" (three nights old: of short stay); and four nights old: "عَتَمَةٌ، رُبَعٌ، لا جائِعٌ ولا مُرْضِعٌ" (the evening-milking time of a young spring-born camel, neither hungry nor suckling). From Ibn al-Aʿrābī: "عَتَمَةُ أُمِّ الرُّبْعِ" (the evening-milking time of the mother of the spring-born calf). Five nights old: "حَدِيثٌ وأُنْسٌ" (conversation and companionship); Abū Zayd said: "عَشا خَلِفاتٍ قُعْسٍ" (the supper-time of pregnant camels with bowed backs). Six nights old: "سِرْوَيِتْ" «[Translator's note: so printed; apparently a corruption of "سِرْ وبِتْ" ("travel and pass the night")]». Seven nights old: "دُلْجَةُ الضَّبْعِ" (the night-journey of the hyena). Eight nights old: "قَمَرُ أضْحَيانِ" (a bright, radiant moon). Nine nights old: from Abū Zayd: "اِنْقَطَعَ الشِّسْعُ" (the sandal-strap broke); from another: "يُلْتَقَطُ فِيهِ الجَزْعُ" (onyx beads can be picked up by it). Ten nights old: "ثُلْثُ الشَّهْرِ" (a third of the month); from Abū Zayd and others: "مُحْنَقُ الفَجْرِ" (the one that vexes the dawn).

After the tenth, the Arabs did not speak of its description night by night as they did in these ten; rather they divided its description into ten parts, giving a description to every three nights. They said: three ghurar — some say ghurr — (the bright-faced); three shuhb (the grey-white); three buhr and bahr (the dazzling); three ʿushr (the tenth-nights) «[Translator's note: as printed]»; three bīḍ (the white); and three durʿ and duruʿ. The meaning of "اَلدُّرْعُ" is blackness of the forepart of a sheep and whiteness of its hindpart; they were called durʿ and duruʿ only because the moon is absent at their beginning, so the beginning of the night is adraʿ, since its beginning is black and what follows is lit. Three khuns, because the moon recedes (yankhanis) in them, that is: falls behind. Three duhm (the dark); they were called duhm only because they become dark until they turn deep black. Some said: three ḥanādis (pitch-dark). Three fuḥm, because the moon "yatafaḥḥam" in them, that is: rises at the end of the night. And three daʾdiyy, which are the last of the month; they are taken from "اَلدَّأْداءِ", which is a kind of gait in which camels hasten to move their hind legs to the place of their forelegs; so daʾdaʾa is the last movement of the legs, and likewise al-daʾdiyy is at the end of the month.

The plural of "هِلالٌ" is "أهِلَّةٌ" for both the small and the large number, because "فِعالٌ" is pluralised for the smallest number on "أفْعِلَةٌ", like "مِثالٌ" and "أمْثِلَةٌ", and "حِمارٌ" and "أحْمِرَةٌ"; and when it goes beyond [the range of] "أفْعِلَةٌ", it is pluralised on "فُعُلٌ", like "حُمُرٌ" and "مُثُلٌ". But they disliked "فُعُلٌ" with doubled [roots], as in "هُلُلٌ" and "خُلُلٌ", so they said "أهِلَّةٌ" and "أخِلَّةٌ", restricting themselves to the plural of the small number, just as they restricted themselves to that in words with wāw and yāʾ [as final radicals], such as "كِساءٌ" and "أكْسِيَةٌ", "رِداءٌ" and "أرْدِيَةٌ".

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلَيْسَ البِرُّ بِأنْ تَأْتُوا البُيُوتَ مِن ظُهُورِها ولَكِنَّ البِرَّ مَنِ اتَّقى﴾ — it was said that there were some people of Quraysh, and a group of Arabs with them, such that when a man of them went out for some need and did not accomplish it and it did not come easy to him, he returned and did not enter by the door of his house for a year, doing that as an evil omen. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made known to them that this is not righteousness; that is, persisting in keeping this custom is not righteousness. Most of the exegetes said: they were the Ḥums, who were some people of Quraysh, the Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa, Thaqīf and Khuzāʿa. When they entered iḥrām they would not make dried curd (aqiṭ), nor pluck camel-hair, nor clarify butter; and when one of them came out of iḥrām he would not enter by the door of his house. They were called "اَلْحُمْسَ" only because they were zealous (taḥammasū) in their religion, that is: they were rigorous. The people of language said: "اَلْحَماسَةُ" is intensity in anger and intensity in fighting, and "اَلْحَماسَةُ" in reality is intensity in everything. Al-ʿAjjāj said:

وَكَمْ قَطَعْنا مِن قِفافٍ حُمْسِ
(How many hard, rugged uplands have we crossed!)

That is: hard. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made known to them that their rigour in this iḥrām is not righteousness, and made known to them that righteousness is piety, and said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ البِرَّ مَنِ اتَّقى﴾; the meaning is: but righteousness is the righteousness of one who guards against contravening the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And He said: ﴿وَأْتُوا البُيُوتَ مِن أبْوابِها﴾; so Allah commanded them to abandon the custom of the Jāhiliyya in this zealotry.

zajjaj:228-228.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿والمُطَلَّقاتُ يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأنْفُسِهِنَّ ثَلاثَةَ قُرُوءٍ﴾. One says ”طَلَقَتِ المَرْأةُ طَلاقًا، فَهي طالِقٌ“ (the woman was divorced, so she is ṭāliq), and they have also reported ”طَلُقَتْ“. Some people claimed that the feminine tāʾ was omitted from ”طالِقَةٌ“ because it is for the feminine only, with no share in it for the masculine. This is worthless, because in the language there is a great deal in which masculine and feminine share and in which the hāʾ is not kept for the feminine, as in their saying ”بَعِيرٌ ضامِرٌ“ and ”ناقَةٌ ضامِرٌ“ (a lean he-camel / she-camel), ”بَعِيرٌ ساعِلٌ“ and ”ناقَةٌ ساعِلٌ“ (a coughing he-camel / she-camel), and this is more than can be counted. Sībawayh and his followers claimed that this occurs in the masculine form as an adjective for the feminine because the meaning is "a ṭāliq thing", and its true nature in their view is that it is by way of relation (nasab), as in their saying ”اِمْرَأةٌ مِذْكارٌ“ and ”رَجُلٌ مِذْكارٌ“, ”اِمْرَأةٌ مِئْناثٌ“ and ”رَجُلٌ مِئْناثٌ“, whose meaning is only "one who has male offspring" and "one who has female offspring"; likewise ”مُطْفِلٌ“ = one who has an infant; and likewise ”طالِقٌ“ means one who has (undergone) divorce. When you make it run on the verb, you say ”طالِقَةٌ“. Al-Aʿshā said:
؎أيا جارَتا بَيْنِي فَإنَّكِ طالِقَةْ ∗∗∗ كَذاكِ أُمُورُ النّاسِ غادٍ وطارِقَةْ
(O my wife, be parted from me, for you are divorced; such are people's affairs — some come in the morning and some by night.)
As for ”ثَلاثَةَ قُرُوءٍ“, the jurists and the authorities on the language have differed on its interpretation. We have mentioned in this book the sum of the jurists' view and the sum of the view of the authorities on the language. The people of Kufa say: al-iqrāʾ (sic) are the menstruations; and the people of the Ḥijāz and Mālik say: al-iqrāʾ are the states of purity. The argument of the people of Kufa that al-iqrāʾ, al-qirāʾ and al-qurūʾ are the menstruations is what is narrated «عَنْ أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ أنَّها اسْتَفْتَتْ لِفاطِمَةَ بِنْتِ أبِي حُبَيْشٍ، وكانَتْ مُسْتَحاضَةً، فَقالَ ﷺ ”تَنْتَظِرُ أيّامَ أقْرائِها، وتَغْتَسِلُ فِيما سِوى ذَلِكَ»“ (from Umm Salama, that she sought a ruling for Fāṭima bint Abī Ḥubaysh, who had chronic bleeding, and he ﷺ said: "She waits for the days of her aqrāʾ and washes in what is other than that"). This means that she is held back from prayer on the days of her menstruation and then washes at times other than the days of menstruation. In another report Fāṭima asked him, and he said: ”إذا أتى قُرْؤُكِ فَلا تُصَلِّي، فَإذا مَرَّ فَتَطَهَّرِي، وصَلِّي ما بَيْنَ القُرْءِ إلى القُرْءِ“ (when your qurʾ comes, do not pray; when it has passed, purify yourself and pray between one qurʾ and the next). This is the doctrine of the Kufans. What strengthens it from the doctrine of the authorities on the language is that al-Aṣmaʿī used to say: ”اَلْقُرْءُ: اَلْحَيْضُ“ (the qurʾ is menstruation), and one says ”أقَرَأتِ المَرْأةُ“ when the woman menstruates. Al-Kisāʾī and the readers (al-qurrāʾ) «[Translator's note: so in the text (والقُرّاءُ); possibly al-Farrāʾ is meant, here and in the next sentence.]» all said: ”أقَرَأتِ المَرْأةُ“ when she menstruates, so she is muqriʾ. The readers said: ”أقَرَأتِ الحاجَّةُ“ when (the need) is delayed. They recited, regarding ”اَلْقُرْءُ“ as menstruation — though it more resembles (the sense of) time:
لَهُ قُرُوءٌ كَقُرُوءِ الحائِضِ
(He has his periodic times, like the periods of a menstruating woman.)
This is the doctrine of the people of Kufa on al-iqrāʾ, and what the authorities on the language adduced that strengthens their doctrine. Al-Akhfash also said: ”أقَرَأتِ المَرْأةُ“ when she menstruates, and ”ما قَرَأتْ حَيْضَةً“ means: her womb has not held together a menstruation.
The people of the Ḥijāz said: al-aqrāʾ and al-qurūʾ are the same, the singular of both being ”قَرْءٌ“, like your saying ”فَرْعٌ“, and they are the states of purity. They argued for that from what is narrated from ʿĀʾisha, that she said: ”اَلْأقْراءُ: اَلْأطْهارُ“ (the aqrāʾ are the states of purity). This is the doctrine of Ibn ʿAmr «[Translator's note: so in the text; Ibn ʿUmar is probably meant.]», Mālik and the jurists of the people of Medina. What strengthens the doctrine of the people of Medina that al-aqrāʾ are the states of purity is the saying of al-Aʿshā:
؎مُوَرِّثَةً مالًا وفي الأصْلِ رِفْعَةً ∗∗∗ لِما ضاعَ فِيها مِن قُرُوءِ نِسائِكا
(…bequeathing wealth, and in lineage high rank, for the qurūʾ of your wives that were wasted in it.)
What was wasted here is the states of purity, not the menstruations. There is another doctrine in this, namely that the qurʾ is purity and the qurʾ is menstruation. Abū ʿUbayda said: "The qurʾ fits both menstruation and purity," and he said: "I think it is from ”أقْرَأتِ النُّجُومُ“, when the stars set." Someone I trust informed me, tracing it back to Yūnus, that al-iqrāʾ in his view fits both menstruation and purity. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ mentioned that the qurʾ is the (appointed) time, and it fits menstruation and fits purity; one says ”هَذا قارِئُ الرِّياحِ“ for the time of the winds' blowing. The authorities on the language recited:
؎شَنِئَتِ العُقْرَ عُقْرَ بَنِي شُلَيْلٍ ∗∗∗ إذا هَبَّتْ لِقارِيها الرِّياحُ
(I hated the ʿuqr, the dwelling of Banū Shulayl, when the winds blow at their appointed time.)
i.e. at the time of their blowing and the severity of their cold. One says ”ما قَرَأتِ النّاقَةُ سَلًا قَطُّ“, i.e. her womb has never held together an offspring. ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm said:
؎تُرِيكَ إذا دَخَلْتَ عَلى خَلاءٍ ∗∗∗ وقَدْ أمِنَتْ عُيُونَ الكاشِحِينا
؎ذِراعَيْ عَيْطَلٍ أدْماءَ بِكْرٍ ∗∗∗ هَجِينِ اللَّوْنِ لَمْ تَقْرَأْ جَنِينا
(She shows you, when you come upon her in privacy and she feels safe from the eyes of the hostile, / the forearms of a long-necked, fair-skinned young she-camel, of pure white colour, whose womb has never held a foetus.)
Most of the authorities on the language hold that (it means) she has never gathered an offspring in her womb. Quṭrub also mentioned this view, and added regarding ”لَمْ تَقْرَأْ جَنِينا“: i.e. she has not cast it out gathered together. This is all that the jurists and the authorities on the language have said on the qurʾ.
My own view is that the qurʾ in the language is gathering, and that their saying ”قَرَيْتُ الماءَ في الحَوْضِ“ (I collected the water in the basin) is from this, even though the (yāʾ form) has become fixed for water; it means "I gathered it". Your saying ”قَرَأْتُ القُرْآنَ“ means: I uttered it gathered together; and ”اَلْقِرْدُ يُقْرِئُ“ (the monkey yuqriʾ), i.e. it gathers what it eats in its cheek-pouch. So ”اَلْقُرْءُ“ is only the gathering of the blood in the body, and that happens only during purity; and its gathering may also be in the womb. Both are good, and this does not depart from the doctrines of the jurists; rather it is the verification of both doctrines. ”اَلْمَقْرَأةُ“ is the basin in which water is "qaraʾ-ed", i.e. gathered; and ”اَلْمَقْرَأُ“ is the vessel in which the guest is entertained (yuqraʾ).
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا يَحِلُّ لَهُنَّ أنْ يَكْتُمْنَ ما خَلَقَ اللَّهُ في أرْحامِهِنَّ﴾. It has been said regarding it: it is not lawful for them to conceal the matter of the child, because if they do that, they only aim at attaching it to someone other than its father. Some said: it is the menstruation. But it more resembles the child, because "what Allah has created in their wombs" points more to the child, since Allah, Majestic and Mighty is He, said: ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي يُصَوِّرُكم في الأرْحامِ كَيْفَ يَشاءُ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 6], and He said: ﴿ثُمَّ خَلَقْنا النُّطْفَةَ عَلَقَةً فَخَلَقْنا العَلَقَةَ مُضْغَةً فَخَلَقْنا المُضْغَةَ عِظامًا﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 14], thus describing the creation of the child.
As for the meaning of ﴿إنْ كُنَّ يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ﴾, its interpretation is: if they believe in Allah and in what He has threatened and warned of, of His punishment for the people of grave sins, then let them not conceal — just as you say to a man who does wrong: "If you are a believer, do not do wrong." It is not that he says this to him permitting wrongdoing to a non-believer; rather the meaning is: if you are a believer, your faith ought to restrain you from wronging me.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَبُعُولَتُهُنَّ أحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ في ذَلِكَ﴾. ”بُعُولَةٌ“ is the plural of ”بَعْلٌ“ (husband), like ”ذَكَرٌ“ / ”ذُكُورَةٌ“; and ”عَمٌّ“ / ”عُمُومَةٌ“ resembles ”بَعْلٌ“ / ”بُعُولَةٌ“ more closely. One also says in the plural of ”ذَكَرٌ“: ”ذِكارَةٌ“, and of ”حَجَرٌ“: ”حِجارَةٌ“. This hāʾ is only an addition reinforcing the sense of the femininity of the group; but you insert it only in the places the authorities on the language have transmitted: you do not say ”كُعُوبَةٌ“ for ”كَعْبٌ“ nor ”كِلابَةٌ“ for ”كَلْبٌ“, because the analogy in these things is known. We have explained much of what is in it earlier in the book. The meaning of ”في ذَلِكَ“ is: in the term during which they were commanded to wait. So the husbands, before the expiry of the three qurūʾ, have more right to take them back, if they take them back by way of setting things right — do you not see His saying: ﴿إنْ أرادُوا إصْلاحًا﴾? And the meaning of His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلَهُنَّ مِثْلُ الَّذِي عَلَيْهِنَّ بِالمَعْرُوفِ﴾ is: women have (rights) like what is upon them, according to what Allah commanded of the man's right over the woman; and that is the meaning of ”بِالمَعْرُوفِ“.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلِلرِّجالِ عَلَيْهِنَّ دَرَجَةٌ﴾. Its meaning is: an increase over what the women have against them, as He the Exalted said: ﴿الرِّجالُ قَوّامُونَ عَلى النِّساءِ بِما فَضَّلَ اللَّهُ بَعْضَهم عَلى بَعْضٍ وبِما أنْفَقُوا مِن أمْوالِهِمْ﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 34]. The meaning is that the woman obtains pleasure from the man just as the man does, and he has the superiority through his maintenance of her and his taking charge of what is good for her.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واللَّهُ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ﴾. Its meaning is: a King who judges as He wills and tests with what He loves, except that this is only ever with consummate wisdom; so He is Mighty, Wise in what He has prescribed for you of that.

zajjaj:190-190.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَقاتِلُوا في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ الَّذِينَ يُقاتِلُونَكُمْ﴾ — they said in its exegesis: fight the people of Mecca. Some said: this was the first obligation of jihād, then it was abrogated by: ﴿وَقاتِلُوا المُشْرِكِينَ كافَّةً كَما يُقاتِلُونَكم كافَّةً﴾ [al-Tawba: 36].

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا تَعْتَدُوا﴾, that is: do not do wrong; iʿtidāʾ (transgression) is exceeding what is right. Two views have been given in its exegesis. It was said: "وَلا تَعْتَدُوا": do not fight anyone other than those you have been commanded to fight, and do not kill others besides them. And it was said: "وَلا تَعْتَدُوا", that is: do not go beyond [them] to killing women and children.

zajjaj:191-191.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿واقْتُلُوهم حَيْثُ ثَقِفْتُمُوهُمْ﴾, that is: wherever you find them. One says: "ثَقِفْتُهُ، أثْقَفُهُ، ثَقْفًا، وثَقافَةً" ("I came upon him"), and one says: "رَجُلٌ ثَقِفٌ، لَقِفٌ" ("a man quick to grasp and catch"). The meaning of the verse is: do not refrain from killing them in the Sanctuary (al-ḥaram) or elsewhere.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿والفِتْنَةُ أشَدُّ مِنَ القَتْلِ﴾, that is: their disbelief in these places is worse than killing.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا تُقاتِلُوهم عِنْدَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ حَتّى يُقاتِلُوكم فِيهِ﴾ — they had been forbidden to initiate killing or fighting against them until the polytheists «[Translator's note: the source has a stray page marker "٩٨]" at this point]» initiated it. It is also read: "وَلا تَقْتُلُوهم عِنْدَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ حَتّى يَقْتُلُوكم فِيهِ" ("do not kill them at the Sacred Mosque until they kill [some of] you in it"), that is: do not begin killing them until they begin it against you. "وَلا تَقْتُلُوهم" is permissible even if the killing falls on some and not others, because in the language it is permissible to say "قَتَلْتُ القَوْمَ" ("I killed the people") when only some of them were killed, provided there is in the speech an indication of the speaker's intent.

zajjaj:193-193.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَقاتِلُوهم حَتّى لا تَكُونَ فِتْنَةٌ﴾ — this is a command from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that every disbeliever be fought, because the meaning of fitna here is disbelief.

zajjaj:194-194.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿الشَّهْرُ الحَرامُ بِالشَّهْرِ الحَرامِ﴾ — "اَلشَّهْرُ" is nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject), and its khabar (predicate) is "بِالشَّهْرِ الحَرامِ"; its meaning is: fighting in the sacred month. It is narrated that the polytheists asked the Prophet ﷺ about the sacred month: is there fighting in it? So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down that killing in it is grave, that is: great in sin. They asked only to take the Muslims by surprise: if they knew that [the Muslims] had not been commanded to fight them, they would fight them. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made known to them that fighting in it is forbidden unless the polytheists initiate fighting in it, in which case the Muslims fight them. So the meaning of His saying "اَلشَّهْرُ الحَرامُ" is: fighting in the sacred month — that is, in the sacred month — for [fighting in] the sacred month. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made known that these sanctities are [subject to] retaliation (qiṣāṣ), that is: [violating them] is not permissible for the Muslims except as retaliation.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فَمَنِ اعْتَدى عَلَيْكُمْ﴾, that is: whoever does wrong and fights has transgressed, so transgress against him in the like of what he transgressed against you. The second was called "اِعْتِداءً" (transgression) because it is the requital of a transgression, so it was called by the like of its name, since the form of the two acts is one, even though one of them is obedience and the other disobedience. The Arabs say: "ظَلَمَنِي فُلانٌ فَظَلَمْتُهُ" ("so-and-so wronged me, so I wronged him"), that is: I requited him for his wrong; and "جَهِلَ عَلَيَّ فَجَهِلْتُ عَلَيْهِ" ("he acted foolishly against me, so I acted foolishly against him"), that is: I requited him for his foolishness. The poet said:

ألا لا يَجْهَلَنْ أحَدٌ عَلَيْنا ∗∗∗ فَنَجْهَلَ فَوْقَ جَهْلِ الجاهِلِينا
(Let no one act rashly against us, lest we act rashly beyond the rashness of the rash.)

That is: lest we repay the rashness with more than its measure. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿وَمَكَرُوا ومَكَرَ اللَّهُ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 54], and He said: ﴿فَيَسْخَرُونَ مِنهم سَخِرَ اللَّهُ مِنهُمْ﴾ [al-Tawba: 79]: He made the name of His requital of them "plotting" (makr), just as they plotted, and made the name of His requital of them for their mockery "mockery"; and likewise: ﴿فَمَنِ اعْتَدى عَلَيْكم فاعْتَدُوا عَلَيْهِ﴾.

zajjaj:195-195.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَأنْفِقُوا في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: in jihād in the way of Allah. Everything good that Allah has commanded is of the way of Allah, that is: of the path to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because "اَلسَّبِيلُ" in the language is the path; it is used more for jihād only because it is the path in which fighting takes place for the sake of the bond of religion.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلا تُلْقُوا بِأيْدِيكم إلى التَّهْلُكَةِ﴾ — the origin of "بِأيْدِيكم" is "بِأيْدِيِكم" with kasra on the yāʾ; but the kasra does not remain on the yāʾ when what precedes it has kasra, because of the heaviness of kasra on yāʾ.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿إلى التَّهْلُكَةِ﴾ — its meaning is: to destruction. One says: "هَلَكَ الرَّجُلُ، يَهْلَكُ، هَلاكًا، وهُلْكًا، وتَهْلُكَةً، وتَهْلِكَةً" ("the man perished"); "تَهْلُكَةٌ" is a noun. Its meaning is: if you do not spend in the way of Allah you will perish, that is: you will disobey Allah and so perish. It may also be: you will perish through strengthening your enemy against you; and Allah knows best.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَأحْسِنُوا إنَّ اللَّهَ يُحِبُّ المُحْسِنِينَ﴾, that is: spend in the way of Allah; whoever spends in the way of Allah is a doer of good (muḥsin).

zajjaj:266-266.t:
His saying, exalted be His praise: ﴿أيَوَدُّ أحَدُكم أنْ تَكُونَ لَهُ جَنَّةٌ مِن نَخِيلٍ وأعْنابٍ﴾: this is a parable Allah struck for them concerning the Hereafter. He made known to them that their need for righteous deeds is like the need of this old man who has weak offspring: if his garden burns while he is old and has weak offspring, he is left stranded. Likewise one who has no deed in the Hereafter to bring him to Paradise: his regret in the Hereafter — with the immensity of regret there — is like the regret of this old man left stranded in this world.
The meaning of ﴿فَأصابَها إعْصارٌ فِيهِ نارٌ﴾: ”اَلْإعْصارُ“ is the wind that blows up from the ground like a column towards the sky, which people call ”اَلزَّوْبَعَةَ“ (the whirlwind). It is a violent wind; it is not called iʿṣār until it blows violently. The poet said:
؎إنْ كُنْتَ رِيحًا فَقَدْ لاقَيْتَ إعْصارا
(If you are a wind, you have met a whirlwind.)
The meaning of «كَذَلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمُ الآياتِ» is: like this clarification which has been made clear — of charity, jihad, the story of Abraham, peace be upon him, the one who passed by a town, and all the preceding verses — that is, like the clarification of these stories Allah makes clear to you the signs, that is, the marks and indications you need in the matter of His oneness, the confirmation of the messages of His messengers, and His reward and punishment, ﴿لَعَلَّكم تَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾.

zajjaj:267-267.t:
His saying, blessed be His name: ﴿أنْفِقُوا مِن طَيِّباتِ ما كَسَبْتُمْ ومِمّا أخْرَجْنا لَكم مِنَ الأرْضِ﴾: the meaning is: spend from the good part of what you have earned from trade, from silver and gold coin, and likewise from the good part of the fruits. The meaning of ”أنْفِقُوا“ is: give in charity. Some people used to bring poor-quality fruit as charity. It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he commanded the collectors not to assess (yukharraṣ) the juʿrūr and the miʿā al-fāra «[Translator's note: two poor varieties of dates; so in the source, «مِعى الفارَّةِ», usually given as «مِعى الفَأْرَةِ», "mouse-gut".]»,
because they are among the poor kinds of date-palm; so he commanded that they not be assessed against them, so that they would not use them as an excuse in charity.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا تَيَمَّمُوا الخَبِيثَ مِنهُ تُنْفِقُونَ﴾ means: do not aim at the poor-quality part of wealth and fruits and give it in charity, while you know that you would not take it yourselves except by shutting your eyes to it.
The meaning of ﴿وَلَسْتُمْ بِآخِذِيهِ إلا أنْ تُغْمِضُوا فِيهِ﴾: He says: you would not take it except at a loss, so how can you give it in charity?! His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿واعْلَمُوا أنَّ اللَّهَ غَنِيٌّ حَمِيدٌ﴾ means: He did not command you to give charity out of need, but in order to test you; and He is praiseworthy for that and for all His blessings. One says ”قَدْ غَنِيَ زَيْدٌ، يَغْنى، غِنًى“ — with short final alif (maqṣūr) — when he is free of need; and ”قَدْ غَنِيَ القَوْمُ“ when they have settled in a place that shelters them, and the place where they settle is a ”مَغْنًى“. And ”قَدْ غَنّى فُلانٌ غِناءً“ when he goes to great lengths in musical modulation in reciting, until the poetry needs nothing added to its melody. And ”قَدْ غَنِيَتِ المَرْأةُ غُنْيانًا“; Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm said:
؎أجَدَّ بِعُمْرَةٍ غُنْيانُها ∗∗∗ فَتَهْجُرُ أمْ شَأْنُنا شَأْنُها
(Has ʿAmra's self-sufficiency become earnest, so that she shuns us, or is our affair still her affair?)
”غُنْيانُها“ means her self-sufficiency. ”اَلْغَوانِي“ are women; it is said that they are called ”غَوانِيَ“ because they are made self-sufficient by their beauty, and it is said by their husbands.

zajjaj:268-268.t:
His saying, Majestic and Exalted is He: ﴿الشَّيْطانُ يَعِدُكُمُ الفَقْرَ﴾: one says both ”اَلْفَقْرُ“ and ”اَلْفَقَرُ“. The meaning is that he urges you to pay poor-quality wealth in charity, making you fear poverty if you give the good. The meaning of ”يَعِدُكُمُ الفَقْرَ“ is "he promises you with poverty", but the bāʾ was omitted and the verb reached [its object] directly and put it in the accusative, as the poet said:
؎أمَرْتُكَ الخَيْرَ فافْعَلْ ما أُمِرْتَ بِهِ ∗∗∗ فَقَدْ تَرَكْتُكَ ذا مالٍ وذا نَشَبِ
(I commanded you [to do] good, so do what you were commanded, for I have left you a man of wealth and property.)
One says ”وَعَدْتُهُ، أعِدُهُ، وعْدًا، وعِدَةً، ومَوْعِدًا، ومَوْعِدَةً، ومَوْعُودًا، ومَوْعُودَةً“. The meaning of ﴿وَيَأْمُرُكم بِالفَحْشاءِ﴾ is: [he commands you] not to give charity, so that you sever ties with one another. The meaning of ﴿واللَّهُ يَعِدُكم مَغْفِرَةً مِنهُ وفَضْلا﴾ is: He promises you that He will requite your charity with forgiveness, and He promises you that He will replace it for you. The meaning of ﴿واللَّهُ واسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾: ”واسِعٌ“ — He gives out of abundance; and ”عَلِيمٌ“ — He knows where He places that, and knows the unseen and the seen.

zajjaj:269-269.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يُؤْتِي الحِكْمَةَ مَن يَشاءُ﴾: the meaning of ”يُؤْتِي“ is "gives". As for ”اَلْحِكْمَةُ“, there are two views on it. Some said: it is prophethood. And it is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd that wisdom is the Qurʾān — and the Qurʾān suffices as wisdom, because through it the community became learned after ignorance, and it is a link to every knowledge that brings one near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and a means to His mercy. That is why Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَمَن يُؤْتَ الحِكْمَةَ فَقَدْ أُوتِيَ خَيْرًا كَثِيرًا﴾, that is: he has been given all knowledge and what leads to the mercy of Allah. ”يُؤْتَ“ is jussive by ”مَن“, and the apodosis (jawāb) is ”فَقَدْ أُوتِيَ خَيْرًا كَثِيرًا“. The meaning of ﴿وَما يَذَّكَّرُ إلا أُولُو الألْبابِ﴾ is: none reflects with a reflection by which he takes heed of the verses of the Qurʾān that have been related except those of understanding (ulū al-albāb), that is, possessors of intellect. The singular of ”اَلْألْبابُ“ is ”لُبٌّ“; one says ”قَدْ لَبِبْتَ يا رَجُلُ“ ("you have become intelligent, man") and ”أنْتَ تَلَبُّ، لَبابَةً، ولُبًّا“. I read with Muḥammad ibn Yazīd [al-Mubarrad], from Yūnus: ”لَبُبْتُ، لَبابَةً“; there is no doubled verb on the pattern ”فَعُلْتُ“ other than this, and no one but Yūnus transmitted it. I asked [scholars] other than the Basrans about it, and they did not know it.

zajjaj:270-270.t:
His saying, Majestic and Mighty is He: ﴿وَما أنْفَقْتُمْ مِن نَفَقَةٍ أوْ نَذَرْتُمْ مِن نَذْرٍ فَإنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُهُ﴾ means: whatever you have given in charity of what is obligatory, because it is in the context of the charity of zakāt, which is the obligation; and ”اَلنَّذْرُ“ (the vow) is the voluntary act — everything a person intends to do voluntarily is a nadhr.
﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُهُ﴾ means: it is not hidden from Him, so He requites it, as He, exalted be His praise, said: ﴿فَمَن يَعْمَلْ مِثْقالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًا يَرَهُ﴾ [al-Zalzala: 7]. One says ”نَذَرْتُ النَّذْرَ، أنْذِرُهُ، وأنْذُرُهُ“, and the plural is ”اَلنُّذُورُ“. And ”أنْذَرْتُ القَوْمَ“ when I informed them and warned them — ”إنْذارًا، ونَذِيرًا، ونَذَرًا“. Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿فَسَتَعْلَمُونَ كَيْفَ نَذِيرِ﴾ [al-Mulk: 17], and He, exalted be His praise, said: ﴿فَكَيْفَ كانَ عَذابِي ونُذُرِ﴾ [al-Qamar: 16]. ”اَلنُّذُرُ“ is like ”اَلنُّكُرُ“, and ”اَلنَّذِيرُ“ is like ”اَلنَّكِيرُ“.

zajjaj:271-271.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنْ تُبْدُوا الصَّدَقاتِ فَنِعِمّا هِيَ﴾: the meaning of ”إنْ تُبْدُوا“ is "if you show openly". One says ”بَدا الشَّيْءُ، يَبْدُو“ when it appears, and ”أبْدَيْتُهُ أنا، إبْداءً“ when I show it; and ”بَدا لِي بُداءً“ when my opinion changes from what it was. ”تُبْدُوا“ is jussive by ”إنْ“, and His saying ”فَنِعِمّا هي“ is the apodosis (jawāb). Abū ʿUbayd transmitted that Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim and Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ read ”فَنِعْمّا هي“, with kasra on the nūn and the ʿayn and a doubled mīm «[Translator's note: so in the source; the vowelling «نِعْمّا» shows sukūn on the ʿayn, which conflicts with the description "kasra on the ʿayn". The discussion below suggests a reading with a quiescent ʿayn is meant.]». And it is narrated that Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb, al-Ashmas «[Translator's note: so in the source, «الأشْمَسَ»; probably a slip for al-Aʿmash.]», Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read ”فَنَعِمّا هي“, with fatḥa on the nūn and kasra on the ʿayn. Abū ʿUbayd mentioned that it is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said to Ibn al-ʿĀṣ: «”نَعْمّا بِالمالِ الصّالِحِ لِلرَّجُلِ الصّالِحِ“» ("how excellent is righteous wealth for a righteous man"), and Abū ʿUbayd mentioned that he prefers this reading because of this narration. I do not think the ḥadīth scholars recorded this accurately, nor is this reading at all permissible according to the Basran grammarians, because it involves combining two sukūns without a letter of prolongation and softness (madd wa-līn). As for what we have read of the reading (ḥarf) of ʿĀṣim and the transmission of Abū ʿAmr, ”فَنِعِمّا هي“, with kasra on the nūn and the ʿayn, this is excellent and fully correct, because here the ʿayn and the nūn have kasra. Likewise the reading of the people of Kufa, ”نَعِمّا هي“, is good, because the original of ”نِعْمَ“ is ”نَعِمَ“, and ”نِعِمَ“.
”نِعْمَ“ has three dialectal forms. With assimilation of the mīm, ”نِعْمّا هي“ is not permissible. ”ما“ has the sense of ”اَلشَّيْءُ“ (the thing); the Basrans held that ”نِعِمّا هي“ means ”نِعْمَ الشَّيْءُ هِيَ“ ("an excellent thing it is"). We have explained this earlier.
The meaning of ﴿وَإنْ تُخْفُوها وتُؤْتُوها الفُقَراءَ فَهو خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾: this was in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when concealment in paying zakāt was better; but today people think ill [of one another], so making zakāt public is better. As for voluntary charity, concealing it is better, because it is a stronger indication that one intends Allah alone by it. One says ”أخْفَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ إخْفاءً“ when I have concealed it, and ”خَفِيَ خَفاءً“ when it is concealed; and ”خَفَيْتُهُ أخْفِيهِ خَفْيًا“ when I have brought it to light. The people of Medina call the grave-robber ”اَلْمُخْتَفِي“. The poet said, concerning ”خَفَيْتُهُ“ in the sense of "I brought it to light":
؎فَإنْ تَدْفِنُوا الدّاءَ لا نَخْفِهِ ∗∗∗ وإنْ تَبْعَثُوا الحَرْبَ لا نَقْعُدِ
(If you bury the malady, we will not bring it to light; and if you stir up war, we will not sit idle.)

zajjaj:229-229.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الطَّلاقُ مَرَّتانِ﴾. ”اَلطَّلاقُ“ is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and ”مَرَّتانِ“ is the khabar (predicate). The meaning is: the divorce in which you retain the right of taking back is twice. This is indicated by ﴿فَإمْساكٌ بِمَعْرُوفٍ﴾; the meaning is: then what is incumbent upon you is retaining in an honourable manner or releasing with kindness. If the wording had been ”فَإمْساكًا بِمَعْرُوفٍ“ it would be permissible, on the sense ”فَأمْسِكُوهُنَّ إمْساكًا بِمَعْرُوفٍ“ (then retain them with an honourable retaining), as He said, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَأمْسِكُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ أوْ سَرِّحُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ﴾ [al-Baqara: 231]. The meaning of ”بِمَعْرُوفٍ“ is: with what is recognised as upholding what is right in retaining the woman.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا يَحِلُّ لَكم أنْ تَأْخُذُوا مِمّا آتَيْتُمُوهُنَّ شَيْئًا﴾, i.e. of what you have given them, of dower and other things.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إلا أنْ يَخافا ألا يُقِيما حُدُودَ اللَّهِ﴾. It has been recited ”يَخافا“ and ”يُخافا“, with fatḥa and with ḍamma. Abū ʿUbayda and others said: the meaning of ”إلّا أنْ يَخافا“ is "unless they are certain". The real sense of His saying ”إلّا أنْ يَخافا ألّا يُقِيما حُدُودَ اللَّهِ“ is that what predominates for them and in their own view, given the causes of estrangement that have appeared between them, is the fear that they will not uphold the limits of Allah. The meaning of ”حُدُودَ اللَّهِ“ is: what Allah, Majestic and Mighty is He, has set as limits, which it is not permissible to overstep to something else. The origin of ”اَلْحَدُّ“ in the language is prevention: one says ”حَدَدْتُ الدّارَ“ and ”حَدَدْتُ حُدُودَ الدّارِ“, i.e. I built the places that prevent others from entering it. ”حَدَدْتُ الرَّجُلَ“ means: I carried out the ḥadd punishment on him; and the ”اَلْحَدُّ“ is that by which people are prevented from entering into what brings them harm and punishment. One says ”أحَدَّتِ المَرْأةُ عَلى زَوْجِها“ and ”حَدَّتْ، فَهي حادٌّ، ومُحِدٌّ“ when a woman abstains from adornment (in mourning for her husband); ”أحْدَدْتُ إلَيْهِ النَّظَرَ“ when I withhold my gaze from anything else and turn it wholly to him; and ”أحْدَدْتُ السِّكِّينَ إحْدادًا“ (I sharpened the knife). The poet said:
؎إنَّ العِبادِيَّ أحَدَّ فَأْسَهُ ∗∗∗ فَعادَ حَدُّ فَأْسِهِ بِرَأْسِهِ
(The ʿIbādī sharpened his axe, and the edge of his axe came back upon his own head.)
Iron is called ”حَدِيدٌ“ only because it is the most protective thing by which one protects oneself. The Arabs call the chamberlain, the doorkeeper and the jailer ”اَلْحَدّادُ“; he is called ”حَدّادٌ“ only because he prevents whoever would enter and whoever would leave. And the saying of al-Aʿshā:
؎فَقُمْنا ولَمّا يَصِحْ دِيكُنا ∗∗∗ إلى خَمْرَةٍ عِنْدَ حَدّادِها
(We rose, before our cock had crowed, to a wine kept by its warden.)
i.e. with its owner, who withholds it except on the terms he wishes. The meaning of ﴿فَلا تَعْتَدُوها﴾ is: do not overstep them.

zajjaj:230-230.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَإنْ طَلَّقَها فَلا تَحِلُّ لَهُ مِن بَعْدُ حَتّى تَنْكِحَ زَوْجًا غَيْرَهُ﴾, i.e. if he divorces her the third time — because the two have already been mentioned — then she is not lawful for him until she marries a husband other than him. Allah did that because of His knowledge of how hard it is for a man that the woman should marry (another); so He forbade him to marry (her) after the three, so that they would not hasten to divorce, and would act with deliberation.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أمْرًا﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1] indicates what we have said.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَإنْ طَلَّقَها فَلا جُناحَ عَلَيْهِما أنْ يَتَراجَعا﴾, i.e. if the second husband divorces her, then there is no sin upon her and upon the first husband in returning to one another. The position of ”أنْ“ is accusative; the meaning is: they do not sin in returning to one another; when ”في“ dropped, the sense of the verb reached (the clause) directly, and so it became accusative. Al-Khalīl permits the position of ”أنْ“ to be genitive, on the dropping of ”في“ while it is still intended in the speech; and al-Kisāʾī said likewise. What the two of them said is correct, because omission occurs with ”أنْ“, and its being made a connected particle (with its ṣila) is a compensation for what was omitted. Do you not see that if you said ”لا جُناحَ عَلَيْهِما الرُّجُوعُ“ it would not be sound? Omission with ”أنْ“ is acceptable; for this reason al-Khalīl and others permitted it to be in the position of the genitive, with ”في“ intended. The meaning of ﴿إنْ ظَنّا أنْ يُقِيما حُدُودَ اللَّهِ﴾ is: if what predominates for them is that they will uphold the limits of Allah.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَتِلْكَ حُدُودُ اللَّهِ يُبَيِّنُها﴾. It is also recited ”نُبَيِّنُها“ — both with yāʾ and with nūn. ﴿لِقَوْمٍ يَعْلَمُونَ﴾, i.e. who know that Allah's promise is true and that what His Messenger brought is truthful.
